timezone_note: Argentina uses UTC-3 year round. The WMO World Weather Information Service lists Buenos Aires at UTC-0300 with daylight saving time 'N'.
passport_validity_rule: Argentina's Direccion Nacional de Migraciones page for tourist entry asks for a valid passport ('vigente') and states no minimum remaining validity. UK FCDO: the passport must be valid for the proposed duration of your stay. Global Affairs Canada: valid for the expected duration of your stay, and notes airlines may apply stricter rules. The six-month minimum and the free blank page (one sheet, two sides) that appear on argentina.gob.ar apply to people applying for a consular tourist visa, not to visa-exempt visitors. Airlines may apply their own margin at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: STAY: Argentina's Migraciones defines a tourist as someone entering for rest or leisure for up to three months ('hasta TRES (3) MESES PRORROGABLE POR OTRO PERIODO SIMILAR'); tourists may not work for pay. argentina.gob.ar says nationals of Mercosur and associated states (Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Panama, Peru, Suriname) can enter without a visa for up to 90 days, and consular offices grant at most 90 days, extendable once for an equal period at a Migraciones office before the first period ends. UK FCDO: UK citizens can visit for tourism without a visa for up to 90 days and should get advice from the Argentine Migration Office before the stay ends if they want a second 90 days; Global Affairs Canada: tourist and business visas are not required for Canadians. The Argentine pages reviewed do not publish a visa-exempt list for other passports, so check the nationality tool on migraciones.gob.ar. AVE: nationals of about 80 listed countries who need a tourist visa can instead apply for the electronic travel authorization (AVE) if they hold a qualifying US visa or meet the other conditions on the Migraciones AVE page; it is valid three months from issue. Chinese, Indian and Dominican citizens holding a valid US visa or green card can enter for up to 90 days. ONWARD TICKET: Argentina's own Migraciones pages do not state an onward or return ticket requirement (hence null, not 'not required'); Global Affairs Canada says customs officials may ask you to show a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds. BIOMETRICS: Global Affairs Canada says all passengers must complete biometric checks at entry and exit. NO ENTRY STAMP: UK FCDO says immigration no longer stamps passports on entry; for proof of entry or exit contact the Argentine Migration Office. Migraciones' exit rules list a valid passport plus proof of valid entry, and a traveller whose permitted stay has expired must pay the exit clearance fee. CASH: UK FCDO says you must declare cash or travellers cheques worth more than 10,000 US dollars; Global Affairs Canada's page does not state a threshold. MINORS: both FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say children under 18 (FCDO: 17 and under) who live in Argentina need written permission from the non-accompanying parents; FCDO adds that non-resident children who have been in Argentina for a year or more need it too. Entry rules are set and enforced by Argentine authorities; confirm with the consulate before travel.

required_vaccinations: None for entry: Argentina's Ministry of Health says Argentina does not require an international vaccination certificate to enter the country, and Global Affairs Canada and the US CDC agree. A yellow fever certificate may be needed for onward travel to other countries (UK FCDO).
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Routine vaccines including measles (MMR)
Typhoid (CDC: consider if visiting areas with poor sanitation or staying a month or longer)
Rabies (CDC: consider pre-exposure vaccination depending on activities)

Yellow fever (CDC: recommended for travellers aged 9 months or older going to Corrientes and Misiones provinces; Argentina's Ministry of Health says to be vaccinated at least ten days before arrival in a transmission-risk area)
health.malaria_risk: CDC: malaria is a risk in some parts of Argentina, but its country page does not name the areas; if travelling to a risk area, see a doctor about prophylaxis before leaving.
health.notes: Yellow fever: the Ministry of Health's national schedule covers residents of Misiones, Corrientes and Formosa and some departments of Chaco, Salta and Jujuy. The CDC recommends the vaccine for Corrientes and Misiones, generally does not recommend it for Formosa and designated areas of Chaco, Jujuy and Salta, and does not recommend it for travel limited to other provinces (CDC page updated 23 April 2025). The Ministry's travel-vaccination article dates from 14 July 2023. Mosquito-borne illness: Global Affairs Canada lists dengue, chikungunya and Zika as risks and says to protect against bites at all times; UK FCDO lists yellow fever, Zika and dengue and says hantavirus is present in Argentina and altitude sickness is a risk in parts (FCDO updated its health page on 7 May 2026 with hantavirus information). The CDC reports increased leptospirosis cases, with higher risk after floods or heavy rain, and advises avoiding swimming or wading in water that may be contaminated with animal urine. Global Affairs Canada: rabies is present, so avoid contact with animals including free-roaming dogs; wash a bite or scratch with soap and clean water for about 15 minutes and seek medical care. Healthcare: Global Affairs Canada says good care is available in Buenos Aires but may be limited elsewhere and hospitals often expect immediate cash payment; UK FCDO says facilities are good but can be expensive and public hospitals tend to be crowded. Both advise comprehensive travel insurance. No official source reviewed gave a statement on whether tap water is safe to drink, so none is made here.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada: foreign credit and debit cards are accepted in main cities; keep your card in sight when paying and you may be asked for photo ID. UK FCDO: you may need to produce your passport when paying by credit card, so keep a copy somewhere safe.
money.cash_culture: Global Affairs Canada says hospitals often expect immediate cash payment, so carry sufficient funds, and advises paying taxi drivers with exact change to reduce the risk of counterfeit bills. No Argentine government source reviewed describes wider cash or card habits or the informal exchange market, so none is described here.
money.atm_notes: Global Affairs Canada: cash withdrawals from foreign bank accounts at ATMs are subject to low limits per withdrawal and per day, and substantial service charges may apply when using non-Argentine bank cards, so check with your bank before leaving. It advises using indoor ATMs and avoiding them at night.

emergency.notes: Numbers come from the UK FCDO (police 911 or 101, ambulance 107, fire 100; 'dial 107 or 911 and ask for an ambulance') and Global Affairs Canada (police 911 or 101; firefighters 911 or 100; medical assistance 107 in Buenos Aires and 911 outside Buenos Aires). The two agree on 911, 101, 107 and 100 but differ on how far 107 reaches, so if 107 does not connect outside Buenos Aires try 911; 911 is not confirmed as a single nationwide all-services line, so 'universal' is left null. The tourist police number is the Buenos Aires Comisaria del Turista, which the FCDO says is staffed 24 hours and works on WhatsApp; Global Affairs Canada lists the same number among its Buenos Aires tourist police contacts (it also lists +54 11 4323 8900 ext. 116311 and +54 911 5050 3293). The FCDO also lists a Mendoza tourist police line, +54 261 413 2135 (24 hours). These come from foreign-government pages because no Argentine government page with a consolidated emergency list was found in the pages reviewed. Calling the Buenos Aires 911 from outside Argentina: +54 11 4309 9600, extension 261099 or 261098 (FCDO). No official source reviewed states whether English is answered.

getting_around.summary: Argentina's tourism ministry describes a very large country with distinct regions (mountains and glaciers in the south, rainforests and wetlands in the north, plains in the centre, deserts and salt flats in the northwest), and points to a transport guide titled 'Como llegar' on its site, which could not be opened for this guide. The UK FCDO says flights from Argentina can be unreliable, so build slack into onward connections. Buenos Aires and other Argentine cities use the SUBE card, described by the national government as a payment system for public passenger transport; the national page says cards can be requested online or bought and topped up through shops and SUBE points, but it does not say whether visitors can use it, which networks accept it, or what it costs. No official source reviewed gave bus, rail or domestic-flight times, fares or timetables, so none are stated.

passes.name: SUBE card
passes.covers: Payment card for public passenger transport; the national SUBE page also describes RED SUBE, which combines transport modes in the Buenos Aires metropolitan area (AMBA) at a discount. Which operators accept it is listed city by city on the 'SUBE en tu ciudad' pages, which were not checked.
passes.worth_it: The official page does not say whether tourists can use SUBE, what the card costs, or how much balance it can hold, so no saving is calculated here. Confirm on argentina.gob.ar/sube or on 0800-777-7823 before relying on it.

timezone_note: Armenia has a single time zone and does not observe daylight saving time; the WMO's country record for Armenia, supplied by the national Hydrometeorology and Monitoring Center SNCO, lists Yerevan at UTC+04:00 with DST flagged 'N'. This agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Yerevan.
passport_validity_rule: Armenia's embassy in India (india.mfa.am, updated 30 June 2026) says the passport must cover the entire stay in Armenia, and the UK FCDO says it 'must be valid for the duration of your stay'; neither names a minimum number of months of remaining validity. Global Affairs Canada instead states the passport 'must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Armenia' and Smartraveller gives only the generic note that many countries want six months. Armenia's own mission and FCDO are the best-supported, so the rule is recorded as validity for the duration of the stay; an airline following the Canadian reading could still ask for six months at check-in, so carry a passport with that margin if you can. Armenia's foreign ministry site (mfa.am) refused connections when checked, so the destination's own main page was not read.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa depends on nationality. The UK FCDO and Australia's Smartraveller both state that their citizens can enter without a visa for up to 180 days (FCDO: 'in a year'; Smartraveller: 'per year'). Global Affairs Canada states that a tourist visa is required for Canadians and points to Armenia's e-visa; Armenia's own pages listing visa-free nationalities could not be opened, so treat Canada, and any nationality not named here, as unconfirmed and check with the Armenian embassy. Armenia's embassy in India states a visa is required for Indian ordinary passports, to be obtained as an e-visa (processing time 'three working days'), at the border for holders of a qualifying residence permit or visa, or at an embassy. Separately, nationals of 111 listed countries who hold a residence permit issued by the USA, an EU/Schengen state, the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait or Oman, valid at least six months from entry, are visa-exempt from 1 July 2026 to 1 July 2027 for up to 180 days in a one-year period; the permit must be shown as a card or a sticker in the passport. The country list is in a PDF that could not be opened, and the page does not name India, so whether this exemption covers Indian citizens is not confirmed. E-visa applicants from India must supply travel insurance and, without a qualifying residence permit or visa, a return air ticket reservation, a local invitation and proof of financial means. No official source consulted states an onward-ticket, proof-of-funds or arrival-card requirement for visa-free visitors, so whether an onward ticket is required is unconfirmed (carry a return booking anyway). The FCDO notes strict customs rules and that entry is refused with an invalid travel document or a passport reported lost or stolen; Smartraveller states cash of USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) is subject to import and export rules. The FCDO notes the land border with Iran is open but can change at short notice. No health declaration is required (armenia.travel: PCR tests and proof of vaccination are no longer required).

Hepatitis A

Rabies (depending on planned activities)

health.notes: The US CDC's Armenia page (last reviewed 25 August 2026) states yellow fever vaccine is 'not required' for country entry and 'not recommended'; Global Affairs Canada likewise says proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required. Everything else is advisory: CDC recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B (under 60), MMR, COVID-19 and routine vaccines, mpox vaccine for travellers with certain risk activities, and says rabies-infected dogs are commonly found in Armenia, so pre-exposure rabies vaccination depends on activities and access to treatment. Global Affairs Canada recommends hepatitis B for all travellers. The CDC Armenia page carries no malaria section, and the FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages do not mention malaria; no official source consulted advises malaria prevention. Smartraveller notes public hospital standards are basic outside Yerevan, serious cases may need medical evacuation, and some medicines (some sleeping tablets, codeine-containing products) are illegal. Armenia's own health ministry was not used as a source here.

money.card_acceptance: Armenia's official tourism board says credit cards are widely accepted in Yerevan, but the country remains largely cash-dependent outside the capital.
money.cash_culture: Carry cash for markets, restaurants and rural areas; the Yerevan metro runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system and is cash only, and taxis are best paid in cash (armenia.travel).
money.tipping: Armenia's official tourism board says it is customary to leave a 10% tip when dining out.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are plentiful in Yerevan, and currency-exchange offices plus kiosks in some major supermarkets are widely available (armenia.travel). No official source was found on ATM fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice, so none is stated.

power.adapter_note: Armenia's official tourism board describes sockets as primarily Type C (European standard) at 220-240V, and says a device labelled 'INPUT: 100-240V, 50/60 Hz' needs only a Type C adaptor. Travellers from a 230V country therefore need a plug adaptor but no voltage converter. Supply frequency is not stated by any official source consulted, so it is left null.

emergency.notes: Armenia's tourism board (armenia.travel) lists 911 as the Emergency Situations Crisis Management Center line alongside the direct services (fire 101, police 102, ambulance 103, gas emergency 104, Yerevan municipality 105, airport hotline 187). The UK FCDO says to call 911 for an ambulance and ask for an English speaker, and its 'Getting help' page lists 911 as the emergency services number. Global Affairs Canada lists police 102, medical assistance 103, firefighters 101 and 'emergency services: 112'; Australia's Smartraveller says 'Call 112 or 911 for the emergency hotline' (fire 101, medical 103, police 102). So 112 is named as an emergency number by two foreign governments but not by Armenia's tourism board; the general emergency number shown is 911 (named by the tourism board and FCDO), and 112 is worth trying if 911 does not connect. Smartraveller warns emergency services may take a long time to reach remote regions. No official source states which languages are answered beyond the FCDO's English-speaker request.

getting_around.summary: Yerevan has a metro that runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system (cash only) plus buses and minibuses, and taxis and ride-hailing are cheap and widely used — the official tourism board names GG and Yandex Taxi as the main apps. For timetables the tourism board points visitors at the T-armenia.com app, which covers both Yerevan and national transport services, and at the A2B Yerevan public-transport listing; Yandex Maps is recommended for navigation and Yerevan Ride for bike sharing. Outside Yerevan, carry cash.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Armenia's official tourism board says SIM cards are very accessible and affordable and can be bought at the airport or from providers in the city, with widespread coverage in both cities and rural areas. It does not state what identification is required to register a SIM, and no official source was found that does.
connectivity.typical_cost: The official tourism board states plans can be bought for up to about USD 12 per month including unlimited data, SMS and domestic and international calls (checked 2026-09-28). No official per-10GB or two-week price is published.

timezone_note: Australia is not on one clock. Tourism Australia lists three standard time zones: Australian Eastern (AEST, UTC+10: Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, ACT), Central (ACST, UTC+9:30: South Australia and the Northern Territory) and Western (AWST, UTC+8: Western Australia). Tourism Australia states that New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT move their clocks forward an hour in summer, while Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not. That matters because the gaps change twice a year: on 17 October 2026 (checked against the IANA tz database) Sydney, Melbourne and Hobart are on AEDT (UTC+11), Brisbane stays on AEST (UTC+10, one hour behind Sydney), Adelaide and Broken Hill are on ACDT (UTC+10:30), Darwin is on ACST (UTC+9:30) and Perth is on AWST (UTC+8, three hours behind Sydney). Per the IANA tz database (not an official page opened for this guide), daylight saving started at 2:00 a.m. on Sunday 4 October 2026 (first Sunday of October) and ends at 3:00 a.m. on Sunday 4 April 2027 (first Sunday of April), when Sydney returns to AEST (UTC+10). Two small zones appear in IANA only: Lord Howe Island (Australia/Lord_Howe, UTC+10:30 standard and UTC+11 in summer) and the Eucla area of Western Australia (Australia/Eucla, UTC+8:45); neither is described on a source opened here. The Bureau of Meteorology and Home Affairs time-zone pages blocked automated retrieval. Book domestic connections against local time at each end. Because Queensland does not move its clocks, the Sydney-Brisbane gap is one hour in summer and zero in winter.
passport_validity_rule: Australia has no six-month rule on the official pages opened. The ABF states all passengers other than Australian and New Zealand citizens must present 'a valid passport or other acceptable travel document' plus a valid visa or authority and a completed Incoming Passenger Card, without giving a minimum number of months. The UK FCDO states: 'To enter Australia, your passport must be valid for the length of your planned stay.' Global Affairs Canada words it as 'Your passport must be valid on the day of entry into the country' and warns that airline or transport rules may be stricter. Home Affairs: an ETA is valid for 12 months or the period the passport is valid, whichever is shorter, is linked to the passport used to apply, and ceases if that passport expires or is replaced, so apply with the passport you will travel on. If you transit a country that wants six months of validity, or your airline applies its own rule at check-in, the stricter rule governs your trip.
entry_requirement_notes: Everyone except Australian citizens needs a visa or electronic authority before travelling. New Zealand citizens are normally granted an electronic Special Category Visa (subclass 444) on arrival, subject to health and character requirements (ABF travel-documents page). Home Affairs: the Electronic Travel Authority (ETA, subclass 601) must be applied for through the Australian ETA app by holders of an ETA-eligible passport, from outside Australia; stay is up to 3 months each entry, valid for 12 months or the life of the passport, whichever is shorter; 'There is a service charge of AUD20 to use the Australian ETA app. There is no other charge payable for an ETA.' The ETA is electronically linked to the passport used to apply and ceases if that passport expires or is replaced. The eVisitor (subclass 651) is free, up to 3 months at a time, for passports from particular (European) countries; the Visitor visa (subclass 600, tourist stream) costs from AUD250 and can be granted for 3, 6 or 12 months. The list of ETA/eVisitor-eligible passports is in an expandable panel on the Home Affairs pages and was not captured here: check it before you book. Arrival card: the ABF states that all arriving passengers must complete an Incoming Passenger Card (IPC), in English, covering identity, address in Australia, customs and quarantine declarations and, for non-citizens, health and character declarations; false information can affect your visa. A digital alternative, the Australia Travel Declaration, is a pilot only (Qantas flights into Brisbane and select flights into Sydney and Melbourne, by invitation through the Qantas app); 'Anyone not invited to apply will continue using the IPC as normal.' So carry/complete the paper IPC unless invited. Cash: AUSTRAC states it is a legal requirement under the AML/CTF Act 2006 to declare currency of AUD 10,000 or more (or foreign-currency equivalent) entering or leaving Australia; failure to report is an offence (AUSTRAC release dated 1 July 2017, the threshold being the figure stated there). Biosecurity (Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry): you must complete a declaration and either declare any risk goods, including food, animal products and plant material (including wooden articles) and footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals, or dispose of them in the bins at the airport or cruise terminal. False or misleading information can bring an infringement notice of up to $7,280, civil penalty proceedings or prosecution, and your visa may be cancelled, with refusal of entry and possibly up to three years before you can return. Yellow fever: see health; Australia does not refuse entry without a certificate. Arrival levy: the ABF lists a Passenger Movement Charge page, but its amount was not read, so it is not stated here. Onward ticket, blank passport pages and proof-of-funds figures were not stated on any official page opened, so none is stated here.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate (ICVP) is requested from travellers over 1 year old who have stayed overnight or longer in an Australia-listed yellow fever declared place within 6 days before arriving; arrivals without one are not refused entry but receive a Yellow Fever Action Card
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (varicella, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19
Diphtheria/tetanus booster within the last 10 years (CDC diphtheria alert for NT, WA, SA)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Japanese encephalitis (mainly Murray River area and Outer Torres Strait Islands; longer stays or higher-risk activities)
Rabies (discuss with a provider; post-exposure vaccine usually available)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: Not addressed on CDC's Australia page; dengue, Ross River virus and melioidosis (northern Australia) are listed there
health.notes: Australian Immunisation Handbook (Department of Health): 'Australia strongly recommends that travellers >1 year of age have a valid ICVP with proof of valid yellow fever vaccination if they: are entering Australia within 6 days of leaving a country that is on Australia's list of yellow fever-declared places [and] stayed in the at-risk area overnight or longer.' Travellers arriving without a valid ICVP 'receive information about yellow fever' and are advised to seek medical assessment if symptoms develop within 6 days. This replaces the CDC wording about layovers over 12 hours, which does not appear on the Australian page. CDC (page reviewed 25 August 2026) also lists dengue, Ross River virus, hantavirus, leptospirosis, ciguatera fish poisoning and melioidosis, and a Level 1 global measles notice. The FCDO health page says essential and urgent hospital treatment is free for UK residents under the UK-Australia Reciprocal Healthcare Agreement but that GP visits, prescriptions, ambulances and medical evacuation are not covered, so travel insurance is advised. Malaria is not addressed on the CDC Australia page and no Australian official page on it was opened, so the entry is unchanged. The recommended list is medical advice, not an entry condition.

money.card_acceptance: Tourism Australia states that cards are widely accepted, that merchants may impose credit card surcharges in some places, and that fees may be charged on transactions, particularly when withdrawing from an international account. It also advises checking with your card company about foreign transaction fees.
money.tipping: Tourism Australia states that hotels and restaurants do not add service charges to your bill, that tipping is always your choice, and that in upmarket restaurants it is common to tip waiters 10 per cent for good service.
money.atm_notes: Tourism Australia notes that fees may be charged on international withdrawals. Declare cash of AUD 10,000 or more (Australian or foreign equivalent) on arrival (Tourism Australia). GST is 10 per cent; Tourism Australia says a refund is possible under the Tourist Refund Scheme if you spent AUD 300 or more with a single business no more than 60 days before departing, claimed in the international departure area.

power.adapter_note: Tourism Australia states Australia uses the Type I plug (two flat pins in an inverted V, sometimes with a third centre pin), with a supply of 220-240 volts AC at 50Hz; its packing page says 230V 50Hz and advises a voltage transformer if your home voltage differs. The IEC's World Plugs was not opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: Australian Government Department of Infrastructure (triplezero.gov.au, opened 18 Oct 2026): 'Triple Zero (000) is Australia's main emergency number for life threatening or time critical situations. You can call 000 from any fixed or mobile phone, satellite phone and certain Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) services.' You say which service you need: police, fire or ambulance. 'In Australia, you can also dial the international standard emergency number (112) from a mobile phone, which will direct you to the same Triple Zero (000) service. This number (112) cannot be called from a fixed landline or satellite phone.' Triple Zero calls are free; with no mobile coverage on any network you cannot reach Triple Zero from a mobile; you cannot contact it by SMS. Deaf or speech-impaired callers can use the National Relay Service via 106 with a TTY. Non-emergency: police assistance line 131 444; State Emergency Service (flood, storm) 132 500. Tourism Australia, Global Affairs Canada and the FCDO also give 000. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: No single national transport pass or intercity rail pass was found on an official page opened for this record, so none is listed. Tourism Australia's budget guide (page last modified 30 April 2025; it says costs are a guide only) says public transport trips cost around AUD 2 compared with AUD 20-30 for a taxi or rideshare for a comparable journey, and that daily fare caps apply in most major cities, with a weekday cap of around AUD 17 in Sydney and around AUD 9 in Melbourne. Distances are continental: no source opened here gives flight or rail times, so none are stated. Fare-cap and per-trip figures vary by city and change, so check the local transport operator before you rely on them.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Tourism Australia states mobile phone network coverage is available across Australia, but coverage may be limited in some remote areas. No official page opened states eSIM support, SIM prices or registration rules.

climate.precipitation_note: 96.0 mm normal rainfall over 12.3 rain days; mean daily max 26.5 C and min 19.6 C (Sydney (station Observatory Hill), 1981-2010 base period, as published by the WMO World Weather Information Service from Bureau of Meteorology data). IMPORTANT: this whole table is Sydney only, not a national average. Australia spans tropical, desert and temperate climates: the north has a wet season and a cyclone season (November to April per FCDO), the interior is arid, and Tasmania and the south are cooler. Seasons are inverted compared with the northern hemisphere, so December to February is summer. Tourism Australia's own Sydney page quotes slightly different monthly figures (for January, 26.4 C max and 18.8 C min), so figures vary with the base period. timezone_note: Austria uses a single zone, Europe/Vienna, from the IANA database (not from a page opened for this guide). Summer time follows the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, so on 18 October 2026 Austria is on CEST (UTC+2) and clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026; that date rests on the last-Sunday rule, not on an Austrian government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Austria is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay your passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years. UK FCDO's Austria entry page gives the same two conditions (issued less than 10 years before arrival; expiry at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area). Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area, and time in other Schengen countries counts. Stays beyond that need an Austrian visa or permit.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; the page also says the fee has been set at EUR 20 (instead of EUR 7) and takes effect once ETIAS is operational. A later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026', that the exact date 'will be officially communicated later this year', and that an approved authorisation is valid for 3 years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first. No page opened for this guide gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel (that site returned no readable text to the fetch tool used here). When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation, not a visa, for visa-exempt nationals. Already live: the Entry/Exit System (EES), which the Commission says became fully operational on 10 April 2026 and replaces passport stamping; UK FCDO says you may need to register fingerprints and a photo at the border and the digital record lasts 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on your nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). Your Europe says border guards may ask for a justification for your visit including proof of sufficient funds, and supporting papers such as proof of accommodation or a return or round-trip ticket; UK FCDO says officers may ask for proof of accommodation, travel insurance, a return or onward ticket and enough money. These are requests, not a fixed condition for visa-exempt visitors, and no page opened for this guide gives a funds figure or a blank-pages requirement, so those fields are left empty. Cash: UK FCDO says declare cash or travellers cheques worth EUR 10,000 or more (you get a certified declaration; without one money could be seized when you leave). No Austrian government page on this was opened for this guide, so that is a foreign-government fallback. FCDO also notes temporary border controls at Germany's land borders, relevant if you travel to Austria overland through Germany.

health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Austria page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Austria page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (that section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. The page has no malaria section and carries the Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025). It also names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis under non-vaccine-preventable risks, advises tick checks after outdoor activity, and says road crashes are a major risk. UK FCDO's health page says a GHIC or EHIC is needed for medically necessary state healthcare in Austria, is not an alternative to travel insurance, and advises insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation; it says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. FCDO's safety page says off-piste skiing can invalidate travel insurance, avalanches are a risk in some areas, and a policy should cover mountain rescue and helicopter costs. CDC and FCDO are used as fallbacks because no page from Austria's health ministry was opened for this guide.

emergency.notes: Numbers are from the Austrian government portal oesterreich.gv.at (page 'Emergency numbers', last update 18/08/2026): 112 single European emergency number, 122 fire service, 133 police, 144 ambulance service, 140 mountain rescue, 141 emergency doctor, 128 gas emergency, 142 crisis hotline, 147 emergency services for children and young people, and poison centre 01 406 43 43. The page says the emergency numbers are free from any phone in Austria and that 112 can be called from a locked mobile phone without a PIN. Deaf and hard-of-hearing people can use the DEC112 app for text-based emergency contact, and the police can be reached by text or fax on 0800 133 133. UK FCDO's Austria page independently lists 133 police, 144 ambulance, 122 fire and 112. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed.

getting_around.summary: Long-distance rail is run by ÖBB, which sells discounted Sparschiene (advance-saver) tickets: ÖBB's Sparschiene page gives Austria fares 'from EUR 9.90' in 2nd class and 'from EUR 19.90' in 1st class, sold only online and in the ÖBB app, bookable up to 6 months (180 days) ahead, valid only for the train chosen at booking, with no cancellation or refund on the standard fare (the Komfort version adds a seat reservation and cancellation options, with a refund fee after 15 days before travel). These are starting prices and the number of cheap tickets per train is limited. No official journey time for any route was opened for this record, so none is given: check the ÖBB timetable on oebb.at. In Vienna, the Wiener Linien network (U-Bahn, tram, bus) and the Vienna City Card are listed on wien.info, but Wiener Linien's own site could not be opened and the wien.info page states no year for its prices, so no Vienna fares are quoted here. On Austrian motorways and expressways a vignette (toll sticker) is required for vehicles, displayed inside the windscreen, per UK FCDO. Regional networks, ferries, and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.name: ÖBB Sparschiene (advance-saver rail tickets)
passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets on ÖBB trains within Austria (and separate Sparschiene fares to other countries). Per ÖBB: from EUR 9.90 (2nd class) and from EUR 19.90 (1st class) for Austria, online and in the ÖBB app only, bookable up to 6 months ahead, valid only for the train selected, and no cancellation or refund on the standard fare.
passes.worth_it: A saving only if your dates are fixed, because the ticket is tied to one train and cannot be refunded; the cheapest fares are limited per train, so buy early. If your plans may change, ÖBB's Komfort fare adds a seat reservation and cancellation options (refund free up to 15 days before the first travel date, then a 50% fee until 1 day before, per ÖBB). Check the current terms in the ÖBB ticket shop before buying.

passes.name: KlimaTicket Österreich (annual nationwide pass)
passes.covers: All scheduled services (public and private rail, city and public transport) across Austria for a year, per klimaticket.at; not valid on tourist railways such as the Schafbergbahn. The Classic ticket is EUR 1,400 for tickets valid from 1 January 2026 (reduced Youth/Senior/Special EUR 1,050).
passes.worth_it: A year-long pass, so it only makes sense for a long stay or residents; it is not a short-visit product. The page sets out eligibility for the reduced rates (25 or younger, 65 or older, certain disabilities).

timezone_note: Europe/Brussels covers all of Belgium. Standard time is CET (UTC+1) and summer time is CEST (UTC+2); Visit Flanders says Belgium is on Central European Time, one hour ahead of GMT (it does not mention summer time). On 19 October 2026 the country is on CEST, and clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026 under the EU last-Sunday-of-October rule; that date comes from the rule and the IANA database, not from a page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Belgium is in the Schengen area. The Belgian Foreign Affairs consular page on visa exemption (Belgian embassy in Japan, page marked last updated 26 March 2024) says the travel document must be valid until at least 'three months after the intended date of departure' and issued within the previous 10 years, and that visa-exempt visits are limited to 'no more than 90 days per period of 180 days'. UK FCDO gives the same two conditions (expiry at least 3 months after you plan to leave the Schengen area; issued less than 10 years before arrival, so some passports renewed before 1 October 2018 may fail) and Global Affairs Canada gives the 3-month condition. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. Airlines may apply stricter rules than the entry rules.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's news item of 28 April 2026 says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be announced later, and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says ETIAS applications were not yet open. No page opened announces an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026, and Belgian Foreign Affairs says it registers non-EU short-stay travellers on each external-border crossing, records biometric data, and that travellers need take no action beforehand; UK FCDO says you may be asked for fingerprints and a photo, the record lasts 3 years, and to allow extra time at the border. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). Funds, purpose and return ticket: the Belgian consular page says you must justify the purpose and conditions of the stay and have sufficient means of subsistence for the stay and for the return; UK FCDO says at Belgian border control you may need to show a return or onward ticket and enough money, and Global Affairs Canada says customs may ask for a return ticket and proof of funds. No Belgian page opened states a fixed daily amount: the Immigration Office (dofi.ibz.be) pages on means of subsistence and reference amounts returned a human-verification page to the fetch tool and were not bypassed, so no figure is stated here. Because the checks are put as things officers 'may' ask for, the onward-ticket field is left null and no blank-page count is stated (no opened page gives a number). Insurance: Global Affairs Canada says to show proof of travel health insurance with at least EUR 30,000 coverage; no Belgian official page opened confirms this as a condition for visa-exempt visitors, so treat it as the Canadian government's advice and carry insurance in any case. Temporary border checks: UK FCDO's entry page says Belgium has additional entry checks 'until December 2025', a date that has passed, and nothing opened confirms whether they continue; carry your passport at all times in Belgium (FCDO) and expect possible ID checks. Cash: UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash into or out of the EU must be declared to customs; the Belgian customs pages (finance.belgium.be) returned a human-verification page and were not bypassed. FCDO also says meat and milk products generally cannot be brought into the EU, and that adults travelling with children aged 17 or under may need proof of the relationship.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose for ages 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (especially for smaller cities, villages, rural areas or street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; unvaccinated travellers 60 and older may be vaccinated)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider; TravelHealthPro advises it only for those at increased risk such as bat handlers, vets and laboratory staff)
Tick-borne encephalitis (TravelHealthPro: recommended for those whose activities raise their risk, such as forestry work, camping, hiking or fieldwork in forested areas)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None stated on the pages opened (CDC's Belgium page has no malaria section; Global Affairs Canada lists no yellow fever risk)
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Belgium page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026), Global Affairs Canada says there is no yellow fever risk and no proof of vaccination is required, and TravelHealthPro says there are no certificate requirements under the International Health Regulations. The recommended list is medical advice only. Global Affairs Canada describes healthcare as excellent and advises insurance covering medical evacuation and hospital stays; it also notes a measles advisory and tick-borne encephalitis risk in some areas, mainly for hikers and campers in forests. TravelHealthPro (updated October 2026) says ticks are most active from early spring to late autumn. For an ambulance UK FCDO says to dial 112. FCDO says a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance (it does not cover repatriation, non-urgent or private care), non-emergency consultations and prescriptions carry a fee, and medicines legal in the UK may have a different legal status in Belgium. CDC, FCDO, TravelHealthPro and Global Affairs Canada are used because no page from the Belgian health authority (FPS Public Health or Sciensano) was opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Flanders (the Flemish tourism board) says cash is accepted in most places and that major debit and credit cards are also accepted, naming Visa, American Express, Diners Club and 'Euro card'. Global Affairs Canada warns that card and ATM fraud occurs and advises using ATMs in public areas or banks, checking for skimmers and covering your PIN. On Brussels public transport, visit.brussels says you can pay with a contactless debit or credit card, smartphone or smartwatch at every STIB bus, tram and metro station device.
money.atm_notes: Visit Flanders says cash is available from banks and a widespread network of ATMs. No fees or limits are stated on any official page opened, so none are given. Global Affairs Canada advises using ATMs in public areas or banks and checking for skimmers.

power.adapter_note: Visit Flanders says plugs may differ from those at home and you may need an adaptor, and describes the supply as 220 volts AC with continental 2-pin round plugs, which is the Type C shape. It does not name plug types by letter or give the frequency, so the type letter is inferred from that description and frequency is left null; the IEC's World Plugs was not opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: The Belgian Federal Public Service Home Affairs page on the 112 emergency centres (securitecivile.be) says 112 is for ambulance and fire department and 101 is for police, that calling 112 for police redirects you to 101 (so call 101 directly for urgent police help), and that calls to 100 currently reach the same EC112 centres as 112, so 100 is worth trying if 112 does not connect. Visit Flanders gives 112 for emergencies and 101 for urgent police help, UK FCDO gives 112 for ambulance, fire and police, and Global Affairs Canada gives police 101 and 112 for all other emergencies. FCDO also recommends the official 112 BE app. A dedicated tourist police line was not confirmed on an official page. Consular help: UK FCDO in London +44 20 7008 5000 (24 hours); the Embassy of Canada in Brussels is +32 (0)2 741-0611, and Canada's after-hours Emergency Watch and Response Centre is 00-800-6633-0000 (toll-free, Global Affairs Canada).

getting_around.summary: Intercity trains are run by Belgian Rail (SNCB/NMBS, belgiantrain.be); its site returned a bot-check page to automated fetches, so no fares, rail pass products or timetables were read from it and none are stated here. Visit Flanders says that by train it often takes less than an hour to travel between two major cities in Flanders, that bicycles can be taken on every train in Belgium (buy the ticket and bicycle supplement in advance), and that Brussels South (Midi) is linked to London in 1h56, Paris in 1h25, Amsterdam in 1h52 and Cologne in 1h50 by the merged Eurostar/Thalys network. For Brussels Airport, Visit Flanders says trains reach Brussels in 20 minutes and Antwerp in 35, and that Brussels South Charleroi Airport is about 60 km from Brussels with a direct bus to Charleroi-South station in 20 minutes and onward train connections. Regional buses are De Lijn in Flanders and, in Brussels, STIB-MIVB runs the bus, tram and metro network. Low emission zones apply in Antwerp, Ghent and the whole Brussels-Capital Region. Check live times on belgiantrain.be or a journey planner; Wallonia's TEC network, intercity fares and rail passes were not researched.

passes.name: STIB-MIVB single ticket (Brussels)

passes.worth_it: A simple option for a few rides in Brussels; the page is undated, so check the STIB-MIVB site for the current fare.

passes.worth_it: Worth considering if you expect four or more rides in a day at the single-ticket price listed (EUR 2.10 from a machine); check the STIB-MIVB site for current prices.

The page does not say what other services the ticket covers.

timezone_note: All of Bolivia uses America/La_Paz, UTC-4 all year with no daylight saving time, according to the IANA time zone database (checked with the tz database on 2026-10-19). Neither the Bolivian government sites reached nor SENAMHI stated the offset on a page that could be read, so this label follows IANA rather than a Bolivian page. La Paz is the seat of government and Sucre the constitutional capital.
passport_validity_rule: Bolivia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states a passport valid for a minimum of six (6) months for visitors, without stating whether the six months run from entry or departure. The UK FCDO says the expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date you arrive, and Global Affairs Canada says at least 6 months from the date you arrive; the record uses 6 months from entry, the stricter practical reading. FCDO also says you need at least two blank pages.
entry_requirement_notes: PASSPORT: Bolivia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs consular visa page (consulados.cancilleria.gob.bo) lists a passport valid for a minimum of six months, and its traveller's guide (Mexico-Bolivia) says the passport must have a minimum validity of six months; neither states the counting basis. The UK FCDO says the expiry date should be at least 6 months after the date you arrive and Global Affairs Canada says valid at least 6 months from the date you arrive, so the record uses 6 months from entry. FCDO also says you need at least two blank pages; no Bolivian page states a blank-page rule, so blank_pages_required carries FCDO's figure only. VISA GROUPS: Bolivia's consular page splits nationalities into Group I (no tourist visa required), Group II (visa required) and Group III (visa required after consulting the consular office, and a DIGEMIG authorisation resolution is needed); the page does not list which countries are in each group, so check your own nationality with a Bolivian consulate or DIGEMIG (migracion.gob.bo returned no readable content to the fetch tool). For visa-required groups the page also lists a return ticket or travel itinerary, proof of funds by bank statement or card, a letter of invitation or hotel reservation, and a yellow fever certificate if visiting high-risk endemic zones. STAY LENGTH: this differs by source. Global Affairs Canada says no tourist visa is needed for stays up to 30 days and a 30-day tourist extension can be obtained twice, for a maximum of 90 days in one calendar year. The UK FCDO says tourists can stay up to 90 days without a visa within a one-year period, that border officials usually issue 30-day stamps, and that you can stay the full 90 days without a new stamp. The decree that sets the rule (Decreto Supremo 4828 of 23 November 2022, amending DS 1923; text read on lexivox.org, which is not an official host) says the tourist entry authorisation lasts 30 calendar days and can be extended by a transitory tourism stay of up to a further 60 days. The stricter reading (30 days on the stamp, extension at DIGEMIG) is what to plan on. Some nationalities have longer treaty periods: Bolivia's own guide says Mexican nationals may stay up to 180 continuous days. REGISTRATION: Global Affairs Canada says you must complete an online SIGEMIG registration before arriving, including lodging details for your whole stay, or you may be fined on leaving; no Bolivian page that could be opened confirms this. FCDO says you may need proof of accommodation, at least for the first night, and that without an entry stamp you may pay a fine on departure. Visitors prove regular status with the entry stamp in the passport, which must be shown on departure (Bolivian traveller's guide). ONWARD TICKET: officials may ask for a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds (Global Affairs Canada), and Bolivia's traveller's guide lists a travel itinerary, a hotel reservation or invitation letter and documented funds among the documents immigration may ask for. No Bolivian page found states it as a fixed requirement for visa-free nationals, so onward_ticket_required is null; carry one. YELLOW FEVER: see the health notes; the certificate rule is conditional on where you travel from and where you go. CASH AND CUSTOMS: the Bolivian traveller's guide says anyone entering or leaving must declare physical entry or exit of foreign currency; amounts of US$10,000 or more need the sworn declaration form for accompanied baggage and physical entry of currency below US$50,000; above US$50,000 needs Banco Central de Bolivia registration and authorisation, and above US$500,000 a ministerial resolution. Duty-free traveller allowances in that guide: used clothing and personal effects, new items for personal use worth US$1,000 or less, up to 3 litres of alcohol, 400 cigarettes, or 50 cigars or 500 g of loose tobacco. Global Affairs Canada says complete the online customs declaration and show the QR code at screening, all luggage is X-rayed; FCDO says declarations use Form 250. Agri-food imports are regulated by SENASAG. LAND BORDERS: get exit and entry stamps on both sides and avoid crossing at night when officials may not be present (Global Affairs Canada, FCDO); FCDO adds that Bolivia no longer stamps at the Argentine border, so register your exit with Argentina's immigration authority. MINORS: Global Affairs Canada says strict entry and exit rules apply to anyone under 18, including special documentation; FCDO says a child travelling with one parent or guardian for more than 90 days needs a judicial permit to leave.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate: Bolivia's Ministry of Health says foreigners who visit high-risk yellow fever zones must hold the certificate or be vaccinated 10 days beforehand; the UK FCDO says a certificate is needed if you arrive from a country with yellow fever transmission risk; the US CDC states proof is required for all arrivals aged 1 year and over. Sources differ, so carry the certificate if you hold one and see notes.
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 year and older, per CDC)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60, per CDC)
Typhoid (areas with poor sanitation including rural areas, stays of a month or more, or visiting friends or relatives)
Rabies (pre-exposure, depending on activities; dogs and bats carry rabies and post-exposure vaccine is often not readily available)

Yellow fever (from 9 months of age, for travel below 2,300 m east of the Andes: all of Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz and designated parts of Chuquisaca, Cochabamba, La Paz and Tarija; not recommended for La Paz city, Sucre or travel limited to above 2,300 m, per CDC)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: CDC: malaria risk in all areas below 2,500 m (about 99% P. vivax, about 1% P. falciparum; chloroquine-resistant); prophylaxis choice depends on itinerary. No transmission in La Paz (the administrative capital).
health.notes: YELLOW FEVER (official sources differ, so the structured list states the conditions). Bolivia's Ministry of Health and Sports (Resolucion Ministerial 0028, dated 5 February 2018 on its resolutions page) says foreigners entering Bolivia who visit high-risk yellow fever areas must hold the yellow fever vaccination certificate or be vaccinated ten days before; the municipality list was not readable on the page. The ministry's February 2025 notice urges anyone travelling to endemic areas for work or tourism to be vaccinated at least ten days beforehand and names La Paz, Beni, Cochabamba, Santa Cruz and Tarija as departments with recorded cases; its 2017 notice says the certificate is checked at air and land entry points. The consular page requires the certificate only for high-risk endemic zones. The UK FCDO says you need a certificate if arriving from a country listed as a yellow fever transmission risk. The US CDC page states that proof is required for all arriving travellers aged 1 year and older and recommends the vaccine from 9 months of age for travel below 2,300 m east of the Andes, including all of Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz and designated parts of Chuquisaca, Cochabamba, La Paz and Tarija; not recommended for La Paz city, Sucre or places above 2,300 m. These readings conflict (CDC is broader than the Bolivian ministry), so if you hold a certificate, carry it; if you plan to visit the lowlands, get vaccinated at least 10 days before. ALTITUDE SICKNESS. Global Affairs Canada: altitude illness is a risk at 2,500 m and above; La Paz is 3,640 m, Uyuni 3,656 m, Oruro 3,735 m and Potosi 4,090 m; high-altitude illnesses can be fatal and you should descend to a lower altitude if symptoms develop. FCDO names La Paz and the Uyuni salt flats as places where altitude sickness is a risk. UK TravelHealthPro (UKHSA) adds: altitude illness usually occurs above 2,500 m; acute mountain sickness (headache plus nausea, dizziness, fatigue or weakness) usually starts 6 to 10 hours after ascending above 2,500 m; avoid going from below 1,200 m to above 3,500 m in one day where possible; above 3,000 m do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a day and take a rest day every three or four days; stop ascending and rest if symptoms appear and descend if they worsen or do not improve in one to two days; confusion, loss of coordination, breathlessness at rest or a wet cough need urgent medical attention and descent. It lists acetazolamide as the preferred preventive drug (unlicensed in the UK; talk to a doctor first) and does not recommend coca or ginkgo for prevention. TravelHealthPro lists La Paz at 3,630 m, Global Affairs Canada at 3,640 m. ROUTINE AND OTHER: CDC recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B for those under 60, typhoid for rural or long stays, rabies pre-exposure depending on activities, and routine vaccines; it notes dengue, Zika, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, leptospirosis, hantavirus and rabies, and advises sun protection at high elevation. FCDO lists Oropouche virus disease and Zika. CARE: FCDO says public healthcare is inconsistent and emergency help in remote areas is limited, private clinics in the main cities work with international insurance, you will usually pay up front and some medicines are in short supply; Global Affairs Canada says many clinics and hospitals accept cash only, prescription medicines are scarce so bring enough in original containers, most providers speak only Spanish, and travel insurance should cover medical evacuation.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada: credit and debit cards are not widely accepted outside urban centres.
money.cash_culture: Global Affairs Canada advises carrying small bills for street food, taxis and tips, and says many clinics and hospitals accept cash only. It also says Canadian dollars are difficult to exchange and to bring U.S. dollars. The UK FCDO says you will usually pay up front for private medical care, so carry funds.

emergency.notes: Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/bolivia) lists police 110, firefighters 119, an ambulance number for La Paz of 165, the La Paz tourist police at +591-2-222-5016 and a gender-based violence line at 800-14-0348. The UK FCDO health page says 'call 118 and ask for an ambulance' without limiting it to a city. The two disagree on the ambulance number: 118 is stored as the nationally worded figure and 165 is the La Paz figure from Canada, so if 118 does not connect in La Paz try 165. These come from foreign-government pages, not a Bolivian government page (the Bolivian police site did not return readable content), and no official source found confirms a single all-purpose number such as 911, so universal is left empty. The tourist police number is for La Paz only. Global Affairs Canada lists the Canadian Embassy in La Paz at 591 218-3030. FCDO warns that many airports outside departmental capitals lack fire and rescue equipment and that emergency medical help in remote areas is limited.

getting_around.summary: No Bolivian transit-pass product was found on an official page, so none is listed. Official advice is mostly about risk. The UK FCDO says roads are poor and mostly unpaved, four-wheel-drive is often needed especially in the rainy season (November to March) when landslides can block roads, long-distance bus accidents are common and affect British nationals, most bus companies and taxis lack seatbelts, tourist-market bus companies often have better safety standards, and you should use established taxi companies or radio taxis. Blockades and protests can happen with little notice and disrupt public transport including roads to airports; do not cross blockades; check the Bolivian road authority's status map. Petrol and diesel shortages are regular with long queues, reducing intercity buses and leaving drivers stranded for days. Lake Titicaca and jungle river boats are often very basic, so check life jackets. Global Affairs Canada says a 90-day nationwide state of emergency was declared on 20 June 2026 (FCDO says it was declared on 21 June), with no curfew but possible local restrictions; its current status was not confirmed from an official page. Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding all travel to the Chapare Region and carrying extra food, water, fuel, medication and warm clothing on road trips. CDC advises avoiding night driving, motorbike taxis and overcrowded vehicles. If arriving by land, use official border posts and get entry stamps (see entry notes).

timezone_note: Botswana uses one time zone, Africa/Gaborone (Central Africa Time, UTC+2), all year, per the IANA tz database. No Botswana government page was opened for this; the label follows IANA, and the live clock in the app uses the same database.
passport_validity_rule: Six months. Two official foreign-government pages state the rule with different reference points: the UK FCDO's Botswana entry-requirements page says the passport must have an expiry date 'at least 6 months after the date you arrive' (and at least 3 blank pages), while Global Affairs Canada (page updated 14 October 2026) says it 'must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Botswana'. Stored as 6 months beyond the date of exit, the stricter reading, so a passport that meets it satisfies both. The Botswana Department of Immigration and Citizenship's own pages could not be opened (gov.bw served an expired TLS certificate), so neither wording is confirmed first-hand. FCDO also says to enter on the same passport you used to leave your previous country and to get the passport stamped on entry.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA (not first-hand): the UK FCDO says British citizens 'can visit Botswana for up to 90 days without a visa' and that work, study or volunteering needs a different visa; Global Affairs Canada says tourist and business visas are not required for Canadians for stays up to 90 days and that longer stays need an extension from local immigration authorities. Both pages speak only for their own nationals. The authoritative list of nationalities that need a visa sits on Botswana government pages (gov.bw, evisa.gov.bw) that could not be read on 19 October 2026: gov.bw served an expired TLS certificate to every fetch, and evisa.gov.bw loaded only a stub page titled 'botswana-evisa' with no list. So Indian ordinary-passport holders and any other nationality not covered by FCDO or GAC must check the Department of Immigration and Citizenship or the nearest Botswana mission before booking. ONLINE VISA / ETA: neither the FCDO page (updated 1 June 2026, still current on 19 October 2026) nor the Global Affairs Canada page (14 October 2026) mentions an eTA or any pre-travel online authorisation for visa-exempt travellers, and no Botswana government page confirming one was found. The national online visa portal is at evisa.gov.bw; its status and content could not be confirmed from that page, so do not assume it is required or unavailable. CHILDREN: FCDO asks for an original or certified copy of the full birth certificate for anyone aged 17 or under entering or leaving, plus, if a parent is not travelling, an affidavit from that parent consenting to the travel. Global Affairs Canada says minors under 18 need a certified copy of the original birth certificate, a valid passport with at least 1 blank page and a written consent form from non-accompanying parent(s) if travelling unaccompanied or with one parent. CASH: BURS (Botswana Unified Revenue Service) says to declare Pula and/or foreign banknotes of P10,000 or more (or equivalent) when entering or leaving; travellers' cheques and other monetary instruments need not be declared. FCDO and Global Affairs Canada give the same threshold. Under the Customs and Excise Duty Act currency counts as goods, so failing to declare may lead to prosecution. BURS also says travellers must declare all goods in their possession and their correct values (including duty-free purchases and items carried for someone else), with seizure, prosecution or penalties of up to three times the goods' value for non-declaration; its prohibited and restricted goods pages were not opened. ONWARD TICKET: none of the official pages opened (FCDO, GAC, BURS, Ministry of Health) states an onward-ticket or proof-of-funds requirement, so it is not confirmed either way. EBOLA: the FCDO (update of 1 June 2026) says the WHO has declared Ebola a Public Health Emergency of International Concern and that Botswana has introduced entry restrictions including health screening for travellers arriving from affected regions. The Botswana government's Daily News (BOPA, 4 July 2026) reports strengthened surveillance and mandatory health screening at all border posts and points of entry (temperature checks, health declaration forms, visual assessments) and does not describe an entry ban or name countries. The Ministry of Health notice of 28 May 2026 that the government site lists could not be opened. That is the position in July 2026; check the Ministry of Health before travel.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate if you have stayed in listed yellow-fever risk countries (Ministry of Health: required for visitors entering Botswana within six days of having stayed in these countries; the page does not name them). FCDO: required if coming from a country listed as a transmission risk. CDC: required for travellers aged 1 year or over arriving from risk countries, including layovers of more than 12 hours.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 year or older; infants 6 to 11 months also)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers of all ages)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Typhoid (consider for areas with poor sanitation, stays of a month or longer, or visiting friends or relatives)
Rabies (discuss pre-exposure vaccination with a provider; CDC notes rabid dogs are commonly found and post-exposure vaccine may only be available in larger urban facilities)
Mpox (only for adults with certain anticipated activities)
health.malaria_risk: CDC lists malaria transmission areas as Bobirwa, Boteti, Chobe (including Chobe National Park), Ghanzi, Mahalapye, Ngamiland, North-East (including Francistown), Okavango, Serowe/Palapye and Tutume, and recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine there; chloroquine resistance is reported, mainly P. falciparum. Rare or sporadic transmission: Kgalagadi North, Kgatleng, Kweneng and Southern (insect-bite precautions only). CDC says Gaborone has no transmission. The Ministry of Health's travel page says malaria is common in northern Botswana and names Okavango, Boteti, Ngami, Tutume and Bobirwa. CDC's page does not give a transmission season, so none is stated here. Global Affairs Canada says antimalarial medication may be recommended depending on itinerary and dates. FCDO notes malaria reported in April 2025 to have spread to areas where it is not usually present.
health.notes: All of this is medical information, not advice. CDC: Travel Health Notice Level 1 'Practice Usual Precautions'; page last reviewed 25 August 2026; malaria and yellow fever sections updated 23 April 2025. CDC does not recommend yellow fever vaccination for Botswana itself and says direct travel from the US does not require it; Global Affairs Canada says there is no yellow fever risk in Botswana but proof is required if you come from or transited through an airport of a country where it occurs. Ministry of Health: foreign visitors are advised to get travel medical insurance covering serious illness and accidents. FCDO: medicine and medical supply shortages are widespread across public health facilities; private hospitals take payment upfront; care is generally good in major towns but limited in rural areas, and serious cases may need evacuation to the UK or South Africa. Other risks named: schistosomiasis (avoid swimming in fresh unchlorinated water), anthrax in wild animals (do not touch carcasses), ticks (African tick-bite fever), leptospirosis, dengue, hantavirus, tuberculosis. EBOLA: see entry_requirement_notes; Botswana was screening cross-border arrivals in July 2026. The Ministry of Health's travel page also dates alerts of 2 December 2019 and 28 January 2020 (rabies outbreak in Ngamiland), which are old.

emergency.notes: Police 999, ambulance 997 and fire 998 are given together by the UK FCDO's Botswana 'Getting help' page and by Global Affairs Canada (police 999, medical assistance 997, firefighters 998, page updated 14 October 2026). The Ministry of Health's emergency-services page separately confirms 997 as the emergency medical services number ('activate the EMERGENCY NUMBER 997 whenever there is an emergency') and lists no police or fire number. No official page opened confirmed a national 112 or a tourist police line, so those are null. Some non-official lists show extra numbers (911, 996); they are not adopted because no official page was found for them.

timezone_note: Brasilia time (America/Sao_Paulo, UTC-3) covers the south-east, south, north-east and the capital, and is the zone to use for most trips. Brazil spans four offsets: Fernando de Noronha is UTC-2 (IANA zone America/Noronha); Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Rondonia and Roraima are UTC-4 (America/Manaus and neighbouring zones); Acre and the far south-west of Amazonas are UTC-5 (America/Rio_Branco). Daylight saving time is not currently observed in the IANA database, so the offsets do not change through the year. Zone names and offsets here follow the IANA tz database; no Brazilian government page was opened for them.
passport_validity_rule: Official sources disagree, so plan for six months. The Brazilian Consulate General in Vancouver (Itamaraty, gov.br/mre, updated 28 September 2026) says passports must be valid for the entire period you intend to stay and that no minimum passport validity is required; Global Affairs Canada says the same (valid for the duration of your stay). The Brazilian Consulate in Zurich (Itamaraty, updated 1 September 2026) tells Swiss citizens the passport must be valid for at least 6 months upon departure, and the UK FCDO says the passport expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date of arrival. The structured fields use the stricter six months from entry because a carrier can refuse boarding on the stricter reading (Global Affairs Canada notes carriers' passport-validity rules may be more stringent than the country's entry rules).
entry_requirement_notes: Visa: Brazil's visa rules follow reciprocity (Itamaraty, 'Informacoes sobre vistos'): the Itamaraty visit visa (VIVIS) covers stays of up to 90 days and Brazil has visa-exemption understandings with about 90 countries, listed in the Quadro Geral de Regime de Vistos. The UK FCDO says British citizens can visit without a visa for up to 90 days for tourism. Brazil's Vancouver consulate states that, since 10 April 2025, a visa is required for Canadian visitors, and that from 30 September 2026 temporary visas for citizens of Australia, Canada and the United States are processed electronically; US and Australian passport holders should check the same Itamaraty page for their own position. Stay: Global Affairs Canada says that to stay beyond 90 days you must obtain an extension from the Federal Police (Policia Federal) before the authorised stay expires, but the Zurich consulate says for Swiss citizens the stay is 90 days within 180 and cannot be extended, so the extension rule depends on nationality; confirm yours. Overstaying incurs a daily fine payable on departure or next visit (FCDO). Get your passport stamped at the border; without the stamp you may be fined when leaving (FCDO). Onward ticket: not confirmed as a stated requirement. Global Affairs Canada says customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds; no Brazilian page opened states it either way, so carry one. Cash: FCDO says cash or travellers' cheques worth US$10,000 or more must be declared online (the Receita Federal page itself could not be opened, so the figure and currency rest on FCDO). Minors: FCDO says dual British-Brazilian minors travelling without both parents need authorisation from both, and non-Brazilian minors travelling without one or both parents should carry the original or a notarised copy of the birth certificate. Dual Brazilian nationals are normally required to travel on their Brazilian passports (FCDO). The Polícia Federal (gov.br/pf) pages opened for this guide only covered issuing Brazilian passports and did not state entry rules, so the Federal Police position rests on the Itamaraty and foreign-government pages above.

The Brazilian consulate in Vancouver says vaccination is recommended for all international travellers visiting Brazil)

health.malaria_risk: CDC: transmission occurs throughout Acre, Amapa, Amazonas, Rondonia and Roraima, is present in Maranhao, Mato Grosso and Para (rare cases in their capitals), and is rare and sporadic in rural and forested parts of several other states. No transmission in Brasilia, Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo or Iguacu Falls. Chloroquine resistance is noted, and CDC lists atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine as prophylaxis options for areas that need it (areas with only rare cases need bite precautions, not prophylaxis). CDC page updated 23 April 2025.
health.notes: No yellow fever vaccination is required for entry: CDC states the vaccine is not required for entry and Global Affairs Canada says proof of vaccination is not required to enter, while also stating there is a risk of yellow fever in the country and that vaccination is recommended depending on your itinerary. The UK FCDO health page lists yellow fever, dengue and Oropouche as health risks and says to check vaccine advice at least 8 weeks before the trip. Brazil's Ministry of Health says Brazil uses a single lifetime dose of the yellow fever vaccine and that symptoms appearing within 15 days of vaccination need medical attention. CDC and the FCDO point out that dengue is spread by mosquito bites, so bite avoidance matters in cities as well as rural areas; CDC also rates chikungunya as elevated risk (vaccination may be considered for stays of about 6 months or more). Healthcare: the FCDO says foreign nationals are entitled to emergency treatment in Brazilian public hospitals, that private hospitals will not accept you unless you can show evidence of enough money or insurance to cover treatment, and that you should hold travel insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation. The ANVISA traveller pages could not be opened (404 on the addresses tried), so no ANVISA statement is relied on.

emergency.notes: Police 190 (FCDO: contact the local police on 190 if you are a crime victim; Global Affairs Canada lists 190 for police) and ambulance 192 (FCDO: call 192 and ask for an ambulance; the Ministry of Health describes SAMU 192 as the free 24-hour emergency medical service reachable from landlines and mobiles). Fire 193 is listed by Global Affairs Canada only; no Brazilian government page that could be opened confirms it. Global Affairs Canada also lists 911 as a general emergency number, but neither the FCDO nor any Brazilian page opened confirms 911 (or 112) connects, so no universal number is shown.
