timezone_note: One offset nationwide, all year. Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism site states the country 'runs at GMT +7 hours, the same time zone as its neighbors Thailand, Vietnam and Laos'. In the IANA time zone database Asia/Phnom_Penh is a link to Asia/Bangkok, so the clock is identical.
passport_validity_rule: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from the date you arrive in Cambodia, and must be undamaged and complete (the UK FCDO says entry is normally refused for a damaged passport or missing pages; Global Affairs Canada also gives 6 months beyond the date of entry). Cambodia's own Ministry of Tourism visa page words it as 'six (6) months from the expiry date', which is ambiguous, so the clearer FCDO/GAC wording is used here. Neither FCDO nor GAC states a minimum number of blank pages. Cambodia's e-visa portal (evisa.gov.kh) sits behind a bot challenge and could not be opened, so this is not a first-hand citation of that site.
entry_requirement_notes: A visa is required for visitors. Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism lists a single-entry tourist (T) visa valid for 30 days at US$30 (business E visa US$35), extendable once for up to one month; the UK FCDO also says a tourist visa is valid 30 days from entry. You can apply for an e-visa online (evisa.gov.kh per the Ministry of Tourism; the FCDO says apply at least 4 days in advance via the Cambodian Embassy UK website or the official e-visa app) or get a visa on arrival at international airports and major land crossings (FCDO; Global Affairs Canada says you may need cash if electronic payment systems are down). Nationals of Afghanistan, Algeria, Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Sudan and Nigeria must apply in advance at a Cambodian embassy (Ministry of Tourism list). From 3 October 2026 the Ministry of Tourism states visa processing and issuance is completely digitalised and physical visa stickers are discontinued; its page does not say what this changes for a traveller, so check the e-visa site before you fly. CAMBODIA E-ARRIVAL CARD: the official form is called the Cambodia e-Arrival Card (CeA), not 'Digital Arrival Card'. It is free at arrival.gov.kh (website or app), replaces the paper immigration, health and customs forms, and the Ministry of Tourism says all travellers must complete it even with a visa. Submit within 7 days before arrival; the General Department of Immigration says travellers can submit it 'within 7 days before or on arrival', and tablets are provided at immigration if you have not done it. The FCDO says it became mandatory on 1 September 2024 for air arrivals at Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and Sihanoukville airports; the Ministry of Tourism says it replaced paper forms from 1 July 2024. Whether it applies at land crossings is not clearly stated by any official source seen. Overstaying: the Ministry of Tourism says US$10 per day; the FCDO says there is no limit on the fine, you can be detained and deported, and an overstay of more than 30 days means you must leave and pay. Get your passport stamped on arrival and keep the departure form (FCDO). Hotels and landlords must register guests through the FPCS app; if you stay with friends or own a property you must register yourself (FCDO). Cash: declare foreign currency over US$10,000 on entry; leaving with more needs a National Bank of Cambodia permit and customs approval unless declared on entry (Ministry of Tourism customs page). Onward ticket and proof of funds: Global Affairs Canada says you need an onward or return ticket and proof of sufficient funds, but neither the FCDO nor Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism or immigration pages state this, so it is left unconfirmed; carry a return booking anyway.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (certificate required only if arriving from, or having transited more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, for travellers aged 1 year or older per CDC; not required for direct travel from the US, and Cambodia itself has no yellow fever risk)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, influenza, varicella, shingles)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Measles (MMR)
Typhoid
Japanese encephalitis (for stays of a month or more, or higher-risk rural activities)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
health.malaria_risk: Mainly in pockets of rural and forested areas, with rare cases in non-forested areas. Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and the main Angkor Wat temple complex have no or negligible malaria transmission (CDC).
health.notes: CDC recommends antimalarial medicine (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, primaquine or tafenoquine) for rural and forested areas and notes chloroquine and mefloquine resistance; areas with rare cases need only bite precautions. CDC also lists schistosomiasis (avoid swimming in fresh water), dengue, Zika, leptospirosis, melioidosis, and common rabid dogs, and warns motorbike crashes are a major risk. CDC does not recommend a yellow fever vaccine for travel to Cambodia. The UK FCDO lists dengue, malaria, Zika, schistosomiasis and biting insects among risks and says to check TravelHealthPro at least 8 weeks before travel. Global Affairs Canada says medical facilities are limited outside Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, hospitals may require cash or a written insurance guarantee upfront, medical evacuation to Thailand or Singapore is often needed, and prescription medicines should be carried in original containers with copies of prescriptions. Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism says no vaccinations are officially required for entry (the page is dated, referring to 2022) and advises bottled water rather than tap water.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada says credit cards are not widely accepted outside major cities. Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism says cards are mainly accepted in major tourist towns, mostly upscale hotels, shops and restaurants, and generally not outside Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, Sihanoukville and the Poipet casinos; Visa, MasterCard and JCB are the most widely accepted and most businesses charge a 2%-4% fee (that page is undated).
money.cash_culture: The official currency is the riel (KHR), but US dollars are widely used (Global Affairs Canada). The Ministry of Tourism says 'US dollars are as commonly used as the Cambodian Riel', that many hotels and some restaurants and shops price in dollars, that small transactions are usually done in riel, and that Thai baht is also accepted in many places. Global Affairs Canada says only newer, undamaged US notes are accepted and notes with even slight tears will be refused.
money.atm_notes: Global Affairs Canada says ATMs are plentiful in Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and Sihanoukville but scarcer elsewhere. The Ministry of Tourism's (undated) money page says ATMs are in Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, Sihanoukville, Kampot and Battambang, that they are open 24 hours and that all ATMs dispense US dollars; banks are open roughly 8:00 to 15:00 or 16:00 Monday to Friday. Money changers 'offer a slightly better rate than the banks' per the same page. No official rate is quoted here.

emergency.notes: Police 117, fire 118 and ambulance 119 are given by the UK FCDO and, for Phnom Penh, by the Ministry of Tourism's useful-contacts page. Global Affairs Canada agrees on 117 and 119 and lists fire as '118 or 666'. No universal 112-style number is published. The FCDO lists the Phnom Penh tourist police on +855 (0)12 942 484 (Ministry of Tourism: 012 942 484; Siem Reap tourist police 012 402 424). Those two tourist-police lines are local mobile numbers for the two cities rather than a national emergency line.

getting_around.summary: Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism lists intercity buses from Phnom Penh to Siem Reap, Sihanoukville, Battambang, Kampot and other provincial towns, and boat services between Phnom Penh and Siem Reap and between Phnom Penh and Chau Doc in Vietnam. Within towns it names taxis, motorcycle taxis, the reumork (motor tricycle) and the cyclo. That page is undated and its schedules and prices are not reproduced here, so confirm times and fares with the operator or your accommodation. The UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both stress road safety, and CDC advises avoiding motorbikes and motorbike taxis and night driving because street lighting may be poor.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Cambodia's Ministry of Tourism says tourists can buy prepaid SIM cards for their phones at the arrival terminal of all airports and at border checkpoints, and that free Wi-Fi is widely available at most hotels, restaurants, mini marts, cafes and shopping malls. The page is undated, so its operator list and prices are not repeated here.

timezone_note: America/Toronto (Eastern) is a representative zone, not the whole country: Canada has six time zones. From east to west the standard offsets are Newfoundland (UTC-3:30), Atlantic (UTC-4), Eastern (UTC-5), Central (UTC-6), Mountain (UTC-7) and Pacific (UTC-8), each one hour later in daylight time (Newfoundland 3:30 behind UTC standard, 2:30 in daylight time). Those numeric offsets are the standard IANA/legal offsets, not read off a page I opened: the National Research Council page lists the zone abbreviations (NST/NDT, AST/ADT, EST/EDT, CST/CDT, MST/MDT) but gives numbers only for Yukon. The NRC states daylight saving time runs from 02:00 on the second Sunday in March to 02:00 on the first Sunday in November (so clocks in Toronto go back on 1 November 2026), is set by provincial legislation, and has exceptions: most of Saskatchewan stays on Central Standard Time all year (Lloydminster-area communities follow Mountain Time with Alberta), Yukon has been on UTC-7 all year since 2020, some areas of Quebec east of 63 degrees W use Atlantic Time, Ontario west of 90 degrees W is on Central Time, and Nunavut covers three zones. British Columbia is changing: the B.C. government states that after clocks moved ahead on 8 March 2026 that was the province's final time change, the 1 November 2026 turn-back will not happen, and B.C.'s new 'Pacific time' is set permanently at UTC-7 (aligned with Yukon). Communities in the northeast (for example Dawson Creek, Fort St. John) stay on UTC-7 year-round and southeastern communities such as Golden, Cranbrook and Fernie keep following Alberta. The practical effect after 1 November is that Vancouver stays on UTC-7 while Toronto drops to UTC-5, a 2-hour gap instead of 3. The NRC page itself warns that from 1 November 2026 some of its content will no longer be accurate and points to provincial and territorial governments. The IANA tz database entry for America/Vancouver was not checked against this change, so do not rely on a device clock alone for B.C. after 1 November 2026. Destination Canada notes that New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are one hour ahead of Eastern Time and Newfoundland is one hour thirty minutes ahead. Book flights and trains against local times at each end.
passport_validity_rule: Canada's official pages state that you must travel with a valid passport (IRCC: 'When you come to Canada, you must travel with a valid passport or travel document') but none that I opened sets a minimum remaining validity or a six-month rule for visitors, so none is stated here. What the rules do tie to the passport is the length of your stay: IRCC says that if you get no stamp or visitor record, your stay runs six months from entry or until your passport (or biometrics) expires, whichever comes first, and IRCC cannot issue a visitor record valid past passport expiry. An eTA is linked to the passport used to apply, so the same passport must be presented at check-in. Practical advice: carry a passport that is valid for your whole stay plus a buffer; airlines may apply their own stricter rules.
entry_requirement_notes: Canada's eTA (Electronic Travel Authorization) is in force today (17 October 2026). IRCC states it is required for visa-exempt foreign nationals who fly to or transit through a Canadian airport; travellers arriving by land, bus, train or boat (including cruise ships) do not need one, though they still need a valid passport. The fee is CAN$7, non-refundable, paid by credit or debit card online for one person at a time, and you need a valid passport, a card and an email address. IRCC says the eTA is valid for up to five years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first, and a new passport needs a new eTA; it allows repeat short stays, normally up to six months at a time. IRCC advises applying before you book your flight; most approvals arrive by email within minutes but some take several days if documents are requested. Apply only on the official canada.ca site. Who is exempt: US citizens do not need an eTA or a visa but IRCC advises carrying a valid US passport (other identity documents showing name, date of birth and citizenship can be shown by those not flying and without a passport); lawful permanent residents of the US with valid status are exempt but must carry proof of status plus a passport from their country of nationality when flying. Canadian citizens (including dual citizens) and permanent residents cannot apply for an eTA and must travel with a Canadian passport or PR documents. Visa-required nationals need a visitor visa (some may use an eTA instead of a visa for air travel only, if they qualify). An eTA or visa does not guarantee entry: a border services officer decides on arrival. IRCC's visitor page says the officer must be satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your authorised stay, have enough money for your stay and have ties (job, home, assets, family) taking you home; most visitors can stay up to six months, and the officer may shorten or lengthen that. That IRCC page sits under the visitor-visa section and does not mention a return ticket, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed; carry proof of onward travel and funds anyway. Cash: the CBSA states there is no limit on money you bring in, but amounts of CAN$10,000 or more (cash or monetary instruments, any currency, combined) must be declared; failing to declare can lead to seizure and penalties of 5% to 50% of the seized funds. Blank pages: IRCC says only travellers from visa-required countries need at least one free page; no requirement is stated for visa-exempt travellers, so none applies. Health insurance: IRCC says Canada does not pay for hospital or medical services for visitors.

health.notes: Sourced from the US CDC because the Public Health Agency of Canada's travel-health pages are written for Canadians leaving the country, not visitors arriving, so there is no PHAC arrival page to cite. CDC's Canada page (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) states yellow fever vaccine is neither recommended nor required for entry, and I found no vaccination that is a condition of entry. CDC also notes rabies in some wild animals and bats (avoid contact; seek care after any bite, scratch or bat exposure), recommends repellent with 20% or more DEET against ticks and mosquitoes, and, at the time of reading, listed a Level 1 notice for a hepatitis A outbreak in Manitoba (dated 4 June 2026) plus a global measles notice; check CDC for the current list. Medical costs: IRCC states 'Canada does not pay for hospital or medical services for visitors' and advises getting health insurance before you come.

money.cash_culture: No Canadian government source I opened describes cash-versus-card habits, so that is left unstated. What is official: Destination Canada says the currency is the Canadian dollar, with a $1 coin (the 'loonie') and a $2 coin (the 'toonie'), and points visitors to the Bank of Canada for live exchange rates. The CBSA requires a declaration of currency or monetary instruments worth CAN$10,000 or more on entering or leaving (no cap on the amount; seizure and 5%-50% penalties if not declared).

emergency.notes: 911 is confirmed as the emergency number for police, fire and ambulance by three official pages: Parks Canada (national parks), the Government of Canada's IRCC driving page (Canada.ca: 'call the emergency number (911) for police and an ambulance') and the Province of British Columbia (gov.bc.ca: 'If you require immediate assistance from the police, fire or ambulance, pull over and call: 911'). The BC page also says 911 is the number for 'most B.C. communities' and advises adding local emergency numbers when travelling in an area without 911 coverage, so some remote communities still use local numbers. I found no official page saying whether 112 works, so it is not listed. Parks Canada warns that cell coverage is not always reliable in the backcountry or in remote areas, so check the park's own page for local contacts. No national tourist-police line was found, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: Canada is very large, so most long hops between regions are by air, and the country has no national rail pass I could verify. VIA Rail is the national passenger operator: its Toronto-Montreal page lists an average travel time of 5 hours 13 minutes over 538 km with 40 departures a week (fares are one-way, per person, excluding taxes, and vary by day and departure time); its Vancouver-to-Toronto page for The Canadian lists 3 days 20 hours 29 minutes over 4,406 km with 2 departures per week. In the Toronto-Montreal-Ottawa-Quebec City corridor rail is competitive with flying, outside it service is infrequent. Domestic flight times, airline fares and bus services were not researched from official sources. City transit is local: Toronto's TTC takes PRESTO, tap-to-pay debit/credit and cash, and some other cities run their own systems. Practical framing (not from a cited source): in most of the country outside big cities a rental car is the usual way to reach national parks.

passes.name: TTC (Toronto) single fare and PRESTO Day Pass
passes.covers: The TTC fares page lists an adult fare of $3.30 with PRESTO or tap with an Interac debit/credit card (including mobile wallet), $3.35 in cash (exact fare only, no change), with a two-hour transfer on tap payments (not cash), and a PRESTO Day Pass at $13.50. Children 12 and under ride free. Starting 2 March 2026 PRESTO cards need enough funds to cover the full fare before tapping.
passes.worth_it: The day pass at $13.50 equals roughly four single fares at $3.30, so it pays off only if you take about five or more separate trips that each fall outside a two-hour transfer window; with tap payment and the two-hour transfer, many visitors will do better paying per trip. TTC also states fares are capped at 47 per month for PRESTO and card payers, a benefit for longer stays. Fares as published on the page at the time of reading; confirm at ttc.ca. Other cities (Montreal, Vancouver, Ottawa) were not researched.

timezone_note: Mainland Chile (IANA America/Santiago) runs on UTC-4 in the southern winter and UTC-3 in the summer. The Interior Ministry fixes the dates by decree; for 2026-27 the clocks go forward 60 minutes from 24:00 on the first Saturday of September 2026 (5 September) until 24:00 on the first Saturday of April 2027 (3 April), according to the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional's listing of Decreto 98 of 2026 (the full decree text could not be opened; the IANA tz database 2026c agrees, giving UTC-3 on 1 October and UTC-4 in July). Two parts of Chile do not follow that pattern. The Magallanes and Antarctic Chilean region (IANA America/Punta_Arenas, covering Punta Arenas and Torres del Paine's Magallanes side) and the Aysén region (IANA America/Coyhaique) are on UTC-3 permanently: Diario Oficial Decreto 93 of 11 March 2025 amends Decreto 1286/2018 so that in both regions the advanced hour is extended indefinitely, 'three hours west of Greenwich (-3)'. Easter Island (Rapa Nui, IANA Pacific/Easter) and Isla Salas y Gomez use a separate zone, UTC-6 standard time advancing one hour in the summer period (UTC-5), per the same decree's recital of Decreto 1142/1980. Travellers going to Patagonia or Rapa Nui should expect the clock to differ from Santiago by one hour in winter or up to two hours on Easter Island.
passport_validity_rule: Chile sets no fixed minimum such as six months. The Global Affairs Canada entry page says the passport must be valid for the duration of the stay in Chile. ChileAtiende (the state services portal) says the Permanencia Transitoria permit cannot run longer than the identity document you enter with. The UK FCDO says the passport expiry date should be after the day you plan to leave Chile. Check your airline's own rule, which can be stricter.
entry_requirement_notes: Mainland Chile: nationals of visa-exempt countries get a tourist permit (Permanencia Transitoria) at the border. ChileAtiende says it allows up to 90 days, that the Policia de Investigaciones (PDI) decides the period at border control even where a prior authorisation exists, and that the proof of the permit is the Tarjeta Unica Migratoria (TUM); the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada describe the same document as a tourist card (tarjeta de turismo) to keep and hand back on departure. Some nationalities need prior authorisation from a Chilean consulate; ChileAtiende refers to a consulate list rather than naming countries. Extension: one extension of up to 90 days, applied for before the first period expires, fee US$100 equivalent in Chilean pesos (nothing for under-18s), through the SERMIG portal (ChileAtiende; serviciomigraciones.cl). Funds: Global Affairs Canada and Chile's tourism board (Sernatur) both say visitors may be asked to show at least US$46 per day of stay. Onward ticket: no source that could be opened states a mainland requirement either way, so it is left unconfirmed; carry one anyway, since airlines check at departure. Easter Island (Rapa Nui) is different: Sernatur says a round-trip ticket covering a stay of at most 30 days (not extendable) is needed, a Single Entry Form (FUI) must be completed within 48 hours before the flight, you need a reservation in a SERNATUR-registered accommodation or a resident's invitation letter, and Rapa Nui National Park tickets should be bought in advance (the UK FCDO also lists the Rapa Nui entry form and a return ticket). Agriculture: every traveller over 18 who carries any plant or animal product, by-product or handicraft of plant or animal origin must declare it under oath to the Servicio Agricola y Ganadero (SAG) on the digital or paper declaration, regardless of quantity or packaging; the inspector decides whether it enters, risky products are refused and destroyed, and a false declaration is punishable by a fine (SAG states no amount). Global Affairs Canada warns that undeclared agricultural items can mean detention and heavy fines. Sernatur adds that honey-derived products are banned on Rapa Nui. Children travelling with one parent or alone need notarised permission from the other parent(s) and an original birth certificate (UK FCDO). No cash-declaration threshold was confirmed from an official page, so none is stated. The PDI website could not be reached by the research tools, so PDI's own wording is not quoted; the tourist-entry page chileatiende.gob.cl/fichas/2084 returned not found.

health.notes: No vaccination is required for entry. Yellow fever: both the US CDC and Global Affairs Canada state Chile does not require proof of yellow fever vaccination and that vaccination is not recommended. Insect-borne illness: Global Affairs Canada says chikungunya and dengue are present (and Chagas disease, generally a low risk for travellers); the UK FCDO says dengue cases are confirmed on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and that hantavirus is present in Chile. Malaria: none of the pages opened addresses it, so no statement is made. Altitude: the UK FCDO warns altitude sickness is a risk in parts of Chile; no official page opened gave specific elevations, so none are stated. Insurance: the UK FCDO advises travel health insurance covering repatriation, and because Rapa Nui has only one limited hospital, cover that includes air ambulance transfer to the mainland.

emergency.notes: Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/chile) lists police 133, medical assistance 131, firefighters 132, maritime search and rescue 137, and a helpline for women victims of violence 1455. The UK FCDO independently confirms the ambulance number ('Call 131 and ask for an ambulance'). The fire number 132 and the police number 133 rest on the Canadian page alone; no Chilean government emergency-numbers page could be opened. No general emergency number such as 112 is confirmed by any official source opened, so none is shown, and no tourist-police number is published on the pages opened. The British Embassy consular line (UK FCDO) is +56 (0) 22 370 4100. Chile is earthquake-prone and has severe wildfires; the FCDO points to the national disaster agency SENAPRED for warnings and says to follow evacuation orders.

getting_around.summary: Chile is a very long country, so most visitors cover big distances by air: Sernatur says an airport network links the extremes in hours, with LATAM, SKY and JetSmart named as the main airlines. Intercity buses are extensive; Santiago has four main terminals (Alameda for most national destinations, Los Heroes mainly for the north, San Borja for north and centre, Santiago Terminal for the south and central coast). In Santiago the Metro is described by Sernatur as the best way around and needs a Bip! card; the RED Movilidad app offers QR payment. Sernatur also lists a Chillan-Estacion Central train, about 400 km south of Santiago in roughly 4 hours 40 minutes. Rapa Nui is reached by air and has its own entry rules (see entry notes). Ferry and Carretera Austral transport were not covered by any page opened, so are not described.

timezone_note: Mainland China keeps one official clock, Beijing Time (UTC+8), and does not use daylight saving time. The IANA database lists Asia/Shanghai for it; IANA also carries a separate Asia/Urumqi zone (UTC+6) for Xinjiang's unofficial local time, so in Xinjiang ask whether a time quoted is Beijing Time or local time. This record covers mainland China only (not Hong Kong or Macao, which have their own entry rules).
passport_validity_rule: Mainland China requires a passport valid for at least 6 months after the date you arrive, with 2 blank pages for visas and stamps (UK FCDO: "expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive"; Global Affairs Canada: "valid for at least 6 months upon entry into China"). Exception: the 240-hour visa-free transit policy only needs a travel document with at least 3 months of validity (National Immigration Administration, NIA). The NIA's own English pages did not state the 6-month rule for ordinary entry when read, so this rests on the UK and Canadian governments' advice; an airline may enforce it at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA-FREE ENTRY IS A TEMPORARY, NATIONALITY-LIST POLICY. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that ordinary passport holders from Canada and the UK may enter without a visa for up to 30 days (business, tourism, visiting family or friends, exchange, transit) from 17 February 2026, effective until 31 December 2026; the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say the same. State media (english.www.gov.cn, 4 November 2025) report the same 30-day unilateral exemption for more than 40 countries extended to 31 December 2026. No source consulted says it will be renewed after that date, so a trip that enters after 31 December 2026 may need a visa: check the National Immigration Administration (en.nia.gov.cn) and the Chinese embassy before booking. Not every nationality is on the list, and a visa is required for work, study, journalism or stays over 30 days. TRANSIT: the NIA's visa-free transit page (dated 20 August 2026) lists 57 countries for a 240-hour (10-day) visa-free transit at 65 designated ports, including the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, Germany, Brazil and Singapore (India is not listed); you need an ordinary passport, a confirmed onward ticket with a date and seat to a third country or region within 240 hours, and the arrival card; work, study and news reporting need a visa. Anyone of any nationality can also transit visa-free for up to 24 hours if they stay in the port's restricted area. ARRIVAL CARD: since 20 November 2025 foreign visitors must complete the Arrival Card for Temporary Entry Foreigners, which can be filed online before arrival (s.nia.gov.cn/ArrivalCardFillingPC/, the NIA 12367 app, or the WeChat/Alipay mini programs), by QR code or port devices on arrival, or on paper; the NIA lists exempt groups (for example holders of a Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card and passengers transiting within 24 hours without leaving the restricted area). NIA hotline: 12367. REGISTRATION: you must register your place of stay with the local Public Security Bureau within 24 hours of arrival; hotels do it at check-in (FCDO, Global Affairs Canada); the NIA has an online registration service for other accommodation. CASH: carrying US$5,000 or more, or RMB 20,000 or more, requires a customs declaration (Global Affairs Canada); declare anything prohibited or dutiable (FCDO). ID: carry your passport at all times; printed copies are not accepted and failure to produce it can lead to a fine or detention (FCDO). TIBET: Global Affairs Canada says you need a permit and must be on an organised tour to travel to Tibet, and that unaccompanied private visits to Tibet are prohibited. Onward ticket for ordinary visa-free entry: not stated by any source consulted, so left unconfirmed (null); it is required for the transit policy. Many Chinese government sites block automated fetches or return partial text, so the UK FCDO, Global Affairs Canada, MFA and NIA English pages were used where they could be read.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate, only for travellers aged 9 months or older arriving from a country with yellow fever transmission risk, including airport transits or layovers of more than 12 hours there (CDC; the UK FCDO says the same for travellers coming from a listed risk country). Not required for direct travel from the US; itineraries limited to Hong Kong or Macao are exempt (CDC).

health.malaria_risk: CDC says malaria is a risk in some parts of China but its page does not name the risk areas or a preventive medicine; Global Affairs Canada's page does not mention malaria. Ask a travel-health clinic about your specific route; no official source consulted lists the major cities as risk areas.
health.notes: Tap water is not safe to drink anywhere in China: the UK FCDO says "Tap water is generally not safe to drink. Drink only bottled water" and CDC says it is not drinkable even in major cities. Dengue and chikungunya are mosquito risks (Global Affairs Canada, CDC). Global Affairs Canada says air pollution can be severe across much of China, and the FCDO notes altitude sickness is a risk in parts of the country. The FCDO says healthcare is not free and can be very costly and advises insurance covering local healthcare, medical evacuation and repatriation; some medicines legal elsewhere may be banned or unavailable, so check with your doctor and the Chinese embassy. CDC's China page was last reviewed 25 August 2026.

money.card_acceptance: Per the UK FCDO, cashless payment through smartphone apps such as WeChat or Alipay is almost universal, but outside major cities credit cards are not always accepted. Global Affairs Canada says international credit cards are accepted in many hotels and larger establishments but not universally, and that major Chinese platforms let foreign travellers link an international credit card and pay by scanning QR codes. Chinese government pages (Beijing government, March 2026) say WeChat Pay accepts Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover Global, JCB, Diners Club and UnionPay cards and waives its 3 percent fee on transactions under 200 yuan; the PBOC raised the per-transaction limit for foreign visitors to US$5,000 and the annual cap to US$50,000 (english.www.gov.cn, March 2024). No source read states that every foreign card will link successfully, so set the app up before you travel and carry a back-up.
money.cash_culture: Foreign currency cannot be used for everyday purchases: Global Affairs Canada says it is illegal to use foreign currency for everyday transactions, so you pay in renminbi (yuan), by app or in cash. The UK FCDO warns that counterfeit banknotes, especially 100 renminbi notes, are common, including from ATMs, and banks will not replace them, and it warns of QR-code phishing. Carrying US$5,000 or RMB 20,000 or more requires a customs declaration.
money.atm_notes: Global Affairs Canada says ATMs that accept foreign cards are widely available in major cities but may be limited in remote areas; the UK FCDO says that outside major cities ATMs are limited. No official source consulted gives withdrawal limits or fees for foreign cards.

power.adapter_note: The Beijing municipal government's visitor FAQ says China uses a 220 volt supply for standard domestic and business purposes, warns not to plug in a device labelled only 120 volts (USA and Japan), and says many outlets accept several plug styles, including straight two-pin rectangular plugs (US and Japan style) and cylindrical plugs (German and European style); these correspond to types A and C (the letters are our mapping, the page does not give them). Hotels generally provide wall outlets in every room, and the page says newer laptop and phone chargers from larger manufacturers are likely to work. It does not state the frequency or mention adapters, and it does not claim to list every plug type in use, so carry a universal adapter and check your charger's label.

emergency.notes: Police 110, ambulance 120, fire 119 (UK FCDO Getting help page; Global Affairs Canada gives the same three). Traffic police 122 and Maritime Search and Rescue 12395 (FCDO). CDC's China page names 999 for an ambulance in Beijing and 120 in Shanghai; 120 is the number both governments give nationally, so 120 is used here, but 999 is worth trying in Beijing if 120 does not connect. No source consulted lists a national 112 or a tourist-police number, so those are left blank. The NIA immigration hotline is 12367. UK consular help from within China: +86 10 5192 4000 (FCDO). The FCDO gives no English-language emergency hotline, so have your hotel or a Chinese speaker place the call if you can.

getting_around.summary: China Railway's official ticketing channels are the 12306 website and its mobile app, and the 12306 English site accepts valid foreign passports (the Beijing government, December 2025, lists a foreign passport as valid ID for online and phone booking and for ticket counters). The same page says self-service ticket machines do not list a foreign passport among accepted documents, so use a staffed counter or the app; a real-name ID is checked to enter stations and on the train. The Beijing page does not say how many days ahead tickets go on sale: the 12306 app shows the release time for your date and can set a reminder. The page says a ticket can be changed once and must be refunded before departure. For taxis the UK FCDO advises against unmarked or unmetered taxis, says to insist on the metered fare and ask for a receipt showing the taxi number. This record gives no fares, speeds or journey times because none were confirmed from an official source.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: No official source consulted states SIM or eSIM availability, SIM registration rules or prices for visitors, so none are given. What the governments do state about the internet: the UK FCDO says the Chinese authorities control internet access, Google, Facebook, YouTube and X are permanently blocked and other sites may be blocked at times, access can be restricted around key political events, and "online products and services (for example, VPNs) need to be licensed by the Chinese government". Global Affairs Canada says China blocks several websites, social media, search engines and online services and that you should not expect internet privacy. Neither page says which VPNs work, so no VPN advice is given. Download maps, translation, payment and messaging apps and set up payments before you travel.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 1.6 C, mean daily minimum -9.4 C, 3 mm precipitation on about 2 days. These are the old 1961-1990 normals that China Meteorological Administration supplies to WMO's World Weather Information Service, so recent years run warmer. Beijing is a continental northern climate; the south (for example Guangzhou, Hainan), the far west and Tibet differ greatly, so treat this as Beijing only.
climate.crowd_note: Cold and dry. Editorial note, not a measurement: the Lunar New Year travel period falls in January or February and is very busy for domestic transport; the exact dates move each year.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 4.0 C, mean daily minimum -6.9 C, 6 mm precipitation on about 3 days.
climate.crowd_note: Cold and very dry. Editorial note: Lunar New Year (late January to mid February, date varies) means heavy domestic travel and many local businesses closing for several days.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 11.3 C, mean daily minimum -0.6 C, 9 mm precipitation on about 4 days.
climate.crowd_note: Still cold early in the month, warming and drying out; shoulder season. Editorial rating.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 19.9 C, mean daily minimum 7.2 C, 26 mm precipitation on about 5 days.

climate.crowd_note: Warm and still relatively dry. Editorial rating: peak season. The Labour Day holiday around 1 May brings domestic crowds (exact days are set each year by the State Council).

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 30.3 C, mean daily minimum 18.2 C, 71 mm precipitation on about 9 days.
climate.crowd_note: Hot and humid, with the rains building. Editorial rating: shoulder season.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 30.8 C, mean daily minimum 21.6 C, 176 mm precipitation on about 14 days.
climate.crowd_note: Wettest, hottest part of the year in Beijing, with heavy summer downpours. Editorial rating: low season for overseas visitors; Chinese school holidays still bring domestic crowds to attractions.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 29.5 C, mean daily minimum 20.4 C, 182 mm precipitation on about 12 days.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 25.8 C, mean daily minimum 14.2 C, 49 mm precipitation on about 7 days.

climate.crowd_note: Cool, dry and clear. Editorial rating: peak season. The National Day holiday in 2026 runs 1 to 7 October (gov.cn report of 22 September 2026), one of the busiest domestic travel weeks of the year, so book transport and rooms well ahead for that week.

climate.precipitation_note: Beijing station normal, 1961-1990 base period: mean daily maximum 10.1 C, mean daily minimum -0.4 C, 6 mm precipitation on about 3 days.

timezone_note: Colombia uses a single time zone across the mainland and the island department of San Andres, Providencia and Santa Catalina, and does not observe daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Colombia sets no fixed minimum validity beyond the stay. UK FCDO: the passport must be valid on entry. Global Affairs Canada: valid for the duration of your stay. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt: valid on entry for at least the intended length of stay. Colombian immigration authorities recommend an expiry date at least 6 months after your planned departure (FCDO), and the German page reports travellers refused entry on passports with no more than six months left beyond planned departure. Airlines may also apply their own margin at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-exempt visitors (Resolucion 5488 of 2022, Article 3, on cancilleria.gov.co) may enter for short-stay activities that involve no paid work; the resolution defines a short stay as under 90 days, extendable to 180 days in the cases the rules set. Official sources describe the extension differently: Global Affairs Canada says a tourist may be granted up to 90 days at entry and can extend to a maximum of 180 days per calendar year; the UK FCDO says up to 90 days, extendable by up to 120 days through Migracion Colombia, capped at 180 days in any 12-month period; Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says 90 days, usually extendable once by a further 90 days with no entitlement to it. The officer sets the length granted at entry. Onward ticket: the FCDO says you must be able to show an onward or return ticket valid within the 90-day period; Global Affairs Canada and Germany say customs or immigration may ask for a return or onward ticket (and Canada adds proof of sufficient funds); CHECK-MIG: the free online pre-registration form (https://apps.migracioncolombia.gov.co/pre-registro/), completed between 72 hours and 1 hour before travel, for entering and leaving. Official sources disagree on whether it is mandatory. Global Affairs Canada says you must complete it within 72 hours to 1 hour before boarding a flight to or from Colombia or crossing by land, maritime or river routes. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says travellers must register within 72 hours before entry and before departure, and that the confirmation must be shown to the airline before departure from Germany. The UK FCDO says it can speed up entry but is not mandatory. Migracion Colombia's own pre-registration page describes it as a way to preload trip details and speed up the immigration interview and does not state that it is compulsory. Safest course: complete it before every flight to or from Colombia, since airlines can ask for it. CURRENCY: the FCDO and Germany's Auswaertiges Amt state you may bring in up to US$10,000 (or equivalent) in any currency, and the FCDO says amounts above that must be declared to DIAN (the tax and customs authority). Other formalities (FCDO): make sure your passport is stamped on arrival by land, sea or river or you could be fined on leaving; visas valid for more than 90 days must be registered within 15 days of arrival; travellers flying to San Andres, Providencia or Santa Catalina buy a tourist card at the boarding gate on the day of the flight unless staying under 24 hours.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate only if arriving from, or transiting an airport in, a country with yellow fever transmission risk (Global Affairs Canada names Angola, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda); not required for direct arrival from Germany (Auswaertiges Amt). See notes - official sources differ.
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid (rural travel or stays of a month or more)
Yellow fever (for travel to at-risk departments and municipalities, given at least 10 days before arrival there)
health.malaria_risk: Present below 1,700 m (5,600 ft) elevation; CDC records no malaria risk in Bogota, Medellin or Cartagena. CDC lists atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine as prophylaxis options for at-risk areas.
health.notes: Official sources state the yellow fever entry rule differently and this guide does not pick silently between them. Colombia's Ministry of Health (Minsalud) says that under the International Health Regulations (2005) Colombia takes a non-restrictive recommendation on yellow fever vaccination for people entering the country - not a blanket entry requirement - but travellers going to Very High and High risk municipalities should be vaccinated 10 days in advance. Colombia's tourism board says there are no mandatory vaccinations and recommends the vaccine for certain areas. The UK FCDO says a certificate is needed if arriving from certain countries with transmission risk and you may be asked for it when travelling to high-risk areas in Colombia. Global Affairs Canada says proof is required only for travellers arriving from or transiting Angola, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says no vaccinations are compulsory for direct entry from Germany, only for arrival from or transit through certain countries, including Brazil, and still recommends the vaccine. The US CDC's country page is the outlier: it states the vaccine is required for all arriving travelers aged 1 year and over (yellow fever notice updated 18 September 2026), while also noting it is generally not recommended for travel limited to Bogota, Barranquilla, Cali, Cartagena, Medellin, San Andres and Providencia, or areas above 2,300 m. The safe course is to carry a yellow fever certificate issued at least 10 days before arrival if you are coming from a risk country or going anywhere outside the high-altitude cities. Colombia's tourism board also notes some domestic routes (for example into the Amazon) ask for a certificate at check-in. Water is described by the tourism board as generally safe to drink in large cities, with bottled water advised in rural areas and small towns.

money.card_acceptance: Colombia's tourism board states that in Bogota, Medellin, Cartagena, Cali and other regional capitals you can pay by card in most hotels, restaurants, shopping centres and tourist services, with Visa and Mastercard the most widely accepted and American Express and Diners Club less frequently taken.
money.cash_culture: Cash remains the most accepted method, especially in markets, small shops, public transport and rural areas. The tourism board advises carrying low-denomination notes (2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 pesos) because many small businesses cannot break large bills, and recommends changing dollars or euros into pesos rather than trying to spend them - foreign cash is taken at exchange houses, not in shops.
money.atm_notes: Colombia's tourism board notes foreign-withdrawal commissions of roughly USD 3-5 per transaction plus surcharges for paying in another currency, and advises always choosing to be charged in Colombian pesos rather than your home currency when a card terminal offers the choice (dynamic currency conversion gives a worse rate). ATMs run 24 hours in major cities and shopping centres, many with an English-language option; it advises using machines inside banks or shopping centres.

power.adapter_note: Colombia's tourism board describes the common outlets as two flat pins, types A and B, as in the United States, and advises travellers from Europe or other 230V regions to bring a universal adapter and, where needed, a voltage regulator; both are sold in stores, airports and department stores.

emergency.notes: 123 is the single national emergency line and reaches police, ambulance and the fire service; 119 is listed separately for fire. Global Affairs Canada's Colombia page (checked 2026-10-17) says 'For emergency assistance, dial 123', which agrees with the UK FCDO's Colombia travel advice, the source for the 119 fire number. The numbers are taken from these foreign-government pages rather than from a Colombian government page - Migracion Colombia and the National Police sites do not publish a consolidated emergency list that was reachable, and the US Embassy in Bogota's page returned 403 to an automated fetch. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt page carries no emergency number. Bogota's city government describes Linea 123 as operating 24/7 with police and civilian operators dispatching police, the Bogota fire brigade and health-secretariat ambulances. No official source was found stating whether English is answered, and no tourist police number was verified, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: Colombia is mountainous and large, so domestic flights (Avianca, LATAM, SATENA and others) are often the fastest way between regions and the only practical way to reach San Andres, Leticia, Nuqui or Cano Cristales; the tourism board advises booking one to two months ahead. An intercity bus network reaches virtually every city and town, with air-conditioned, wi-fi-equipped reclining-seat coaches on main routes - good value for medium distances, but mountain crossings take many hours and road conditions are worth checking in the rainy season. In cities, Bogota runs the TransMilenio articulated-bus trunk network plus the SITP local buses, and Medellin has the country's only metro, linked to the Metrocable gondolas serving the hillside neighbourhoods; Cali's MIO is a similar bus-plus-cable system. Taxis and ride apps are widely available, and in smaller cities like Pereira, Manizales and Bucaramanga transport is simpler and mostly cash.

passes.name: Tu Llave card (Bogota)
passes.covers: TransMilenio trunk services and the SITP city buses in Bogota
passes.worth_it: Required rather than optional - Colombia's tourism board states you need the card to use the network. It is a stored-value card you top up, sold at system stations; it is not a time-limited tourist pass and there is no saving to calculate.

passes.name: Civica card (Medellin)
passes.covers: Metro de Medellin and connecting services including the Metrocable
passes.worth_it: Also a requirement rather than a discount product - the tourism board states you need the Civica card to use the system. Available at metro stations.

climate.precipitation_note: READ FIRST - this table is Bogota only, and Bogota is not Colombia. Colombia's official tourism board states there are no seasons in Colombia: climate is set by altitude and region, not by time of year, so temperatures barely move month to month and it is elevation that changes them. Bogota sits at 2,600 m and is cool all year (highs 15-17C); Medellin at about 1,500 m is mild all year; Cartagena on the Caribbean coast is hot and humid all year. Treat every figure below as a Bogota figure only - no verified month-by-month normals for Medellin or Cartagena were obtained, so no offset is given here rather than an invented one; pack for the altitude of each place you are going, not for the month. What does vary is rain: the Andean interior has two wetter periods (roughly March-May and September-November) and two drier ones. January itself is one of Bogota's driest months: 29 mm over about 8 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Colombian school holidays run into mid-January, so domestic destinations and coastal flights stay busy in the first half of the month.

climate.precipitation_note: Still dry in Bogota: 44 mm over about 11 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Quiet nationally outside Barranquilla, where Carnival fills the city and its hotels for several days.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota's first rainy period builds: 66 mm over about 14 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Semana Santa falls in late March or April and is the heaviest domestic travel week of the year; book transport and rooms well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota's wettest stretch: 101 mm over about 18 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Semana Santa crowds if Easter lands here; otherwise quiet once the holiday passes.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet in Bogota: 93 mm over about 20 rain days - the highest count of rain days in the year (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Low domestic travel; good value, with afternoon rain the main constraint.

climate.precipitation_note: Drying out in Bogota: 54 mm over about 18 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Mid-year school holidays begin toward the end of the month and lift domestic demand.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota's dry mid-year window: 43 mm over about 17 rain days, and the coolest average high of the year (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: School holidays plus international summer travel make this one of the busiest months.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry and windy in Bogota: 46 mm over about 16 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Medellin's Feria de las Flores fills that city; nationally still a busy month.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota's second rainy period begins: 72 mm over about 16 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Domestic travel drops sharply after the holidays end - one of the calmer months.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota's wettest month: 107 mm over about 18 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and cheap, at the cost of frequent afternoon rain and some Andean road disruption.

climate.precipitation_note: Still wet in Bogota: 91 mm over about 17 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Low season; a few long weekends produce short domestic surges.

climate.precipitation_note: Bogota dries out again: 53 mm over about 12 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: From roughly mid-month, Christmas and New Year drive the year's strongest domestic travel and the highest coastal prices.

timezone_note: One zone nationwide; Costa Rica does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset from North American and European clocks shifts when those countries change.
passport_validity_rule: Costa Rica does not impose a six-month rule. The Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería (DGME) Directrices Generales de Visas de Ingreso y Permanencia para No Residentes (Alcance 148 a La Gaceta 216, 17 November 2025) set the minimum passport validity for First Group nationalities at 'hasta un día' (up to one day), counted from the day of entry; the same text adds that the stay the border officer grants will not exceed the passport's validity. First Group includes the USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil among others. The UK FCDO states the same rule as 'your passport must have an expiry date at least 1 day after the day you plan to leave Costa Rica', so a passport valid at least a day past the planned departure satisfies both. Only machine-readable or biometric ICAO passports are accepted. Second Group nationals (e.g. Belize, Bolivia, El Salvador) need 90 days of validity from entry, and Third and Fourth Group nationals 180 days; check the directive if you hold one of those passports. Sourcing note: the DGME site (migracion.go.cr) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the directive was read first-hand from the identical copy of the same Gaceta document hosted on icoder.go.cr (a Costa Rican government domain), and cross-checked against the UK FCDO page.
entry_requirement_notes: Source of the rules below: DGME Directrices Generales de Visas (Alcance 148 a La Gaceta 216, 17 November 2025), read from the copy at icoder.go.cr because the DGME site (migracion.go.cr) blocks automated fetches (HTTP 403). Section 4 of the directive lists the entry requirements for every non-resident: a valid machine-readable or biometric passport; a visa where required; proof of economic means of at least US$100 per month or part-month of legal stay; a return ticket to the country of origin or an onward ticket (or a navigation plan naming the destination port); and no bar to entry. Costa Rica enforces onward travel at the border, not just at airline check-in: the tourism board (ICT) says all travelers must have a ticket for return or onward travel, and accepts a pre-purchased bus or flight ticket or cruise documentation. Stay length: First Group nationalities (which include the USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil) enter visa-free for up to 180 calendar days, non-extendable, with the exact period set by the immigration officer at the border; the directive allows an extension only for someone granted fewer than 90 days, and only up to a total of 90. The UK FCDO also says up to 180 days. The older 90-day figure for Canada and others is not in the current directive. Do not book non-refundable travel past the days actually stamped. Second to Fourth Group nationalities get at most 30 days (Second Group extendable to 90). FCDO additionally notes a currency declaration for amounts of US$10,000 or more, a departure tax of about US$29 (usually included in the airfare), and overstay fines of US$100 per month.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — required only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, Tdap, polio, varicella, influenza)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid (rural travel or longer stays)
Chikungunya (per CDC, tied to an outbreak in the northwest)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the provinces of Alajuela and Limón; rare to no transmission elsewhere (CDC).
health.notes: Yellow fever is checked at the border, not merely advised. Costa Rica's Ministerio de Salud states that foreigners arriving from a risk zone who do not present the Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla to the immigration authority cannot enter the country ('los extranjeros que lleguen a Costa Rica y no presenten el Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla ante la autoridad migratoria, no podrán ingresar al territorio'). The Americas risk list named by the Ministerio de Salud is Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, French Guiana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela, plus a set of African countries; CDC states the requirement applies to travellers aged 9 months and older. A separate and easily confused rule runs the other way: since 2026 Costa Rican citizens and residents departing Costa Rica for those same destinations must themselves be vaccinated at least 10 days before travel — that obligation does not apply to foreign visitors arriving. Neither the Ministerio de Salud article read here nor CDC stated a minimum number of days between vaccination and arrival for inbound foreign travellers, so no figure is given. Everything else listed under recommended vaccinations is advice, not a border check.

money.card_acceptance: The official tourism board states that all major credit cards are widely accepted and that US dollars are also widely accepted alongside the colón. No official source was found on where cards stop working, so assume cash for small rural businesses and buses.
money.cash_culture: Intercity buses are privately operated with no central terminal, and the tourism board advises bringing cash for lines that sell tickets only at the station — so carry colones for bus travel and small purchases even though cards are common.
money.tipping: Restaurant and hotel prices already include a 13% value added tax and a 10% service charge, per the official tourism board: an additional tip is optional and only for exceptional service, not expected.
money.atm_notes: The tourism board states ATMs are located throughout the country. No official source was found on fees, bank networks or dynamic currency conversion, so none is asserted.

power.adapter_note: The official tourism board specifies 110V outlets with standard US two-prong plugs (Type A). Grounded three-prong Type B outlets are also in general use but no official source confirmed that, so only Type A is listed. A traveller from a 230V country needs a plug adapter and must check that each device is rated for 110V — many hairdryers and kettles are not. Mains frequency is left null because no official source stated it.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single national emergency number. Costa Rica's Sistema de Emergencias 9-1-1 (operated by ICE) confirms nationwide 9-1-1 coverage, and the UK FCDO lists '911 (ambulance, fire, police)' for Costa Rica. No official source confirmed a separate tourist-police line or whether English is answered, so neither is claimed.

getting_around.summary: There is no national rail network for visitors and no countrywide transit pass. Intercity buses, run by several private companies rather than a government operator, reach nearly every popular destination cheaply, but there is no central terminal in San José — each line has its own terminal, and some sell tickets only at the station, for cash. Over ten domestic airports are served by Sansa and Green Airways, which is how travellers skip long drives between the Pacific coast, the Caribbean and the northern volcanoes. All of the above is as stated by the official tourism board; road-condition and drive-time claims are deliberately omitted because no official source was found for them.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry season; about 9 mm for the month, the second-driest of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement, not sourced: the busiest stretch of the high season, with the first week still carrying New Year demand.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month of the year, about 5 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: peak dry-season demand; book lodging and car hire well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Still dry, about 12 mm, and warming.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: busy, with an extra surge around Semana Santa when that falls in March.

climate.precipitation_note: Transition month; about 44 mm as the rains begin to return.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: Semana Santa is the domestic travel peak; outside it, prices start easing.

climate.precipitation_note: Green season begins in earnest — about 222 mm, a fivefold jump on April.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: quiet and cheaper; rain is typically afternoon-weighted rather than all-day.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet, about 283 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: low visitor numbers, good value, landscapes at their greenest.

climate.precipitation_note: About 208 mm — a dip against June and August that corresponds to the mid-year veranillo.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: a secondary high season driven by northern-hemisphere summer holidays.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain picks back up, about 252 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: moderate; summer-holiday traffic tapers through the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 325 mm, among the wettest months on the Pacific side and in the Central Valley.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: the quietest month; the Caribbean coast is the drier exception at this time of year.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month, about 326 mm; road and trail closures are most likely now.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: lowest demand and lowest prices, with some lodges and tour operators closed.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain drops sharply to about 139 mm as the dry season approaches.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: an underrated window — drying out but not yet busy or expensive.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry season returns, about 40 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Editorial judgement: fills up steeply from mid-month; the Christmas and New Year weeks are the most expensive of the year.

phrases.phrase_en: No worries / You're welcome (Costa Rican expression)

timezone_note: Croatia uses a single time zone, Europe/Zagreb in the IANA database (Central European Time, UTC+1 in winter). The European Commission's summertime page states that under Directive 2000/84/EC Member States switch to summer time on the last Sunday of March and back to standard time on the last Sunday of October; the last Sunday of October 2026 is 25 October, so Croatia returns from CEST (UTC+2) to CET (UTC+1) on 25 October 2026. The label above reflects the state on 18 October 2026. That Commission page does not list members by name, so Croatia's membership of Central European Time rests on the IANA zone, not on a page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Croatia is in the Schengen area (the Croatian Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs states that the Schengen acquis has applied in full since 1 January 2023). The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (page last checked 19 August 2026). The UK FCDO says the same: issued less than 10 years before arrival and expiring at least three months after your planned exit from the Schengen area. The Government of Canada also states the 3-month margin beyond the date you expect to leave the Schengen area. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area, whether or not a visa is required, and time in Croatia counts toward that total (mvep.gov.hr).
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS: no confirmed start date was found. The European Commission's ETIAS page on home-affairs.ec.europa.eu (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; the Government of Canada's Croatia advice (updated 11 August 2026) says applications are not yet open and to apply only through the official EU website once it launches. The UK FCDO entry page (undated) does not mention ETIAS. Re-check the Commission page before travelling; when it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation for visa-exempt nationals, not a visa. Entry/Exit System (EES): Canada's advice says the system collects information about your trip when you enter the Schengen area and that nothing needs doing before travel; the FCDO says it is being implemented across the Schengen area, that fingerprints and a photo may be taken at no cost, and that the digital record is valid for 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality: see the visa rules for your passport and mvep.gov.hr. Onward ticket and funds: the FCDO says border control may ask you to show a return or onward ticket and to prove you have enough money for your stay, with the amount depending on your accommodation; no Croatian government page opened for this guide states an onward-ticket rule, a minimum number of blank pages or a proof-of-funds figure, so none is stated here. Police registration: the FCDO says your accommodation provider must register your arrival with the police within 48 hours and usually does it for you; if you are on a boat, presence in Croatia must also be registered (tour operators usually handle it, otherwise form 16a at a police station). Cash: the FCDO and the Government of Canada both say that if you carry EUR 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) you must declare it to customs when you enter or leave the EU; Canada adds this does not apply to travel within the EU. Without a certified declaration the FCDO says money could be seized on departure. Unexploded mines: the FCDO says to beware of mines in previously war-affected areas, which it lists as Eastern Slavonia, Brod-Posavina County, Karlovac County, areas around Zadar County and remote parts of Plitvice Lakes National Park, and not to step off marked paths. mup.gov.hr (interior ministry) was reachable but its opened page did not state entry rules, so this guide relies on the EU, mvep.gov.hr, UK, Canadian and croatia.hr (Croatian National Tourist Board) pages.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged one year or older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; the Government of Canada recommends it for all travellers)

Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from outdoor activities; the Government of Canada says it is a risk in some areas, higher from April to November for hikers and campers in forested areas, and that the vaccine is not available in Canada)
Rabies (discuss with a clinician depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for adults with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: No malaria section appears on CDC's Croatia page or in the Government of Canada's Croatia advice, so none is stated here.
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Croatia page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry and not recommended; the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) and carries a Level 1 notice about rising global measles cases dated 28 May 2025. The UK FCDO says UK travellers need a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that it is not an alternative to travel insurance, and advises insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation; its health page lists no mandatory vaccines. To call an ambulance dial 194 (hakom.hr, croatia.hr) or 112; the FCDO says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. The Croatian Institute of Public Health and the Ministry of Health were not opened for this guide, so CDC, the FCDO and Canada are used as fallbacks; no official statement on tap water was opened.

money.card_acceptance: The Croatian National Tourist Board (croatia.hr) states that Croatia is one of the leading European countries for card and other electronic payment in hospitality, hotels, shops and agencies, that all major credit card companies are represented, that debit and credit cards and wallets such as Google Pay are accepted at a growing number of outlets with no additional or hidden costs for customers, and that ATMs can be found everywhere, especially in tourist destinations, for places that do not take cards.
money.tipping: The Croatian National Tourist Board states that tipping is optional and not mandatory, that prices in cafes, restaurants and hotels are clear and final with no service fee, and recommends rounding up to at least the nearest whole number in cafes and bars, leaving at least 10-15% in restaurants or for larger amounts, and giving hotel staff at least EUR 3.00 to 5.00.
money.atm_notes: croatia.hr's currency page states that the euro (EUR) has been the only official means of payment since 1 January 2023, replacing the kuna; banknotes of 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 euros and coins of 1 and 2 euros and 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 cents are in use, and the 500 euro note, discontinued in 2019, is still legal tender. The European Central Bank states that Croatia joined the euro area on 1 January 2023. ATMs: croatia.hr says they can be found everywhere, especially in tourist destinations; no official source opened gave withdrawal fees or limits, VAT-refund thresholds or bank opening hours, so those are not stated.

power.adapter_note: The Croatian National Tourist Board (croatia.hr, Electricity page) states that Croatia's installations supply alternating current of 220V/50Hz and that the sockets are type F (so-called Schuko), so European visitors (except those from Great Britain and Ireland) will not need adapters, while visitors from other systems should use standard EU adapters; visitors from 110V countries should check whether their devices work on 220V. The page says 220V, not the 230V figure used elsewhere in the EU, and it names only type F, so those are reported as written.

emergency.notes: Two official Croatian sources agree: HAKOM, the national telecom regulator (hakom.hr), lists 112 as the unified emergency number (free from all public networks) with 192 police, 193 fire brigade, 194 emergency medical services, 195 maritime rescue and 1987 the Croatian Automobile Club; the Croatian National Tourist Board's emergency page (croatia.hr) lists 112 plus 192 police, 193 firefighters, 194 emergency medical assistance, 195 search and rescue at sea and 1987 road assistance. The UK FCDO and the Government of Canada both point to 112 as the number to call, and the FCDO says to call 112 for the Croatian Mountain Rescue Service and, if you see a wildfire, to call 112. A Croatian-run tourist police number was not found on any official page opened, so tourist_police is null. Some non-official sites list 93/94 for fire/ambulance; the official pages give 193/194.

getting_around.summary: Ferries: the Government of Canada says ferry services operate between the mainland and several Adriatic islands, particularly in summer. Jadrolinija, whose site sells tickets online, lists international Dubrovnik-Bari, Split-Bari and Split-Ancona ferries and a Zadar-Ancona high-speed route, and on 15 October 2026 its home page carried notices that international ferry services would not operate until 21 October 2026 and that Split-Ancona was further interrupted until 2 November 2026, plus a 14 October notice on interrupted lines; some lines are reservation-only, so check the sailing schedule on jadrolinija.hr close to your date. No domestic journey time or fare could be confirmed from an official page, so none is given. Trains: HZPP (Croatian railways) says Zagreb Main Station to Split and back is served by daytime trains 523, 520 and 522 and night trains 1821 and 1820, with Sibenik connections changing at Perkovic; seats on the daytime Zagreb-Split-Zagreb trains must be reserved for EUR 1.06 and the page was last changed on 2 October 2026. HZPP's timetable page says the 2025/2026 timetable runs to 12 December 2026 and a fifth set of amendments takes effect on 5 October 2026; no Zagreb-Split journey time is shown on the pages opened, so none is given. Zagreb: ZET runs the city tram and bus network (fares below). Buses: no operator timetable or fare was opened, so none is given. Safety on the move: the FCDO reports taxi-related sexual assaults and advises photographing the taxi's number and sharing your ride; it also says to sail by the most direct route to a port of entry when arriving by boat and not to drink alcohol if in charge of a vessel.

passes.name: ZET Zagreb tram and bus tickets (single, daily, multi-day)
passes.covers: ZET's fares page lists, in EUR, prepaid single tickets of 0.53 (30 minutes), 0.93 (60 minutes) and 1.33 (90 minutes) and a night single of 1.99; tickets bought from the driver cost 0.80, 1.33 and 1.99 for 30/60/90 minutes; a daily ticket is 3.98, and multi-day tickets are 9.29 (3 days), 19.91 (7 days), 26.54 (15 days) and 53.09 (30 days). The funicular is 0.66 one way.
passes.worth_it: A daily ticket (3.98) costs about the same as four 60-minute prepaid singles (4 x 0.93 = 3.72) plus a little more, so it pays off only on a day of five or more rides; a 3-day ticket works out at 3.10 per day. The fares page carries no effective date and contains a note dated 2017, so confirm current fares at zet.hr or from the driver; contactless payment and airport-bus fares were not stated on the pages opened.

passes.name: HZPP seaside rail offer (Zagreb to Split and back)
passes.covers: HZPP's 'To the seaside by rail' page offers a 40% discount on tickets bought at HZPP ticket offices for the Zagreb-Split routes and says online tickets are 10% cheaper than tickets at the counter. It is not valid for journeys under 25 km; the day-train seat reservation costs EUR 1.06; night-train berths cost extra (EUR 9 three-berth, EUR 13 two-berth, EUR 25 single, EUR 7 couchette); a bicycle costs EUR 1.99 on trains 520, 522 and 523.
passes.worth_it: A discount offer, not a pass. The page was last changed on 2 October 2026 and several trains run only on stated dates (for example train 520 does not run on Sundays and public holidays until 27 June and from 31 August), so check the dates for your day on hzpp.hr. No standard fare or journey time was stated, so no saving is calculated.
