timezone_label: CST (UTC-5; CDT UTC-4 in daylight saving time)
timezone_note: One zone nationwide. The IANA tz database gives Cuba standard time of UTC-5 and daylight saving time (UTC-4) from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (so UTC-4 applies on 19 October 2026). The WMO World Weather Information Service listing for Havana also shows the offset as -0400 with daylight saving in effect. No Cuban government page stating the changeover dates was reachable, so the dates come from the IANA database; the live clock follows that database automatically.
passport_validity_rule: Official Cuban sources are not fully consistent, so the structured rule uses the strictest wording a Cuban government page states. The Cuban consular office in Panama (misiones.cubaminrex.cu, note dated 13 February 2026) states the passport's expiry date 'no debe ser inferior a 6 meses'. The UK FCDO says the passport must expire at least 6 months after the date you arrive and 3 months after the planned departure date. Global Affairs Canada says it must be valid for the expected duration of the stay, and the Cuban eVisa portal (evisacuba.cu) says the electronic visa is linked to a passport valid during the stay. Practical advice: carry a passport with at least 6 months of validity beyond your arrival date; that satisfies every wording above for stays of up to 3 months. Sourcing note: the six-month figure comes from the Cuban consular note read first-hand; the consular note does not say whether the six months run from arrival or from departure, so entry is used as the basis, with FCDO's extra 3-months-after-departure wording recorded here.
entry_requirement_notes: Entry documents. (1) A tourist visa: the Cuban consular office in Panama (note of 13 February 2026) states that from 1 January the paper 'carta de turismo' ceased to apply for travel to Cuba and that visitors need a tourist visa, which can be bought as an electronic visa at the official site evisacuba.cu, requested before the 72 hours preceding travel; the result is an email with the visa number and a link to the D'Viajeros form. The tourist visa is valid for 1 year from purchase until entry, becomes effective on entry, allows one entry and a stay of 90 days, extendable by a further 90 days inside Cuba. evisacuba.cu itself states 'una sola entrada a Cuba, para una estancia de 90 días, prorrogables por 90 días' and says a reply comes within 72 working hours, so request it well ahead. The UK FCDO page still calls this document a tourist visa 'also known as a tourist card' obtainable from the Cuban Embassy, a travel agent or evisa-Cuba; Global Affairs Canada says transit passengers must obtain the electronic visa in advance because its code is needed for the customs form. Cuba's older D'Viajeros manual says citizens of countries with visa-free agreements with Cuba are excepted; no visa-free list was read, so check your nationality with the Cuban embassy. Business, journalism and long or work stays need special visas from a Cuban consulate or embassy (D'Viajeros manual, immigration page). (2) D'Viajeros: the digital advance traveller information form (dviajeros.mitrans.gob.cu) is stated by Cuba to be mandatory for every passenger, with truthful information for immigration (Dirección de Identificación, Inmigración y Extranjería), customs (Aduana General de la República) and the Ministry of Public Health. The Cuban consular note says it produces a PDF with a QR code to show to airlines before boarding and at the border, and can be edited before arrival. Time window: FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say within 72 hours before arrival (FCDO: show the emailed QR code, and download or print it first as Wi-Fi may be unavailable on arrival); the D'Viajeros home page read here does not state the window. (3) Return or onward travel: FCDO states you must show proof of onward or return travel, and Global Affairs Canada says officials may ask for a return or onward ticket and proof of accommodation; no Cuban government page read here states it, so true reflects FCDO's wording. (4) Health insurance: Global Affairs Canada says you must be able to show proof of medical insurance on entry and may be required to buy Cuban coverage on arrival; the Cuban consular note recommends travel insurance, asks you to check whether your insurer has a contract with the Cuban insurer ASISTUR and says it can also be bought at the airport of entry. Money and customs. FCDO: declare foreign currency over US$5,000. Global Affairs Canada: you cannot leave Cuba with more than US$5,000 or its equivalent, or more than 5,000 CUP. Cuban customs (aduana.gob.cu) says the following may not be imported: narcotics, psychotropic or hallucinogenic substances, precursors, explosives, blood derivatives, obscene or pornographic material and anything against the nation's interests, plus electric stoves and hotplates beyond stated wattage limits, air conditioners above 1 tonne or 12,000 BTU, light motor vehicles, and animal products from ungulates that can carry disease; lobster in any quantity cannot be exported. Drones: Global Affairs Canada says they are prohibited and confiscated on entry; FCDO says they are not allowed. Liquids over 100 ml must go in hold baggage when leaving Cuba by air (Aduana). Medicines: Cuban customs (D'Viajeros manual, 2022 text) exempts up to 10 kg of medicines from duty if carried separately from other baggage; CDC advises that some prescriptions may be illegal in Cuba and to check with the embassy. US government travel restrictions: the US Treasury (OFAC) Cuba sanctions FAQs, read here, state that tourism is not authorised for US persons, that travel-related transactions are permitted only within 12 listed categories (travel outside them needs a specific OFAC licence), and list changes effective 30 September 2026 (professional meetings authorisation removed; group people-to-people travel only for travellers who completed a travel-related transaction before 30 September 2026; individual people-to-people travel never permitted). The US State Department advisory page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches and was not read. Current conditions: as of 19 October 2026 the UK FCDO advises against all but essential travel to Cuba (last updated 25 September 2026), citing shortages of fuel, electricity, water and basic necessities and likely further grid collapses, and says authorities report all international airports are without aviation fuel and several airlines have suspended flights; Global Affairs Canada (updated 5 October 2026) advises avoiding non-essential travel and says all Canadian airlines have suspended service. Check that your flight is operating before relying on any rule above. Sourcing note: cubatravel.cu, the Ministry of Tourism site and the Cuban immigration site (diie.minint.gob.cu) could not be reached, so stay length and visa mechanics come from evisacuba.cu and a Cuban consular note, with FCDO and Global Affairs Canada as fallbacks where stated.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever: required only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from, or transiting for more than 12 hours through, a country with yellow fever transmission risk (CDC); not required for direct travel from the US
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, flu, MMR, polio, shingles) and COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (under 60; may be given at 60 and over)
Typhoid (poor sanitation areas, stays of a month or longer, or visiting friends or relatives)
Rabies pre-exposure, depending on animal contact and access to care
Measles (MMR) fully up to date
health.malaria_risk: The CDC Cuba page read here does not state malaria status. The UK FCDO lists malaria among the mosquito-borne illnesses 'circulating' in Cuba without quantifying the risk; check the CDC Yellow Book country table and TravelHealthPro before travelling.
health.notes: Yellow fever is checked at the border for people coming from risk countries (FCDO; CDC; Global Affairs Canada, which says proof is needed only if you come from or transit through an airport in a country where yellow fever occurs). Neither CDC nor Global Affairs Canada recommends the vaccine for Cuba itself. Mosquito-borne disease: CDC lists dengue and Zika, and Global Affairs Canada lists dengue, chikungunya and Oropouche as risks; FCDO says authorities may fumigate. Cuba's own health ministry (MINSAP, salud.msp.gob.cu, 14 October 2026) reports a rise in respiratory infections and acute diarrhoeal disease, and its 9 October 2026 article stresses safe water and well-cooked food. CDC also lists leptospirosis (avoid floodwater), rabies in dogs and wildlife, tuberculosis, hantavirus and New World screwworm. Medical care: FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say facilities are poor and basic medicines are in severe shortage; foreigners pay or are expected to pay in foreign currency (FCDO: likely US dollars, and Visa and Mastercard are not accepted; Global Affairs Canada: cash in US dollars only). Bring enough of your own medication; FCDO suggests a GP letter listing treatment and doses. Make sure travel insurance covers local treatment and medical evacuation. The old COVID-19 entry rules (test or vaccination certificate) were removed according to the D'Viajeros manual's MINSAP page, but that manual's text is dated 2022 and the current D'Viajeros home page does not mention any COVID-19 requirement.

money.card_acceptance: International Visa and Mastercard cards are not accepted. FCDO (page current at 19 October 2026) says 'international cards such as Visa and Mastercard are no longer accepted in Cuba' and that you cannot withdraw cash with an international card; Global Affairs Canada says that starting 6 June 2026 Visa and Mastercard credit and debit cards are no longer accepted and that cards issued by or affiliated with US banks are not accepted. Accepted payment is cash and Cuban domestic prepaid cards (FCDO: CLASICA; Global Affairs Canada: Clásica and Tropical, which may not always work reliably). Ask hotels and tour providers how they take payment and whether you can pay in advance by international bank transfer (FCDO).
money.cash_culture: Bring enough cash for the whole stay plus a reserve for emergencies such as medical costs or a delayed departure (FCDO). The local currency is the Cuban peso (CUP). FCDO says US dollars and euros are widely accepted and can be exchanged; Global Affairs Canada says US dollars or euros are more widely accepted and Canadian dollars are not widely accepted or easily exchanged. Exchange only through official channels: FCDO says only at Cadeca exchange houses and that unauthorised exchange, including with individuals, can bring a fine or prison sentence; Global Affairs Canada lists airport exchange bureaus, banks, major hotels or official exchange bureaus and says street exchange is illegal. The Banco Central de Cuba publishes exchange rates daily (reproduced by Granma, 'Vigente 16/10/2026'); the rate figures were an image and were not read, so no rate is stated here. Neither FCDO nor Global Affairs Canada describes separate official, floating or informal exchange segments, and no official page describing them was opened, so none are asserted. Leaving Cuba with more than US$5,000 or its equivalent, or more than 5,000 CUP, is not allowed (Global Affairs Canada).
money.atm_notes: FCDO says you cannot withdraw cash from ATMs with an international card. Global Affairs Canada adds that credit cards and ATMs may not work during power outages, so carry cash.

emergency.notes: Police 106, ambulance 104 and fire 105, as listed by the UK FCDO 'Getting help' page and by Global Affairs Canada (which lists police 106, medical assistance 104, firefighters 105); the two sources agree. FCDO health advice says the ambulance service is 'limited and generally unreliable', especially outside urban areas. No single national emergency number and no tourist-police line were confirmed by an official source, so those are left null. Embassy of Canada in Havana: +53 7 204-2516 (Global Affairs Canada).

getting_around.summary: Transport is heavily affected by fuel shortages. Global Affairs Canada (updated 5 October 2026) says local transport is limited and costly because of fuel shortages, public buses are unreliable, scarce, overcrowded and poorly maintained, the rail network is unreliable and slow, and roads are poor throughout the island except the west-east Central Highway; taxis have no meters (agree the fare first) and it advises using only officially marked taxis. FCDO says official yellow taxis are generally reliable, three-wheel Coco-taxis may be unsafe, fake taxi drivers operate at the airport and in Old Havana, a UK licence is valid for up to 6 months, and night driving is best avoided because of poor street lighting. FCDO also notes fuel shortages make petrol or diesel hard to get. Both governments warn that international flights may be limited or cancelled at short notice. No official source read gave domestic flight, intercity bus or train timetables or journey times, so none are given.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Global Affairs Canada says the telecommunications network is poor, connections are often interrupted during power outages, foreign mobile phones may not work even in large cities, and internet or social media may be blocked or restricted, especially during unrest; it advises installing a VPN before leaving home and not relying only on your phone in an emergency. FCDO says Wi-Fi and data signal is limited. Neither page mentions ETECSA SIM cards, so no SIM, price or registration facts are given.

timezone_note: Czechia has one time zone (IANA Europe/Prague). On 18 October 2026 it is on central European summer time (CEST, UTC+2); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Czech government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Czechia is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (counted from the day you enter). UK FCDO's Czechia entry page gives the same two conditions (expiry at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area; issued less than 10 years before arrival). Visa-free short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. No page from Czechia's own foreign ministry or interior ministry stating this rule could be opened for this guide, so the EU and FCDO pages are the sources.
entry_requirement_notes: CURRENCY: Czechia is in the EU and Schengen area but its currency is the Czech koruna (CZK), not the euro. The Czech National Bank (CNB) states that adoption of the euro has been postponed to a later, as yet unspecified, date (an older FAQ page), and a CNB news release of 9 April 2025 says the government accepted the Ministry of Finance and CNB recommendation not to set a euro adoption date for the time being. ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point', says the start date will be announced several months ahead, and gives a fee of EUR 20. A later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be communicated later, and that the authorisation will be valid for 3 years or until the passport expires. No page opened for this guide gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; UK FCDO's Czechia entry page does not mention ETIAS. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it 'became fully operational on 10 April 2026'; per UK FCDO it requires biometric registration (fingerprints and a photo), usually at a booth on first entry, there is no cost, the digital record is valid for 3 years and longer border waits are possible. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). Border checks: per UK FCDO, Czech border control may ask you to show a return or onward ticket and to prove you have enough money (the amount depending on your accommodation), and the Your Europe portal lists a return ticket and proof of means among documents officers may ask for; no page opened for this guide states that an onward ticket or a specific funds figure is a fixed condition for visa-exempt visitors, and none states a blank-page requirement, so those fields are not stated. Registration: per UK FCDO, if you do not hold a Czech residence permit you must register your address with the foreign police within 3 days of arrival, or have your accommodation do it, and the fine for not registering can be up to 3,000 CZK. ID: FCDO says carrying ID is a legal requirement in Czechia and you should always carry your passport, though police will normally accept a scan of it. Cash: the Czech customs administration's factsheet (in Czech) and UK FCDO say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash or equivalent (any currency, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes; since 3 June 2021 also certain gold coins and bars) into or out of the EU must be declared in writing to customs; undeclared cash can be seized and a fine imposed. Food: FCDO says meat and milk products cannot be brought into the EU, with exceptions such as baby food.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 and older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from outdoor activities; may be considered for others outdoors where ticks are likely)

health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Czechia page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Czechia page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page carries a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis among non-vaccine-preventable risks; it says dogs with rabies are not commonly found in Czechia and post-exposure vaccines are typically available. Emergency care: dial 112 and ask for an ambulance (UK FCDO). FCDO says a UK GHIC or EHIC is needed for medically necessary state healthcare, covers state care only, and is not an alternative to travel insurance; FCDO lists no non-emergency health helpline. CDC and FCDO are used as fallbacks because no page from the Czech health ministry was opened for this guide.

money.cash_culture: Prices are in Czech koruna (CZK); see the entry notes for the status of euro adoption. UK FCDO advises exchanging currency at a bank or exchange office rather than on the street, where it says counterfeits are common, and being cautious at cash machines. Card acceptance, tipping and ATM fees were not stated on any official page opened for this guide.

power.adapter_note: CzechTourism's visitczechia.com states that the electrical network in the Czech Republic has a voltage of 230 V and frequency of 50 Hz, that the sockets are the same as in France, Germany, Belgium or Poland, and that for a different plug you should use a universal adaptor (ordinary, or one that also changes voltage and frequency). The page does not name plug type letters, so none are listed here.

emergency.notes: The Czech government portal (portal.gov.cz) lists 112 (single European emergency number), 150 (fire and rescue, Hasicsky zachranny sbor), 155 (ambulance, Zdravotnicka zachranna sluzba) and 158 (Czech Police), and says these lines run around the clock and are free. It also lists 156 for municipal police (obecni / mestska policie); it does not say whether 156 is free and municipal police do not exist in every municipality. UK FCDO's Czechia page lists only 112 for ambulance, fire and police, so 112 is a safe single number if unsure. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page. UK FCDO says Prague's main police station (Jungmannovo namesti 9) is open 24 hours and can provide English-speaking interpreters, that theft should be reported in person to the nearest police station within 24 hours to get a crime number, and warns that fake plainclothes 'police' asking to see your passport and foreign currency are a known scam (call 112 to verify).

getting_around.summary: Prague's integrated public transport (PID) sells time tickets valid across the capital; the official PID page counts Prague as 3 fare zones (P, 0, B) and gives the 2026 prices below. UK FCDO says paper tickets must be validated in a machine before boarding and that on-the-spot fines are issued by inspectors (FCDO quotes 1,000 CZK rising to 1,500 CZK; the PID tariff page states Prague surcharges of 1,200 CZK on the spot, 1,500 CZK within 15 days or 2,000 CZK otherwise, so treat the PID figures as the operator's and check before travelling). The national rail operator is Ceske drahy (cd.cz); its English homepage shows sample connections only, not a timetable, for example Brno-Praha 2 h 59 min (railjet), Plzen-Praha 1 h 21 min (InterCity) and Praha-Dresden 2 h 26 min (EuroCity), and it lists no rail pass or fares on that page, so check cd.cz for the journey you want. The PID page gives the Praha main railway station to Vaclav Havel Airport fare as 200 CZK (100 CZK for children aged 6-15). Regional buses, other city networks and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.name: Prague PID 24-hour and 72-hour tickets
passes.covers: PID's 2026 tariff (from 1 January 2026) lists, for Prague (full fare, ages 15-60), a 24-hour ticket at 140 CZK in the PID Litacka app or 150 CZK on paper, and a 72-hour ticket at 340 CZK in the app or 350 CZK on paper; the discounted (half-price) 24-hour ticket is 70 CZK app / 75 CZK paper and there is no discounted 72-hour ticket. Shorter tickets are 30 minutes (36 CZK app / 39 CZK paper) and 90 minutes (46 CZK app / 50 CZK paper). Prague counts as zones P, 0 and B. One large piece of luggage travels free with a 24-hour or season ticket for Prague.
passes.worth_it: A 24-hour ticket at 140 CZK (app) costs about three 46 CZK 90-minute tickets, so it pays off on a day of three or more separate journeys; the 72-hour ticket suits a three-day stay. Buying in the app is cheaper than paper. Whether the airport fare or particular lines fall outside these tickets was not confirmed here; check pid.cz.

passes.name: Ceske drahy long-distance tickets
passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets for Czech Railways trains, sold through cd.cz and its apps; no national rail pass was found on the pages opened for this guide.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey on cd.cz. Fares and any advance-purchase discounts were not read for this guide.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: CzechTourism's visitczechia.com says operators offer postpaid packages as well as prepaid cards for those who want to use a phone without a contract, and advises checking that your phone is not blocked by another operator before buying a prepaid SIM. It says wireless internet is available in many places, typically restaurants, cafes, hotels, libraries and some public transport. It notes an EU rule banning extra roaming fees, which applies within the EU; it does not cover travellers from outside the EU. It does not mention eSIM, prices or registration.

timezone_note: Mainland Denmark has one time zone (IANA Europe/Copenhagen). On 19 October 2026 it is on central European summer time (CEST, UTC+2); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The Faroe Islands (IANA Atlantic/Faroe) and Greenland (several IANA zones) are parts of the Kingdom of Denmark but keep different clock times; this guide covers mainland Denmark. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Danish government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Denmark is in the Schengen area. The Danish Immigration Service (nyidanmark.dk, page last updated 15-10-2025) states that a visa-exempt visitor needs a valid passport or other travel document that is valid for three months past the planned departure from the Schengen area and was issued within the past 10 years. UK FCDO's Denmark entry page gives the same two conditions (expiry at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area; issued less than 10 years before arrival). Visa-free stays are limited to 90 days within any 180-day period across the Schengen area, Greenland and the Faroe Islands combined (nyidanmark.dk); both the entry day and the exit day count. Citizens of Australia, Canada, Israel, Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, the USA, New Zealand, Chile and South Korea have a separate, differently counted allowance of 3 months (90 days for Chile and South Korea) counted from first entry into Denmark or another Nordic country (details in the entry notes).
entry_requirement_notes: CURRENCY: Denmark is in the EU and Schengen area but its currency is the Danish krone (DKK), not the euro. Danmarks Nationalbank states that Denmark pursues a fixed exchange rate policy against the euro, participates in ERM II at a central rate of 746.038 kroner per 100 euro with a +/- 2.25 per cent band, and 'does not participate with a view to joining the euro'. ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and gives a fee of EUR 20; a Commission news item of 28 April 2026 says ETIAS is 'scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026', with the exact date to be announced, and that an authorisation is valid for 3 years or until the passport expires. No page opened for this guide gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is live: the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; per UK FCDO it can require a photo and fingerprints, there is no cost, the digital record is valid for 3 years and longer border waits are possible. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). LONGER NORDIC STAYS: the Danish Immigration Service says citizens of Australia, Canada, Israel, Japan and Singapore may stay 3 months counted from first entry into Denmark or another Nordic country (time spent in Denmark or another Nordic country in the 6 months before entry is deducted); Malaysia is the same but excluding Iceland; the USA and New Zealand get 3 months from first entry into Denmark (time in Denmark in the previous 6 months deducted); Chile gets 90 days and South Korea 90 days from first entry into Denmark or another Nordic country. It says these citizens may stay regardless of earlier stays in other Schengen countries. FUNDS AND PURPOSE: nyidanmark.dk requires enough money for the stay and the return trip, giving a general guideline of about DKK 350 per day (about DKK 500 per day at a hotel; less if a host in a private home covers all costs), and that you can explain and, where required, document your purpose of stay; these must be met at entry and throughout the stay. It lists no fixed onward-ticket or blank-page requirement, so those fields are not stated; UK FCDO adds that at Danish border control you may be asked to show a return or onward ticket and prove you have enough money. BORDERS: per UK FCDO, temporary border controls apply to entry by land into Germany and travel between Denmark and Sweden has its own border controls, and Copenhagen Airport may have passport-control delays on flights to or from non-Schengen countries including the UK. Neither the Faroe Islands nor Greenland is in the EU; FCDO says tourists need no visa there, and nyidanmark.dk says the same funds conditions apply and that days there count toward the 90/180 limit. CASH: the Danish Customs Agency (toldst.dk) says you must declare cash or cheques worth EUR 10,000 or more (any currency, including in transit) when entering or leaving Denmark; you must visit a customs office even if you declare online in advance, and undeclared cash can be fined and seized. CUSTOMS ALLOWANCES (toldst.dk, arriving from outside the EU): goods up to DKK 3,250 by plane or ship (DKK 2,250 by other means); alcohol only for those aged 17 or over: 1 litre of spirits, 2 litres fortified or sparkling wine, 4 litres table wine, 16 litres beer; tobacco for those aged 17 or over: 200 cigarettes, 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g smoking tobacco; the customs page does not cover meat and dairy, but UK FCDO says meat, milk and their products cannot be taken into EU countries (exceptions include baby food and special medical foods).

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early dose for infants aged 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (CDC lists it for higher-risk activities such as visiting smaller cities, villages or rural areas, or eating street food, and says to consider it for most travellers)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; those 60 and older may get it)
Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from planned outdoor activities; may be considered for others outdoors where ticks are likely)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Denmark page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Denmark page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. CDC shows a Level 1 'practice usual precautions' notice and a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025), and says rabid dogs are not commonly found in Denmark and rabies vaccines are typically available throughout most of the country after an exposure. Emergency care: dial 112 and ask for an ambulance (UK FCDO). FCDO says UK nationals need a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that it does not replace travel insurance, that the cards generally do not cover costs in Greenland and cannot be used in the Faroe Islands, and that Denmark does not recognise UK prescriptions (see a local pharmacist, an apotek). Other nationalities should check what their own insurer covers. CDC and FCDO are used as sources because no page from Sundhedsstyrelsen (the Danish Health Authority) with visitor health advice could be opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: VisitDenmark says many shops, cafes and restaurants are now cashless and some accept only cards or mobile payments such as MobilePay or Apple Pay, but also that many smaller shops and supermarkets do not accept international credit cards. Carry a debit card and check before you order or shop.
money.cash_culture: The Danish krone is the official currency of Denmark, Greenland and the Faroe Islands (VisitDenmark). Banknotes are 50, 100, 200 and 500 kr; coins are 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 kr plus a 50 ore coin. VisitDenmark says some kiosks and supermarkets stop accepting cash after 8 PM. It does not say whether euros are accepted. Amounts of EUR 10,000 (about 75,000 kr per VisitDenmark) or more must be declared on entry or exit.
money.tipping: VisitDenmark states that service charges are included in hotel, restaurant and taxi bills, that tipping is optional, and that how much you tip is entirely up to you with no set etiquette.

power.adapter_note: VisitDenmark's travel essentials page states that Denmark uses two-pin continental plugs and 220 volt (50 Hz) like most other European countries, that visitors from Ireland or the UK need adaptors, and that North American visitors need a transformer for 110/125 volt appliances. The page does not name plug type letters, so none are listed. VisitDenmark quotes 220 V; the nominal figure used across the EU is 230 V, which no official page opened for this guide states, so check any single-voltage device before plugging it in.

emergency.notes: The Danish police (politi.dk) say 112 is the number for the emergency services in Denmark, and UK FCDO's Denmark page lists 112 for ambulance, fire and police, so all three are shown as 112. VisitDenmark describes 112 as the number for life-threatening emergencies. For non-emergency police matters the police give (+45) 114 as the service number for general enquiries (dial +45 114 from a foreign phone), and VisitDenmark also gives 114 for non-emergency police matters. politi.dk says that if you are the victim of a crime you should report it to the police and that in many cases you can report online. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page opened for this guide. A medical out-of-hours line (1813 in the Capital Region) exists but was not confirmed on a page opened for this guide, so it is not listed as a structured number. UK FCDO's 24-hour line for British nationals in difficulty is +44 20 7008 5000.

getting_around.summary: VisitDenmark says public transport in Denmark is easy, fast and convenient and that distances are small. The Rejseplanen journey planner suggests routes and sells train and bus tickets, and DSB (the national rail operator) takes bookings on its website or by phone (+45 70 13 14 15). VisitDenmark gives rough DSB journey times from Copenhagen of about 3 hours to Aarhus, 4 hours to Aalborg and 1.5 hours to Odense, and says DSB Orange off-peak tickets are the best value, with booking up to two months ahead recommended; no train fares are listed there. From Copenhagen Airport, VisitDenmark says regional train or metro reach central Copenhagen in under 15 minutes on a 3-zone ticket costing approximately DKK 36 (a figure that may be dated; check at the airport). Bikes are allowed on the metro except weekdays 7:00-9:00 and 15:30-17:30, and on regional trains with a ticket for the bike. Ferries serve many smaller islands. TICKETING IS IN TRANSITION: the older Rejsekort card is being replaced; DSB's page says the Rejsekort app replaces the physical Rejsekort and lists an anonymous Basiskort at 80 kr, and the national DOT page says the DOT Tickets app is closing and points users to the Rejsebillet app. VisitCopenhagen's page still describes Rejsekort Anonymous (DKK 80 card plus DKK 70 balance), which may be out of date. Closing dates for the Rejsekort could not be read on an official page for this guide, so check dinoffentligetransport.dk or rejsekort.dk before relying on a card. Regional buses and other cities were not researched.

passes.name: Copenhagen City Pass
passes.covers: VisitDenmark describes City Pass as a digital ticket for unlimited travel valid 24 to 120 hours, with adult and child (over 12) versions, costing from DKK 80 for 24 hours in Copenhagen zones 1-4, including the airport. You buy it online and need to keep your phone charged. The national journey-planning site dinoffentligetransport.dk has a City Pass page for tourists and travellers, but its prices could not be read for this guide.
passes.worth_it: Not worked out here: the 24-hour price quoted is 'from' DKK 80 and fares may have changed, so compare against single tickets on the day. It suits a visitor staying within Copenhagen's zones 1-4 who also needs the airport leg.

passes.name: Copenhagen Card
passes.covers: VisitDenmark says it gives unlimited public transport in the capital region plus free entry to more than 80 attractions, valid 24, 48, 72 or 120 hours, costing EUR 54-133 for adults, with a cheaper child version for ages 10-15.
passes.worth_it: Only pays off if you visit several of the included attractions; the attraction list and per-entry prices were not checked for this guide.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: VisitDenmark says your home provider needs a roaming agreement with a Danish operator to use your phone in Denmark, advises checking availability and cost before you travel, and notes that in some cases it might be cheaper to buy a Danish SIM card. timezone_note: One zone nationwide (Atlantic Standard Time, per the IANA database); the Dominican Republic does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset from North American and European clocks shifts when those countries change.
passport_validity_rule: General rule: the tourism board (Ministry of Tourism) lists a passport with a minimum validity of six months for tourists, and Global Affairs Canada says regular passports must be valid for at least 6 months after the date of arrival. There is an exceptional, time-limited relaxation: nationals of the European Union, the UK, Canada, the USA, Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Colombia and Ecuador entering exclusively as tourists may enter with a passport that is merely valid and stays valid during their stay and departure, under a measure the tourism board says remains in force until 31 December 2026 (its page prints the start as 1 December 2024; Spanish-language press reports a 1 December 2025 start, which this record could not confirm from an official page). UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both repeat the 31 December 2026 end date. From 1 January 2027 the six-month rule applies again unless the measure is renewed, so re-check before any 2027 trip. The relaxation covers US, UK, Canadian, German (EU) and Brazilian passports among the NextStamp set; Australian, Singaporean and Indian passport holders are not named in it and should assume six months. Global Affairs Canada adds that non-tourism purposes need six months' validity. Sourcing note: the DGM site (migracion.gob.do) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the rule is taken from the Ministry of Tourism page, which reproduces the DGM resolution, and cross-checked against UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada.
entry_requirement_notes: E-TICKET (electronic entry and exit form): the Ministry of Tourism says all foreign and Dominican passengers entering or leaving on commercial flights must complete the free electronic entry and exit form at eticket.migracion.gob.do (the Dirección General de Migración portal, which describes it as mandatory and as serving Immigration, Customs and the Ministry of Public Health). It is no longer limited to 72 hours before travel: it can be completed as soon as flight details are known, even months ahead, but must be done before reaching the airline check-in counter, and the airline asks for it. Complete one for arrival and one for departure; a QR code is generated and can be saved as PDF or screenshot. One account can cover a family of up to 7 people per form (the Customs section is for adults 18+ only). Passengers on private flights, non-commercial vessels, ferries and cruise ships use the paper Customs and embarkation/disembarkation forms instead. UK FCDO says the form can be submitted up to 7 days before arrival; the tourism board's later-worded page says it can be filled in months ahead, so the safe course is to complete it after booking and before check-in. Treat only eticket.migracion.gob.do as the official site. TOURIST CARD FEE: the DGII (tax authority) states the Tarjeta de Turista costs US$10.00 (its FAQ also gives EUR 10.00 for euro payments at ports and borders), is valid for a single entry, and since 25 April 2018 is included in every air ticket issued outside the Dominican Republic, so air arrivals do not buy it at the airport; Global Affairs Canada says the same. It is not included for tickets sold in the Dominican Republic or for transit passengers whose final destination is elsewhere, and visitors arriving by land or sea buy it at DGII points of sale at the port or border. Exempt: Dominican citizens, residents, holders of a valid Dominican visa and some others. It authorises a stay of up to 30 days. The tourism board also says a departure tax of US$20 is already included in the airline ticket fare. STAY AND EXTENSION: visa-free tourist stays are limited to 30 days; beyond 30 days a fee on a sliding scale by total length of stay is payable before departure or at the airport immigration section; UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say an extension to up to 120 days can be requested through immigration (Canada: in Santo Domingo, before the tourist card expires). RETURN TICKET: since 28 April 2023 air carriers must ensure foreign passengers hold a round-trip air ticket to and from the Dominican Republic (residents exempt); the tourism board also lists a ticket of entrance and return, a permanent address in the country and proof of sufficient funds as tourist requirements, and FCDO and Canada say officers may ask for return or onward proof and funds. VISAS: the tourism board says most visitors, including from the US, Canada, UK, EU, Russia, Mexico and Japan, need no visa, and that a legal resident of, or holder of a valid visa for, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom or the Schengen area may visit without applying; the DGII lists nationalities that must obtain a consular visa instead of the tourist card (it includes India and China). CUSTOMS: per the Dirección General de Aduanas (DGA) traveller FAQ, cash or bearer instruments of US$10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared on entry or exit with proof of lawful origin, and no tax is charged simply for carrying money; gifts up to US$500 once every three months and 20 packs of cigarettes, or 25 cigars, or 200 g of tobacco are allowed; the DGA FAQ states a 5 litre alcohol allowance while the tourism board page says 3 litres in total, so take the lower figure. Medicines for personal use are allowed; carry the prescription for psychotropic medicines.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate (International Certificate of Vaccination) for travellers arriving from the Brazilian states of Espírito Santo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, vaccinated at least 10 days before arrival (children under 10 months, pregnant women and people transiting under 12 hours are exempt, per the tourism board; CDC says travellers 1 year and older)
Yellow fever vaccination card for travellers arriving from Venezuela or who were there in the previous 14 days, aged 1 year or over (tourism board page, notice dated 15 October 2021)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, Tdap/Td, polio, varicella, influenza)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid (poor sanitation or rural travel, stays of a month or more)
Rabies (case by case, per CDC)
health.malaria_risk: Present mainly in the provinces of Azua, Elías Piña, La Altagracia (which includes the resort area of Punta Cana), San Juan and Santo Domingo; in the Distrito Nacional mainly in La Ciénaga and Los Tres Brazos; rare in other provinces (CDC, updated 23 April 2025). Prophylaxis is recommended by CDC for the listed provinces only.
health.notes: Yellow fever vaccination is only an entry condition for arrivals from the places named above; Global Affairs Canada states there is no yellow fever risk in the Dominican Republic itself and CDC does not recommend the vaccine for travel to it. Other risks named by CDC and Global Affairs Canada: dengue, Zika, chikungunya, Oropouche virus, leptospirosis, rabies, hepatitis A and B and travellers' diarrhoea. The tourism board and UK FCDO both state that tap water is not safe to drink. UK FCDO says public medical facilities are limited and private hospitals can be expensive, and advises insurance covering treatment and repatriation. The tourism board's entry page still carries a 2023 notice suspending entry of passengers and crew coming from Equatorial Guinea (Marburg virus); it is undated as to current status, so check before travelling from there. CDC's Level 1 measles notice (28 May 2025) advises MMR for all travellers.

money.cash_culture: The tourism board says most prices are in Dominican pesos; US dollars are widely accepted in tourist areas but at a worse rate than at banks, which use the Central Bank's daily rate. Banks close at 5pm on weekdays, though branches inside shopping malls stay open until around 7pm-8pm. Airport exchange is described as fine for small immediate needs only.
money.tipping: The tourism board says a 10% service charge is automatically added in restaurants, bars and hotels (plus 18% ITBIS sales tax) and, on its travel-tips page, that it is customary to leave an additional 10% in restaurants; taxi drivers do not receive a gratuity though exceptional service may be rewarded.
money.atm_notes: The tourism board says ATMs are available at supermarkets and shopping malls until later hours, advises using exchange services or ATMs as needed rather than carrying large sums, and notes that several banks' ATMs accept North American bank cards. UK FCDO warns that bank card cloning and identity theft are a risk: keep your card in sight when paying or pay in cash. No official source was found on ATM fees or on which merchants take cards, so neither is asserted.

power.adapter_note: The official tourism board states electricity operates at 110 volts, that visitors from the US and Canada will not need adapters, and that travellers from 220-volt regions such as Europe will need adapters and converters. It does not name plug types or mains frequency, so both are left null.

emergency.notes: 911 covers police, ambulance and fire per the tourism board and UK FCDO. FCDO warns 911 does not have full coverage across the country and says that outside Santo Domingo you should call the tourist police (Politur) on +1 809 200 3500; Global Affairs Canada lists the same number as CESTUR (Cuerpo Especializado de Seguridad Turística). Global Affairs Canada also lists road assistance on 1 829 688 1000 (free on major toll highways, 24 hours).

getting_around.summary: As stated by the official tourism board (page undated, so fares may have moved): the Santo Domingo metro has two lines, Line 1 north-south along Máximo Gómez avenue and Line 2 east-west along John F. Kennedy avenue, running daily 6am-10:30pm, with a rechargeable card at RD$15 and fares of RD$40 round trip or RD$80 for a day pass. Uber runs in Santo Domingo, Santiago and Puerto Plata and Cabify in Santo Domingo only. Taxis are set by the taxi association; confirm the fare before riding. Intercity coaches (Metro Tours, Caribe Tours, Expreso Bávaro) run RD$200-500 one way; long-distance minivans (guaguas) are cheaper, and the white in-city guaguas are the slowest. Motoconchos (motorbike taxis) are cheap but UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada warn they are often unsafe, and Canada advises avoiding them. Highways: Autopista Duarte, Santo Domingo to Santiago (about two hours per the tourism board); Autopista del Coral, Santo Domingo to Punta Cana in under three hours; tolls RD$60-100 per booth. Car rental requires age 25+ and a valid home licence; FCDO says a UK photocard licence is valid for up to 3 months and warns of poor night-time road lighting. Domestic flights use airports such as La Isabela (JBQ), Arroyo Barril (MDAB) and María Montez (BRX) mainly via charter operators. No ferry information was found on the tourism board page, so none is given.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: The tourism board says GSM phones work but roaming is costly, and that a local SIM can be bought with your passport from carriers such as Claro and Altice, then topped up with credit. It does not state any registration rule or eSIM support.
connectivity.typical_cost: Under US$5 for a local SIM, per the tourism board (page undated).

timezone_note: Mainland Ecuador (including Quito and Guayaquil) uses America/Guayaquil, UTC-5 all year with no daylight saving time. The Galapagos Islands are one hour behind the mainland on Pacific/Galapagos (UTC-6), also without daylight saving, so a flight from Quito or Guayaquil to the islands crosses that boundary. The US dollar is Ecuador's official currency (Global Affairs Canada: the U.S. dollar is the currency).
passport_validity_rule: The Ministry of Government states that foreign nationals need a valid passport with six months of validity (Art. 131, Organic Law on Human Mobility), and ecuador.travel repeats 'valid for 6 months'. The UK FCDO says the passport expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date you arrive; Global Affairs Canada says valid at least 6 months beyond your planned departure date. South American citizens may enter on a national ID card instead of a passport.
entry_requirement_notes: Ecuador's own pages do not state the tourist stay length; the stay figures below come from the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada, which agree. Visa-free visitors can stay up to 90 days in any 12-month period (FCDO and Global Affairs Canada); FCDO says you can pay to extend by a further 90 days and must apply before the first period ends or risk a fine, and Global Affairs Canada says one extension of 90 days is possible and the visa must be obtained before the entry stamp expires. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Human Mobility (cancilleria.gob.ec) publishes a list of 45 nationalities that must hold a visa before entering Ecuador (it includes India, China, Philippines, Vietnam, Cuba, Venezuela and Egypt) and the list is undated, so check your own nationality there. Passport: the Ministry of Government states a valid passport with six months of validity under Art. 131 of the Organic Law on Human Mobility; FCDO counts the six months from the date of arrival while Global Affairs Canada counts them from the planned departure date, so the record uses the stricter practical reading and you should carry a passport that clears both. Citizens of South American countries may enter on a national ID card. Onward ticket: no Ecuadorian authority page found states it either way. FCDO says it is not a stated entry requirement but you may be asked to show a return or onward journey at border control; Global Affairs Canada does not mention it for the mainland, so it is left unconfirmed here. Carry one anyway. Customs: FCDO says adults carrying taxable goods or cash of US$10,000 or more must register online and present the QR form, ideally at least three days before travelling; ecuador.travel also says USD 10,000 or more must be declared. Land arrivals from Peru or Colombia: FCDO says you need a criminal record certificate from your last five years of residence, apostilled and translated into Spanish if needed (ecuador.travel mentions the same, with an alternative SIMIEC review at the border), and must enter at an official checkpoint to get an entry stamp; an overstay is fined on departure. Children aged 17 and under who live in Ecuador or have been there more than 90 days need a notarised consent letter to leave if travelling alone or with one parent or guardian (FCDO). GALAPAGOS (a separate entry regime, source: Galapagos Governing Council, gobiernogalapagos.gob.ec): tourists need a valid passport or ID, a personal, non-transferable return air ticket between the mainland and Galapagos that does not exceed 60 days, available tourist days, and a Transit Control Card (Tarjeta de Control de Transito, TCT) costing US$20, paid on every trip. Tourists may stay up to 60 days per year counted from first entry, can enter several times, and the days cannot be extended. The TCT is bought at the Galapagos Governing Council counter at Quito or Guayaquil airport before check-in (ecuador.travel and Global Affairs Canada; the Council's FAQ says advance online purchase applies only through travel agencies, 48 hours ahead). FCDO also lists evidence of a hotel booking or host invitation and travel health insurance; ecuador.travel and FCDO both say foreign tourists must have private or travel health insurance for Galapagos, although the Council FAQ page does not mention insurance. Galapagos National Park conservation entry fee (Ministry of Environment and Energy table dated 14 April 2026, galapagos.gob.ec): foreign tourists over 12 US$200, foreign tourists under 12 US$100; nationals of Andean Community or Mercosur countries (Bolivia, Colombia, Peru, Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) over 12 US$100 and under 12 US$50; residents of Ecuador over 12 US$30; children under 2 and transit travellers are exempt. The Ministry of Health (salud.gob.ec) recommends, but does not require, a Traveler's Health Declaration for arrivals with symptoms (fever, cough, malaise, loss of smell or taste, rash).

recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged one year and older, per CDC)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers younger than 60, per CDC)
Typhoid (if visiting rural areas, staying a month or more, or visiting friends or relatives)
Rabies (pre-exposure, depending on activities; dogs and bats may carry rabies)

Yellow fever (for travel below 2,300 m east of the Andes, e.g. Napo, Orellana, Pastaza, Sucumbios, Morona-Santiago, Zamora-Chinchipe, Tungurahua; not recommended for Quito, Guayaquil or the Galapagos)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: CDC: transmission below 1,500 m in Cotopaxi, Esmeraldas, Morona-Santiago, Orellana, Pastaza and Sucumbios, with rare cases below 1,500 m elsewhere; chemoprophylaxis is recommended only in those provinces. No transmission in Guayaquil, Quito or the Galapagos Islands.
health.notes: Ecuador's own authorities treat yellow fever vaccination as a recommendation for tourists, not an entry requirement: the Ministry of Health urges national and foreign visitors to Orellana, Sucumbios, Pastaza, Napo, Morona Santiago, Zamora Chinchipe and Esmeraldas to be vaccinated at least 10 days before arrival, and the Ministry of Government says the vaccine is recommended for all travellers and required only for visitors from certain countries with active outbreaks. Foreign governments state the conditions differently, so the structured required_vaccinations list is left empty and both are recorded here: the US CDC says travellers aged 1 to 60 who stayed more than 10 days in Colombia, Peru, Brazil or Bolivia need proof of vaccination given at least 10 days before entry; Global Affairs Canada says proof is required if you arrive from, or transited through an airport in, the Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. If you are coming from any of those countries, carry the certificate. CDC recommends yellow fever vaccine for travellers aged 9 months or older going below 2,300 m east of the Andes (Morona-Santiago, Napo, Orellana, Pastaza, Sucumbios, Tungurahua, Zamora-Chinchipe); it is generally not recommended for travel limited to below 2,300 m west of the Andes, and not recommended above 2,300 m, in Quito, Guayaquil or the Galapagos. Altitude: FCDO says altitude sickness is a risk in parts of Ecuador and advises climbing at a moderate pace and staying hydrated (it gives the Pichincha volcano cable car station at 4,050 m as an example); the CDC page consulted had no altitude section. Medical care: FCDO says facilities in Galapagos are limited and Isabela Island has only a very small, basic health centre, and advises insurance that includes air ambulance evacuation; Global Affairs Canada says care is limited outside major cities and serious conditions in Galapagos require medical evacuation. Other risks noted by Global Affairs Canada: dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche, rabies and malaria in certain areas and seasons.

emergency.notes: 911 is the number given by the UK FCDO (police, 'call 911 and ask for an ambulance', 'call 911 if you see a fire') and Global Affairs Canada (National Police and emergency help). FCDO names ECU 911 as the emergency services body but gives no separate police, ambulance, fire or tourist-police numbers, so none is shown; ecu911.gob.ec could not be opened. Global Affairs Canada lists the Canadian Embassy in Quito at 593 (2) 245-5499. In Galapagos sirens sound for a tsunami alert (FCDO).

getting_around.summary: The islands are reached only by air from the mainland: the Galapagos Governing Council says tourists must arrive at Quito or Guayaquil airport with a personal, non-transferable return air ticket between the mainland and Galapagos of no more than 60 days, plus the US$20 Transit Control Card. Ecuador's tourism board lists Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca and Manta airports on the mainland and Baltra and San Cristobal airports in Galapagos. FCDO warns that several serious accidents in Galapagos have involved tour boats and smaller vessels, that some may lack licences or enough life vests, and advises using reputable operators. Global Affairs Canada and FCDO say land arrivals must use an official immigration checkpoint to get an entry stamp. No official source consulted describes a transit pass or fare product, so none is listed.

timezone_label: EET (UTC+2) in winter, EEST (UTC+3) on daylight saving time — currently UTC+3
timezone_note: Egypt has a single nationwide time zone (IANA Africa/Cairo). Egypt's State Information Service states that Egypt reintroduced daylight saving time in 2023 after a seven-year hiatus and now runs it annually, clocks going forward on the last Friday of April and back at the end of the last Thursday in October. Daylight saving time is therefore in effect on this guide's verification date (28 September 2026), putting Egypt at UTC+3; clocks return to UTC+2 at the end of October 2026.
passport_validity_rule: The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office states: "To enter Egypt, your passport must have an 'expiry date' at least 6 months after the date you arrive and have at least one blank page." Global Affairs Canada words the same six-month rule from the other end: valid at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Egypt (it does not mention blank pages). The two differ only on the counting basis; the stricter, safe reading for a long stay is six months beyond departure. Egypt's own e-visa portal (visa2egypt.gov.eg) does not publish the rule on its public pages, so this is sourced from foreign governments' pages about Egypt rather than first-hand from an Egyptian authority.
entry_requirement_notes: Per UK FCDO guidance on Egypt (page checked 2026-10-17): most visitors need a visa, available as an e-visa applied for online through Egypt's official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg (valid up to 3 months; the portal says to apply at least 7 days before departure) or as a visa on arrival at approved airports (30 US dollars, cash only, valid up to 30 days). Since 1 August 2026, travellers arriving at Cairo International Airport can instead buy a digital visa on arrival from self-service machines, card payment only, 36 US dollars including a 6 US dollar digital service fee. Global Affairs Canada, which does not mention the Cairo machines, quotes the cash visa on arrival at roughly 60 to 100 US dollars per person depending on travel plans, so the fee differs between official sources: carry cash or a card for the higher figure and confirm on visa2egypt.gov.eg. Travellers arriving by air at Sharm El-Sheikh and staying under 15 days within the Sharm El-Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba and Taba resort area receive a free entry stamp instead of a visa; Canada also describes a 14-day Sinai-only stamp at the Taba land border. Keep the entry stamp: Global Affairs Canada warns exit can be denied without proof of it. A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from, or transiting through, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Foreign currency worth more than 10,000 US dollars must be declared on arrival; up to 5,000 Egyptian pounds may be brought in or taken out. Drones are prohibited and satellite phones, radios and large video cameras can be confiscated (Global Affairs Canada). No arrival card, health declaration, proof of funds, hotel booking, travel insurance or onward ticket requirement is stated by FCDO. This is a foreign government's summary, not a first-hand Egyptian citation: confirm against visa2egypt.gov.eg or an Egyptian consulate before travel.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever: certificate required only for travellers arriving from, or with a long layover (CDC: over 12 hours) in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from the United States

health.notes: The only vaccination actually checked at the Egyptian border is the yellow fever certificate, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country (UK FCDO, US CDC and Global Affairs Canada agree on this; CDC page reviewed 25 August 2026 and does not recommend the vaccine for Egypt itself). Everything else on the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. Global Affairs Canada adds that some foreigners staying longer than a month for study, work or training may need an HIV test, and the FCDO says HIV test results are required for work permits, not for tourist entry. No malaria risk level is stated: the CDC and FCDO health pages consulted carry no malaria statement for Egypt and Global Affairs Canada's entry page does not mention it, so no risk level is asserted here.

emergency.notes: The US Embassy in Cairo gives the Egyptian police hotline as 122, the tourist police as 126 and the ambulance service hotline as 123, and lists no fire number. The UK FCDO (gov.uk Egypt 'Getting help' page, checked 2026-10-17) lists the same police 122, tourist police 126 and ambulance 123 together with fire 180, so fire is set to 180 on that single official source. Note a genuine discrepancy in official guidance: Global Affairs Canada's Egypt page lists police 112, medical assistance 113 and firefighters 110, with no separate tourist police number; if 122, 123 or 180 do not connect, those are worth trying. Whether English is answered on any of these lines is not stated by any official source consulted.

getting_around.summary: In Cairo the metro is the practical way to cross the city; its state operator, Cairo Metro Company, runs the first, second and third lines and publishes fares and station lists on its own site. Intercity travel between Cairo, Alexandria and Upper Egypt is by Egyptian National Railways, which sells tickets through its official portal at enr.gov.eg. No nationwide tourist transport pass could be found on any official Egyptian source, so none is listed below.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Egypt's National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (NTRA) requires every mobile line to be registered against an identified person's data, and enforces it — in August 2026 it referred all four Egyptian mobile operators to the Public Prosecution over lines registered under users' personal data without their consent. NTRA does not state on its site whether a visitor can register a line on a foreign passport, where, or what it costs, so none of that is asserted here.

timezone_label: EEST (UTC+3, summer time in effect); EET (UTC+2) from 25 October 2026
timezone_note: Finland (mainland) has one time zone, IANA Europe/Helsinki. On 19 October 2026 it is on eastern European summer time (EEST, UTC+3); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to EET (UTC+2) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Finnish government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Finland is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (counted from the day you enter). UK FCDO's Finland entry page gives the same two conditions (expiry at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area; issued less than 10 years before arrival) and notes that passports renewed before 1 October 2018 may show an issue date more than 10 years old. Global Affairs Canada's Finland page also gives the 3 months beyond planned departure and adds that airlines may apply stricter validity rules. Visa-free short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. No page from the Finnish Immigration Service or the Finnish Border Guard could be opened for this guide (both returned 403 / a Cloudflare check), so the EU, FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages are the sources.
entry_requirement_notes: CURRENCY: Finland is in the EU and Schengen area and uses the euro (Visit Finland: the euro was officially introduced in 2002; totals are rounded to the nearest five cents). ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point', and that the start date will be announced several months ahead. A later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be communicated later this year, and that an approved authorisation is valid for 3 years or until the passport expires. Global Affairs Canada's Finland page (updated 11 August 2026) likewise says applications were not yet open. No page opened gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it became fully operational on 10 April 2026, and Visit Finland says the same for all external Schengen borders. It applies to non-EU nationals making a short stay (visa-holders and visa-exempt travellers staying up to 90 days in any 180). Per UK FCDO it means fingerprints and a photo at a booth on first entry, no fee, a digital record valid for 3 years, and possibly longer border waits. RUSSIAN BORDER: UK FCDO says all land border crossings between Finland and Russia are closed 'until further notice' with no reopening date, a border-zone permit from the Finnish Border Guard is needed to enter areas near the border, and the maritime crossings at Haapasaari, Nuijamaa and Santio are closed to leisure boating. Global Affairs Canada says the same and adds that an EU entry ban applies to Russian-registered private vehicles with some exceptions. Do not plan to enter or leave Finland by land via Russia. The Finnish Border Guard's own pages (raja.fi) sit behind a Cloudflare check and could not be opened, and were not bypassed, so these two foreign-government pages are the sources. Border checks: per UK FCDO, officers may ask for proof of accommodation, a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds (the amount depending on your accommodation); the EU Your Europe portal lists an invitation letter, proof of lodging and a return ticket among documents you may be asked for, and Global Affairs Canada says officials may ask for a return ticket or proof of funds. No page opened states that an onward ticket or a specific funds figure is a fixed condition for visa-exempt visitors, and none states a blank-page requirement, so those fields are not stated. Schengen members can temporarily reintroduce internal border checks (Global Affairs Canada), so you may be checked even when arriving from another Schengen country. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). The Finnish Immigration Service (migri.fi) pages returned 403 / a Cloudflare check and could not be opened, so the passport rule is taken from the EU Your Europe portal, UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada. Cash: UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash or equivalent into or out of the EU must be declared (FCDO: get a certified declaration, or the money could be seized on exit). The Finnish Customs (tulli.fi) page returned 403 and could not be opened. Food: UK FCDO says meat and milk products cannot be taken into the EU, with exceptions such as powdered baby milk, baby food and medically required special foods. Winter driving: Global Affairs Canada says winter tyres are mandatory from 1 November to 31 March; Visit Finland says snow tyres are required in the winter months and headlights must be used at all times.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose for ages 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (consider for most travellers; recommended for higher-risk activities such as visiting rural areas or eating street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; those 60 and older may get vaccinated before travel)
Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from outdoor activities; may be considered for others outdoors where ticks are likely)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Finland page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Finland page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. Global Affairs Canada says tick-borne encephalitis risk exists in some areas from April to November, highest for people hiking or camping in forests, and that the vaccine is not available in Canada; it also recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all travellers and says rabies is present in some wildlife including bats. CDC's page carries a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis among non-vaccine-preventable risks, and recommends repellents and tick checks after outdoor activity. Emergency care: dial 112 and ask for an ambulance (UK FCDO). FCDO says a UK GHIC or EHIC is needed for medically necessary state healthcare, covers state care only, and is not an alternative to travel insurance. Global Affairs Canada describes health care as excellent and available nationwide, advises insurance covering medical evacuation, and says emergency response can be slow in isolated and Arctic regions. CDC, FCDO and Global Affairs Canada are used as fallbacks because the THL (Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare) page returned 403 and no page from a Finnish health authority could be opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Finland says cards and mobile payments are accepted almost everywhere (taxis, cafes, market stalls, roadside berry stands), that Finland is a contactless-friendly country, and that Visa and Mastercard are the most widely accepted cards. Its FAQ says all major credit cards are accepted in most places.
money.cash_culture: Visit Finland says cash is still technically accepted but most Finns have barely used it recently; it recommends carrying a few coins or small bills because some rural spots may prefer cash, and says a sign reading 'Ei käteistä' (no cash) means cash is not accepted. Totals are rounded to the nearest five cents, so 1 and 2 cent coins are rarely used. Displayed prices include VAT; Visit Finland says visitors from outside the EU can claim VAT back on purchases over 40 euros in one store, with receipts, when leaving the country. Public-transport tickets can be bought in mobile apps such as HSL in Helsinki, at ticket machines, or with a contactless card in many areas.
money.tipping: Visit Finland says tipping is not expected and that service is always included in the bill; a small tip, rounding up or a couple of euros, is appreciated for good service.

emergency.notes: Visit Finland's FAQ says to call 112 for urgent medical attention or help from firefighters or police, and UK FCDO's Finland page lists 112 for ambulance, fire and police, so all three are shown as 112. Global Affairs Canada also gives 112 for police, ambulance and fire and advises installing the 112 Suomi app (it says debris and drones from the Ukraine conflict have entered Finnish airspace and to follow air raid siren instructions). The Emergency Response Centre Agency's own site (112.fi) and the stm.fi emergency-response page returned 403 and could not be opened. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed. For non-urgent medical advice no number was confirmed on an official page opened for this guide. Global Affairs Canada's page gives the Canadian Embassy in Helsinki as +358 (0) 9 228 530 (business hours); its 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre number appeared malformed on the page and is not repeated here.

getting_around.summary: Visit Finland says Helsinki-Vantaa (HEL) is the main international gateway, 18 km north of the centre and about 30 minutes or less away: commuter trains on lines I and P reach Helsinki Central Station in about 30 minutes, every 10 minutes during the day; a taxi takes about 25 minutes; local and regional buses also serve the airport. Visit Finland says the VR train network runs from Helsinki to Kolari in Lapland, with overnight sleeping cars recommended for long journeys and car carriers on some trains; the coach network covers more than 90 percent of public roads (operators named: Matkahuolto, OnniBus, Express Bus, Perille); there are ferries to Germany, Sweden and Estonia, a steamboat on Lake Saimaa and sea cruisers to the Aland Islands; and Finland has over 20 airports. VR's English homepage (vr.fi/en) lists single, multi and season tickets plus night and car trains, and showed long-distance tickets on sale until 14 February 2027; it shows only 'from' prices, so check vr.fi for the journey you want. Driving: Visit Finland says Finland drives on the right, snow tyres are required in the winter months, headlights must be used at all times, and to watch for elk and reindeer at dusk and dawn; Global Affairs Canada gives the winter-tyre period as 1 November to 31 March and warns of icy conditions, short winter days and wildlife on roads. No Helsinki (HSL) fare, zone or journey-time figure was read from an official page (hsl.fi returned 403 / a Cloudflare check), and intercity journey times were not confirmed, so none are given here.

passes.covers: Visit Finland says Helsinki's tickets can be bought in the HSL mobile app, at ticket machines, or with a contactless card in many areas. Zones, prices and validity were not read from an official page (hsl.fi blocked automated access), so none are stated.
passes.worth_it: Not assessed: no fare table was available. Check hsl.fi for current single and day-ticket prices for the zones you need.

passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets for VR trains, sold through vr.fi and its apps, including night trains with sleeping cars and car trains; VR also lists multi and season tickets. No national rail pass was found on the pages opened for this guide.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey on vr.fi. Fares and any advance-purchase discounts were not read for this guide.

timezone_note: This guide covers metropolitan France only (mainland France and Corsica), which uses a single time zone, Europe/Paris. France's overseas departments and territories use other zones (France.fr lists Guadeloupe and Martinique at -5, Mayotte and La Reunion at +3, New Caledonia at +11) and are not covered here. Per service-public.gouv.fr, clocks go back one hour on the night of 24 to 25 October 2026 (3 a.m. becomes 2 a.m.), so metropolitan France returns to CET (UTC+1) on 25 October 2026; the label above reflects the state on 17 October 2026, and the same page says the switches follow the last Sundays of March and October.
passport_validity_rule: France is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years; France's service-public.gouv.fr states the same ten-year issue limit and a margin of at least three months beyond planned departure. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. This applies to metropolitan France.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (17 October 2026). The European Commission's ETIAS page states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; that page is dated 6 October 2025. France's diplomatie.gouv.fr page (April 2026) said it expected ETIAS in the last quarter of 2026, but the EU's official portal (travel-europe.europa.eu, opened 18 October 2026) now gives no launch window and no start date, and Global Affairs Canada says 'Applications are not yet open', so treat no date as fact and check travel-europe.europa.eu before travelling. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation (not a visa) for visa-exempt nationals; the French MFA page gives a fee of EUR 20, validity of three years or until the passport expires, and exemption for people under 18 or over 70. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): per diplomatie.gouv.fr it was phased in from 12 October 2025 and fully operational from 10 April 2026, replaces passport stamping, and records entry, exit and length of stay with a facial image and (except for under-12s) fingerprints; holders of long-stay visas and residence permits are not registered. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and france-visas.gouv.fr). The UK FCDO page says border officers may ask you to show a return or onward ticket, proof of enough money for your stay, accommodation and travel insurance, which is a possibility at the border rather than a stated requirement, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. Official pages opened for this guide did not state an onward-ticket requirement, a minimum number of blank passport pages for visa-exempt visitors, or a proof-of-funds figure, so none is stated here. Cash or travellers cheques worth EUR 10,000 or more must be declared to customs when entering or leaving the EU (UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada, both opened 18 October 2026). EES full operation from 10 April 2026 is also stated by the European Commission's Migration and Home Affairs news item.
