health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's France page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's France page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry, and everything in the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page, last updated 23 April 2025, has no malaria section; it notes bug bites can spread disease in France (use repellent) and lists a Level 1 notice mainly about rising global measles cases (28 May 2025). Tick-borne encephalitis appears on the page with no France-specific recommendation. CDC is used as a fallback because no French health-ministry page was opened for this guide. Global Affairs Canada's France page (18 October 2026) independently states proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required to enter, and the UK FCDO health page names no required vaccine and no malaria.

money.card_acceptance: France.fr states 'Credit cards are accepted in a large number of shops, hotels, and restaurants' and that shopkeepers often state a minimum charge, and that virtually all ATMs take Visa and MasterCard. The article was last updated on 6 March 2019, so treat contactless and minimum-spend details as unverified.
money.tipping: France.fr states that almost all restaurants include tax and a 15% service charge in their prices (service compris), that a 15% tip is appropriate where service is not included (service non compris), 10-15% of the metered fare for taxi drivers, and about 1.50 EUR each for hotel porters and chambermaids (article last updated 6 March 2019). Tips are customary, not mandatory; the consumer agency DGCCRF's page could not be opened to confirm the legal position.
money.atm_notes: France.fr advises that ATMs often have the best exchange rates, that withdrawing cash on a credit card is treated as a cash advance, that most French ATM keypads have numbers only (convert any letters in a PIN), and to tell your card company you will be abroad. Non-EU residents can claim VAT refunds on purchases over 175 EUR at a single store (per the same 2019 article; check current thresholds).

power.adapter_note: France.fr states electricity runs on a 220-volt, 50-hertz AC current, that France uses a Type E plug (a round pin plus a grounding pin), that visitors bringing appliances need a plug adapter, and that a voltage transformer may also be needed though most major appliances now have one built in. The article is dated 22 March 2012, so the 220V figure is the tourism board's wording; the IEC's World Plugs could not be opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: service-public.gouv.fr lists 15 as the Samu (emergency medical assistance), 17 as police or gendarmerie, 18 as firefighters and 112 as the European emergency number. The same page lists 114 for deaf and hard-of-hearing callers (France.fr's German-language page says this works by SMS or chat), 196 for maritime rescue, 191 for aeronautical rescue, 115 for social emergencies and 119 for children in danger. France.fr describes 112 as working without an active SIM or credit and routing you to police, ambulance or fire. 0 800 112 112 is a free callback line and does not take emergency calls. 116 117 is for urgent non-life-threatening care outside surgery hours. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed here. Cross-checked on 18 October 2026 against the French Gendarmerie nationale's emergency-numbers page (15 medical/SAMU, 17 police-gendarmerie, 18 fire, 112 European number; also 114, 115, 119, 191, 196, 197); Global Affairs Canada confirms 112 and 17 and the UK FCDO says to call 112 for an ambulance.

getting_around.summary: Metropolitan France's long-distance backbone is rail. France.fr describes TGV INOUI as high-speed travel at up to 300 km/h linking Paris with Lyon, Marseille, Strasbourg and Bordeaux in roughly 2 to 3 hours, and Paris to Nice in under 6 hours; slower regional TER trains serve towns, vineyards and coastal villages. SNCF Connect states tickets for TGV INOUI and Intercites open on set dates (12 November 2026 for TGV INOUI travel from 7 January to 2 July 2027, and for Intercites travel through 31 March 2027), and that OUIGO Classique tickets go on sale 60 days before departure. No official fare for any TGV, Intercites or OUIGO journey was found, so none is given here: fares vary by date and booking time, so check SNCF Connect. In Paris and the Ile-de-France, Ile-de-France Mobilites runs the metro, RER, trains, trams and buses on a shared ticket and pass system.

passes.name: Ile-de-France single tickets (metro-train-RER and bus-tram)
passes.covers: Ile-de-France Mobilites' 2026 tariff release lists a metro-train-RER ticket at 2.55 EUR (reduced 1.30 EUR) and a bus-tram ticket at 2.05 EUR (reduced 1.05 EUR).
passes.worth_it: Fine for occasional trips. The release was published ahead of the IDFM board vote of 10 December 2025 and states the fares are for entry into force on 1 January 2026; confirm at the station or on iledefrance-mobilites.fr, and note the airport fare and Paris Visite tourist pass were not verified and are not listed.

passes.name: Navigo Semaine (weekly) and Navigo Mois (monthly) passes
passes.covers: All-zone Navigo passes for the Ile-de-France network; IDFM's 2026 release lists Navigo Semaine at 32.40 EUR (reduced 16.20 EUR) and Navigo Mois at 90.80 EUR (reduced 45.40 EUR).
passes.worth_it: At the 2.55 EUR single-ticket fare the weekly price equals about 13 single trips, so it pays off only if you ride the network heavily across a week. Same caveat as above: figures come from a release dated before the December 2025 vote.

passes.name: SNCF long-distance tickets (TGV INOUI, Intercites, OUIGO)
passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets for France's high-speed and intercity trains, sold on SNCF Connect; no national pass was found on an official page.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey. Sales open on the dates SNCF Connect lists (see summary), so for peak travel dates buy as soon as sales open.

timezone_note: Georgia uses a single time zone year-round and does not observe daylight saving time. The WMO station record for Tbilisi, supplied by Georgia's Department of Hydrometeorology, lists the zone as +0400 with DST = N; this agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Tbilisi (+04 all year). Note that the de facto authorities in Abkhazia and South Ossetia keep Moscow time (UTC+3); those regions are not accessible from the rest of Georgia and Georgian law treats entry to them from Russia as illegal.
passport_validity_rule: Georgia's national tourism board (georgia.travel) states that travellers from most countries need a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond their date of entry into Georgia, and that entry requires an ordinary or biometric national passport unless a treaty provides otherwise. The UK FCDO instead says only that your passport should be valid for the duration of your stay, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs entry page (geoconsul.gov.ge), which was read in full, states no passport-validity rule for visa-free entry; the 6-month figure is kept as the best-supported destination-side statement, so carry a passport with 6 months left. For an e-Visa the passport must be valid 3 months beyond the visa's validity (evisa.gov.ge).
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-free stay is unusually long: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs consular portal (geoconsul.gov.ge, 'Visa free countries' page) lists most eligible nationalities, including the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Japan, Singapore, Brazil and the other EU states, at 'Full 1 (one) year' (365 days) without a visa, under Government of Georgia Ordinance No. 255 of 5 June 2015 (Legislative Herald of Georgia; last amended 24 Feb 2026). A few listed nationalities get less (for example Chile 90 days in any 180, Uruguay 90 days, Iran 45 days), and India is not on the list. Holders of valid visas or residence permits of listed countries (including Australia, Canada, the UK, the USA, Japan, South Korea, the Schengen states and Gulf states) may enter and stay 90 days in any 180 without a Georgian visa, if the visa or permit is valid when they cross the border. Nationals not covered may apply for an e-Visa at evisa.gov.ge: fee 20 USD plus a 2% service fee (non-refundable), decision in at least 5 working days, travel document valid at least 3 months beyond the visa's validity, at least two blank pages and issued within the previous 10 years; a short-term single-entry visa is for at most 30 days and the total stay under a short-term visa may not exceed 90 days in any 180. MANDATORY INSURANCE: under the Law on Tourism, since 1 January 2026 every tourist entering Georgia must hold a valid health and accident insurance policy (paper or electronic, in Georgian or English, from a Georgian or foreign insurer) with cover of at least 30,000 GEL for the whole stay including arrival and departure dates, and must present it on entry; exempt are diplomatic/official/special passport and visa holders, accredited diplomatic and international-organisation staff, persons entering under international treaties, and international road freight and passenger drivers (MFA geoconsul.gov.ge; UK FCDO says the same and that proof may be asked at check-in or immigration). The tourism board page (georgia.travel) still calls insurance 'not mandatory'; that page predates or lags the MFA notice, so follow the MFA. The tourism board says proof of sufficient funds may be requested in some cases and that a return or onward ticket is recommended rather than required, so no onward ticket is treated as required; the MFA entry page does not state an onward-ticket rule. Work, including remote work and running a business, needs a work permit under rules changed on 1 March 2026 (MFA, FCDO). No mandatory online arrival form or pre-registration was found.

emergency.notes: 112 is Georgia's single emergency number for all services. The Public Safety Command Center 112, an entity of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, states that it takes calls 24/7 nationwide from landline or mobile with no prefix, and dispatches police, fire/rescue teams and emergency medical crews. Operators answer in Georgian, English, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Turkish and Russian. A free 112 Georgia app (Android and iOS) and a video-call/SMS channel for deaf and hard-of-hearing callers also exist. No separate legacy service numbers were confirmed by an official source, so none are listed here.

getting_around.summary: Georgian Railway runs the main intercity links, including fast trains between Tbilisi and Batumi on the Black Sea coast (train 802/801, roughly 5.5 hours: 08:00-13:35 westbound, 16:30-21:55 eastbound). Tickets go on sale up to 20 days before departure and can be bought at station ticket offices, at pay boxes, online at ticket.railway.ge or through the operator's mobile app; sales close 10 minutes before departure and a passport or personal ID number is required to book. Georgian Railway also operates international services. Marshrutka minibuses cover routes the railway does not, but no official source for their fares or schedules was found, so none are described here.

timezone_note: Germany uses a single time zone, Europe/Berlin. The Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) states that summer time (MESZ) starts on the last Sunday in March at 2:00 and ends on the last Sunday in October at 3:00, when clocks go back to 2:00. Applying that rule, summer time ends on Sunday 25 October 2026 and Germany returns to CET (UTC+1); PTB's separate table for the years since 1980 lists 25 October 2026 at 3:00 MESZ as the end. The label above reflects the state on 18 October 2026.
passport_validity_rule: Germany is in the Schengen area. Germany's Federal Foreign Office states that a passport must still be valid for at least three months on the planned date of departure from Germany and must have been issued within the last 10 years; the EU's Your Europe portal states the same (valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU, issued within the last 10 years, counted from the day you enter). Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. Border officers decide on admission; the Federal Foreign Office says there is no legal entitlement to enter the Schengen area.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026). The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says applications are not yet open. No start date is stated here because none was confirmed; check the EU's official ETIAS pages before travelling. What is live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the European Commission states it became fully operational across all Schengen countries on 10 April 2026, replaces passport stamping and records facial images, fingerprints and travel-document data of non-EU short-stay visitors; UK FCDO says fingerprints and a photo may be taken at a booth on your first visit at no cost, with children aged 11 or younger photographed but not fingerprinted. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). UK FCDO says that at German border control you may need to show a return or onward ticket and proof of enough money for your stay; that is a possibility at the border, not a stated requirement, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. The Federal Foreign Office says proof of funds depends on the purpose and length of stay with no fixed daily rates, and recommends health insurance that also covers repatriation. Official pages opened did not state a minimum number of blank passport pages for visa-exempt visitors. Germany has temporary border controls at its land borders (UK FCDO; no start or end date given there), so carry your passport even when arriving by road or rail from a neighbouring country. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more (or equivalent) entering Germany from a non-EU country must be declared to customs in writing without being asked, using the cash declaration form (free; at airports in the red exit); failure to declare is an administrative offence with a fine of up to EUR 1 million (zoll.de). UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada state the same EUR 10,000 threshold, and Canada states that proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required.

Tick-borne encephalitis (for travellers with extensive tick exposure from outdoor activities)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)

health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Germany page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Germany page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry, and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) independently says Germany poses no yellow fever risk and proof of vaccination is not required. UK FCDO's health page lists no mandatory vaccine. Everything in the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page (last reviewed 25 August 2026) carries a Level 2 Global Polio notice (23 September 2026) and a Level 1 Global Measles notice (28 May 2025), and says to use repellent and check for ticks after outdoor activity; it has no malaria section. UK FCDO states that a UK GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance, which should cover medical evacuation and private care. CDC is used as the main health source because no German health-ministry traveller page was opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: The Deutsche Bundesbank's payment-behaviour study for 2025 (press release of 17 June 2026) reports that cashless payments were possible for 86% of the purchases recorded at physical locations, and that about one quarter of respondents had been unable to pay cashlessly at least once in the past month when they wanted to. It gives no retailer acceptance rate, so carry some cash.
money.cash_culture: The Bundesbank study for 2025 (published 17 June 2026) found cash was still used for 45% of payments (six points lower than in 2023) and 23% of turnover, with cashless methods overtaking cash in the share of transactions for the first time (55%); debit cards accounted for 26% of transactions and mobile payments 10%. These are national survey figures, not a rule about any particular shop.

emergency.notes: The Bundespolizei states that 110 is the free emergency number for the police and that 112 is the Europe-wide free emergency number for ambulance, fire and police (works from landlines and mobiles in all EU countries). The federal civil-protection office BBK states that fire and rescue are reached free of charge on 112 in Germany and Europe, and that an emergency fax can be sent to 110 or 112. Global Affairs Canada lists police 110, medical assistance 112 and firefighters 112; UK FCDO says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. 116 117 is the nationwide number for urgent but non-life-threatening medical help (the Federal Health Ministry, 15 October 2026, describes it as an acute-care line being expanded; 112 stays the number for life-threatening emergencies). Germany.travel also confirms 112 works across Europe, free from any network. The BBK recommends the free NINA warning app (in English and six other languages) and says the 'nora' app is the official emergency-call app of the 16 federal states. No dedicated tourist police number was found on an official page, so none is listed.

getting_around.summary: Deutsche Bahn (bahn.de) runs the long-distance (ICE, IC, EC) and much regional rail network; FlixTrain is a separate long-distance operator. No official fare for any long-distance journey was found on a page opened for this guide, so none is given: fares vary by date and booking time, so check bahn.de. For local travel, the Deutschlandticket is a nationwide monthly pass for local buses, U-Bahn, S-Bahn and regional trains, but it is not valid on DB long-distance trains (IC, EC, ICE) or other long-distance operators such as FlixTrain; local legs before or after a long-distance trip are covered, while the long-distance part needs a separate ticket. City transport tickets and day passes vary by transport association and were not researched here.

passes.name: Deutschlandticket (Deutschland-Ticket)
passes.covers: Local buses, U-Bahn, S-Bahn and regional trains nationwide. bahn.de (Stand: October 2026) gives the price as EUR 63 per month through 31 December 2026, rising to EUR 66.80 per month from 1 January 2027. Not valid on IC, EC or ICE trains or other long-distance operators such as FlixTrain, nor on vehicles run mainly for tourist or historic purposes.
passes.worth_it: bahn.de states the ticket is available only as a subscription, cancellable monthly (by the 10th of each month, with the final month still usable), so it is not a one-off tourist ticket; the page does not say whether short-stay visitors can buy it. It pays off only for a month or more of heavy local and regional travel. Check bahn.de or your local transport association for single, day and group tickets.

timezone_note: Ghana uses a single zone, Africa/Accra, at UTC+0 all year with no daylight saving, per the IANA time zone database. No Ghanaian government page opened for this guide states the time zone, so this rests on the IANA database rather than an official citation.
passport_validity_rule: Passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you intend to leave Ghana, with at least 3 blank pages. The Ghana e-visa applicant guide (Ghana Immigration Service / Ministry of Foreign Affairs) states 'valid for at least 6 months beyond the intended departure date from Ghana' and at least 3 blank pages. Global Affairs Canada says 'valid for at least six months beyond the date you expect to leave Ghana' and notes airlines may apply stricter rules; the UK FCDO says the expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date you arrive. The stricter, departure-based reading is stored. Neither foreign advisory mentions blank pages; the 3-page figure comes only from the Ghana portal's guide for e-visa applicants.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA: most travellers need a visa. Global Affairs Canada lists visas as required for tourist, business and student travel, the UK FCDO says 'You must have a visa to visit Ghana', and Visit Ghana (Ghana Tourism Authority) says most non-residents need one and ECOWAS nationals are exempt. Ghana Immigration Service's visa page lists a visa-free regime for ECOWAS states and selected African countries; in its table Singapore is shown as 'visa not required' for any passport type with a listed stay of 60 days, while Germany and Brazil are shown as visa-free only for service and diplomatic passports (90 days). USA, UK, Canada, Australia and India are not in that table, so assume a visa is needed. The table is undated and the e-visa portal's eligibility checker (by nationality) was not readable, so confirm your own nationality there before booking. E-VISA: the Ghana Immigration Service runs the e-visa portal at evisa.immigration.gov.gh, which says it is an official Government of Ghana service of the Immigration Service and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; the visa.mfa.gov.gh address named in the research brief did not resolve (DNS not found) when tried. The portal's fee page states flat fees, not based on nationality: Standard USD 260 (processed within 96 hours), Priority USD 338 (48 hours) and Express USD 442 (5 hours). Its applicant guide summary says 90 days to enter Ghana and up to 60 days' stay set at the border; the specimen e-visa on the site shows a 30-day single-entry tourist visa, so the stay granted can differ from 60 days. It also says an e-visa does not guarantee entry, which is at the Immigration Officer's discretion. The UK FCDO page still describes an online form plus posted hard copies and does not mention the e-visa, so it is behind the portal. PASSPORT AND DOCUMENTS (e-visa applicant guide): passport valid at least 6 months beyond the intended departure date and with at least 3 blank pages; tourist (B2) applicants must provide a confirmed return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation covering the full stay and a bank or credit-card statement covering the last 3 months. These are the portal's requirements for applicants; the FCDO page says 6 months after arrival and Global Affairs Canada says 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave, so the stricter reading (6 months beyond departure) is stored. Neither mentions blank pages or an onward ticket. YELLOW FEVER: Global Affairs Canada says proof of yellow fever vaccination is required for travellers from all countries and the UK FCDO says you must have a certificate (and upload it with the visa application); CDC says it is mandatory for arriving travellers aged 9 months and older. The e-visa portal lists a yellow-fever FAQ question but its answer was not readable. OUTBREAK: Ghana Health Service reported (15 October 2026) a reactive yellow fever vaccination campaign in Wa West, Sissala East and Sissala West districts of the Upper West Region (14-18 October 2026), and CDC has a Level 2 notice (16 October 2026) for a yellow fever outbreak in the Upper West Region advising vaccination at least 10 days before travel. MONEY AND CUSTOMS: Global Affairs Canada says there is no restriction on bringing in or taking out foreign currency but it must be declared on arrival on an Exchange Control Form T-5 that you keep for departure, and that Ghanaian cedis cannot be exported. The UK FCDO says hard currency must be declared on a form provided on arrival and that carrying US$10,000 or more in foreign currency risks confiscation of the entire amount. Ghana Revenue Authority's passenger page says foreign currency above US$1,000 may be declared on the Bank of Ghana Currency Declaration Form (CDF Form 4A); the three pages differ, so declare any foreign cash you carry. GRA duty-free allowances: spirits up to 37.5 cl, wine up to 75 cl, and tobacco up to 0.5 kg combined; arms and ammunition must be declared and need a special permit. SAFETY NOTES (FCDO/GAC): FCDO advises against all but essential travel to the Bawku Municipal area in the Upper East region, and Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding non-essential travel within 25 km of the Burkina Faso border; wearing military clothing including camouflage is illegal (FCDO); carry ID or a photocopy of the passport photo page (FCDO). FCDO's latest update on its main page is 2 July 2026 (still current on 19 October 2026); Global Affairs Canada's page was updated 26 May 2026.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever vaccination certificate: Global Affairs Canada says proof is required for travellers from all countries; CDC says entry is mandatory for travellers aged 9 months and older; the UK FCDO says you must have a certificate. Check the e-visa portal and your nearest Ghanaian mission for current wording.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (CDC; COVID-19 recommended for eligible travellers)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 year or older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers of all ages)
Typhoid (recommended for most travellers)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Meningococcal (travellers aged 2 months and older going to meningitis-belt areas in the dry season, about December to June)
Cholera (may be considered for travellers to areas with active transmission, including Ashanti, Central, Greater Accra, Northern and Western regions)
Rabies (dogs with rabies are common; discuss pre-exposure vaccination with a provider)
health.malaria_risk: CDC lists the whole of Ghana as a malaria transmission area, primarily Plasmodium falciparum, with chloroquine resistance, and recommends prescription prevention (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine; some must be started days before travel). Global Affairs Canada says malaria is a risk throughout the country and recommends antimalarial medication for most travellers, ideally discussed with a doctor or travel clinic about six weeks before travel. CDC's malaria section was updated 23 April 2025.
health.notes: ENTRY: see the yellow fever wording in the entry requirements; the Ghana Ministry of Health / Ghana Health Service pages opened (ghs.gov.gh) did not state the traveller certificate rule, so the requirement is sourced to Global Affairs Canada, the UK FCDO and CDC. OUTBREAK: Ghana Health Service's article of 15 October 2026 reports a five-day reactive yellow fever vaccination campaign (14-18 October 2026) in Wa West, Sissala East and Sissala West districts of the Upper West Region targeting about 244,869 people aged 9 months to 60 years; CDC has a Level 2 'Practice Enhanced Precautions' notice dated 16 October 2026 for the Upper West outbreak and says travellers there should be vaccinated at least 10 days before travel. CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 and also carries a Level 1 global measles notice. UK FCDO says medical facilities are poor outside towns and serious treatment may require medical evacuation, so travel insurance should cover that. All of this is medical information, not advice.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Ghana (Ghana Tourism Authority) says Visa and Mastercard are the most widely accepted cards and are taken by major hotels, restaurants, banks, airlines and supermarkets. The UK FCDO says many hotels, guesthouses and shops accept credit cards but Mastercard is not widely accepted, so check ahead and carry back-up funds. The two sources differ on Mastercard.
money.tipping: Visit Ghana (Ghana Tourism Authority) says tipping is permitted in hotels and restaurants and is rarely added to the bill; where it is not, tip according to service quality for waiters, taxi drivers, porters and tour guides. No percentage is given.
money.atm_notes: UK FCDO: ATMs are common in large towns but may be unavailable in rural areas; avoid carrying large sums of cash, be alert at ATMs and watch for card skimming devices; contact your card issuer before travelling in case your account is blocked. Global Affairs Canada: exchange money only at banks or licensed bureaus (dealing with private citizens is illegal). Visit Ghana: banks and forex bureaux accept traveller's cheques, possibly at a slightly lower rate than cash.

power.adapter_note: Visit Ghana (Ghana Tourism Authority) says appliances should run on or be adaptable to 220/240 volts, that outlets are typically 3-pronged and sometimes 2-pronged, and that visitors should bring British or Continental European plug adapters or converters. It does not name plug type letters or the frequency, so those are left null.

emergency.notes: Sources differ. Global Affairs Canada lists emergency services 112, police 191 or 18555, ambulance 193 and firefighters 192. The National Ambulance Service (nas.gov.gh) lists 112 as its emergency number and NADMO (nadmo.gov.gh) shows 112 as its emergency hotline (and 0302964884 as 'National Emergency'); neither page lists 191, 193 or a fire number. The UK FCDO's getting-help page lists '999 or 112' for all services and gives 192 as the police number, which contradicts Global Affairs Canada's 192 for fire. Because 192 is claimed for two different services, no fire number is shown; 112 is supported by four official pages, police 191 and ambulance 193 only by Global Affairs Canada (a foreign-government fallback). If 191 or 193 do not connect, try 112 or 999. No tourist police number was found. The Ghana Police Service contact page opened lists only administrative lines (+233 302 773906, +233 302 787373), not an emergency number.

getting_around.summary: No Ghanaian government or tourism-board page opened for this guide described public transport (the Visit Ghana 'Getting around Ghana' page is empty apart from a note that international airlines including British Airways and Delta operate scheduled flights to Ghana). The UK FCDO says road conditions can be poor, especially in rural areas, street lighting is poor or absent so avoid driving outside main towns after dark, and impromptu police checkpoints occur at night. It also says crime has occurred in all taxi types (licensed taxis, tro-tros and app-based services), that tro-tro and app-based taxi drivers are not centrally licensed, that licensed taxis and pre-booked vehicles from reputable companies are safer outside major towns, and that you should avoid travelling alone in taxis after dark. A 1949 international driving permit or a Ghanaian licence is accepted for driving. No fares, passes or schedules were found.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visit Ghana (Ghana Tourism Authority) says that with a valid ID or passport you can buy a SIM card from any of the six telecom companies. It names no operators, prices or eSIM support.

phrases_language: Mixed sample: Twi (Akan) greetings and basics with the common English phrases. Ghana has many languages (Twi, Ga, Ewe and others) and English is widely used; every Ghanaian government page opened for this guide is published in English, but no page was opened that states the official-language status. The Twi phrases were written from general knowledge and not taken from an official page, so spellings may vary; treat this as a small sample for greetings and basic needs, not a phrasebook.

timezone_note: Greece uses a single time zone, Europe/Athens. The European Commission's summertime page lists Greece among the Eastern European Time (EET) members and states that Member States switch to summer time on the last Sunday of March and back to standard time on the last Sunday of October; the last Sunday of October 2026 is 25 October, so Greece returns from EEST (UTC+3) to EET (UTC+2) on 25 October 2026. The label above reflects the state on 17 October 2026. The WMO World Weather Information Service entry for Athens shows +0300 with daylight saving in effect.
passport_validity_rule: Greece is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (the page was last checked 19 August 2026); the UK FCDO and the Government of Canada state the same 3-month margin beyond the date you leave the Schengen area. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. The Greek National Tourism Organisation (visitgreece.gr) describes the same 90-days-within-six-months limit for visa-exempt nationals and refers other nationals to the Greek embassy or consulate.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026; re-checked on travel-europe.europa.eu, which still says it is not in operation and no applications are collected). The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The Government of Canada's Greece advice, modified 5 October 2026, says applications are not yet open and to apply only through the official EU website once the system is launched. France's diplomatie.gouv.fr (April 2026) says ETIAS is expected in the last quarter of 2026 with a EUR 20 fee (free under 18 or over 70); that is an expectation, not a confirmed start date, and no confirmed date was found on any page opened for this guide, so check travel-europe.europa.eu before travelling. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation, not a visa, for visa-exempt nationals. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is already live: per diplomatie.gouv.fr it has been phased in since 12 October 2025 and is fully operational from 10 April 2026, replacing passport stamping, and Canada's advice says facial image and fingerprints are collected on entry with nothing to do before you travel. The UK FCDO page (undated in the text opened) says Greek authorities indicated they would not collect fingerprints and photos from UK travellers under EES; treat that as a statement about UK travellers that may have changed. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and the Greek embassy or consulate in your country). The FCDO says you may need to show a return or onward ticket and prove you have enough money; no Greek government page opened for this guide states an onward-ticket rule, a minimum number of blank pages, or a proof-of-funds figure, so none is stated here. mfa.gr returned errors to automated fetches, so this guide relies on EU, UK, Canadian, Australian, French and Greek tourism-board (GNTO) pages. Cash: the Government of Canada's Greece page (updated 5 October 2026) says that if you carry EUR 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) you must declare it to customs when you enter or leave the European Union; this does not apply to travel within the EU. Smartraveller (Australia, still current 18 October 2026) also says travellers on short stays must register fingerprints and a photo under EES on arrival, with nothing to do beforehand. No arrival card or health declaration is mentioned on the Canadian page.

COVID-19
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose for babies 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (especially for smaller cities, villages, rural areas or street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Rabies (discuss with a clinician depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: CDC's Greece page has no malaria section; the Government of Canada's advice says limited malaria transmission may occur but risk to travellers is very low
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Greece page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry and not recommended; everything in the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) and carries a Level 1 notice about rising global measles cases (28 May 2025). EU travellers should carry an EHIC or equivalent, per visitgreece.gr; the UK FCDO says UK travellers need a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that it is not a substitute for travel insurance, and advises insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation. The Government of Canada says health care is adequate but varies across the country. FCDO says to dial 112 or 166 for an ambulance. EODY (eody.gov.gr), the national public health organisation, returned an error to automated fetches, so CDC, FCDO and GNTO are used as fallbacks; no official statement on tap water or West Nile virus was opened.

money.atm_notes: visitgreece.gr's travel tips state that credit card holders may take money from the ATMs of the collaborating banks, that its currency is the euro (banknotes 5 to 500 EUR; coins 1 and 2 EUR and 1 to 50 cents), and that bank hours are Mon-Thu 8:00-14:30 and Fri 8:00-13:30, closed on public holidays. Its 'Before you travel' page advises calling your bank or card company before travelling so they know you will use the card in Greece. No official source opened gave card-acceptance levels, tipping norms or VAT-refund thresholds, so those are null.

power.adapter_note: visitgreece.gr states electric power in Greece is 230 V / 50 Hz and the plugs are type F; its 'Before you travel' page adds that North American appliances need a transformer and British appliances need an adaptor. Non-official guides say type C plugs also fit the sockets; that was not confirmed by an official source, so only type F is listed here.

emergency.notes: visitgreece.gr (Greek National Tourism Organisation) lists 112 as the European emergency number, 100 police, 166 First Aid National Center (ambulances), 199 Fire Authority, 1571 Tourist Police (24/7), 1016 SOS Doctors and 210 77 93 777 for the Poisoning Phone Center. The Government of Canada's Greece page confirms 112 and 100 and 1571 for tourist police but does not list 166 or 199; the UK FCDO says to call 112 in immediate danger and to dial 112 or 166 for an ambulance, to call 112 if you see a wildfire, and to make sure your phone can receive emergency alerts (it points to @112Greece for official updates). Some non-official websites list 171 for the tourist police; the two official pages opened (GNTO and Canada) give 1571, so 1571 is used. No official page opened gave a coast guard number, so none is listed. Confirmed on official Greek pages opened 18 October 2026: civilprotection.gov.gr/en/112 (112, free, works across the EU); Hellenic Police direct-lines page astynomia.gr/citizens-guide/direct-lines (100 for emergencies nationwide; 1571 tourist line in Greek, English, French and German; 1033 for police services in Attica, Thessaloniki, Serres, Pieria and Pella); gov.gr national emergency numbers pages titled '166 - Medical Emergency Service (EKAB) Number' and '199 - Hellenic Fire Service Number'; and the Hellenic Fire Service site header shows 199. Government of Canada (updated 5 October 2026): 112, 1571 tourist police, 100 police.

getting_around.summary: Islands: the Government of Canada's Greece advice states that ferries between mainland Greece and its islands meet European safety standards but that weather conditions and strong winds can cause cancellations or significant delays, and that the meltemi wind may bring high waves and disrupt transportation; the UK FCDO warns of regular strikes, sometimes called at short notice, that can disrupt buses, trains, ferries and air travel. No ferry operator timetable or the Ministry of Maritime Affairs' ferry pages could be opened (that ministry's passenger-rights portal and Coast Guard site returned HTTP 403 and the ministry site had an expired certificate), so no operator, route, journey time or fare is given here; check each operator's own page close to the date. Athens: OASA (the Athens urban transport organisation) runs buses and trolleybuses and sells the ATH.ENA ticket and card used across the city's transport; its Visit Athens page says Metro Line 3 connects the airport directly to Syntagma and that Airport Express buses X93, X95, X96 and X97 run on a 24-hour basis, and that you can pay with a contactless bank card or mobile wallet without pre-buying a ticket. Intercity rail: Hellenic Train runs the national passenger trains; its Athens-Thessaloniki page says the route runs daily with frequent services but states no journey time or fare, and links a timetable PDF, so no journey time is given here (third-party sites disagree). Hellenic Train sells single journeys, multi-trip cards and OASA interoperable tickets and offers online ticket purchase.

timezone_note: Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China and keeps its own clock, Hong Kong Time (Asia/Hong_Kong in the IANA database), UTC+8, with no daylight saving. No government page opened for this guide states the offset or the absence of daylight saving in so many words; the label follows the IANA tz database, which is what the app's live clock uses, and the Hong Kong Observatory publishes its observations in Hong Kong Time.
passport_validity_rule: The Immigration Department's visit-visa page (immd.gov.hk) sets no minimum remaining validity for visitors: it only says a visitor needs a valid travel document. Hong Kong government offices abroad state a six-month rule: the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Offices in Sydney and Berlin say passports must be valid for at least six months after the planned departure date from Hong Kong, and the Immigration Department's own pre-arrival registration page for Indian nationals requires an Indian passport valid for at least six months. Two foreign governments state a lower figure: UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say at least one month beyond the date you plan to leave. The record uses the stricter figure the Hong Kong side itself states (six months after departure), because a shorter margin risks being turned back by an airline or officer applying that rule. Your airline may apply its own rule regardless.
entry_requirement_notes: CHECKED 19 October 2026. Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China with its own immigration control and its own visit-visa rules, set by the Hong Kong Immigration Department; the Chinese Mainland's rules do not apply here, and a trip to the Mainland is a separate entry that this guide does not cover. (1) Stay length by nationality (Immigration Department visit-visa page): United States 90 days, Canada 90, Australia 90, Germany 90, Singapore 90, Brazil 90; United Kingdom 180 days for British citizens (90 days for other British nationality categories); India 14 days and only after completing online pre-arrival registration (PAR). The HKETO pages say nationals of about 170 countries and territories can visit without a visa for periods from 7 to 180 days. (2) Funds and onward ticket: the Immigration Department says visitors must have adequate funds to cover their stay without working and, unless in transit to the Chinese Mainland or Macao, must hold onward or return tickets. Meeting the conditions does not guarantee entry. UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada do not mention an onward-ticket rule; the requirement rests on the Immigration Department page. (3) No arrival card, entry declaration or visa-free authorisation is mentioned on the Immigration Department visit-visa page for non-Indian visitors; Indian nationals need PAR, which is free, issued instantly online, valid six months for multiple visits of up to 14 days each, requires a passport valid at least six months, and must be redone if the passport is renewed or replaced (immd.gov.hk). Visitors may not work, run a business or study on a visit entry and generally cannot change status after arrival. Anyone wanting to stay longer than the visa-free period must apply for a visa before travelling. (4) Health: the HKETO Singapore page says vaccination, quarantine and isolation requirements have been removed; Global Affairs Canada says all travellers are screened for temperature on arrival. A yellow fever certificate is the one point where sources differ (see health.notes). (5) Customs: Hong Kong Customs and Excise requires a written declaration through the Red Channel by anyone arriving at a specified control point with currency and bearer negotiable instruments worth more than HKD 120,000 in total (foreign currency is declared in its original currency); a first-time failure can be settled for HKD 2,000, otherwise the maximum penalty is a fine of HKD 500,000 and two years in prison. Red Channel is also for prohibited or controlled items and dutiable goods above the exempt quantities (the exempt quantities were not found on a page that could be opened). UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say bringing e-cigarettes, heated tobacco and related devices into Hong Kong is prohibited, including in luggage, and FCDO says that from 30 April 2026 possessing any e-cigarette or alternative smoking product in a public place is illegal even if not in use (travellers transiting without passing immigration are exempt). FCDO also lists stun guns, sharp-edged objects and martial arts equipment as illegal to bring in, and CBD products (oils, creams, capsules, foods) as illegal. (6) UK FCDO states that BN(O) passports are no longer accepted for immigration clearance or as proof of identity, and that dual nationals must return to the UK on a British passport. (7) Contacts: Immigration Department enquiry hotline (852) 2824 6111. Stay periods, PAR rules and the e-cigarette law can change; re-check immd.gov.hk before departure.

health.notes: No vaccination is required for entry on the evidence of CDC (last reviewed 25 August 2026: the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and Hong Kong does not require it for entry) and Global Affairs Canada (proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required). UK FCDO's entry page says a yellow fever certificate is required if you arrive from a country listed as a transmission risk; neither the Department of Health's Centre for Health Protection yellow fever page nor its Travel Health Service page, both opened for this guide, states an entry rule, so the sources disagree and the record cannot settle it. If you are arriving from a yellow-fever-risk country, carry a valid certificate to be safe. CDC carries a Level 1 (usual precautions) travel health notice for global measles. Global Affairs Canada notes dengue and chikungunya are present (use mosquito protection) and advises travel insurance that covers medical evacuation; the Centre for Health Protection runs a dengue topic page and advises travellers who return from affected areas and feel unwell to seek medical advice promptly. The recommended list is CDC's medical advice, not something checked at immigration. No malaria information appeared on the CDC page opened, so none is stated.

power.adapter_note: HK Electric's Supply Rules state a supply frequency of 50 Hertz and a single-phase voltage of 220 volts in HK Electric's rules (the other utility, CLP Power, was not checked). The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) household safety handbook says appliances must be fitted with a 3-pin plug that meets Hong Kong's safety requirements, and warns that appliances rated below 200V a.c. (for example 110V audio-video equipment) must not be connected directly to the 220V household supply. No official page opened names a plug-type letter, so none is recorded. Check that chargers say 100-240V or bring a transformer for 110V-only appliances, and a plug adapter for a 3-pin socket.

emergency.notes: The Hong Kong government's HKEngage page states that police, fire services and ambulance care are reached by calling 999, and that 992 is an emergency SMS service for people with a speech or hearing impairment. Global Affairs Canada's Hong Kong page also says to dial 999 for emergency assistance. The HKEngage page also lists an HKSOS app for police service. No official page opened states whether 112 works from a foreign SIM, so none is claimed. No tourist-police number was confirmed on an official page opened for this guide, so none is listed.

getting_around.summary: Hong Kong's MTR runs the Airport Express: MTR's tickets page lists a single journey from Hong Kong Station to the Airport at HKD 120 for an adult paying with Octopus, a contactless bank card or a QR code (HKD 130 with a Smart Ticket), HKD 60 for a child aged 3-11 with Octopus or QR code, and children under 3 free; the page gives no journey time, so none is stated here. The Octopus stored-value card pays for MTR, buses, ferries, trams, minibuses and coaches, and is accepted in many shops, restaurants and attractions. Fares and card prices change, so confirm on mtr.com.hk and octopus.com.hk. Typhoons and heavy rain can disrupt transport: the Hong Kong Observatory issues tropical cyclone warning signals (Signal No. 8 is the gale or storm signal) and a black rainstorm warning; check hko.gov.hk.

passes.name: Tourist Octopus
passes.covers: Octopus Hong Kong describes the sold Tourist Octopus as priced at HKD 39 with no initial stored value and no deposit, sold at Hung Fook Tong stores. It works on public transport (MTR, bus, ferry, public light bus, coach, tram) and at shops, restaurants and attractions that accept Octopus. MTR's own page separately lists a Tourist Octopus (China T-Union Card) sold at the Airport Station Customer Service Centre, Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau at HKD 170 for an adult, HKD 110 for a child, and a version with two Airport Express single journeys at HKD 260. Prices differ by version and outlet.
passes.worth_it: A practical default for city transport rather than a discount pass: tap-and-go on trains, buses and ferries without exact change. Octopus says remaining value can be refunded but the card is then deactivated, and it can be kept as a souvenir. No verdict on value for money is offered because the prices above differ by version.

passes.covers: MTR: the Airport Express links Hong Kong Station and the Airport; adult HKD 120 with Octopus, contactless bank card or QR code (HKD 130 with a Smart Ticket), as listed on MTR's tickets page.
passes.worth_it: The page opened does not state journey times or compare alternatives, so no verdict is offered. Check mtr.com.hk for the current fare and timetable.

timezone_note: Hungary has one time zone (IANA Europe/Budapest). On 19 October 2026 it is on central European summer time (CEST, UTC+2); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Hungarian government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Hungary is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay your passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years. The Hungarian police border-crossing page (dated 18 July 2017) gives the same two conditions for non-EU travellers (valid at least three months after the intended date of departure, issued within the previous 10 years), and UK FCDO's Hungary page and Global Affairs Canada agree on the 3-month rule. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area, and time spent in other Schengen countries counts. Stays beyond that need a Hungarian visa or residence permit. Airlines can apply stricter rules at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; it also says the fee has been set at EUR 20 once ETIAS is operational. A later Commission item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026', that the exact date 'will be officially communicated later this year', and that an authorisation is valid for 3 years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first. No page opened for this guide gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation, not a visa, for visa-exempt nationals; Global Affairs Canada (page updated 11 August 2026) likewise says applications are not yet open and warns about fraudulent sites selling ETIAS authorisations. Already live: the Entry/Exit System (EES), which the Commission says has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; UK FCDO says you must give fingerprints and a photo at the border, with no fee, that waits may be longer, and that the record lasts 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on your nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). The Hungarian police border-crossing page says travellers should carry documents proving the purpose of the visit (for example a hotel reservation or invitation) and must be able to show sufficient means of subsistence (cash, cards, traveller's cheques); that page is dated 2017 and predates EES. The EU's Your Europe portal says border guards may ask for proof of sufficient funds, lodging and a return or round-trip ticket, and UK FCDO says you may be asked for a return or onward ticket, funds and accommodation. These are requests, not a fixed condition for visa-exempt visitors, and no page opened for this guide gives a funds figure or a blank-pages requirement, so those fields are left empty and the onward-ticket field is null (not confirmed either way). Global Affairs Canada adds that Hungarian authorities may deny entry if you have an unpaid previous fine. Cash: NAV, the Hungarian tax and customs authority, says a cash declaration form must be completed when carrying EUR 10,000 or more (or the equivalent in other currencies) in cash on entering or leaving the EU (Regulation (EU) 2018/1672); UK FCDO says cash or travellers cheques of that size must be declared and undeclared money could be seized. Currency: Hungary is in the EU but its official currency is the forint (HUF), not the euro; the Hungarian Tourism Agency says many stores accept euros but some do not and change comes back in forint. Border controls: the European Commission's list of temporarily reintroduced internal border controls (no as-of date shown) does not list Hungary as imposing controls, but lists Austria's controls on its land borders with Czechia, Hungary and Slovenia for 16 September 2026 to 15 March 2027, so expect possible checks if entering or leaving Hungary overland from Austria. The Hungarian consular service site (konzuliszolgalat.kormany.hu) could not be opened by the fetch tool used for this guide (certificate error), so the Hungarian police page, the EU portals and UK/Canadian government pages are the sources.

Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from planned outdoor activities; may be considered for others outdoors where ticks are likely)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination depending on occupational or recreational animal exposure and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Hungary page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Hungary page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (that section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026), and the Hungarian Tourism Agency says Hungary is a low-risk country for health and has no required vaccines for entering. The recommended list is CDC's medical advice only. CDC's page has no malaria section, carries the Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025), names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis among non-vaccine-preventable risks, and advises preventing bug bites. Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a risk in some areas, higher from April to November especially for hikers and campers in forested areas, and that the vaccine may be available in Hungary. The Hungarian Tourism Agency says Hungarian healthcare is publicly funded, that foreign citizens are eligible for free public care only if they come from certain countries (the text opened did not name them), that private care is not free, and that you should have accident and health insurance before your trip. The Hungarian health agency NNGYK was searched but no NNGYK page was opened for this guide, so the advice here rests on CDC, Global Affairs Canada and the Hungarian Tourism Agency.

money.card_acceptance: The Hungarian Tourism Agency says you can pay by debit or credit card in most stores, that each city has ATMs accepting major debit and credit cards (often in bank lobbies where you need your card to open the door), and that only a few banks will cash traveller's cheques. It also says smaller shops and country guesthouses may accept only cash.
money.cash_culture: The official currency is the forint (HUF). The Hungarian Tourism Agency says many stores accept euros but markets, small grocery shops, bakeries, souvenir shops and some restaurants do not, and that change comes back in forint. It advises against exchanging money at the airport or on the street and to ask about commission at banks, private exchange points, hotels or travel agencies; it warns smaller shops may lack change for large notes. Global Affairs Canada says euros are accepted in Budapest and some major cities where a sign is posted but rates may be poor, and not to use unofficial moneychangers. ATM fees were not stated on any page opened for this guide.
money.tipping: The Hungarian Tourism Agency says the usual tip is 10% in cabs and restaurants; if a service charge is already on the bill you do not need to tip, and if you pay by card the staff prefer the tip in cash. Global Affairs Canada's Hungary page carries no tipping guidance.

power.adapter_note: The Hungarian Tourism Agency states that the electric current in Hungary is 230 V and 50 Hz and that plug types C and F are used. It suggests buying any adapter at home or at an international airport, because Hungarian hardware stores mostly stock adapters meant for Hungarians travelling abroad.

emergency.notes: The Hungarian Tourism Agency lists 112 (free emergency hotline, 24/7), 104 (ambulance), 105 (fire service), 107 (police) and 188 (emergency tow truck service), and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) lists the same four emergency numbers independently. The national disaster management directorate (katasztrofavedelem.hu) says 112 can be called around the clock in Hungarian, English and German and its banner says to call 112 or 105 in case of danger; it does not mention 104 or 107. The Hungarian police site tells people to call 112 for urgent police help, calls it the European free emergency number, and gives a separate SMS line for hearing-impaired people (+36-20/9000-107), a 24/7 victim support line (+36-80/225-225) and the police switchboard (+36-1/443-5500). If unsure which number to use, 112 reaches all services. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page opened for this guide, so none is listed. Global Affairs Canada warns about restaurant and club overcharging, taxi-driver-linked bar scams and pickpocketing on public transport, at stations and at markets, and advises using only officially marked taxis ordered through a dispatcher.

getting_around.summary: Budapest's public transport is run by BKK, whose English price page (copyright 2011-2026, no 'applies from' date shown) lists a single ticket at 500 Ft, a 30-minute ticket at 600 Ft, a 90-minute ticket at 850 Ft, a 24-hour Budapest-travelcard at 2,750 Ft and a 72-hour Budapest-travelcard at 5,750 Ft; the single ticket bought on the spot is listed at 700 Ft. The Hungarian Tourism Agency's transport page still quotes older fares (HUF 350 single), so treat BKK's own page as the one to trust and check bkk.hu before you travel. The Budapest Card (24, 48, 72 and 96 hours, with FLEXI and PLUS variants) is sold by BKK with product addresses marked 'valid from 1 May 2026' and includes public transport. National rail is run by MAV; the Hungarian Tourism Agency says intercity trains need a ticket plus a seat ticket and that tickets can be bought at stations, at machines or online at mavcsoport.hu/en. MAV's English homepage links to an online ticket shop, a live map and timetable (mavplusz.hu) and customer service on +36 1 349 49 49, and mentions the Adria InterCity night train between Budapest and Split; no official journey time for any route was opened for this record, so none is given. For driving, the Hungarian Tourism Agency says cars need a motorway e-vignette bought before entering the motorway (at petrol stations or on the official Hungarian Public Roads website), available as daily, weekly (10-day), monthly, annual and county vignettes, and that if you forget you have 60 minutes to buy one; it gives no prices. Budapest's airport is Liszt Ferenc International Airport, about 24 km south-east of the city, with Terminal 2A mainly for Schengen flights and 2B mainly for low-cost flights from outside the Schengen area (check the airport's site). Regional buses, other city networks and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.covers: BKK's English price page lists a 24-hour Budapest-travelcard at 2,750 Ft and a 72-hour Budapest-travelcard at 5,750 Ft, against a single ticket of 500 Ft (700 Ft bought on the spot), a 30-minute ticket of 600 Ft and a 90-minute ticket of 850 Ft. The page shows no 'applies from' date and does not describe the validity rules for the travelcards beyond their names. The Hungarian Tourism Agency says single tickets are valid across metro, bus, trolleybus, tram and the HEV suburban railway within Budapest and must be validated.
passes.worth_it: At the listed fares, a 24-hour travelcard (2,750 Ft) equals about 5.5 single tickets (500 Ft each), so it pays off from about six rides in a day. Fares and 'valid from' dates may change, so confirm the current price at bkk.hu before buying.

passes.name: Budapest Card (24 to 96 hours)
passes.covers: BKK's price page lists Budapest Card products at 17,990 Ft (24 hours), 23,990 Ft (48 hours), 29,990 Ft (72 hours), 27,990 Ft (72 hours FLEXI), 39,990 Ft (72 hours PLUS) and 38,990 Ft (96 hours); the product addresses are marked 'valid from 1 May 2026'. The Hungarian Tourism Agency says the 24-hour and 7-day versions give free use of public transport for the validity period and a discount or free ride on the airport minibus depending on the card type. What each card includes beyond transport was not read for this record.
passes.worth_it: Whether the card pays for itself depends on how many included attractions you use; compare its price with the 24-hour (2,750 Ft) and 72-hour (5,750 Ft) travelcards, which cover transport only, and check the card's current inclusions at budapestcard.org or bkk.hu before buying.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: The Hungarian Tourism Agency's useful-links page lists the mobile operators Telenor, Telekom and Vodafone (as named on that page) and says nothing about SIM cards, eSIM, prices or registration. Roaming for EU residents is not covered by any page opened for this guide.

timezone_note: Iceland is on UTC+0 all year and does not change its clocks; this comes from the IANA time zone database (Atlantic/Reykjavik), not from a page opened for this guide. It means Iceland is on the same clock as the UK in winter and one hour behind the UK in summer.
passport_validity_rule: Iceland is in the Schengen area but is not an EU member (the EU's Your Europe portal lists it as one of four non-EU Schengen countries with Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland). For a short stay UK FCDO says the passport must have an expiry date at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area and a date of issue less than 10 years before you arrive. Global Affairs Canada states the same 3-month rule, and island.is, the Icelandic government's service portal, states the same two conditions for visa applicants (valid at least 3 months beyond intended departure, issued within the last 10 years). Visa-free short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area (FCDO; Global Affairs Canada). Global Affairs Canada adds that transport companies may apply stricter passport rules.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point'; a later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says it 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be announced later; Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says applications 'are not yet open'. No page opened gives a start date, so do not treat any date as fact. No page opened for this guide names Iceland in a list of ETIAS countries (the Commission counts 30 countries, the Schengen area plus Cyprus), but Iceland is a Schengen state and Global Affairs Canada's Iceland page covers it, so visa-exempt visitors should expect to need it once it starts; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel. When it starts the Commission says it will be valid for 3 years or until the passport expires, and an earlier Commission page gives a fee of EUR 20. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is already live: the Commission says it became fully operational on 10 April 2026 and records name, travel document data, fingerprints and facial images at the border and replaces passport stamping; UK FCDO says the digital record is valid for 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality; island.is says visas are issued by Icelandic or other Schengen embassies and consulates. UK FCDO says that at Icelandic border control you may need to show a return or onward ticket and enough money for your stay, but no page opened for this guide states either as a fixed condition for visa-exempt visitors or gives a funds figure or a blank-page requirement, so those fields are left unset. Cash: the Icelandic customs authority (skatturinn.is) says cash of more than EUR 10,000 (or the equivalent in other currencies), travellers' cheques or bearer negotiable instruments must be declared on entering or leaving Iceland; UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada word the threshold as EUR 10,000 or more, so declare if you are at or near that amount. Global Affairs Canada also notes that border controls may be temporarily reintroduced within the Schengen area.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (especially for rural areas or street food)
Hepatitis B (CDC: unvaccinated travellers of all ages; Global Affairs Canada: recommended for all travellers)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Iceland page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Iceland page says yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026), and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says Iceland has no yellow fever risk. CDC lists a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and no malaria section. CDC says dogs with rabies are not commonly found in Iceland; Global Affairs Canada says rabies may be present in some wildlife, including bats. Global Affairs Canada says health care is excellent but services can be limited outside urban areas and upfront payment may be required, and warns that hot springs can be dangerously hot. UK FCDO says a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance; the FCDO and Canada both advise insurance covering medical evacuation. Emergency care is via 112. Safetravel.is lists a 24-hour health line on 00354 5131700 (taken from that page; its scope was not stated). No page from Iceland's health authorities was opened for this guide, so UK FCDO, CDC and Global Affairs Canada are used as fallbacks.

emergency.notes: The Icelandic emergency service (112.is) says to call 112 for an emergency, 24 hours a day all year, and UK FCDO's Iceland page gives 112 for ambulance, fire and police. Police, ambulance and fire are therefore all shown as 112. 112.is also offers a text message (SMS) option, an online chat and a 112 Iceland app, and says that if you have trouble calling 112 you can use the chat or call +354 599 0112. Safetravel.is says hikers using its Safetravel app can send their GPS position to 112. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed. For road and weather information the road authority's site (umferdin.is, which road.is redirects to) shows a traffic service number, 1777. Global Affairs Canada lists the Embassy of Canada in Reykjavik at +354 575 6500 and its Emergency Watch and Response Centre at 800-8042 (toll-free from Canada).

getting_around.summary: The pages opened for this guide describe Iceland as a place where road conditions drive travel plans. UK FCDO says distances between towns are long, speed limits are lower than in the UK, some single-lane routes and bridges have passing places, and the weather can change quickly and make driving challenging. It says some highland and interior roads require 4-wheel drive, many highland tracks only open for part of the summer, river crossings should be made slowly (5 to 10 km/h) because levels can change within a day, off-road driving is strictly controlled, and wind-blown sand or ash can damage hire cars with damage possibly not covered by insurance. It points to road.is (now umferdin.is) for road and weather information; umferdin.is lists a traffic service number, 1777. Safetravel.is shows current travel conditions and weather alerts and asks travellers to share a travel plan with someone who can act for them. In the capital area, the city bus operator Straeto uses Klapp, which its site describes as an account-based ticketing system. No fare, journey time or timetable was read from any official page, so none is given here. Intercity buses, domestic flights, ferries, the Keflavik airport transfer and car-hire rules were not researched.
