timezone_note: One time zone for the whole country, 30 minutes off whole hours, with no daylight saving. WMO's World Weather page for New Delhi lists +0530 with DST 'N'.
passport_validity_rule: India's e-Visa site states that the passport must have at least six months' validity when you apply for an e-Visa and recommends two blank pages for stamping. The UK FCDO states the stricter-sounding entry rule for British travellers: the passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the day you arrive, with at least 2 blank pages. A paper visa from an Indian mission may be assessed differently; the six months from arrival is used here as the safe planning figure.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa: nearly every foreign visitor needs a visa; the UK FCDO says you must have one unless you are an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, and Incredible India states that all foreign nationals entering India must hold a valid passport and visa (Nepal and Bhutan nationals are exempt, with exceptions for arrivals from China, Macau, Hong Kong or Pakistan; Maldivian citizens with a Maldivian passport can visit for tourism for up to 90 days without a visa, per Incredible India). The e-Visa (indianvisaonline.gov.in) is open to nationals of about 175 listed countries and regions and is non-extendable and non-convertible; holders of Pakistani passports or people of Pakistani origin, diplomatic/official passports and travel documents are not eligible. Types published include e-Tourist for 30 days (one month, multiple entries), e-Tourist for 1 year or 5 years (stay capped at 180 days per calendar year), e-Business, e-Medical and others; the e-Visa site's own text is inconsistent in places (for example the validity of e-Medical visas), so check the current FAQ before paying. Apply at least 4 days before arrival; the fee must be paid at least 4 days before travel or the application is not processed; the site's FAQ says the 120-day advance window applies to the 1-year/5-year tourist and several other types, while its instructions mention it only for medical visas. The e-Visa site states that you need a return or onward ticket and sufficient money for your stay. The e-Visa is valid only at the airports, seaports and land border points listed in its FAQ (FCDO: check the FAQs for restrictions on ports of entry). E-ARRIVAL CARD: an Indian embassy notice (eoimanila.gov.in) states that effective October 1, 2025 foreigners and OCI cardholders arriving in India are required to submit an e-Arrival Card (digital disembarkation card) online within 72 hours before arrival, through boi.gov.in, indianvisaonline.gov.in or the Indian Visa Su-Swagatam app; the UK FCDO says foreign nationals must complete it before reaching immigration, and that it is not a visa. The boi.gov.in home page returned an error when checked on 2026-10-18, so the Bureau of Immigration's own wording was not read first-hand; check the e-Arrival status on indianvisaonline.gov.in before flying. Other items from the FCDO page (second-hand, not read on an Indian government site): complete a Self-Declaration Form on the Air Suvidha portal up to 24 hours before arrival (failure may cause delays); foreign guests must be registered by accommodation providers; visitors staying over 180 days without an OCI card must register within 14 days of arrival; restricted and protected areas need special permits (apply about 3 months ahead); and if you have no entry stamp you need a special exit permit from within India. Cash: FCDO says to declare cash above 5,000 US dollars in notes (10,000 US dollars combined with travellers' cheques) and to follow Reserve Bank of India guidelines on rupees; the thresholds were not checked on an Indian customs or RBI page.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever: certificate required for travellers aged 9 months and over arriving from a yellow-fever-risk country as notified by the Government of India (not required for direct travel from a non-risk country such as the USA)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines including MMR (CDC urges all travellers to be fully vaccinated against measles), COVID-19, polio
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Typhoid
Japanese encephalitis (for a month or more in affected areas or higher-risk activities)
Rabies (risk-based, decide with a clinician)
Cholera (consider for areas with active transmission)
Chikungunya (consider for stays of about 6 months or more)
health.malaria_risk: CDC recommends prescription antimalarial medication for travellers to certain areas of India; chloroquine resistance is reported. CDC lists areas above 2,000 m (6,500 ft) as having no malaria transmission. Which areas count depends on the itinerary, so ask a travel-health clinician with your route.
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccine tied to entry. MoHFW's quarantine rule: a traveller without a valid certificate from a risk country can be quarantined until six days have passed since the last possible exposure, or until the certificate becomes valid, whichever is earlier, and a medical exemption letter does not prevent quarantine. The certificate is valid from 10 days after vaccination (Indian High Commission, Accra, notice). The current list of risk countries is on ihpoe.mohfw.gov.in/vaccination.php, which showed a WHO list dated 3 January 2023 (Africa and Central/South America), so the live list of countries should be checked before travel; CDC also says India adds any country that reports a yellow fever case. Other CDC notes: dengue, Zika, leptospirosis and other water- and mosquito-borne illness are present; infected dogs are common, so rabies matters; CDC reported counterfeit rabies vaccine in Delhi; trauma care is limited outside urban areas, and CDC recommends medical evacuation insurance. FCDO adds that medical facilities are less advanced than in the UK outside major cities and that air pollution is a major health hazard, especially from October to February.

money.card_acceptance: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism) states that foreign credit and debit cards are widely accepted in India, and that mobile wallets and UPI payments are popular. It says foreign currency can be exchanged at airports, hotels and Reserve Bank of India approved money changers.

emergency.notes: Incredible India (Ministry of Tourism) lists the national emergency number 112, police 100, fire 101, ambulance 102, road accident 1073, disaster management 108, women in distress 1091, medical helpline 104, railway security 1322 and the tourist helpline 1363. The UK FCDO lists police 100, the national emergency number 112 and women's helpline 1091, and says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance, with English and Hindi available. The Ministry of Tourism's 24x7 multilingual tourist helpline is 1800111363 (toll-free) or 1363, in English, Hindi and ten foreign languages, free from within India (Indian consulate Sao Paulo page). No tourist police number is published on those pages, so none is given.

getting_around.summary: Incredible India states that air, rail and road are the main modes of transport in India, and that tickets can be booked through websites and apps including IRCTC (irctc.co.in) or through authorised tour operators and travel agents. Foreign visitors with a valid international driving permit or licence can drive during their stay. No official source read for this guide states fares, rail passes for foreigners or city transit details, so none are stated here.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Incredible India says visitors can use local SIM cards or portable Wi-Fi devices for internet access, and that cafes and hotels offer Wi-Fi hotspots. No official source read for this guide states registration rules or prices.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 20.9mm. Cool, dry winter. New Delhi's mean daily minimum is around 8C, so mornings are cold and often hazy. FCDO notes severe air pollution in India from October to February, with northern cities most affected. Base period: India Meteorological Department data published via WMO World Weather Information Service; WMO states the rainfall base as 1901-2000 and gives no base period for temperatures. One city only: India spans very different climates (Himalaya, Rajasthan desert, Kerala coast), so these figures do not describe the whole country.
climate.crowd_note: Cool-season peak for travel in northern India. Editorial judgement, not a sourced measurement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 21.0mm. Still dry and mild; daytime highs climb into the mid-20s C. Air pollution warning from FCDO (October to February) still applies.
climate.crowd_note: Cool-season peak. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 14.5mm. Warming quickly; highs reach about 30C and the dry season is ending.
climate.crowd_note: Pleasant and busy before the heat; editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 10.7mm. Hot and dry: highs around 36C and very little rain (about 11mm).
climate.crowd_note: Heat starts to cut visitor numbers on the plains; editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 14.1mm. Hottest month on these figures, with an average high of about 40C and minimums of 26C. Rainfall is only about 14mm.
climate.crowd_note: Extreme heat; most visitors head to hill stations instead. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 66.3mm. Still extremely hot (average high about 39C, minimum 28C); the first monsoon rain begins, about 66mm for the month.
climate.crowd_note: Extreme heat then monsoon onset; low demand on the plains. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 198.4mm. Monsoon: about 198mm of rain and hot, humid conditions (high about 35C).
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon; rain can disrupt road and rail travel. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 206.5mm. Wettest month on these figures at about 207mm; humid with highs around 34C.
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon; editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 130.3mm. Monsoon tails off but is still wet (about 130mm); highs around 34C.
climate.crowd_note: End of monsoon; editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 20.8mm. Monsoon has gone: rainfall falls to about 21mm and nights start to cool, though highs remain near 33C. FCDO's October-to-February air pollution warning begins to apply.
climate.crowd_note: Post-monsoon and festival season; demand rises through the month. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 3.9mm. Driest month on these figures (about 4mm) with pleasant days around 28C and cool nights of 13C. FCDO's air pollution warning applies.
climate.crowd_note: Start of the main cool-weather season. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: New Delhi (Safdarjung) rainfall averages 8.8mm. Cool and dry (high about 23C, low about 8C); very little rain (about 9mm). FCDO's air pollution warning applies.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season including the year-end holidays. Editorial judgement.

timezone_note: Indonesia spans three zones and none of them observe daylight saving. WIB / Western Indonesia Time (UTC+7, IANA Asia/Jakarta) covers Sumatra, Java — including Jakarta and Yogyakarta — and West and Central Kalimantan. WITA / Central Indonesia Time (UTC+8, IANA Asia/Makassar) covers Bali, Lombok and the rest of Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and South/East/North Kalimantan. WIT / Eastern Indonesia Time (UTC+9, IANA Asia/Jayapura) covers Maluku and Papua. This guide uses WITA because Bali (Denpasar) is the single most likely arrival point for a visitor; if you are landing in Jakarta instead, set your clock an hour earlier to UTC+7. The WMO/BMKG station records confirm Denpasar at +0800 and Jakarta at +0700, both with no DST.
passport_validity_rule: Indonesia's Directorate General of Immigration requires a national passport valid for at least six months from the date of arrival. The official e-Visa portal states the passport biodata page must show "a minimum validity of 6 months from the date of your arrival to Indonesia", and the same six-month-from-arrival rule is stated for Visa on Arrival issued at the border.
entry_requirement_notes: Three things beyond the visa itself. (1) ALL INDONESIA ARRIVAL CARD — mandatory. Since 1 October 2025 every passenger arriving from abroad, regardless of nationality or visa type, must submit an arrival declaration through the All Indonesia system at allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id or the All Indonesia app. It is free, can be completed up to three days before arrival, and replaces the separate immigration, customs, health and quarantine forms (including the old electronic customs declaration). Only allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id is official. (2) BALI TOURIST LEVY — still in force. Every foreign tourist entering Bali pays a one-off IDR 150,000 levy under Bali Provincial Regulation No. 2 of 2025 (amending Regional Regulation No. 6 of 2023). Pay before or on arrival through the Bali provincial government's Love Bali portal at lovebali.baliprov.go.id, which issues a QR voucher; an exemption application route exists on the same portal. Copycat payment sites exist — use only the baliprov.go.id domain. (3) ONWARD TICKET AND FEES — Immigration states that VOA applicants must show a return ticket or a ticket onward to another country, and officers reserve the right to ask for a printed return ticket on arrival. Visa on Arrival / e-VOA costs IDR 500,000, permits a 30-day stay for tourism, and can be extended once for a further 30 days at an immigration office; it cannot be converted to another stay permit. Separately, bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 in cash requires a customs declaration. (4) FEE STATUS — the fee stated on Immigration's own VOA page and by the UK FCDO today is IDR 500,000; a higher fee (reported as IDR 750,000 for e-VOA and IDR 1,000,000 for VOA on arrival) was proposed by the Directorate General of Immigration in August 2026 but is not confirmed as in force, so check evisa.imigrasi.go.id before paying. (5) BLANK PAGES — Indonesia's own pages do not state a figure; UK FCDO says at least two blank pages and Global Affairs Canada says at least one, so carry two.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required only for travellers arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid
Routine vaccinations up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Rabies (for some travellers and itineraries)
Japanese encephalitis (for some activities and longer stays)
health.malaria_risk: None in Jakarta or Ubud, and none in the resort areas of Bali and Java, the Gili Islands or the Thousand Islands (Pulau Seribu). Transmission is present in all eastern provinces (Maluku, North Maluku, East Nusa Tenggara, Papua, West Papua), in rural Kalimantan, West Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and Sumatra, and at low levels in rural Java.
health.notes: The yellow fever certificate is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only if you are arriving from a yellow-fever risk country — everything else on this list is medical advice, not an entry condition. A typical Bali or Jakarta trip needs no malaria prophylaxis. Note that a 2022 Immigration article on counter Visa on Arrival still lists a full-dose COVID-19 vaccination certificate among its requirements, while the current official e-VOA document list does not mention one; if you want certainty on that point, check evisa.imigrasi.go.id shortly before you fly.

money.card_acceptance: Visa and Mastercard are the most widely accepted and work at merchants across the major cities and tourist areas including Bali, Jakarta and Yogyakarta; JCB is accepted through BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri and BRI affiliations, and American Express acceptance is limited, largely via Bank Danamon. Cards are reliable in hotels, larger restaurants and larger stores but not in warungs, markets or small local businesses. Shops do not always display which cards they take, so ask before ordering.
money.cash_culture: Carry rupiah in cash, especially outside the main cities — the national tourism board recommends withdrawing cash in a major city before heading anywhere remote. ATMs dispense IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes, and those larger notes can be hard to break in rural and non-tourist areas, so deliberately keep a stock of small notes. Notes in circulation run from IDR 1,000 to IDR 100,000. Bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 (roughly USD 6,500) in cash must be declared to customs.
money.tipping: Tipping is discretionary rather than an obligation. Hotels and restaurants inside hotels operate a regulated service charge ("uang servis") added to the bill under Ministry of Manpower Regulation No. 7 of 2016, which requires that charge to be distributed to the staff — so where you see a service charge on the bill, the staff are already receiving it and a further tip is optional. No official Indonesian source sets a tipping percentage, and this record deliberately does not invent one.
money.atm_notes: ATMs on the Cirrus, Maestro and Plus networks are widespread in major cities and tourist areas. JCB cardholders can withdraw at affiliated bank ATMs (BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri, BRI) and American Express cardholders at Bank Danamon ATMs. Machines dispense either IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes. No official source for per-withdrawal fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice was available, so none is stated here — as everywhere, decline any ATM offer to bill you in your home currency.

power.adapter_note: Indonesia uses the two-pin European plug at 230 V / 50 Hz. Travellers from continental Europe and most of Asia need no adapter; UK (type G) visitors need a simple plug adapter only. Visitors from the United States, Canada and most of South America should check that their devices are dual-voltage (phone and laptop chargers usually are) and otherwise bring a voltage converter — the official tourism board advises exactly this. Adapters are sold in local minimarkets throughout Indonesia if you forget one.

emergency.notes: 112 is Indonesia's national emergency number, reachable from mobile and satellite phones, and is the number to use if you are unsure which service you need. Ambulance and medical emergencies can also be reached on 118 as well as 119. Two other numbers are worth saving: 115 for BASARNAS search and rescue (relevant for sea, diving and mountain incidents) and 129 for natural-disaster assistance. No separate national tourist-police number is published by the tourism board. Whether an English speaker answers is not guaranteed by any official source, so having your accommodation call on your behalf is often faster.

getting_around.summary: Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 13,000 islands, so moving between regions means flying or taking a ferry. The busiest gateways are Soekarno-Hatta (Jakarta), Juanda (Surabaya), I Gusti Ngurah Rai (Bali), Sultan Hasanuddin (Makassar) and Kualanamu (Medan), with connecting flights onward to smaller islands; PELNI runs multi-port inter-island ferries and ASDP runs single-route vehicle and passenger ferries. PT Kereta Api Indonesia (KAI) is the national rail operator, running intercity trains, Greater Jakarta commuter services and airport rail links, but its network covers Java and parts of Sumatra and does not extend to Bali, so getting around that island means ride-hailing, a hired car with driver, or a scooter. In cities, Damri buses serve the airports and metered taxis, ride-hailing apps, ojek (motorbike taxi) and bemo (minivan) fill in the rest. Indonesia has no nationwide tourist rail or transit pass — KAI lists no such product — so journeys are bought point to point.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Prepaid SIMs are sold from operator booths in the arrivals halls of the main international airports — Telkomsel, Indosat/IM3, XL, Smartfren, 3/Tri and Axis all have a presence. Registration is compulsory and the booth staff do it for you: a visitor registers with their passport, while residents use a KITAS or KITAP. eSIM does exist on Indonesian networks (Telkomsel sells prepaid eSIM starter packs), but Telkomsel's own prepaid eSIM registration page asks for an Indonesian KTP and family card, so a visitor is usually better off with a physical SIM registered against a passport at the airport, or an international travel eSIM bought before departure. Pocket wifi rental is offered as an alternative, orderable online for airport pickup or mailing. Free wifi is common at major airports, hotels, Jakarta train stations, malls, cafés and tourist sites.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official price list for a ~10 GB / two-week visitor bundle could be verified from an operator or government source, so none is invented here. For scale: the national tourism board states airport SIM prices "vary for each provider starting from IDR 10,000", and Telkomsel lists its SIMPATI eSIM starter pack (3 GB, plus call and SMS allowance) from IDR 25,000 (roughly USD 1.50). Checked 28 September 2026.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month: about 345 mm across roughly 27 rain days. Expect heavy, short downpours rather than all-day rain, plus high humidity.
climate.crowd_note: Busy through the first week for the New Year period, then noticeably quieter for the rest of the month.

climate.precipitation_note: Still deep in the wet season — around 274 mm over about 22 rain days, with humid, overcast stretches.
climate.crowd_note: One of the quietest months on the island; accommodation is at its most available.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain easing but still substantial, about 234 mm over roughly 20 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Nyepi, the Balinese Day of Silence, usually falls in March. I Gusti Ngurah Rai airport closes completely for 24 hours from 06:00 WITA (medical evacuation and emergency landings excepted), and for that day nobody — visitors included — may leave their accommodation, with lights and noise restricted island-wide. Check the exact date before booking flights around it.

climate.precipitation_note: The switch to the dry season: rainfall drops sharply to about 88 mm over roughly 9 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Good weather before the northern-summer rush arrives; prices and crowds are still moderate.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry season proper, around 93 mm over about 8 rain days, with lower humidity than the wet months.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best value of the year — dry weather without peak-season numbers.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry and a couple of degrees cooler: roughly 53 mm over about 6 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Numbers climb through the month as the northern-hemisphere and Australian holidays begin.

climate.precipitation_note: Coolest and among the driest months, about 55 mm over roughly 4 rain days, often breezy.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest stretch of the year alongside August — book accommodation, drivers and popular restaurants well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month of the year — only about 25 mm over roughly 4 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season continues; Indonesian Independence Day on 17 August brings nationwide celebrations and domestic travel.

climate.precipitation_note: Still firmly dry, around 47 mm over about 8 rain days, with temperatures starting to climb again.
climate.crowd_note: Crowds thin out after the school holidays while the weather stays reliable — one of the better windows.

climate.precipitation_note: Hot, with the rains returning late in the month: about 63 mm over roughly 12 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Quieter than the mid-year peak; a good month if you can take the heat and occasional afternoon storms.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet season resumes in earnest, roughly 179 mm over about 16 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: A genuinely quiet month between the dry-season and Christmas peaks.

climate.precipitation_note: Very wet — around 276 mm over roughly 22 rain days, humid throughout.
climate.crowd_note: Wet and busy at the same time: the Christmas and New Year fortnight is one of the most crowded and expensive periods of the year, so this is a peak-price month rather than a peak-weather one.

timezone_label: IST (UTC+1, summer time in effect); GMT (UTC+0) from 25 October 2026
timezone_note: The whole Republic of Ireland is on one clock. Citizens Information (page edited 6 January 2026) states that clocks go back one hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October (25 October 2026) and forward one hour at 1am on the last Sunday of March (29 March 2026 was the 2026 date), that Ireland has the same time as the UK and Portugal, and that this is one hour behind Central European Time. Today (18 October 2026) Ireland is therefore on summer time, UTC+1, switching to GMT (UTC+0) on 25 October 2026. The IANA zone Europe/Dublin is used for the live clock. Northern Ireland is part of the UK and uses the same clock, but it has its own entry rules (see entry notes). The 2027 spring change date is not stated on the page; it follows the 'last Sunday of March' rule.
passport_validity_rule: Ireland's Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) pages opened for this guide do not state a minimum passport validity for visa-exempt visitors. They say you must present your passport (plus a visa if one is needed and your boarding card) to the immigration officer on arrival. Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca, updated 26 May 2026) says: 'Your passport must be valid for the expected duration of your stay in Ireland', and that transport companies may apply stricter rules. The app therefore encodes duration-of-stay with no extra months. Practical points: airlines or ferry operators can apply their own stricter checks at boarding; for visa-required nationals applying for an Irish visa the requirement may be stricter (a search result summarising an Irish visit-visa checklist PDF suggested 6 months beyond departure, but that PDF returned HTTP 403 and was not read, so it is not confirmed here). EU/EEA/Swiss citizens may use a valid national identity card as well as a passport (ISD, page last updated 19 May 2023).
entry_requirement_notes: NO IRISH ETA OR E-VISA: Ireland has no pre-travel electronic authorisation in force for visitors. The ISD visit-visa page states that Ireland does not issue 'E-visas'; the only pre-arrival document is the Short Stay 'C' visa, and only for 'visa required' nationalities. Tourism Ireland's practical page (ireland.com, undated, (c) 2026) says 'You do not need an ETA to visit the Republic of Ireland', and Global Affairs Canada (26 May 2026) mentions no ETA for Ireland. The Republic of Ireland is in the EU but NOT in the Schengen Area and runs its own immigration and visa policy: ISD's Entry/Exit System page (last updated 8 October 2025) says Ireland is not participating in the EES, so travellers coming directly to Ireland are not bound by the scheme. The EU's official ETIAS site (opened 2026-10-18) says ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are collected; no official page opened for this guide says whether ETIAS applies to Ireland, so do not assume either way and check the ISD site before travel. A Schengen visa or Schengen stay is not an Irish permission, and Ireland's days do not use the Schengen 90/180 count. WHO NEEDS A VISA: ISD says that if you are from a 'visa required' country you must apply for a Short Stay C visa before travelling (up to 3 months before travel, from the country where you ordinarily live, via the AVATS online system; the visa covers stays of up to 90 days), unless you hold an in-date EUFAM card or a BIVS visa. Which nationalities are visa-required is shown by ISD's 'Visit Ireland - Travel Path' country list, which is an interactive page not readable here, so check your own nationality there. Global Affairs Canada states that tourist and business visas are not required for stays up to 90 days for Canadians. PERMISSION TO STAY: Permission is given at the border, not by the visa. ISD says the immigration officer stamps your passport with the length and conditions of stay at their discretion 'up to a maximum of 3 months', and its extension page says the maximum an officer can give at the border is 90 days 'regardless of whether or not you require a visa'. An Irish visa allows travel only and does not itself give permission to enter; an officer can refuse entry even to a visa holder. A temporary extension of up to 90 more days is possible only after an unexpected change of circumstances (ISD extension page). ON ARRIVAL: ISD says non-EU, non-EEA, non-Swiss and non-UK nationals arriving by air or sea from outside the State must present to an immigration officer with, at a minimum, passport, visa (if necessary) and boarding card. Useful extras it lists are a travel itinerary, proof of sufficient funds, proof of health insurance covering the stay, accommodation details and invitation letters. Global Affairs Canada adds that officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket and proof of funds. ISD does not state that an onward ticket is required, so that field is null. COMMON TRAVEL AREA (CTA): ISD describes the CTA as the UK, the Channel Islands, the Isle of Man and Ireland, within which Irish and British citizens can travel freely. There is generally no separation of arriving passengers at Irish airports and seaports, so officers cannot tell where a passenger flew from and may ask about nationality and port of embarkation; British and Irish citizens arriving from the UK can show a boarding card or documentary evidence of name and nationality. UK citizens do not need a visa to live, work or study in Ireland (GOV.UK foreign travel advice). The CTA does not extend your permission: ISD says an Irish short stay visa does not let a person who needs a UK visa enter the UK (the British-Irish Visa Scheme, BIVS, is an exception for some Chinese and Indian residents), and the Short Stay Visa Waiver Programme lets nationals of listed countries who entered the UK on a UK short stay visa visit Ireland on the remainder of that UK leave. NORTHERN IRELAND: it is part of the UK, not the Republic. Tourism Ireland (ireland.com) says you need a UK Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to visit Northern Ireland whether you arrive directly or via the Republic; GOV.UK says people who live in Ireland and travel from Ireland are exempt if they show an original valid Irish government-issued document (age 16+). Check gov.uk/eta for the live UK rule and fee. ISD also says non-EU nationals who arrive in the Republic via the Northern Ireland land border must report to an immigration officer (Dundalk Immigration Office, Dublin Airport or Port, or a local Garda immigration office) within 30 days, or within 7 days if engaging in business or employment. Airlines and ferry operators may apply their own ID rules on Ireland-UK routes (GOV.UK foreign travel advice). EU/EEA/SWISS AND UK CITIZENS: EU/EEA/Swiss nationals show a passport or valid national identity card; those over 18 with a biometric passport can use the Dublin Airport eGates (ISD). WORK: a visitor visa or landing permission does not allow paid or unpaid work, and ISD says the visa conditions include having travel/medical insurance and not using publicly funded services such as a hospital. PAGE DATES: the ISD pages cited carry 'last updated' dates between 2023 and 2025 (for example the FAQ 14 February 2024, non-EU entry page 27 June 2024, EES page 8 October 2025), so confirm on irishimmigration.ie before booking.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose at 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (travellers doing higher-risk activities such as visiting rural areas or eating street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Ireland page
health.notes: No vaccination is required to enter Ireland: CDC's Ireland page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry, and Global Affairs Canada (updated 26 May 2026) says 'Proof of vaccination is not required to enter this country'. The recommendations above are CDC medical advice, not entry conditions; CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 and carries a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025). CDC and Global Affairs Canada are used as fallbacks because no HSE page listing vaccines for visitors was opened for this guide. Global Affairs Canada additionally recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all travellers and a flu shot at least 2 weeks before travel. Healthcare: the HSE says that visitors with a European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) can get necessary medical treatment in Ireland free of charge, but that an EHIC only covers public healthcare, not private healthcare (HSE EHIC page, review date not shown). That page does not address visitors from outside the EU/EEA, and no official page opened for this guide states what a non-EU visitor is charged, so those charges are not given here; ISD's visa conditions say visa holders must have appropriate travel/medical insurance for the duration of the trip, so take insurance. For emergencies call 112 or 999 (HSE: both free from any phone).

money.card_acceptance: Tourism Ireland (ireland.com, undated, (c) 2026) states: 'The euro is used in the Republic of Ireland' (Northern Ireland uses pound sterling), that 'Visa and Mastercard are widely accepted throughout the island of Ireland' and that 'American Express is accepted in some places but not all'. It also says you can 'tap' a debit card for purchases of up to 50 euro (or 45 pounds in Northern Ireland); this contactless limit comes from an undated page, so treat it as indicative.
money.atm_notes: Tourism Ireland states that ATMs are located at most banks and in cities, towns and villages and accept most credit and debit cards; the page says fees are charged for ATM use and that credit cards pay 'Fees will still be charged but at a lower rate to credit cards', without giving amounts, so check your own bank's charges. The page is undated.

power.adapter_note: Tourism Ireland's travel checklist (ireland.com, undated, (c) 2026) states: 'Plugs in Ireland are three-pronged and the electricity supply is 230v/50hz, so bring an adapter.' The page does not give the IEC plug-type letter and the IEC World Plugs listing was not opened, so plug_types is left null.

emergency.notes: Both 112 and 999 reach the emergency services in Ireland. The HSE says: 'Phone the emergency services by calling 112 or 999 from any phone. Both numbers are free of charge' and that 112 works in any EU country (page last reviewed 19 October 2022). An Garda Siochana says 'Always call 112 or 999 in an emergency' and that you should state which service you need (page undated); Global Affairs Canada (26 May 2026) says 'Dial 112 or 999'. The same call-takers answer either number, so the per-service fields show 999 and the universal field 112 only for convenience: either number works for police (Garda), ambulance, fire and coastguard. Deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired people can use the 112 SMS service, which sends texts through the Emergency Call Answering Service to the Garda, ambulance, fire service or Irish Coastguard; Garda warns SMS is not real-time and delivery is not guaranteed, so use voice if you can. No tourist-police line was found, so that field is null.

getting_around.summary: This guide researched only urban public transport fare products from Transport for Ireland (TFI) and the Leap Card pages; intercity rail (Irish Rail), Bus Eireann coach fares and journey times, taxis and driving rules were not researched, so none are stated here. TFI describes the Leap Visitor Card as a Dublin-area ticket for unlimited travel for a chosen period on Dublin City Bus (Dublin Bus and Go-Ahead Ireland), Luas, DART and Commuter Rail. The ordinary TFI Leap Card has fare capping: for adults the Dublin daily cap is 6.00 euro and the weekly cap 24.00 euro (Dublin City buses, Luas, DART and Commuter Rail within Zone 1), and the Cork daily cap is 5.10 euro and weekly cap 20.40 euro (eligible TFI Cork City buses only), with Nitelink, tours, Bus Eireann and Go-Ahead commuter services excluded in Dublin (Leap Card fare-capping page, undated). The TFI 90 Minute Fare is 2.00 euro for adults in Dublin and 1.70 euro in Cork City, covering the same Dublin services (excluding Express and Nitelink buses) with later journeys free if you tap on within 90 minutes; it is not available on rail services in Cork (Leap Card page, undated). Most of these pages carry no date, so confirm fares before travel.

passes.name: TFI Leap Card (adult fare capping)
passes.covers: Pay-as-you-go travel on Dublin City buses (Dublin Bus and Go-Ahead Ireland, including Xpresso), Luas, and DART and Commuter Rail within Zone 1, with a daily cap of 6.00 euro and weekly cap of 24.00 euro for adults; in Cork the daily cap is 5.10 euro and the weekly cap 20.40 euro on eligible TFI Cork City buses only. Excludes Nitelink, tours, Bus Eireann and Go-Ahead Ireland commuter services in Dublin.
passes.worth_it: On the same Dublin services the adult daily cap (6.00 euro) is lower than the 24-hour Visitor Card price (8.00 euro), so for short Dublin city stays a standard Leap Card with capping looks cheaper on these figures. The price of buying a Leap Card itself was not checked, so the comparison is incomplete.

passes.name: TFI Leap Visitor Card
passes.covers: Unlimited travel for a chosen period on Dublin Bus scheduled services (not tours), Go-Ahead Ireland Dublin City services, all Luas services, and DART and Commuter Rail within Zone 1. Prices per Leap Card page: 24 hours 8.00 euro, 72 hours 18.00 euro, 7 days (168 hours) 24.00 euro; the period starts at first use. Not valid on Bus Eireann or Hop-on Hop-off and other tour services.
passes.worth_it: Useful if you want one prepaid ticket with no top-ups, but it is not an e-ticket: it is delivered by post (Ireland 3-5 working days, UK up to 7, Europe up to 10, rest of world up to 14 after dispatch) or bought at listed Dublin outlets including Dublin Airport. Unused cards expire 12 months after purchase. Whether airport bus services are included could not be confirmed: the English text does not say, while translated sections say airport travel is included, so verify before relying on it.

timezone_label: UTC+2 (Israel Standard Time) in winter, UTC+3 (Israel Daylight Time) in summer
timezone_note: Israel has a single nationwide zone (IANA Asia/Jerusalem, standard time UTC+2) and uses daylight saving time. Per the IANA tz database 'asia' file, summer time (UTC+3) starts at 02:00 on the Friday before the last Sunday of March (rule 'Fri>=23 Mar') and ends at 02:00 on the last Sunday of October, rules in force from 2013 with no end year. At the date of this record (19 October 2026) Israel is on UTC+3; the clocks go back to UTC+2 on Sunday 25 October 2026 and forward again on Friday 26 March 2027. Source is the IANA tz database 'asia' file; no Israeli government page stating the rule could be opened (gov.il returned 403). Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, Eilat and the West Bank use the same IANA zone in the database.
passport_validity_rule: Sources disagree. israel.travel (Israel Ministry of Tourism, a page that still carries pandemic-era text) says a passport valid at least six months beyond the date of arrival, stated for US and Canadian citizens. UK FCDO says expiry at least 90 days after the date you arrive, and Global Affairs Canada says at least 90 days beyond the date of entry. The stricter six months from entry is encoded. No source consulted states a blank-page requirement. The Population and Immigration Authority's own page could not be opened (gov.il returned 403; israel-entry.piba.gov.il shows only a title to fetchers), so the rule is not confirmed first-hand; visa-waiver travellers must also hold a machine-readable passport and an approved ETA-IL.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa and authorisation: no visa is needed for a tourist visit. UK FCDO says visitors get permission to stay up to 3 months on entry, and Global Affairs Canada says no visa is needed for tourist stays of up to 90 days (work needs a visa). Citizens of visa-exempt countries must also hold an approved ETA-IL (electronic travel authorisation) before arrival. Status today: in force. FCDO's entry page, opened on 19 October 2026, states ETA-IL has been required since 1 January 2025, costs 25 new Israeli shekels, is valid for 2 years and covers a visit of 90 days, applied for through the Israel Population and Immigration Authority. Global Affairs Canada (updated 29 July 2026) says Canadians need an ETA-IL, should apply at least 72 hours before arrival, and can stay up to 90 days if approved. Neither page lists exemptions. The Population and Immigration Authority's own application site (israel-entry.piba.gov.il) loads only a page title for automated fetchers and the gov.il pages returned 403, so the fee, validity and lead time are from FCDO and Global Affairs Canada rather than first-hand; apply only through the official gov.il or piba.gov.il address and confirm the current fee there. The Israel Ministry of Tourism's English page (israel.travel) is out of date (it still carries pandemic-era entry text and does not mention ETA-IL), so it was not used for the ETA. Visa-waiver travellers must present a machine-readable passport (israel.travel). Passport validity: the sources disagree. israel.travel says a passport valid at least six months beyond the date of arrival is needed (stated for US and Canadian citizens). FCDO says expiry at least 90 days after the date you arrive, and Global Affairs Canada says at least 90 days beyond the date of entry. The stricter six months from entry is encoded; carry a passport with at least six months left to avoid being turned away at check-in. Border questioning and refusal (FCDO): officials may question you at length, search baggage and devices, ask for access to personal email or social media accounts and may withhold devices; foreign nationals can be refused entry for publicly calling for a boycott of Israel or its settlements, or for Holocaust denial statements; if refused you are booked on the next flight back with the same airline and may be held at the Immigration Detention Centre. Working without proper permission can lead to detention and deportation. Israel sets the entry rules for the West Bank too (Global Affairs Canada: Palestine issues no visas of its own, entry is through Israeli ports of entry, some visitors need specific permits and entry is not guaranteed; Gaza entry and exit are extremely limited); FCDO says violating the Palestinian Authority entry restriction can mean deportation and a ban of up to 10 years. Customs and cash: FCDO says to declare anything prohibited, taxable or dutiable and points to the Israel Tax Authority's guidance on taking money in or out, giving no figure. The gov.il Form 84 page ('Declare bringing money into and out of Israel') was reported by a search result as setting the threshold at 50,000 NIS, or 12,000 NIS at a land border, but that page returned 403 to the fetch tool and was not opened, so confirm the figure with the Israel Tax Authority before travel. No duty-free allowance was confirmed from an official page. No source consulted states a blank-page requirement, an arrival card or an onward ticket requirement. Travel advisories (re-check both before departure; they can change within days): UK FCDO (page showing updated 22 July 2026, still current at 19 October 2026) advises against all travel to Gaza and within 500m of the Gaza border; Tulkarm, Jenin and Tubas Governorates in the West Bank (except Route 90); northern Israel and the occupied Golan Heights north of Route 89 between Nahariyya and Dalton, north of a line from Dalton to Route 91, and north of Route 91 across the Golan (excluding Routes 89 and 91); within 500m of the Golan Area of Separation ('Alpha line'); and Sheba'a Farms and Ghajja. FCDO advises against all but essential travel to most of the rest of the West Bank, with exceptions including East Jerusalem, Bethlehem Governorate, Ramallah Municipality, Jericho municipality and areas south of Jericho (including the Allenby crossing), Highway 1 and the areas south and west of it (including Highway 3), Route 443 and Highway 45. It lists no all-travel or all-but-essential-travel warning for the rest of Israel (including Tel Aviv and Jerusalem). FCDO's headline text reports Iranian strikes and retaliatory attacks across the region since 8 July, says the situation is unpredictable with a risk of further attacks, and tells travellers to expect possible flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures and disruption at Ben Gurion Airport, with international air and land borders possibly closing. It notes attacks have become less frequent but rocket and drone attacks remain a risk across Israel, with shrapnel from intercepted missiles possible; follow Home Front Command instructions and shelter when told. FCDO's separate safety page carries differently dated regional-tension text (Iran-Israel ceasefire of 8 April 2026, Hizballah cessation of hostilities announced 16 April 2026 with fighting continuing, Houthi missile and drone risk), so the pages are not fully consistent; read the live advice. FCDO also says terrorist attacks are 'very likely' in Israel and Palestine, protests can turn violent at short notice, and travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against FCDO advice. Global Affairs Canada (updated 29 July 2026; the advisory index lists 'Israel and Palestine' at 'avoid non-essential travel' with regional advisories): Israel - avoid non-essential travel because of the volatile security situation in the region; Jerusalem - avoid non-essential travel; Golan Heights - avoid all travel to the parts bordering Syria east of Highway 98; avoid all travel within 5 km of the Lebanon border and within 10 km of the Gaza Strip border; Palestine - avoid all travel, except Highway 1 and Route 90 from its junction with Highway 1 to the King Hussein (Allenby) Bridge near Jericho, where non-essential travel should be avoided. The Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Population and Immigration Authority and the Israel Tax Authority pages on gov.il returned 403 to the fetch tool, so no first-hand Israeli confirmation of any entry rule above was possible.

health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC says yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and entry requirements do not require it, and Global Affairs Canada says there is no yellow fever risk and no proof of vaccination is required. FCDO lists no required vaccines and refers travellers to TravelHealthPro at least 8 weeks before travel. CDC (page reviewed 25 August 2026) carries a rabies alert for an increase in rabies cases in dogs and jackals (avoid wild animals and unfamiliar dogs and cats), a Level 2 global polio notice and a Level 1 global measles notice; it does not mention malaria, so no malaria risk level is asserted. FCDO: healthcare is not free and treatment can be expensive, hospitals will insist on payment and may take legal action to stop you leaving until bills are paid, so carry travel health insurance that covers treatment and repatriation. Ambulance number: FCDO's health page, as read, gives 100 for an ambulance in Israel and 101 in the West Bank and Gaza, while FCDO's getting-help page and Global Affairs Canada both give 101 for medical assistance in Israel; see emergency notes. The Israel Ministry of Health site (gov.il) returned 403 and could not be opened, so no Israeli health-ministry statement is cited.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Getting help page lists police 100, ambulance 101 and fire 102 for Israel and Palestine and no tourist police number; Global Affairs Canada gives the same three (police 100, medical assistance 101, fire 102). One FCDO page (health) as read says to dial 100 for an ambulance in Israel and 101 in the West Bank and Gaza, which conflicts with the other two sources; 101 is encoded, and if 101 does not connect try the other number. israel.travel also tells people with symptoms to call the 101 MDA hotline. No single all-purpose number and no tourist police number is confirmed by an official source consulted, so both are left null. FCDO's getting-help page says English-speaking lawyers and interpreters are listed on FCDO pages; no source states whether English is answered on the emergency lines. Embassy of Canada, Tel Aviv: +972 3 636 3300 (Global Affairs Canada). The Israeli police and MDA sites could not be opened, so these are foreign-government sources rather than first-hand Israeli ones.

getting_around.summary: No Israeli transport authority or operator page could be opened (gov.il and rail.co.il returned 403), so this record carries no fares, timetables or pass details. What the sources state: FCDO advises UK drivers that they need a UK licence, the 1968 International Driving Permit and a green card; it warns against driving into ultra-Orthodox areas of Jerusalem from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall because residents have thrown stones at cars; and its travel warnings restrict travel on and around parts of Highway 1, Route 443 and Highway 45 for the West Bank (see entry notes). israel.travel says passengers on El Al, and on certain European flights by Arkia or Israir, face a security interview at check-in. Ben Gurion Airport can be disrupted at short notice, and FCDO notes demonstrations can affect access to it.

timezone_note: Italy has a single time zone, Central European Time (CET, UTC+1), and moves to UTC+2 for summer time (italia.it). The Italian tourism portal says the clocks change overnight between Saturday and Sunday and the exact dates change each year. Under the EU-wide rule as recorded in the IANA tz database for Europe/Rome, summer time (CEST, UTC+2) began on 29 March 2026 and ends on 25 October 2026, when clocks return to CET (UTC+1); that date pair is the IANA/EU schedule and was not read off an Italian government page. The label above reflects the state on 2026-10-17.
passport_validity_rule: Italy applies the Schengen rule. The Italian tourism portal (italia.it) states that non-EU visitors need a passport valid for at least three months after the planned date of departure from the Schengen Area; the UK FCDO's Italy entry guidance adds that the passport must also have been issued less than 10 years before the date of arrival (passports renewed before 1 October 2018 may fail this test). The three months run from leaving the Schengen Area, not from arriving in Italy. EU and Schengen-country citizens may use a valid national ID card instead of a passport.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-free short stays are Schengen-wide: the UK FCDO states that visitors who do not need a visa may stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area, with earlier Schengen visits in the previous 180 days counting toward the 90. ETIAS is NOT in force today (checked 2026-10-18): the official EU ETIAS site (travel-europe.europa.eu/en/etias) states "ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point" and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; it gives no start date (the earlier "last quarter of 2026" target no longer appears on that page, so no start date should be assumed). Canada's travel advice likewise says ETIAS applications are not yet open. The UK government warns that websites selling ETIAS authorisations now are fraudulent. The separate Entry/Exit System (EES) IS operating: the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026 (the UK government dates its start to 12 October 2025), so non-EU visitors may be asked for fingerprints and a photo at the border, free of charge, and should allow longer queues. The FCDO says that at Italian border control you may be asked to show accommodation proof, travel insurance, a return or onward ticket and enough money for the stay; this is stated as something you may need to show, not as a fixed rule with a published amount, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. Cash or travellers' cheques worth 10,000 euros or more must be declared on entry or exit (FCDO); Global Affairs Canada says the same for 10,000 euros or more when entering or leaving the EU, and Smartraveller adds that this covers all forms of currency and that no declaration is needed travelling to or from another EU country. Smartraveller (12 Oct 2026) also reports temporary border checks on arrivals from Spain and at the Slovenia land border, so allow extra time. Registration: hotels and other accommodation providers register guests with the police; a visitor arriving from another Schengen country who is not staying somewhere that does so must file a declaration of presence with the local questura within 8 days (FCDO and italia.it). Italian police can stop you for an identity check at any time, so carry photo ID (FCDO). Tourist tax: many major Italian cities charge a small per-night tourist tax that varies by city and hotel star rating and is usually collected by the hotel, often in cash (FCDO). Italy's own foreign ministry pages (esteri.it, viaggiaresicuri.it) and travel-europe.europa.eu could not be read by an automated fetch, so the rules above come from the italia.it tourism portal, the European Commission's home-affairs pages and the UK FCDO as fallbacks.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19
Measles (MMR), including an early dose for infants 6-11 months
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Mpox (for adults expecting certain activities, per CDC)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Tick-borne encephalitis (for extensive tick exposure in endemic areas)
health.malaria_risk: None listed - the CDC's Italy page lists no malaria risk or prevention guidance.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the border: the CDC states Italy does not require yellow fever vaccination and does not recommend it for Italy. Other CDC-listed risks are dengue and leishmaniasis (insect and sand-fly bites) and leptospirosis from contaminated water or soil; the UK FCDO adds ticks, West Nile disease and altitude sickness in the Alps and Dolomites. Italy's tourism portal says medical assistance is guaranteed to anyone who goes to a public hospital or similar facility, that foreign nationals temporarily visiting are entitled to basic dental care, and recommends buying travel health insurance before departure. The FCDO notes that UK prescriptions are not accepted, that pharmacies are marked with a green cross, and that a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not a substitute for travel insurance. Call 118 for an ambulance. No official source reached here stated whether tap water is safe to drink, so this guide does not say.

money.card_acceptance: The Italian tourism portal states that in addition to cash you can pay with the most popular credit cards (Visa, Mastercard/Cirrus/Maestro, American Express, and the domestic Bancomat, Postamat and PagoBancomat systems), and that in larger centres you can pay with your smartphone through dedicated apps. It does not say how universal acceptance is among small businesses.
money.cash_culture: The tourism portal gives no view on how cash-reliant Italy is. One official note on cash: the UK FCDO says hotels often ask for the city tourist tax in cash and advises getting a receipt.
money.tipping: Italy's tourism portal states that tipping is not compulsory and there are no established rules; it says it is customary to leave about 10% of the bill if you were satisfied with the service.
money.atm_notes: The tourism portal says banks with 24/7 ATMs are spread across Italy and that you can exchange currency or withdraw cash at airports, large train stations and banks or exchange agencies. It states no fee or limit information.

power.voltage: 220 V AC as stated by italia.it
power.adapter_note: italia.it says Italian sockets follow standard CEI 23-50 and are symmetrical and non-polarised, so a plug fits either way. It names the C-type socket (2 or 3 round holes) and the L-type socket (larger pins), and says the multistandard socket accepts all types of Italian plugs and the German Schuko plug. Adapters are sold in supermarkets, dedicated shops and most hotels. Check your device's rated input voltage before plugging in; the portal gives 220 V and 50 Hz.

emergency.notes: italia.it states that the single number for emergencies in Italy is 112, free and dialled without a prefix, and lists State Police 113 (accidents, thefts, etc.), fire brigade 115 (fires, weather emergencies) and urgent medical help 118 (also relevant to mountain or cave rescue). Other numbers on the same page: sea rescue 1530, forest ranger 1515, travel information 1518, and Automobile Club d'Italia roadside assistance 803.116. The UK FCDO's Italy page lists the numbers slightly differently (118 ambulance, 115 fire, and 112 for police) and mentions the 112 Where ARE U app, which works only in some parts of Italy; both sources agree 112, 115 and 118, so 112 is the safe first call and the operator routes you. No official source consulted confirmed a dedicated tourist police line, so none is listed here. Smartraveller (opened 2026-10-18) lists 112 for emergency assistance, 113 police, 115 fire and rescue, 118 medical, and Global Affairs Canada gives 112; FCDO lists 112 for police, so 113 (State Police) is kept as the structured police value.

getting_around.summary: Rail is the backbone for visitors. italia.it says Trenitalia and Italo Treno run more than 300 daily connections between the big cities, and that Milan to Rome by high-speed train takes just over three hours; Italo's own site lists Rome-Florence 1h 30min, Milan-Florence 1h 55min, Rome-Naples 1h and Milan-Venice 2h 30min, and says its trains connect 51 major cities via 58 stations. Trenitalia's high-speed brand is Frecciarossa, alongside Frecciargento, Frecciabianca, Intercity and Regionale services. Tickets can be bought on each operator's website, via apps, at travel agencies or at station offices; check on regional tickets whether you must validate them at a station machine before boarding. In cities, italia.it says it is compulsory to buy a bus, tram or metro ticket at an authorised outlet (tobacconists, newsagents, bars) before boarding and validate it once on board; metros exist in Milan, Rome, Naples, Brescia, Turin, Catania and Genoa. No official operator page reached here gave a city transit pass price, so none is listed. Driving: the FCDO says you need a pass to drive into the historic centre of many Italian cities in a private or hire car; the boundaries are usually marked ZTL in black on a yellow background and passing the sign without a pass can lead to a fine. Italy's consulate in Toronto adds that ZTL cameras issue fines that are mailed to the owner's home country and that a rental company can pass on the driver's details. italia.it says ZTL rules vary by city, with signs at each entrance. Transport strikes are often called at short notice (FCDO).

connectivity.local_sim_notes: italia.it says you can use a SIM card from an Italian operator with your chosen amount of data, and recommends buying an Italian SIM for longer stays to keep costs down. It also says hotels, transport providers and many bars, restaurants and attractions offer free Wi-Fi, and that Piazza Wi-Fi Italia is a national free network with an offline hotspot map in the wifi.italia.it app. It advises checking roaming tariffs beforehand and points to europa.eu for roaming cost details. It does not mention eSIM or any ID requirement to buy a SIM.

timezone_note: One zone nationwide. The Jamaica Tourist Board states Jamaica is on UTC/GMT -5 and does not observe daylight saving time (the IANA zone America/Jamaica agrees), so the offset from US Eastern, Canadian and European clocks changes when those places move their clocks: Jamaica matches US Eastern time in winter and is one hour behind it in summer.
passport_validity_rule: Jamaica does not state a six-month rule in any source read. The Jamaica Tourist Board says a US passport 'must be valid at the time of entry and exit' and that UK travellers need a passport valid for the duration of their stay; PICA's travel-documents page asks only for a 'valid' passport and sets no minimum remaining period; UK FCDO says the passport must be valid for the stay and have two blank pages for entry and exit stamps. The six-month figure on PICA's extension-of-stay page applies only to people asking to extend their stay (passport valid at least six months beyond the extension request's expiry), not to entry. Some airlines apply their own validity checks at check-in, so travelling with a passport that expires soon after your return date is not advisable.
entry_requirement_notes: C5 DECLARATION (mandatory): the Jamaica Customs Agency says all arriving passengers must complete and submit the Electronic Passenger Declaration (C5) at enterjamaica.gov.jm, in force since 1 September 2023, free of charge, and the C5 is required for final clearance at Jamaica's international airports. The Jamaica Tourist Board adds that all passengers arriving by air or cruise ship must complete the online C5; there is NO COST for it, so do not pay a third-party site; it can be submitted up to 30 days before the trip; every traveller regardless of age needs their own form (children included); and a new form is needed for each trip. It combines the immigration form and a Customs Declaration section of Yes/No questions on currency, agricultural goods and restricted items. The Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency (PICA) lists the C5 'either online or a physical form' among the documents presented at the immigration interview. A Jamaica Information Service article (31 May 2024) quotes PICA saying the form can still be completed on arrival (airport Wi-Fi, tablets and officer help are provided) but that completing it beforehand shortens the immigration queue. UK FCDO also says to complete it online before arrival where possible. The C5 portal c5online.pica.gov.jm returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so enterjamaica.gov.jm (the address given by the Customs Agency and the tourist board) is the one read here. VISA: PICA's entry-visa page says no visa is required for the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, India and Singapore passport holders (Commonwealth countries are listed as 'NO visa required'), and for Germany and Brazil 'NO visa required for 90 days'. STAY LENGTH SOURCES DISAGREE: PICA's page says the USA is 'NO visa required for 6 months' (the page footer carries 'Last updated July 19, 2023'), whereas the Jamaica Tourist Board says US and Canadian citizens need no visa for stays of up to 90 days and that UK entry 'may be granted for up to 90 days', and UK FCDO also says usually up to 90 days with the leave-by date stamped in the passport. The officer sets the period at the border; plan around the date actually stamped, and treat 90 days as the safe working figure. EXTENSIONS: PICA says an extension must be applied for before the landing period ends, takes three working days, and requires a return ticket, a letter giving the reason, the fee and a passport valid for at least six months beyond the expiry date of the extension request; maximum total stay is 12 months for Commonwealth citizens and 6 months for non-Commonwealth visitors. Overstaying is a breach of immigration law. ONWARD TICKET: the Jamaica Tourist Board states that all visitors are required to show a return or onward ticket for entry into Jamaica (PICA's travel-documents page does not mention it). PASSPORT: the sources found state no minimum remaining validity; the Tourist Board says a US passport must be valid at entry and exit and a UK passport valid for the duration of the stay, and UK FCDO asks for two blank pages for stamps. No proof-of-funds rule was stated by the PICA, Tourist Board or FCDO pages read. CURRENCY AND CUSTOMS: the C5 asks whether you carry currency or monetary instruments over US$10,000 or equivalent, and UK FCDO says undeclared sums can be seized and fined. The Customs Agency allows arriving passengers aged 18 and over duty-free personal and household goods up to US$1,000 in total value (excess may be charged), and minors do not get that allowance. The C5 also asks about fruit, plants, cut flowers, vegetables, soil, meat, live animals, honey and wildlife products; UK FCDO notes meat and dairy products may not be brought in. The Customs Agency pages read did not list tobacco or alcohol limits or the full prohibited-goods list, so none is stated here; declare anything in doubt. HURRICANE SEASON (official note): the Atlantic hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November (Jamaica Meteorological Service, via the Jamaica Information Service, 28 May 2026; the Jamaica Tourist Board gives the same dates and says peak activity is August to October, and monitoring is by the Meteorological Service, the US National Hurricane Center and CDEMA). The Meteorological Service's 2026 outlook was a 55% likelihood of a below-normal season (8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes, 1-3 major hurricanes) but warned against complacency, citing Hurricane Melissa, which made landfall in October 2025. UK FCDO (page current at 19 October 2026, last updated 6 May 2026) says all Western parishes suffered significant damage, some communities were still without electricity and piped water, and healthcare access is limited in the worst-affected areas. The Jamaica Tourist Board alerts page (undated) says the three international airports are fully operating, seaports are open and most resort areas are up and running while some repairs continue, so confirm your own hotel and transfers before travel. Hurricanes can cause fallen trees, blocked roads and flooding (FCDO); buy insurance that covers weather disruption and monitor the Meteorological Service (metservice.gov.jm) and the National Hurricane Center.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate: required of travellers older than one year arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, and of those transiting such a country for more than 12 hours (Ministry of Health & Wellness, 23 June 2025). Not required for travel direct from the USA (CDC).
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines, including MMR (CDC: all international travellers fully vaccinated against measles)
COVID-19 (CDC: all eligible travellers current)
Hepatitis A (CDC: unvaccinated travellers aged one year and over)
Hepatitis B (CDC: unvaccinated travellers under 60; 60 and over may be vaccinated)
Typhoid (CDC: consider if staying a month or longer, visiting poor-sanitation areas, or visiting friends or relatives)
Rabies (CDC: ask a clinician about pre-exposure vaccination)
Mpox (CDC: for adults expecting certain activities)
health.notes: The Ministry of Health & Wellness (23 June 2025) says Jamaica is yellow-fever-free and names the countries whose arrivals must show proof: Angola, Argentina, Benin, Bolivia, Brazil, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Colombia, Congo, Cote d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ecuador, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, French Guiana, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Guyana, Kenya, Liberia, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Sudan, Sudan, Suriname, Togo, Trinidad & Tobago, Uganda and Venezuela. Vaccinate at least 10 days before travel. A 2016 Jamaica Information Service article says a traveller without a valid certificate may be refused entry or quarantined for up to six days, with medical-exemption holders given a Health Alert Card and daily symptom reporting; that article is old, so treat the penalty as indicative. The CDC page (last reviewed 25 August 2026) does not mention malaria, so no malaria-risk statement is made here. CDC lists leptospirosis (contaminated water and soil), dengue and Zika (mosquito bites), hantavirus and tuberculosis. After Hurricane Melissa, UK FCDO warns of water-borne and mosquito-borne disease risks from debris and standing water, and the Jamaica Tourist Board alerts page reports suspected leptospirosis cases and advises visitors outside resorts to avoid floodwater and see a health centre for flu-like symptoms. Jamaican Tourist Board says drinking water is purified and safe to drink. FCDO says medical facilities, private and public, vary and may not meet UK standards, providers may expect immediate cash payment, and travellers should hold insurance covering treatment and medical evacuation.

money.cash_culture: UK FCDO says health providers may expect immediate cash payment for treatment, so insurance and a payment method for upfront fees matter. No official source read states how widely cards are accepted by shops, restaurants or taxis.
money.atm_notes: The Jamaica Tourist Board states most Jamaican ATMs accept international bank cards with Visa, MasterCard, Cirrus and Plus logos; banks give credit-card cash advances and cash traveller's cheques; and licensed cambios and commercial banks operate in resort areas, with official exchange rates varying daily (compare before exchanging). No official source on ATM fees or dynamic currency conversion was found, so none is asserted.

power.adapter_note: The Jamaica Tourist Board states the electrical supply is 110 volts/50 cycles standard with flat two-pronged plugs like those in the USA and Canada (Type A). It says adaptors and converters are available locally but may not be easy to find, so bring them if your appliances use another voltage or plug. Whether grounded three-pin sockets are also in use was not stated by an official source, so only Type A is listed. North American 60 Hz devices run on 50 Hz mains, which is fine for most electronics but check any motor-driven or clock-timed device.

emergency.notes: The Jamaica Constabulary Force gives 119 for crimes in progress and life-threatening emergencies (free from any phone) and 311 for anonymous Crime Stop tips. UK FCDO lists police 119, ambulance 110 and fire 110, and Jamaica Information Service articles (2019, 2023) say to dial 110 for fire and ambulance. A 2023 Jamaica Information Service article says 112 routes to the emergency services of the country you are in and works even when your own network signal is lost; the JCF page did not list ambulance or fire. Jamaica Fire Brigade's direct Kingston lines in a 2019 article are (876) 922-2121 and 922-2122 (may be out of date). No official source read confirmed a dedicated tourist-police number, so none is claimed. For UK nationals the British High Commission in Kingston is +1 (876) 936 0700 (FCDO).

getting_around.summary: As described by the Jamaica Tourist Board: the government-owned JUTC runs yellow buses on set routes around Kingston and nearby areas and takes cash or a JUTC Smartercard; privately operated coaster minibuses link most towns from depots and bus parks and are licensed by the Transport Authority, with Kingston's Half Way Tree Transport Centre as the central hub. Licensed route taxis (red 'PPV' or white 'P' plates, checkered black-and-white marking) run fixed routes at regulated fares and pick up several passengers. Chartered taxis, usually air-conditioned, can be booked through hotels with the fare confirmed at booking. Knutsford Express runs scheduled air-conditioned coaches to over 20 locations including the international airports. Rental cars are available at the international airports and in town centres, and drivers keep to the left. UK FCDO advises using Jamaica Tourist Board approved taxis and minibuses for excursions and airport transfers and licensed providers. No official source read gave fares, journey times, domestic flight or ferry details, or a driving-licence rule, so none are stated.
