timezone_note: Japan observes a single time zone nationwide, from Okinawa to Hokkaido, and does not use daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Japan sets no minimum remaining validity beyond the trip itself: the passport only has to stay valid for the length of the stay. UK government entry guidance for Japan states "your passport must be valid for the length of your stay. No additional period of validity is required." JNTO's own visa page says only that all foreign visitors must hold a valid passport. Note that an onward airline or a transit country may still apply its own six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Nationals of the 74 countries and regions on Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs visa-exemption list (page dated 1 September 2025) may enter for short-term stays without a visa, normally 90 days (15 days for Indonesia and Thailand, 30 for Brunei and Qatar); some listed countries (Brazil, Peru, Serbia, Thailand and others) are exempt only with an ICAO-compliant ePassport, and others need a visa. No pre-travel electronic travel authorisation is in force for Japan today. A scheme called JESTA has been announced but is not operating: Japan's Immigration Services Agency plan says it aims to introduce it in FY2028 (earlier than the original 2030), and no start date, eligible nationalities or fee have been published, so do not pay any site selling a "JESTA" or "Japan ETA". Visit Japan Web registration is not mandatory (JNTO: "Registration is not required, but advance registration makes procedures like tax-free shopping more convenient"), but every arriving passenger must make a customs declaration (Japan Customs: all passengers entering Japan are required to declare their belongings; paper forms are given on the plane or at Customs, and Visit Japan Web is the recommended electronic route). Cash or other means of payment (cheques, travellers cheques, securities) worth more than 1,000,000 yen must be declared to Customs on a separate form. Practical trap: if you plan to use a Japan Rail Pass you need the "Temporary Visitor" stamp or sticker in your passport, and the automated immigration gates do not apply one — use a staffed counter or ask a clerk to stamp it.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Japanese encephalitis (longer stays or extensive rural/outdoor exposure)
Measles
Mpox (for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry to Japan — CDC lists yellow fever vaccine as both "not required" and "not recommended" for Japan, and its Japan destination page carries no malaria section and no antimalarial recommendation. Everything in the recommended list above is medical advice only; nothing on it is checked at immigration.

money.card_acceptance: International credit, debit and prepaid cards are generally accepted across the country and increasingly in shops and restaurants, and work for long-distance rail such as the shinkansen and the Narita Express. Short-distance train and subway fares typically cannot be paid by card, and smaller independent businesses may still be yen-only.
money.cash_culture: Japan remains, in JNTO's own words, "still very much a cash culture" — carrying some cash is recommended for the whole trip, and many smaller establishments accept only yen. A prepaid IC card (Suica, Pasmo) covers public transport, convenience stores and a growing number of shops, and is the usual way to avoid carrying coins, though it is not accepted everywhere either.
money.tipping: Not practised and best avoided. JNTO states "In Japan, it's not common to tip for services such as those provided in bars, cafes, restaurants, taxis, and hotels" and that tipping "can cause discomfort and confusion if you do." The one traditional exception is a gratuity called kokorozuke, which is given in an envelope rather than as loose cash; a private guide or interpreter used to overseas practice may also accept a tip.
money.atm_notes: Not every Japanese ATM takes foreign cards. The two networks JNTO names as accepting them are Japan Post Bank ATMs and Seven Bank ATMs in 7-Eleven stores (the latter offer 12-language menus). JNTO also warns that ATMs often charge for withdrawals, that many are not open 24 hours, and that they can occasionally run out of cash — so do not leave a withdrawal to the last minute.

power.frequency: 50Hz (eastern Japan, including Tokyo) / 60Hz (western Japan, including Nagoya, Kyoto and Osaka)
power.adapter_note: JNTO describes Japanese outlets as taking two flat parallel prongs (the Type A pattern) and states "The voltage used throughout Japan is uniformly 100 volts, A.C." Coming from a 230V country you need a plug adapter, and voltage matters more than the plug: dual-voltage devices such as phone and laptop chargers, hair dryers and shavers work nationwide, but any single-voltage 230V appliance needs a step-down transformer. Adapters and transformers are sold in electronics districts such as Tokyo's Akihabara and at major appliance retailers.

emergency.notes: Police 110; fire and ambulance 119 (UK FCDO Getting help page for Japan). The JNTO safety page now names only 110 as the emergency number, so 119 rests on FCDO. No official source consulted lists 112 for Japan, so do not rely on it. For English-language help, the JNTO Japan Visitor Hotline on 050-3816-2787 runs 24 hours a day for emergencies such as illness and disasters, in English, Chinese, Korean and Japanese; the Tokyo Metropolitan Police English helpline is 03-3501-0110, 24 hours, 365 days a year.

getting_around.summary: Almost every visitor moves by rail. The JR network plus the shinkansen links the major cities, city subways and private lines cover everything inside them, and a prepaid IC card (Suica or Pasmo) tapped at the gate is the simplest way to pay for short hops — short-distance rail and subway fares generally will not take a foreign credit card. Buses, ferries, domestic flights and taxis fill the gaps, and a rental car is mainly worth it outside the major cities.

passes.name: Japan Rail Pass
passes.covers: A joint product of the six JR Group companies giving nationwide travel on JR lines, with Ordinary Car and Green Car versions in 7, 14 and 21-day durations. Special conditions apply to the fastest NOZOMI and MIZUHO shinkansen services, which the pass does not simply cover.
passes.worth_it: An Ordinary 7-day pass is 50,000 yen through 30 September 2026 and 53,000 yen from 1 October 2026 (14-day 80,000 rising to 84,000; 21-day 100,000 rising to 105,000). JNTO's own guidance is that the regional passes are better value if you are staying in one area, so the nationwide pass really only pays off on a multi-region, long-distance itinerary.

passes.name: Regional JR passes (JR TOKYO Wide Pass, JR EAST PASS, JR-West, JR-Central, JR Kyushu, Hokkaido, ALL SHIKOKU, Hokuriku Arch)
passes.covers: Each covers one region — for example the JR TOKYO Wide Pass covers greater Tokyo including Mt. Fuji, Nikko and the Izu Peninsula, and the Hokuriku Arch Pass links Tokyo and Osaka via Nagano, Toyama, Ishikawa and Fukui.
passes.worth_it: JNTO states that regional passes offer better value than the nationwide pass when you are exploring a single area.

passes.name: Suica / Pasmo IC card
passes.covers: Prepaid tap-to-pay for public transport nationwide, plus convenience stores and a growing number of shops and restaurants.
passes.worth_it: Not a discount pass but the practical default for city travel and short hops, and the usual alternative to carrying cash. Not accepted absolutely everywhere.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a prepaid SIM. JNTO's official Mobile Tips site states the handset must be SIM-free (unlocked) and must carry Japan's technical standards conformity certification mark for wireless equipment; nano, micro and standard SIM sizes are sold. JNTO points visitors to major airports, electronics megastores such as Bic Camera and Yodobashi Camera, and travel agencies. JNTO does not state any ID, passport or registration requirement for a prepaid tourist data SIM. Rented pocket Wi-Fi is the common alternative and is available at every major airport or by online reservation for hotel delivery; SoftBank's Free Wi-Fi Passport also gives two weeks of free access to about 400,000 hotspots.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official figure for a ~10GB / 2-week plan could be verified. The only price JNTO publishes is roughly 3,000 yen for a 1GB, 30-day data plan (checked 28 September 2026).

climate.precipitation_note: Tokyo's normal monthly precipitation is 59.7 mm. JMA notes that northwesterly winter winds leave the Pacific side sunny while the Sea of Japan side gets heavy snow.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO names 27 December to 4 January (plus adjacent weekends) as a peak period to avoid; from roughly the second week the month is one of the quietest of the year.

climate.precipitation_note: 56.5 mm — the lowest monthly normal of the year in Tokyo. Heavy snow continues on the Sea of Japan side, and inland Hokkaido regularly falls to around -20C.
climate.crowd_note: Falls outside all three of JNTO's named peak periods; among the least crowded months for visitors.

climate.precipitation_note: 116.0 mm. JMA describes spring as alternating cyclones and anticyclones with large short-term temperature swings.
climate.crowd_note: Demand builds sharply in the second half of the month as cherry blossom season starts: JNTO's 2026 forecast puts first bloom at 19 March in Tokyo, 24 March in Fukuoka and 26 March in Osaka.

climate.precipitation_note: 133.7 mm, with JMA noting increasing sunshine towards late spring.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest blossom weeks in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka fall in early April, with Tohoku and Hokkaido following from mid-April (Sapporo forecast around 19 April). Golden Week begins 29 April — JNTO names 29 April to 5 May and adjacent weekends as a period to avoid.

climate.precipitation_note: 139.7 mm. JMA notes the rainy season already starts in early May in Okinawa and mid-May in Amami, well before mainland Japan.
climate.crowd_note: Golden Week (29 April to 5 May plus adjacent weekends) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid; after it, mid and late May is one of the best-value stretches of the year. Kushiro's late-blooming cherries are forecast around 5 May.

climate.precipitation_note: 167.8 mm. The Baiu rainy season begins in the Kanto/Koshin region around 7 June on the JMA 1991-2020 average — a cloudy, rainy early-summer period caused by a stationary front.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak period; visitor numbers are low, largely because of the rain.

climate.precipitation_note: 156.2 mm. The Kanto Baiu ends around 19 July on average (JMA), after which the North Pacific High brings intense heat — western Japan regularly exceeds 35C.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak until mid-August, but heat and humidity make long sightseeing days hard work.

climate.precipitation_note: 154.7 mm. JMA records August as the peak of typhoon formation (5.7 per month on the 1991-2020 average) and the hottest month.
climate.crowd_note: The week centred on 15 August (Obon) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid — domestic travel and transport are heavily booked. Combined with the heat and typhoon risk, this is the hardest month to visit.

climate.precipitation_note: 224.9 mm. JMA notes September brings heavy rain from the autumnal front and from tropical cyclones, with typhoon formation still near its annual peak.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods. Autumn colour begins in northern Hokkaido and the high mountains from late September.

climate.precipitation_note: 234.8 mm — the highest monthly normal in Tokyo, inflated by late-season tropical cyclones, though JMA describes October itself as generally sunny under frequent anticyclones.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods; comfortable temperatures and the start of the autumn-colour season working south from Hokkaido.

climate.precipitation_note: 96.3 mm — dry and settled in Tokyo, though JMA notes cold northwesterly flows and rising precipitation on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO calls November the best month to see autumn colour in most of Japan, so famous temple gardens and mountain areas get busy — but it is not one of JNTO's three named domestic travel peaks.

climate.precipitation_note: 57.9 mm — among the driest months in Tokyo, with heavy snow starting on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and clear until about 27 December, when JNTO's New Year peak period (27 December to 4 January) begins and many businesses close.

timezone_note: Jordan has a single nationwide zone (IANA Asia/Amman). Jordan used to move between UTC+2 in winter and UTC+3 in summer, but the IANA time zone database records that Jordan's Council of Ministers decided on 5 October 2022 that daylight saving time would apply throughout the year, which IANA models as a switch from summer time to plain UTC+3 at 00:00 on 28 October 2022 with no further changes in the zone. Jordan therefore stays at UTC+3 all year and does not change its clocks. Source is the IANA tz database 'asia' file; no Jordanian government page announcing the decision could be opened. The Jordan Tourism Board's 'Just the Facts' page also lists the time zone as GMT+03:00.
passport_validity_rule: Global Affairs Canada states a passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond your planned departure from Jordan and notes airlines may apply stricter rules. UK FCDO words it as an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive. The two differ only in the counting basis; the stricter reading (six months beyond departure) is encoded. FCDO does not mention blank pages and no source consulted states a blank-page requirement. Jordan's own immigration pages (moi.gov.jo) do not publish the rule, so this is sourced from foreign governments' pages about Jordan rather than first-hand from a Jordanian authority.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa: Jordan's Ministry of Interior e-services page (moi.gov.jo) lists e-applications for visit, transit, exit/entry, study and work visas but states no fees, durations or on-arrival rules, and its separate list names 53 'restricted' nationalities that need prior approval (none of the eight passports NextStamp models is on it; check the list for others). On fees and stay length the sources differ. FCDO: a single-entry visit visa costs 40 JOD, valid 3 months, bought on arrival at a Jordanian airport or at the Sheikh Hussein (North Border) crossing. The Jordan Tourism Board's border-crossing page: 40 JOD single entry, valid one month and extendable at the nearest police station, or a six-month multiple-entry visa at 120 JOD (not extendable), and says all crossing rules are subject to change. Global Affairs Canada: a tourist visa is required, valid 3 months, and visas on arrival are issued only at international airports, Sheikh Hussein and Wadi Araba (Aqaba); at the King Hussein (Allenby) Bridge you must have the visa online or from a Jordanian mission beforehand. The tourism board's page says the Wadi Araba and Allenby crossings need a visa arranged in advance, which contradicts Global Affairs Canada on Wadi Araba: arrange the visa before using any land crossing. Jordan Pass (jordanpass.jo): 70 JOD (Wanderer, 1 day at Petra), 75 JOD (Explorer, 2 consecutive Petra days) or 80 JOD (Expert, 3 consecutive Petra days), with entry to over 40 attractions. Tourist entry visa fees are waived if the pass is bought before arriving and you stay a minimum of two nights (3 days) per the pass site; FCDO says at least 3 nights. The pass site says it must be used within 3 months of purchase and expires 1 month after its first scan at an attraction (FCDO says valid 3 months from entry). The pass site names Queen Alia Airport and Sheikh Hussein Bridge as visa-on-arrival points and says to show the pass at the airport visa office. Other stated rules: departure tax 10 JOD in cash at land borders, not at airports (tourism board, FCDO); an HIV test (20 JOD per FCDO) for stays over 30 days; FCDO says stays over 14 days need police registration within 14 days (fine 200 JOD), while Global Affairs Canada says to request registration within 13 days or be fined on departure, so register early; drones need a permit applied for at least 10 working days ahead (FCDO). A yellow fever certificate is required only when arriving from a country with yellow fever transmission risk (CDC). No source consulted states a currency-declaration threshold, an arrival card, proof of funds, a hotel booking or an onward ticket. Regional security (read both before booking): FCDO (updated 10 September 2026, current at 19 October 2026) advises against all travel to within 3km of the border with Syria and lists no other area; it reports Iranian strikes and retaliatory attacks across the region including Jordan from 8 July, renewed attacks and interceptions in and around Aqaba in early September, warns of a risk of more attacks and escalation, says the greatest risk is falling debris from intercepts, advises being ready for flight cancellations and airspace closures at short notice, and says travel insurance could be invalidated if you travel against FCDO advice. Global Affairs Canada (updated 16 October 2026): exercise a high degree of caution overall; avoid all travel within 5km of the Iraq and Syria borders and east of Ruwaished including Highway 10 past Ruwaished; avoid non-essential travel to Zarqa governorate and western Mafraq governorate; stay vigilant around Aqaba Port and King Hussein International Airport in Aqaba. These advisories can change within days, so re-check both before departure. The Jordan Ministry of Interior and Public Security Directorate pages could not supply fees or registration rules (psd.gov.jo refused connection), so the figures above are from the Jordan Tourism Board, jordanpass.jo and foreign governments, and should be confirmed with a Jordanian mission or moi.gov.jo before travel.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever: certificate required for travellers aged 1 year and older arriving from, or with a layover or transit of more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from the United States (CDC)
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Typhoid
Measles-Mumps-Rubella (MMR)
Rabies (pre-exposure, discuss with a clinician; CDC notes infected dogs are common)
Routine vaccines (COVID-19, influenza, polio, DTaP/Tdap, chickenpox, shingles)
health.notes: The only vaccination condition of entry found is the yellow fever certificate for arrivals from transmission-risk countries (CDC; Global Affairs Canada says there is no yellow fever risk in Jordan and does not recommend the vaccine; UK FCDO lists no required vaccines). Everything else listed is advice, not an entry condition. CDC's page (reviewed 25 August 2026) carries no malaria recommendation for Jordan and only links to a separate resource, so no malaria risk level is asserted. FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both list MERS (Middle East respiratory syndrome) as a risk; Global Affairs Canada advises avoiding camels and camel products and notes rabies is present. FCDO says medical facilities outside Amman and Aqaba are basic; Global Affairs Canada says modern care is available in Amman, immediate payment is often required, and medical evacuation can be costly, so insurance covering evacuation is advised. FCDO also warns that methanol poisoning is a risk and that even small amounts can kill. Stays over 30 days require an HIV test (FCDO). Jordan's Ministry of Health site (moh.gov.jo) states its content is not available in English and its pages opened list no entry vaccination rule for visitors.

money.atm_notes: FCDO says cash machines are mainly available in Amman and major cities. The Jordan Tourism Board says currency can be exchanged at major banks, exchange booths and most hotels, and that street money-changers are best avoided. The dinar is divided into 100 piasters or 1,000 fils (tourism board). The tourism board's page does not mention ATMs or card acceptance.

power.adapter_note: The Jordan Tourism Board's 'Just the Facts' page states 220 AC volts, 50 cycles, requiring rounded two-prong wall plugs, and says visitors from the US will need a transformer, which most hotels can provide. It gives no plug type letters, so plug types are left null; check your devices' input range and bring an adaptor for two-round-pin sockets.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Getting help page lists 911 for ambulance, fire and police, and its safety page gives 911 for police and for Civil Defence (flash floods). Global Affairs Canada also says to dial 911 for emergency assistance and lists no separate police, ambulance, fire or tourist-police numbers. No official source consulted lists a tourist police number, so it is left null. Jordan's Public Security Directorate site (psd.gov.jo) refused connection, so these are foreign-government sources rather than first-hand Jordanian ones. No source states whether English is answered. Canada's embassy in Amman: +962 6 590 1500 (ext. 3341 or 3342) in business hours (Global Affairs Canada).

getting_around.summary: Per the Jordan Tourism Board: yellow private taxis can be hailed or found outside larger hotels and the drivers usually speak English; white service taxis share rides on fixed routes. Taxis have meters but they are not always used after 11pm, so agree the fare beforehand. Careem operates in Amman, Irbid, Zarqa, Madaba and Salt; Uber and Jeeny are also listed. JETT (Jordan Express Tourist Transport, Amman 7th Circle) and other tourist-transport firms run trips to Petra, the Dead Sea and Ma'in Hot Springs, some daily and some weekly; the board publishes no fares or timetables, so ask the operator or your hotel. For driving, a licence valid in your country of origin is accepted if held for at least one year; driving is on the right; fuel is plentiful in cities and on most highways but not on the Dead Sea to Aqaba road, so fill up before long drives. Land crossings have their own hours and visa rules (see entry notes). The Hejaz Railway is described by the board only as history; no current passenger rail service was found, and no official journey times or fares were opened for this record.

passes.name: Jordan Pass
passes.covers: Official sightseeing pass sold at jordanpass.jo: entry to over 40 attractions including Petra (70 JOD for 1 Petra day, 75 JOD for 2 consecutive days, 80 JOD for 3 consecutive days) and the tourist entry visa fee, if bought before arrival and you stay at least two nights. Not a transport pass.
passes.worth_it: Depends on how many included sites you visit; no official source states a break-even, so none is given. The visa-fee waiver only works if the pass is bought before arriving. Check the included-attractions list at jordanpass.jo against your plan.

timezone_note: Kenya uses a single time zone, Africa/Nairobi (East Africa Time, UTC+3), all year, per the IANA tz database. No Kenyan government page was opened for this guide that states the offset, so the label rests on IANA rather than on a first-hand Kenyan citation.
passport_validity_rule: Passport must be valid for at least 6 months from the date you enter Kenya. The Kenya eTA portal's document list says: 'Valid passport (minimum 6 months validity with at least one blank page)'. The UK FCDO says the passport must expire 'at least 6 months after the date you arrive' and have 'at least 2 blank pages'; Global Affairs Canada says 'at least 6 months from the date of entry into Kenya'. Blank pages: the destination's own eTA page says one, FCDO says two, so two is stored as the safer figure and the eTA portal's one is the stated minimum.
entry_requirement_notes: ETA (IN FORCE): Kenya has an Electronic Travel Authorisation, applied for only through the official site (etakenya.go.ke) or the 'Kenya Travel Authorisation' app, one application per traveller including children and infants; the portal says you may travel only after approval and must present the approved eTA at departure and arrival. Global Affairs Canada says tourists do not need a visa but must apply for an eTA before departure, and the only exemption it names is transiting an airport without passing border control. FCDO says to apply online in advance and the portal recommends at least two weeks before travel. Processing: the eTA FAQ says normal applications are generally processed within three business days (72 hours) though verification can take longer, expedited applications are processed immediately. FEE: the FAQ says normal processing 'starts at $30' and expedited processing costs an additional $100; the General Information page does not state a fee and neither FCDO nor Global Affairs Canada states one. eTA validity period and permitted stay for a standard eTA holder are NOT stated on any page opened, so they are not given here. The portal lists exempt groups with stay limits (East African Community partner-state citizens up to 180 days, a long list of countries up to 90 days, listed African countries up to 60 days); possession of an eTA is 'not the final authority to enter' and admissibility is decided at the port of entry. Documents the portal asks for: passport, a selfie or passport-type photo, contact details, travel itinerary (arrival and departure), accommodation booking confirmation and a payment method. MANDATORY KENYAN TRAVEL HEALTH INSURANCE (reported in force from 5 October 2026): FCDO says most travellers visiting for less than 12 months must have Kenyan Government-provided travel health insurance from 5 October 2026, that foreign policies are not accepted instead, that it is valid for 90 days with multiple entries, and that it is bought during the eTA application or, for someone who already holds a valid eTA, through the eCitizen insurance portal; exempt are Kenyan citizens, holders of valid Kenyan residence status, East African Community partner-state citizens and transit passengers who do not pass Kenyan immigration. Global Affairs Canada says 'As of October 5, 2026, the eTA application includes a mandatory travel health insurance' for stays under 12 months. No Kenyan government page opened for this guide (the eTA portal's How to Apply and FAQ pages do not mention it) states the rule, the price or the cover, so the price and benefit limits are deliberately not given; some press reports mention a court challenge, which no official page opened here confirms or rules out, so check etakenya.go.ke and the airline before departure. EBOLA (changing situation): FCDO's health page says that on 6 October 2026 the Kenyan Ministry of Health confirmed its first imported case of Ebola, and its entry-requirements page says travellers arriving from Uganda, Ethiopia or the Democratic Republic of the Congo may face enhanced health screening; Global Affairs Canada (updated 15 October 2026) says a case was reported in Nairobi linked to the ongoing outbreak in the DRC and advises monitoring your health in Kenya and for 21 days after leaving. The CDC Kenya page (last reviewed 25 August 2026) pre-dates this and carries no Ebola alert. Re-check before travel. YELLOW FEVER certificate: see health. CURRENCY: Global Affairs Canada says amounts exceeding the equivalent of USD 10 000 must be declared to customs on both arrival and departure; the FCDO page does not mention a currency rule. CUSTOMS AND DRONES: FCDO says to declare anything that may be prohibited or taxable and that importing or exporting a drone needs prior approval from the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority. PHOTOGRAPHY: FCDO says it is illegal to photograph official buildings including embassies, or airports. ONWARD TICKET: not stated on any official page opened (the eTA asks for an itinerary with arrival and departure details and accommodation, which is not the same as a ticket requirement), so left null; carry a return or onward booking anyway. SAFETY ADVISORIES: FCDO advises against all travel to Mandera County, Tarbaj and Wajir East constituencies (except Wajir Town), areas of Wajir County within 60 km of the Somali border, most of Garissa County and Lamu County (except Lamu and Manda islands), and against all but essential travel to Garissa Town, Tana River County north of the Tana River as far as Saka, and areas within 15 km of the coast between the Tana and Galana rivers, because of terrorism from Somalia-based groups. FCDO page updated 16 October 2026. NOT VERIFIED: Kenya Wildlife Service park fees could not be sourced from an official page (kws.go.ke fee page failed certificate verification and the Magical Kenya and Kenya Airports Authority pages returned 403), so no park fee is stated.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate if you are arriving from a country listed as a yellow fever transmission risk (UK FCDO, Global Affairs Canada, CDC); CDC says required for travellers aged 1 year and older arriving from risk countries and not required for direct travel from the US; Kenyan authorities spot-check, so carry the proof (Global Affairs Canada)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (varicella, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)

Yellow fever vaccine for travellers aged 9 months and older (CDC), except those whose travel is limited to Nairobi, Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa or Tana River counties; Taita-Taveta is not part of that exception
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 year and older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Typhoid (recommended for most travellers)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Meningococcal (2 months and older visiting meningitis-belt areas in the dry season, about December to June)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be discussed with a provider)
Cholera (may be considered for travel to areas of active transmission: Garissa, Migori, Mombasa, Nairobi, Narok and Turkana counties)
Mpox (only for adults with certain anticipated activities)
health.malaria_risk: CDC says malaria transmission occurs in all areas of Kenya below 2,500 m (8,200 ft), including game parks, with cases rare in the highly urbanized central part of Nairobi; mainly P. falciparum, with chloroquine resistance noted. CDC recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine for risk areas, and insect-bite precautions only for central Nairobi. Global Affairs Canada says antimalarials may be recommended depending on itinerary and dates; consult a health professional ideally about 6 weeks before travel. Several medicines must be started days before travel.
health.notes: ENTRY: FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say a yellow fever vaccination certificate is needed when arriving from a transmission-risk country; FCDO links to a list and Global Affairs Canada recommends carrying a copy because authorities spot-check. The Kenyan Ministry of Health's own page (health.go.ke) could not be fetched (certificate error) and the Kenya Airports Authority page returned 403, so the Kenyan primary text and its list of risk countries was not read: check the WHO list of countries with yellow fever risk. Do not rely on press reports about a 10-day rule or transit hours. EBOLA: see entry_requirement_notes; Global Affairs Canada advises monitoring your health for 21 days after leaving Kenya. OTHER RISKS: FCDO lists malaria, dengue, Zika, schistosomiasis, mpox and altitude sickness. FCDO says medicines legal in the UK may be regulated differently in Kenya, and that you should check travel insurance covers local treatment and medical evacuation. CDC malaria and yellow fever sections were updated 23 April 2025 and the page last reviewed 25 August 2026. All of this is medical information, not advice.

emergency.notes: Global Affairs Canada says 'Dial 999 or 112 for emergency assistance' (page updated 15 October 2026) and does not list separate police, ambulance or fire numbers. FCDO's health page says 'Dial 999 and ask for an ambulance'. 999 is therefore stored for police and ambulance and 112 as the general number; no page opened gave a fire-brigade number, so fire is left empty rather than guessed, and no tourist-police number was confirmed. FCDO's safety page says the Kenya Tourism Federation Safety and Communication Center offers tourist advice and emergency help but gives no number.

timezone_note: One offset nationwide, all year. The Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism's tourism site (tourismlaos.org) gives the time zone as GMT+7. In the IANA time zone database Asia/Vientiane is a link to Asia/Bangkok, so the clock is identical to Thailand's.
passport_validity_rule: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from the date you arrive in Laos. The Lao e-visa portal's terms (laoevisa.gov.la) say at least 6 months beyond the arrival date and its FAQ says more than 180 days from arrival; the UK FCDO says an expiry date at least 6 months after arrival. Global Affairs Canada words it as 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Laos, which is stricter on a long stay, so a passport with comfortably more than 6 months after your departure date satisfies every version. Blank pages: the FCDO states at least 2 blank pages (and airlines may refuse boarding without enough); the e-visa terms say at least one blank page and room for the return trip.
entry_requirement_notes: A visa is required for tourism (UK FCDO; Global Affairs Canada). E-VISA: apply at laoevisa.gov.la; single entry only, accepted at 9 ports of entry: Wattay International Airport (Vientiane), Lao-Thai Friendship Bridge I (Vientiane), Luang Prabang International Airport, Lao-Thai Friendship Bridge II (Savannakhet), Pakse International Airport, Lao-Thai Friendship Bridge IV (Bokeo), Boten International Checkpoint, Boten Railway Station (Luang Namtha) and Khamsavath Railway Station (Vientiane). The portal says processing is within 3 working days of a complete application and full payment; the FCDO advises applying at least 5 days in advance, so allow the longer. Needs a 4x6 cm ICAO-standard photo taken within the last 6 months and a scan of the passport bio page including the two MRZ lines. The e-visa fee is per applicant, excludes bank charges and is non-refundable whether the application is approved, denied or cancelled; the amount is shown only in the portal's fee calculator, which could not be read, so no figure is given here. The approval letter is valid for entry for 60 days and the stay runs 30 days from arrival (portal FAQ and terms). If you enter at a port without e-visa service you must get a visa on arrival and the e-visa fee is not refunded. Eligibility is limited to nationalities on the portal's 'eligible countries' list, which was not readable here. VISA ON ARRIVAL: single entry at many entry points including Vientiane Wattay airport, Luang Prabang airport and Pakse airport (FCDO); Global Affairs Canada says bring a passport photo and pay a fee on arrival. No official fee figure could be confirmed, and some nationalities are visa-exempt under bilateral rules that were not checked here. STAY AND EXTENSION: the FCDO says tourist visas are for 30 days from arrival (from 1 January 2025) and can be extended twice in Laos for a total of 60 additional days. Overstay: the FCDO says a fine in Lao kip worth US$2,000, deportation and a ban on returning. Get an entry stamp on arrival: Global Affairs Canada says a missing stamp can mean fines, detention or deportation. LAO DIGITAL IMMIGRATION FORM (LDIF): the FCDO says it is mandatory for all foreign nationals, to be completed digitally within 3 days before arrival (and before departure), and that it does not replace visa requirements; Global Affairs Canada says paper forms can still be completed on arrival or departure and online forms must be submitted within 3 days. Customs: the FCDO says rules are strict and anything that may be prohibited or taxable must be declared; it states no currency-declaration threshold, and none could be confirmed from an official source. Onward ticket and proof of funds: neither the FCDO, Global Affairs Canada nor the e-visa portal's FAQ states a requirement, so it is left unconfirmed; carry a return booking anyway. DRUGS AND VAPES: the FCDO says zero tolerance for drugs including cannabis and that e-cigarettes and vapes are illegal, with possession punishable by fines or imprisonment. REGIONAL ADVICE: as of the FCDO page last updated 13 August 2026, it advises against all but essential travel to Xaisomboun Province (attacks on infrastructure and armed clashes), notes the Thailand-Cambodia land crossings remain suspended after fighting in 2025, and warns of airspace disruption linked to the Middle East.

required_vaccinations: None required for entry. CDC states a yellow fever vaccine is not required and not recommended for Laos; the UK FCDO's entry page states no health entry requirement.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, influenza, varicella, shingles)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Measles (MMR), including an early dose for infants 6 to 11 months
Polio (CDC notes poliovirus has been identified in Laos in the past year)
Typhoid (recommended for most travellers)
Japanese encephalitis (for a month or more, or frequent travel, or higher-risk rural activities)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the southern provinces of Attapeu, Champasak, Khammouane, Salavan, Savannakhet and Sekong, where CDC recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline or tafenoquine. Rare cases in the north, where only bite precautions are advised. No malaria transmission in Luang Prabang or Vientiane (CDC). Chloroquine and mefloquine resistance is reported.
health.notes: CDC also lists leptospirosis and melioidosis (avoid floodwater and muddy soil), schistosomiasis (avoid fresh water swimming), dengue, Zika, hantavirus, tuberculosis, and commonly rabid dogs, and warns that motorbike crashes are a leading cause of death; it recommends medical evacuation insurance because trauma care is uncommon outside urban areas. The UK FCDO says dengue and malaria are endemic (dengue rises in the rainy season), warns of anthrax in cattle and buffalo near the 4,000 Islands, Pakse and the Bolaven Plateau, notes air pollution can worsen heart and lung conditions, and says care outside the capital is limited with no reliable emergency facilities and medical evacuation is difficult and costly. Global Affairs Canada says medical facilities are scarce and below Canadian standards, basic care is available in Vientiane and Luang Prabang, and complex cases need evacuation to Thailand. You may be asked to pay upfront. The FCDO says only trust responders in uniforms marked Vientiane Rescue or Lao Red Cross, as bogus companies have charged fees. The FCDO also warns that methanol cannot be detected by taste or smell and that authorities have banned Tiger Vodka and Tiger Whisky.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada says major credit cards are accepted at some international hotels and tourist businesses. The Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism's tourism site says Visa, Mastercard and American Express are accepted mainly in larger hotels, restaurants and souvenir shops in big cities such as Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Savannakhet and Champasak. Global Affairs Canada warns that card and ATM fraud occurs frequently.
money.cash_culture: The kip (LAK) is the official currency, with notes in circulation from 500 to 100,000 kip (tourismlaos.org). Global Affairs Canada says the kip is not easily obtained outside Laos and that US dollars and Thai baht are commonly accepted; tourismlaos.org says US dollars, euros and Thai baht are the best currencies to bring for exchange, at banks, airports or foreign exchange offices. The tourism site names the EzyKip app and LOCA Pay (links a card to Lao standard QR codes) as payment options.
money.atm_notes: Global Affairs Canada says ATMs are widely available and cash advances are available at some banks but with high commission. It advises using ATMs in public areas or inside banks and covering the keypad. No official ATM limits or fees are quoted here.

emergency.notes: Police 1191, ambulance 1195 and fire 1190 are given by both the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada. The FCDO also lists a second ambulance number, 030 525 7239; Vientiane Rescue 1623 or 020 5666 8825; Lao Red Cross Rescue 020 5996 6111 or 020 2200 5563; and alternative Vientiane police station lines 241162, 241163, 241164 and 212703. The tourist police number 021 251 128 is for Vientiane. The FCDO gives +856 20 5666 9090 as the number to report road accidents to the police. No universal 112-style number is published by the sources read. The FCDO says local police responses may be limited. Canada's embassy in Vientiane: +856 21 35 38 34.

getting_around.summary: The tourism site (tourismlaos.org) says Wattay International Airport (Vientiane) has flights to regional destinations including Bangkok, Hanoi, Kunming and Singapore, Luang Prabang International Airport has international flights including to Bangkok and Hanoi, and Pakse flies to Phnom Penh and Ho Chi Minh City. It lists land crossings with Thailand (Friendship Bridges I-IV, Thanaleng), China (Lantuy, Boten and the Lao-China Railway crossing in Luang Namtha), Vietnam, Cambodia (Nong Nok Khian) and Myanmar, and rail border stations at Thanaleng (to Thailand) and the Lao-China Railway crossing (to Bohan, Yunnan); the e-visa portal lists Boten and Khamsavath railway stations as e-visa entry points. The Lao-China railway timetable and fares are not on any page read here, so none are given: check the operator. The FCDO describes the China-Laos Expressway between Vientiane and Vang Vieng as the country's first high-speed road with limits of 80 to 120 km/h. ROAD AND RIVER SAFETY: the FCDO says roads are often poor, driving after dark greatly raises risk because many vehicles lack lights, livestock strays onto roads, rental motorbikes may not include helmets, and Mekong river levels and currents change quickly (avoid overcrowded boats; check life jackets). You need a 1949 International Driving Permit to drive. Global Affairs Canada advises hiring a driver, avoiding travel after dark, and never leaving your passport as rental collateral. UNEXPLODED ORDNANCE (UXO): the FCDO says landmines and unexploded weapons kill a number of people each year; keep to main routes in rural areas and do not pick up metal objects; the risk is higher after floods or landslides. Global Affairs Canada says the risk is throughout the country but particularly at the Plain of Jars site, in Xiengkhouang province and in the Lao-Vietnam border areas; stay on main roads, avoid walking in fields, roadside ditches and unmarked trails, and report suspicious items to local authorities.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: No official source read states SIM or eSIM availability or prices. The tourism site (tourismlaos.org) names the LOCA app for taxis and electric motorbikes. The FCDO notes that remote roads can have limited mobile coverage in the rainy season.

timezone_note: Tourism Malaysia states Malaysia is 8 hours ahead of GMT (GMT+8), and the WMO World Weather Information Service lists Kuala Lumpur at +0800 with no daylight saving. Peninsular and East Malaysia share this one time zone.
passport_validity_rule: Passport must be valid for at least six months from the date of entry. The Immigration Department of Malaysia's MYVISA portal (announcement dated 28 September 2026) says: all foreign nationals must register the MDAC within 3 days before arriving, and the passport must be valid for at least six (6) months from the date of entry. The UK FCDO gives the same reading (expiry at least 6 months after arrival; passport undamaged with no pages missing). Global Affairs Canada words it more strictly, at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Malaysia, and a Malaysian consulate's visa-application page also counts from departure; for a longer stay that reading asks for more, and airlines may apply stricter checks, so a passport with a margin beyond that is safest.
entry_requirement_notes: Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC): all foreign nationals travelling to Malaysia must complete it online, up to 3 days before arrival (Immigration Department MYVISA announcement of 28 September 2026; Tourism Malaysia and the Malaysian consulate in Vancouver give the same 3-day window). Exempt: citizens of Singapore, diplomatic and official passport holders, Malaysian permanent residents and long-term pass holders, Brunei GCI holders, Brunei-Malaysia Frequent Traveller Facility holders, Thailand Border Pass holders and Indonesia Cross-Border Pass (PLB) holders. It is free (Global Affairs Canada, which warns against third-party sites that charge fees for arrival cards), is not a visa, and a visa-requiring traveller must still get one separately. Submit it before travel at imigresen-online.imi.gov.my/mdac/main; the UK FCDO notes airlines may ask for it at check-in, and travellers show a valid passport and the completed MDAC to border officers. Visa-free stay length depends on nationality (the UK FCDO says British citizens are normally allowed 90 days for tourism); longer stays and non-tourist purposes need a visa from a Malaysian mission before travel, and the eVisa portal is malaysiavisa.imi.gov.my. Onward ticket and funds: the eVisa portal lists a round-trip flight ticket or proof of journey, proof of paid accommodation and proof of financial support among documents for visa applicants, but no Malaysian, UK or Canadian page found states an onward-ticket or proof-of-funds rule for visa-free arrivals, so onward_ticket_required is left null; carrying a return or onward booking is sensible, since the immigration officer makes the final decision. Cash: the Royal Malaysian Customs Department says to declare cash and bearer negotiable instruments of USD 10,000 or more on Customs Form No. 7 (the Immigration MDAC page words it as more than USD 10,000, so declare at the threshold); importing or exporting ringgit needs written Bank Negara Malaysia permission; the penalty can be a fine up to RM3 million, up to 5 years in prison, or both. Duty-free alcohol is up to 1 litre in total (RMCD). Yellow fever: a certificate is required if you are arriving from, or have transited more than 12 hours through, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission (CDC; UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say the same in general terms); not required for direct travel from the US. The UK FCDO also warns that officials may require a urine drug test on arrival and that Malaysia has a zero-tolerance drug policy, and that overstaying even briefly can bring fines, detention or a re-entry ban.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from, or after a layover of more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, for travellers aged 1 year or older; not required for direct travel from the United States, and the CDC does not recommend the vaccine for travel to Malaysia itself)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, polio, influenza, chickenpox, shingles)

health.malaria_risk: Localised. The CDC reports zoonotic transmission of P. knowlesi malaria in rural, forested areas, with prevention medicine (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine) advised for those areas. It reports no malaria transmission in other areas, including Kuala Lumpur and Penang State (Penang Island and George Town).
health.notes: None of these is checked at the Malaysian border for an ordinary arrival; the only vaccination that can be required on entry is yellow fever, and only for arrivals from risk countries. Dengue is a year-round risk in many parts of the world and the CDC advises preventing mosquito bites; chikungunya and Zika are also present. The CDC reports increased human rabies cases in Sarawak. Global Affairs Canada notes good medical care is mainly in major cities and payment is expected at the time of service; the UK FCDO says government and private hospitals charge for all services, so travel insurance with medical evacuation cover is effectively essential. The UK FCDO also notes forest-fire haze from Indonesia can occur between June and October. In an emergency call 999 and ask for an ambulance (UK FCDO).

money.card_acceptance: Tourism Malaysia states that most hotels, shopping complexes, restaurants and shops accept international credit cards (Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Diners Club), and that digital payment methods such as Touch N Go, GrabPay and Boost, plus bank transfers, are widely used by locals and tourists. Banknotes are RM1, 5, 10, 20, 50 and 100; coins are 5, 10, 20 and 50 sen.
money.atm_notes: Card and ATM fraud is widespread (UK FCDO). Global Affairs Canada advises using ATMs in well-lit public areas or inside a bank or business, covering the keypad when entering your PIN, avoiding card readers with an irregular or unusual feature, watching your card when others handle it, and checking statements for unauthorised transactions; it reports card skimming has occurred, including at international hotels. Cash and bearer instruments of USD 10,000 or more must be declared on entry (see entry notes).

power.adapter_note: Tourism Malaysia states the supply is 240V at 50 Hz and that a standard 3-pin plug and socket is commonly used. Malaysia's Energy Commission (Suruhanjaya Tenaga) lists the permitted plug tops as the 13A fused plug (MS 589-1 / BS 1363-1), a 15A round-pin plug (MS 1577) and a 2-pin 2.5A plug for non-metallic-body equipment; BS 1363 is the UK-style plug usually labelled Type G, a letter neither source prints. Travellers from the UK need no adapter; others from 220-240V countries need a plug adapter if their plug shape differs. Travellers from 100-127V countries (US, Canada, Japan) need equipment rated for 240V or a converter; most modern phone and laptop chargers are dual-voltage, but check the label.

emergency.notes: Tourism Malaysia: dial 999 for ambulance and police and 994 for fire; Global Affairs Canada gives 999 as the general emergency number and the UK FCDO says call 999 and ask for an ambulance. Tourism Malaysia's Tourism Infoline is 1300 885 050 for tourism enquiries, not emergencies. A tourist-police line, a 112 service and which lines are answered in English could not be confirmed from an official source, so they are not listed.

getting_around.summary: Tourism Malaysia advises using only transport services and tour operators licensed by the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture and licensed guides, and notes that cashless e-wallets such as Touch N Go are widely used. The UK FCDO advises: at airports pay for taxis with the fixed-price coupon from the terminal counter, and elsewhere taxis should use a meter; motorbike riders do not always stop at traffic lights or pedestrian crossings and helmets are required for rented motorbikes; several fatal bus crashes have occurred, especially on overnight journeys, so choose a reputable operator; road conditions in East Malaysia are poorer than in Peninsular Malaysia; British visitors driving need a 1949 international driving permit as well as a UK licence. Carry your passport when travelling between Peninsular and East Malaysia, as you pass through immigration control (UK FCDO). Rail, metro and ferry timetables and passes were not researched from an official operator page here, so none are listed.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Tourism Malaysia names CelcomDigi, Maxis, Umobile and Tune Talk as the main telecom operators, says prepaid SIM cards can be bought easily at airports, malls and city centres, and that traveller SIM packages with preloaded credit, call minutes and data are available. It also says free WiFi is available in shopping centres, terminals and cafes, though some networks require a sign-in or registration.
