phrases_language: Afrikaans only, a small sample for greetings and basic needs, each labelled. These phrases were written from general knowledge, not taken from an official page, and no Namibian government page opened for this guide states which languages are official or most spoken, so the choice of Afrikaans (widely understood in Namibia) and the status of English are not sourced here. Namibia has many other languages (for example Oshiwambo, Otjiherero, Khoekhoegowab and German) that are not covered.

timezone_note: One zone for the whole country, offset by 45 minutes from the half-hour zones: 15 minutes ahead of India (UTC+5:30) and 5 hours 45 minutes ahead of UTC, with no daylight saving. The odd offset is the IANA Asia/Kathmandu rule, which this record follows.
passport_validity_rule: Nepal's Department of Immigration says the passport must be valid for at least 6 months prior to the date of travel (and the uploaded passport scan valid 6 months or more). The UK FCDO says the passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after your date of entry; Global Affairs Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Nepal. The wordings differ, so have 6 months beyond your planned departure date to satisfy all three. No minimum blank pages is published.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA. Nepal's Department of Immigration (DoI) says tourist visas are available on arrival at Tribhuvan International Airport (TIA) and other designated entry points, or from a Nepali diplomatic mission before travel, or by online application. DoI's visa page gives the on-arrival fees as US$30 for 15 days, US$50 for 30 days and US$125 for 90 days, all multiple-entry and counted from the day of entry. DoI's three-step on-arrival process: fill in the arrival card and online tourist-visa form (on its website before arrival or at kiosks at TIA), print the receipt with barcode (valid 15 days), pay at the bank counter ("carrying some cash is advised"), then present form, receipt and passport at the immigration desk. DoI's eVisa/ETA page offers an online route through the Nepali Port portal (pay by card in US dollars; approved visa sent by email; print and carry it) and says a visa must be used within 6 months of issue, cannot be withdrawn once issued and the fee is non-refundable. The UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both state a visa is required for visits of up to 90 days. STAY LIMIT AND EXTENSION. DoI: a tourist visa can be extended inside Nepal at the Department of Immigration in Kathmandu or the Immigration Office in Pokhara at US$3 a day (minimum 15 days) up to a combined maximum of 150 days per visa year (January to December); overstay is fined US$5 a day and a re-entry add-on of US$25 is listed. FCDO: overstaying is a serious crime. WHO DOES NOT NEED, OR CANNOT GET, A VISA ON ARRIVAL. DoI states Indian citizens do not require a visa. It lists free (gratis) visas for children under 10, SAARC citizens (except Afghanistan) for up to 30 days on a first visit in a visa year, Chinese nationals and NRN card holders. DoI's list of passports that cannot get a visa on arrival and must apply at a Nepali mission in advance: Nigeria, Ghana, Zimbabwe, Swaziland, Cameroon, Somalia, Liberia, Ethiopia, Iraq, Palestine, Afghanistan, Syria; Nepal Tourism Board's (NTB) visa page also names Iran and refugees with travel documents, so the two official lists differ. US PASSPORTS: DoI's fee table separately lists a 'reciprocity' tourist visa for US citizens (US$160, five years, 180 days of stay per year; documents listed include a bank statement of at least US$10,000, a health-insurance certificate and a police report), and its gratis-visa note for children excludes US citizens. Whether that US visa replaces the 15/30/90-day on-arrival visa for a US passport holder on an ordinary short trip could not be confirmed from the pages opened, so check with DoI or a Nepali mission before travel. PASSPORT VALIDITY. DoI's eVisa page says the passport must be valid for at least 6 months prior to the date of travel and the scanned passport copy uploaded must be valid 6 months or more; FCDO says the expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date of entry; Global Affairs Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Nepal. These wordings differ, so the record uses 6 months from entry as the stated minimum and recommends having 6 months beyond your planned departure to satisfy all three. No minimum number of blank pages is published by any source opened. ONWARD TICKET: neither DoI, NTB, FCDO nor Global Affairs Canada states an onward or return ticket requirement, so onward_ticket_required is null (could not confirm either way). FCDO adds that at border checks you may need proof of travel insurance covering healthcare including repatriation, and proof of your first night's accommodation. MONEY AT THE BORDER. FCDO: declare on arrival any amount above US$5,000 in banknotes, or US$10,000 in notes and travellers' cheques combined; keep the certified declaration and convert all Nepali currency before leaving. Global Affairs Canada: declare more than US$5,000 in cash, taking Nepali rupee banknotes out of the country is illegal and Indian rupee notes above 100 INR are prohibited. FCDO: gold ornaments up to 50 g and silver up to 100 g may be carried; undeclared precious metals risk fines, prison or confiscation. TREKKING PERMITS - WHAT THE OFFICIAL PAGES SAY TODAY (checked 2026-10-18). There are three separate layers. (1) RESTRICTED-AREA TREKKING PERMIT (Department of Immigration): DoI's trekking-permit page (updated 8 June 2026 by the page's own date) says foreign tourists who want to trek in certain restricted areas must obtain a trekking permit from DoI, that it is issued only through a registered trekking agency via the Nepali Port system, and that the service now runs fully faceless, paperless and cashless; the agency uploads each trekker's passport and valid visa, the trekkers' and guides'/porters' insurance papers and a signed itinerary. DoI's FAQ says individual trekkers cannot get a permit for a restricted area themselves, that trekking alone is not permitted in those areas, that the passport and permit must be carried throughout, and that going anywhere other than the route or place named on the permit is prohibited. DoI's fee table (per person, USD) lists: Upper Mustang US$50 a day; Upper Dolpa US$500 for the first 10 days then US$50 a day; Gorkha-Manaslu US$100 a week in September-November (US$15 a day beyond one week) and US$75 a week in December-August (US$10 a day beyond one week); Manang US$100 a week in September-November and US$75 a week in December-August (US$15 a day beyond a week); Gorkha-Tsum Valley US$40 a week in September-November and US$30 a week in December-August (US$7 a day beyond a week); Humla US$50 a week; Mugu US$100 a week; Bajhang US$90 a week; Darchula US$90 a week; Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha and Solukhumbu (the listed Khumbu ward) US$20 a week for the first four weeks; Lower Dolpa US$20 a week; Dolakha and Rasuwa (Gosaikunda) US$20 a week. (2) TIMS CARD AND LICENSED GUIDE (Nepal Tourism Board): NTB's TIMS page says that under the 'Revised TIMS Provision effective from March 31, 2023', specific protected-area routes require the trekker to be accompanied by a licensed trekking guide and to carry an agency-issued TIMS card; the routes it lists include Everest Base Camp, Gokyo, Three Passes, Annapurna Circuit, Poon Hill-ABC, Mardi Himal, Langtang, Manaslu, Upper Mustang, Round Dhaulagiri, Kanchenjunga and Makalu. The card costs NPR 2,000 (NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals), is bought online by the agency, and an eCard with a QR code is issued per trekker. UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both repeat that a TIMS card and permit are needed in the main trekking regions and that independent trekkers must use a licensed guide or porter. IMPORTANT: some trekker information says TIMS and the Annapurna permit have been replaced by local permits; NTB's page, which carries no end date, does NOT say that. Non-official trekking-agency pages claim that local rural-municipality entry fees (for example in Khumbu) now replace TIMS in some areas, but no government page opened here confirms it, so it is not stated as fact: confirm the exact permit set for your route with a registered trekking agency and the relevant local office. (3) PROTECTED-AREA ENTRY FEES: NTB's park-fee table (foreigners, per entry) lists NPR 3,000 for Annapurna Conservation Area, Sagarmatha (Everest) National Park, Langtang National Park, Manaslu Conservation Area, Makalu-Barun, Shey-Phoksundo, Rara, Khaptad and Gaurishankar; NPR 2,000 for Chitwan National Park and Kanchenjunga Conservation Area; NPR 1,000 for Shivapuri-Nagarjun; fees can be paid at the Tourist Service Center in Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, or at park entry points, and children under 10 are free. CURRENT SITUATION (UK FCDO, latest update 1 October 2026): major flash flooding on 26 August 2026 damaged buildings, roads and communications in Rasuwa district and at the Nepal-China border, with Gorkha, Nuwakot and Dhading also affected; authorities warn of further flooding and affected areas may be unstable. FCDO also says Middle East airspace disruption has delayed or cancelled flights and that Nepal's Immigration Department says foreign nationals whose visas lapsed because of this get a free extension arranged at the airport.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever - certificate required if arriving from, or transiting, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
Polio - certificate required if arriving from certain countries with a polio transmission risk (UK FCDO; the list of countries was not published on the page opened)
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid
Japanese encephalitis (longer stays or higher-risk rural/outdoor activity)
Rabies (risk-based; infected dogs are common)
Cholera (may be considered; transmission is active but rare in travellers)
Routine vaccines including MMR/measles and COVID-19
health.malaria_risk: Limited. CDC: prophylaxis recommended only for areas under 2,000 m in Sudurpashchim and Karnali provinces; Kathmandu, Pokhara and typical Himalayan treks have no malaria transmission (CDC malaria section updated 23 April 2025). Global Affairs Canada says there is risk in certain areas or times of year.
health.notes: ALTITUDE SICKNESS (acute mountain sickness, AMS) is the main trekking health risk and the entry requirements do not screen for it. FCDO: altitude sickness is a risk in tourist and trekking areas, hazards exist all year and especially above 3,000 m, and travellers should be wary of guides who take trekkers to high altitude too quickly and then call expensive helicopter evacuations. Global Affairs Canada: acute mountain sickness can be deadly; know the symptoms and carry medical and first-aid kits. Nepal Tourism Board's 'Safety in the Mountains' page: if you feel unwell above 2,500 m treat it as AMS until proven otherwise; early symptoms are headache, loss of appetite, nausea, fatigue on minimal exertion and dizziness; severe headache, vomiting, altered mental state, severe fatigue or breathlessness at rest mean descend; stop climbing, rest and drink fluids (not alcohol); ascend slowly with a sleeping altitude no more than 300 to 500 m higher per day above 2,500 m, and a rest day for every 1,000 m gained; NTB says to consider acetazolamide (Diamox) 250 mg twice a day, which is a prescription-medicine decision to take to a clinician before travel. NTB says the Himalayan Rescue Association runs aid posts at Pheriche (4,250 m) and Manang (3,550 m) staffed by volunteer doctors during the spring and autumn trekking seasons, and an Everest ER clinic at Everest Base Camp (5,350 m). The CDC destination page opened carries no altitude-illness guidance of its own, so none is attributed to it. MEDICAL CARE AND EVACUATION (FCDO): there is no central public ambulance service; some private providers operate in main cities; healthcare is poor in most places outside the Kathmandu Valley and Pokhara; helicopter evacuation may be hard to arrange in remote areas and usually costs between GBP 1,000 and GBP 2,000 or more per flying hour, so insurance is strongly advised. FCDO's safety page: make sure your insurance covers mountain rescue services and helicopter costs. ENTRY VACCINES: FCDO states a yellow-fever certificate is needed if arriving from a country listed as a transmission risk, and a polio certificate if arriving from certain countries with a transmission risk. CDC and Global Affairs Canada both say there is no yellow fever risk in Nepal and proof is required only on arrival from or transit through a risk country (CDC includes layovers longer than 12 hours). Everything in the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. OTHER RISKS: FCDO lists dengue among Nepal's health risks and CDC says to avoid mosquito bites (repellent with 20% or more DEET), notes infected dogs are common so rabies advice matters (post-exposure vaccine may only be available at larger urban facilities), and says cholera transmission is active but rare in travellers. Global Affairs Canada notes malaria risk in certain areas and times; CDC (page updated 23 April 2025 for malaria) says Kathmandu, Pokhara and typical Himalayan treks have no malaria transmission and recommends prophylaxis only for areas under 2,000 m in Sudurpashchim and Karnali provinces.

money.tipping: Nepal Tourism Board says no tip is expected for taxis. No official source opened states tipping norms for restaurants, guides or porters, so none are asserted.
money.atm_notes: UK FCDO says ATMs and card payments may be unavailable in remote areas, so carry enough cash for flight delays on treks. Global Affairs Canada says taking Nepali rupee banknotes out of the country is illegal and that Indian rupee notes above 100 INR are prohibited; Nepal Tourism Board's tourist police advice is to exchange foreign currency only at government-authorised financial institutions. Cash over US$5,000 (or US$10,000 in notes and travellers' cheques combined, per FCDO) must be declared on arrival. No official source opened gives ATM limits or card-acceptance rates.

emergency.notes: Police 100 and the tourist police hotline 1144 are given by Nepal Tourism Board (which also lists 103 for traffic police), and Global Affairs Canada lists police 100, ambulance 102 and firefighters 101 plus tourist police 1144. UK FCDO says there is NO central public ambulance service in Nepal and tells people to go to or call the nearest hospital, so 102 is taken from Global Affairs Canada alone and may not connect everywhere; 101 for fire is likewise from Global Affairs Canada alone. Nepal Tourism Board says Tourist Police are available 24/7 inside Kathmandu Valley and Pokhara and publishes unit numbers: head office Bhrikutimandap +977 9851289445 or +977-01-5347041, Airport 9851289450, Thamel 9851289453, Pokhara 061-462761 or 9856082761, Lukla 9852821304. FCDO (1 October 2026) also says the government set up the toll-free number 1234 alongside 1144 during the August 2026 flooding. No official source confirmed a single general emergency number (such as 112), so none is shown, and no source stated whether English is answered.

getting_around.summary: Nepal Tourism Board describes government-run green Sajha buses on the main roads of Kathmandu Valley that stop only at designated stops, taxis recognisable by a sign on top and a black licence plate (no tip expected), battery-run three-wheelers, rickshaws in old Kathmandu and hired bicycles in Thamel, Jhochhen and Pokhara. Tourist buses run to Pokhara and Chitwan and other long-distance day and night buses leave from the New Bus Park at Gongabu, Kathmandu. Nepal Airlines and more than 18 other domestic airlines serve popular destinations and offer mountain flights. No official source opened gives fares, timetables or booking rules, and none lists a transport pass, so passes is empty. FCDO adds that mobile coverage is limited on long stretches of the Annapurna Circuit and that flights and roads in the hills can be disrupted by flooding and landslides.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Nepal Tourism Board says to bring an extra passport photo to get a local SIM card at the arrival halls of Kathmandu's international airport, and that mobile carriers have service centres elsewhere and at road borders. FCDO says mobile coverage is limited on long stretches of the Annapurna Circuit and suggests considering a satellite phone.

climate.precipitation_note: Base period not disclosed: temperatures and rainfall are from the World Meteorological Organization's World Weather Information Service record for Kathmandu, whose monthly figures carry a submission date of 30 April 2001 and no stated base period; Nepal's own Department of Hydrology and Meteorology normals page (dhm.gov.np, 1991-2020 layer) returned an error when queried and its data is sold on request. WMO record: 14 mm of rain over about 2 days. Dry, cold and clear in the Kathmandu Valley with sharp nights; NTB says winter in the Valley averages 2-12 C and that sunshine and clear views continue despite the cold. NTB also says temperature drops about 6 C for every 1,000 m of altitude gained, so trekking altitudes are far colder than these valley figures and can fall below freezing.
climate.crowd_note: Cold, dry season; trekking is possible but high passes and camps are bitterly cold (editorial judgement, not a sourced measurement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 17 mm over about 3 days. Still dry and cold at night in the Valley; NTB notes winter rain is heavier in the western hills.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet period before the spring trekking season (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 31 mm over about 4 days. Warming quickly; start of spring, which NTB names as one of the two best seasons to visit, with rhododendrons in bloom.
climate.crowd_note: Spring season is starting and trails begin to fill (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 54 mm over about 6 days. Spring: NTB says rhododendrons bloom; afternoon haze and the first pre-monsoon showers can appear in the lowlands.
climate.crowd_note: Peak spring trekking season (editorial judgement; NTB names spring as a best time to visit).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 114 mm over about 12 days. Pre-monsoon heat and thunderstorms build; this month falls inside NTB's May-July summer figures for Kathmandu (28.1 C max, 19.5 C min, 312 mm).
climate.crowd_note: Hot and increasingly showery; fewer trekkers by late May (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 256 mm over about 17 days. NTB says 80 percent of Nepal's rain falls in the June-September monsoon.
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon onset; clouds hide the mountains and trails and roads get slippery or washed out (editorial judgement; FCDO warns of flood and landslide risk).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 360 mm over about 23 days, the wettest month of the year. NTB says Manang and Mustang sit in a rain shadow and stay mostly dry, with rainfall under 300 mm a year in Mustang.
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon; the rain-shadow regions are the usual exception for trekkers (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 314 mm over about 22 days. FCDO reports major flash flooding on 26 August 2026 in Rasuwa and at the Nepal-China border, a reminder that landslide and flood risk peaks in the monsoon.
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon; landslide-prone roads and trails (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 183 mm over about 15 days. NTB's June-September monsoon window is ending, but rain can still be heavy early in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Monsoon tail; the autumn season is about to begin (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 59 mm over about 4 days. NTB says autumn gives the clearest skies, especially in October and November, and names autumn as a best season for trekking.
climate.crowd_note: Peak trekking season; flights, lodges and permits book up early (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 8 mm over about 1 day, the driest month. NTB says October and November have the clearest skies of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season continues but cold builds at altitude (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: WMO record: 14 mm over about 1 day. Dry, cold and clear in the Valley (NTB: winter 2-12 C in Kathmandu Valley). Winter in the mountains can fall below freezing and NTB says the Himalaya blocks cold Central Asian winds.
climate.crowd_note: Cold, quieter season for trekkers (editorial judgement).

timezone_note: Europe/Amsterdam covers the European Netherlands. Standard time is CET (UTC+1) and summer time is CEST (UTC+2); Holland.com's FAQ says the Netherlands is on 'GMT +1' and applies daylight saving time in summer. On 18 October 2026 the country is on CEST, and clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026 under the EU last-Sunday-of-October rule; that date comes from the rule and the IANA database, not from a page opened for this guide. The Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) are outside this guide: UK FCDO says they have separate travel advice pages, and their time zone and currency were not researched here.
passport_validity_rule: The Netherlands is in the Schengen area. For a short stay, IND (the Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service, last updated 10 June 2026) says for visa-exempt travellers: 'Your passport may not have been issued more than 10 years ago' and the passport must be valid for at least another 3 months after your departure from the Netherlands. The EU's Your Europe portal (last checked 19 August 2026) and UK FCDO give the same two conditions (issued within the previous 10 years; valid at least 3 months after you leave). Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. Airlines may apply stricter rules than the entry rules (Global Affairs Canada).
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's news item of 28 April 2026 says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be announced later, and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says ETIAS applications are 'not yet open'. No page opened for this guide announces an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it has been fully operational across the Schengen states since 10 April 2026; per IND it replaces entry and exit passport stamps, and per UK FCDO you may be asked to register fingerprints and a photo, the record is valid for 3 years, and you should expect longer waits at the border. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). Return ticket, funds and insurance: IND says a return ticket alone is not enough and you must also show ties to your home country, that a border check may ask for an option on or reservation of a return ticket, and that for a holiday or family visit by a visa-exempt traveller you need at least EUR 55 per person per day for the stay (bank statements, travel cheques or cash accepted, or a guarantor in the Netherlands). IND is inconsistent on insurance: it says cover of at least EUR 30,000 for medical expenses in the Schengen area is needed for visa applicants but also that it is not required if you do not need a visa and 'not compulsory, but recommended' in its checklist; travel insurance is recommended in any case (UK FCDO, Global Affairs Canada). Your Europe says border guards may ask for proof of lodging, a return or round-trip ticket and proof of sufficient financial means. Because the checks are put as things officers 'may' ask for rather than a fixed condition for every visa-exempt visitor, the onward-ticket field is left null and blank passport pages are not stated (no opened page gives a number). Temporary border checks: UK FCDO's entry page (opened for this guide) says the Netherlands has extra entry checks in place 'until 8 June 2026', a date that has passed; a web search surfaced a later Dutch notification extending them to 30 September 2026 but that document was not opened here, and nothing opened confirms whether checks continue after that, so expect possible ID checks on arrival by land from Belgium or Germany and carry your passport. Cash: Dutch Customs (douane.nl, last updated 7 April 2026) and the Dutch government say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash (or gold) into or out of the EU must be declared to customs, and UK FCDO adds that without a certified declaration your money could be seized when you leave; this does not apply to travel within the EU. Global Affairs Canada notes that credit cards are not widely accepted, so carry some cash (see the money block). Customs: UK FCDO says meat and milk products generally cannot be brought into the EU.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose for ages 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (especially for smaller cities, villages, rural areas or street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; unvaccinated travellers 60 and older may be vaccinated)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Netherlands page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Netherlands page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (that section last updated 23 April 2025; the page was last reviewed 25 August 2026), and Global Affairs Canada also says no proof of yellow fever vaccination is needed. The recommended list is medical advice only; Global Affairs Canada separately says hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all travellers and describes health care as excellent. The CDC page has no malaria section, carries only a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025), and names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis under non-vaccine-preventable risks. For urgent care, UK FCDO says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. FCDO says a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance, and may not cover private healthcare, repatriation or prescription charges; Global Affairs Canada advises insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays. FCDO also notes that medicine rules can differ from the UK. CDC, FCDO and Global Affairs Canada are used because no page from the Dutch health ministry or RIVM was opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: Holland.com (the Netherlands' national tourism site) says you can pay with cash or a debit card, and often with your phone via NFC, Apple Pay or Google Wallet, and that you can pay with a debit card in just about any store. It says the Dutch hardly use credit cards in daily life, though they remain useful for car hire, hotel rooms and flights, and that some (often small) hospitality businesses are pin-only with no cash on site. Global Affairs Canada says credit cards are not widely accepted and advises carrying enough cash. The two do not fully agree, so carry both a debit card and some cash. Holland.com's public-transport page adds that foreign debit cards may not work on OVpay and advises international visitors to use a credit card; check with your bank.
money.cash_culture: Holland.com says more than three quarters of stores, pubs, bars and accommodation offer the option to pay in cash, and advises checking in advance. Very few stores accept or exchange EUR 500 notes, and cash totals are rounded to the nearest 5 cents because 1- and 2-cent coins are no longer in circulation.
money.tipping: Holland.com says a tip of about 10% is quite acceptable in the Netherlands, and card users can simply add the tip to the bill (some terminals ask if and how much). It is not presented as a fixed rule.
money.atm_notes: Holland.com says the number of ATMs is decreasing considerably because of contactless payments, and that yellow 'Geldmaten' ATMs accept almost all bank cards. It does not give fees or limits, so none are stated here.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Netherlands getting-help page (a fallback; no Dutch government emergency page could be opened, the government.nl and politie.nl addresses tried returned 404) gives one emergency number: 112 for ambulance, fire and police. The European Commission (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/112) says 112 is the European emergency number, available everywhere in the EU free of charge, reaching ambulance, fire brigade or police from landlines or mobiles, for real emergencies only. Global Affairs Canada independently says 'Dial 112 for emergency assistance'. A separate non-emergency police number and any dedicated tourist police line were not confirmed on an official page opened for this guide, so none is listed. For urgent consular help for a British national, FCDO lists +44 20 7008 5000 (24 hours); the Embassy of Canada in The Hague is +31 70 311-1600 (Global Affairs Canada).

getting_around.summary: The national train network is run by NS (Nederlandse Spoorwegen). Holland.com, the national tourism site, says the country has about 400 train stations, that Amsterdam to Utrecht takes no more than half an hour, Amsterdam to The Hague Central Station 50 minutes, and that you can reach the other side of the country within two hours; it also says delays generally do not last more than about 25 minutes. Those times come from the tourism site, not from an NS timetable, so check live times on ns.nl or 9292.nl (both named by Holland.com for journey planning). Payment for trains, trams, metro and buses is moving to OVpay (tapping a contactless bank card, phone or watch), because the anonymous OV-chipkaart is no longer sold. Trains have 1st and 2nd class; OVpay is 2nd class only. Regional operators, Schiphol airport train services, domestic flights and the Caribbean Netherlands were not researched.

passes.name: OVpay (contactless bank card, phone or watch)
passes.covers: OV-chipkaart.nl says you check in with a contactless card, phone or smartwatch and always use the same card or device to check in and out; you do not top up a balance but must keep enough funds in your account. NS says that when you travel on a payment card you travel 2nd class and without a discount, and Holland.com says OVpay can only be used in 2nd class and that existing season tickets cannot be used with it. A double check-in can happen if your wallet holds both a contactless card and an OV-chipkaart; OV-chipkaart.nl points to zelfregelen.ovpay.nl to correct it. Holland.com advises international visitors to use a credit card because debit cards may only work if Dutch-issued; the Dutch Payments Association says otherwise, so check with your bank.
passes.worth_it: Official pages call OVpay the simplest option for visitors because there is nothing to buy or top up; no fare figures were read for this record, so check the live fare on ns.nl or 9292.nl.

passes.name: Anonymous OV-chipkaart (no longer sold)
passes.covers: OV-chipkaart.nl says that from 1 July 2026 you can no longer buy an anonymous OV-chipkaart and that existing cards can be used as usual; NS says existing anonymous cards remain usable until the end of 2027. Holland.com (an older page) says the card needs a balance of at least EUR 20 to travel by train and, being anonymous, a lost card's balance cannot be refunded.
passes.worth_it: Only relevant if you already hold one or are lent one; a new visitor cannot buy it, so use OVpay or a single-use ticket instead.

passes.name: Single-use chip card ticket
passes.covers: Holland.com says single-use chip cards cost EUR 1 extra per trip and can be bought at an NS ticketing machine or service desk; NS says its single-use tickets are valid up to one week in advance (except for travel to Germany, Belgium or Luxembourg). Holland.com describes them as meant for single trips and less practical if you travel to several places.
passes.worth_it: Useful for a one-off train journey or if you would rather not use a bank card; it costs more per trip than the other options (EUR 1 extra per trip, per Holland.com). Other pass products (day tickets, city cards, regional passes) were not researched.

climate.precipitation_note: 63.1 mm normal rainfall (11.0 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 7.0 C and min 0.7 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table).
climate.crowd_note: Still cold; quiet apart from school-holiday weeks (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 57.8 mm normal rainfall (10.2 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 10.5 C and min 2.4 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table). The mean max of 10.5 C is rounded up to 11 in the structured field.
climate.crowd_note: Cool, with visitor numbers building through the month (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 41.6 mm normal rainfall (8.4 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 14.8 C and min 4.5 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table). The mean min of 4.5 C is rounded up to 5 in the structured field.
climate.crowd_note: Mild spring weather and a busy month for visitors; book rooms and trains early (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 59.3 mm normal rainfall (9.3 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 18.3 C and min 8.0 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table).
climate.crowd_note: Mild and the driest-feeling spring month; busy at the main sights (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 70.5 mm normal rainfall (10.0 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 20.9 C and min 10.8 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table).
climate.crowd_note: Long days and warm afternoons; busy in Amsterdam and the coast (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 85.2 mm normal rainfall (10.7 days with 1 mm or more); mean daily max 23.1 C and min 13.0 C (1991-2020 normal, De Bilt, KNMI station 260, from KNMI's published long-term averages table). timezone_note: Tourism New Zealand states New Zealand is 12 hours ahead of GMT, that daylight saving puts clocks forward one hour to GMT+13, and that daylight saving 'begins on the last Sunday in September and ends on the first Sunday of the following April, when clocks are put back to GMT+12'. Applying that to 2026-27 (checked against the IANA tz database, not a dated official page): daylight saving began on Sunday 27 September 2026, so on 18 October 2026 Auckland, Wellington and Queenstown are on NZDT (UTC+13); it ends on Sunday 4 April 2027, when clocks go back to NZST (UTC+12). The main islands share one clock, so there is no time-zone change between Auckland and Queenstown. The Chatham Islands (IANA zone Pacific/Chatham) keep their own time 45 minutes ahead of the main islands (UTC+12:45 standard, UTC+13:45 in summer); the Tourism New Zealand page opened does not mention them, so that comes from the IANA database only.
passport_validity_rule: Immigration New Zealand: 'Check that your passport or other travel document will not expire until 3 months after the date you plan to leave New Zealand.' When you request an NZeTA, your passport 'must be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave New Zealand', and you may not be allowed to check in if it is close to expiring. The NZeTA is linked to the passport used to request it, so travel on that same passport; a new passport needs a change request before you fly. New Zealand citizens, residents and Australian citizens only need a passport valid for travel to New Zealand. UK FCDO gives the same 3-months-after-departure rule. If you transit a country that wants six months of validity, or your airline applies its own rule at check-in, the stricter rule governs your trip.
entry_requirement_notes: Who needs what: Australian citizens need neither a visa nor an NZeTA. Citizens of visa waiver countries (INZ's list includes Brazil, Canada, Germany, Singapore, the UK (citizens and other British passport holders with the right to reside permanently in the UK) and the USA among others, and does not include India) must hold a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority (NZeTA) before they travel, unless exempt; everyone else needs a visitor visa. NZeTA: it is not a visa; at the border INZ gives visa waiver travellers a visitor visa on arrival if they meet the requirements. Cost: NZD $23 on the INZ website or NZD $17 on the official NZeTA mobile app (INZ news item of 10 January 2024 and INZ fee table in force from 1 October 2024; the NZeTA page itself now shows 'From NZD $17'), plus the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy (IVL) of NZD $100, paid at the same time; the IVL is non-refundable even if the application is declined. INZ's IVL page says you do not pay it if you hold an Australian or New Zealand passport or many Pacific Island passports, are a transit passenger at Auckland, or hold a New Zealand or Australian resident visa, among other exemptions. Timing and validity: INZ says allow 72 hours (up to 3 days) for a decision, longer if checks are needed; the NZeTA is valid for 2 years for most travellers and allows multiple visits, each up to 3 months (6 months for UK citizens), with no more than 6 months in any 12-month period. The NZeTA is not a visa and does not guarantee entry: INZ can refuse entry on character, genuine-visitor or evidence grounds. Use only the official INZ website or app; INZ warns that some third-party sites are not legitimate and cannot speed up an application. Onward ticket and funds: INZ says that on an NZeTA you must show a ticket out of New Zealand to a country you have the right to enter, 'already paid for', at check-in, and that your departure date must fall within 3 months of arrival (6 months for UK citizens). At check-in or on arrival you may be asked to prove you have enough money: at least NZD $1,000 a month, or NZD $400 a month if accommodation is prepaid (bank or card statements, prepaid accommodation, bank drafts or traveller's cheques count as evidence). Visa waiver travellers cannot use an NZeTA if they need a sponsor to cover costs. Arrival declaration: everyone, including New Zealand citizens and children, must complete the free New Zealand Traveller Declaration (NZTD) online or in the NZTD app, no earlier than 24 hours before the journey starts and by the time you reach passport control; it covers customs, immigration and biosecurity, and a paper form is available if you cannot do it online. Customs states that false or incorrect declarations or failing to declare restricted or prohibited items can bring a $400 instant fine; the NZTD page says false declarations can lead to confiscation, a minimum instant fine of NZ$400, prosecution, imprisonment and deportation. What to declare (Customs): more than three months' supply of medicine or medicine not prescribed to you; goods obtained overseas or duty-free worth more than NZ$700; more than 3 bottles of spirits (up to 1.125 litres each) plus 4.5 litres of wine or beer; more than 50 cigarettes or 50 grams of tobacco; goods carried for business or for another person; and cash of NZ$10,000 or more (or foreign equivalent), including travellers cheques, bank drafts and money orders, which also needs a Border Cash Report (paper form NZCS 337 or online within 72 hours of travel; failing to declare cash is an offence that can bring a fine, imprisonment or seizure). Biosecurity: the NZTD page says some foods, used outdoor equipment, and animal and plant products carry pests and diseases and must be declared; the Ministry for Primary Industries pages that list the rules returned a bot-check to automated fetches and were not read, so no biosecurity detail beyond the NZTD and Customs wording is given here. Not stated: the Customs travel page lists a border processing levy payable on arrival and departure, but its amount was not read, so none is stated; blank passport pages and any other proof-of-funds figures were not found on an official page opened.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (varicella, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR; CDC Level 1 global measles notice)
Hepatitis A (most travellers; especially those visiting smaller towns or rural areas or eating street food)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)

health.malaria_risk: Not addressed on CDC's New Zealand page; CDC lists no malaria risk or antimalarial recommendation there
health.notes: CDC (page reviewed 25 August 2026): yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and, under country entry requirements, 'Vaccine is not required' (CDC entry for New Zealand updated 23 April 2025). No entry vaccination is required. CDC also lists leptospirosis (fresh water, soil and mud contaminated by animal urine), hantavirus, tuberculosis and a Level 1 global measles notice, and says bug bites can still spread disease so use repellent. UK FCDO: call 111 and ask for an ambulance; essential and urgent care is covered for UK residents on short visits under the reciprocal health agreement, but not routine, non-emergency treatment including prescriptions, so travel insurance is advised; Healthline offers free 24-hour medical advice; all products containing codeine are prescription-only controlled drugs, and prescription medicines must be declared. Immigration New Zealand: you must pay for any health care in New Zealand and it recommends full medical insurance; NZeTA applicants coming for medical treatment need a Medical Treatment Visitor Visa instead, and there are extra rules if you are pregnant. The Ministry of Health, Health NZ and ACC pages were blocked to automated fetches (Cloudflare or bot check) and were not read, so ACC accident-cover rules for visitors are not stated here. The recommended list is medical advice, not an entry condition.

money.card_acceptance: Tourism New Zealand states that all major credit cards are accepted, with Visa and Mastercard the most widely used, many retailers in main centres also have Apple Pay, and travellers' cheques are no longer accepted.
money.tipping: Tourism New Zealand states that tipping is not obligatory, even in restaurants and bars, that tipping for good service is at the visitor's discretion, and that hotels and restaurants do not add service charges to their bills.
money.atm_notes: Tourism New Zealand: ATMs are at bank branches, main shopping streets and malls; international credit and ATM cards work as long as they have a four-digit PIN encoded, so check with your bank before you leave. Goods and Services Tax (GST) is 15% and is included in displayed prices; Tourism New Zealand says visitors cannot claim it back. Prices are rounded to the nearest 10 cents in cash because 1c, 2c and 5c coins were withdrawn. There is no limit on foreign currency brought in, but cash of NZ$10,000 or more (Customs; Tourism New Zealand words it as more than NZ$10,000) needs a Border Cash Report.

power.adapter_note: Tourism New Zealand states New Zealand uses Type I plugs (three flat pins, two angled in an inverted V with one straight below), the same as Australia and the Pacific Islands, at 230/240 volts and 50Hz. Visitors from lower-voltage countries such as the USA, Canada or Japan should check that the appliance is rated for up to 240 volts or use a voltage converter. Most hotels and motels provide 110 volt sockets in bathrooms for electric razors only. The IEC's World Plugs was not opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: New Zealand Police: 'Call 111 and ask for Police when: people are injured or in danger; or there is a serious, immediate, or imminent risk to life or property; or a crime is being or has just been committed.' The police page states 111 is operated by Spark and that Police, FENZ (Fire and Emergency) and Ambulance Services are all users of the 111 service, and UK FCDO gives 'Telephone: 111 (ambulance, fire, police)', so one number covers all three; you say which service you need. Texting 111 does not work unless you are deaf, hearing or speech impaired and have registered for the 111 TXT service in advance. Non-emergency: Police 105 (free, nationwide, 24/7, from any mobile or landline, or online at 105.police.govt.nz) is for things that do not need urgent help, such as a burglary that has already happened or a lost wallet. No official page opened states whether 112 connects, so no universal number is listed. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed.

getting_around.summary: No national transport pass or intercity rail pass was found on an official page opened for this record, so none is listed. Tourism New Zealand's driving page states that New Zealanders drive on the left, that many roads are hilly, narrow and winding so distances may take longer than expected, that outside the main cities there are very few motorways and most roads are single carriageway with one lane each way, that speed signs are in kilometres per hour, that seatbelts are compulsory in front and back seats, that using a hand-held phone while driving is illegal, and that roads are busiest from December to April, with snow, ice or heavy rain possible in winter. It says a current driver's licence lets a visitor drive for up to 18 months (carry an accurate English translation if it is not in English) and an English-language International Driving Permit alongside the home licence works for up to 12 months. The alcohol limit is zero for drivers under 20 and 50 mg per 100 ml of blood (250 micrograms per litre of breath) for those 20 and over. No source opened gives flight, ferry or rail times, so none are stated; use the NZTA Journey Planner for road times.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Tourism New Zealand states you need a SIM card from one of the main local phone companies (2degrees, Skinny, Spark, Vodafone) to use an overseas phone on the network, and recommends a pre-paid plan. Coverage is good in all main centres and surrounding towns but may not be available in some rural and wilderness areas. Free WiFi is limited (central Auckland, Rotorua, Wellington, Dunedin, main airports, public libraries and many i-SITE centres). The page does not state eSIM support or any registration rules, so none are claimed.
connectivity.typical_cost: Tourism New Zealand states pre-paid data and mobile packs start from around NZ$15 per month depending on data, with some weekly options (page not dated; check current plans).

New Zealand spans about 1,600 km north to south and the climate varies a lot: the north is subtropical-leaning and humid, the South Island has alpine and snow country, and the west coast is far wetter than the east. Seasons are inverted compared with the northern hemisphere, so December to February is summer. timezone_note: Norway uses Central European Time and changes its clocks for summer time; the zone comes from the IANA time zone database (Europe/Oslo). Visit Norway's A-Z page says 'All of Norway uses Central European Time (CET)'.
passport_validity_rule: Norway is in the Schengen area but is not an EU member. For a short stay UK FCDO's Norway page says the passport must have an expiry date at least 3 months after the day you plan to leave the Schengen area and a date of issue less than 10 years before you arrive, and that visa-free stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period (stays beyond that may lead to a ban of up to 3 years, FCDO). Global Affairs Canada's Norway page states the same 3-month rule and adds that some transport companies may apply stricter passport rules. Visit Norway says UDI (the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration) is the authority on who needs a visa. UDI's own pages could not be opened for this guide (see entry_requirement_notes), so the rule is cited from FCDO and Global Affairs Canada.
entry_requirement_notes: UDI (udi.no) and its visitor-rules page returned HTTP 403 / an Azure web-application-firewall block to both the fetch tool and the built-in browser, so nothing in this record is read first-hand from UDI. Visit Norway (opened) says citizens of EU/EEA countries and listed countries including the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan and Singapore can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period without a visa but must also meet additional UDI conditions; a Schengen visa is needed for other nationalities (see the visa rules for your passport). ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026): the official ETIAS site (travel-europe.europa.eu, opened 19 October 2026) says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months ahead; Visit Norway says it is 'expected to begin operating in the last quarter of 2026'; Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says applications are not yet open. No date is given here because no opened official page states one; the ETIAS site says the fee is EUR 20 and that it covers 30 European countries, and Global Affairs Canada's Norway page covers it, so visa-exempt visitors should expect to need it once it starts. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is operating: Visit Norway says it is 'now fully operational' and records facial image, fingerprints, passport details and time and place of entry and exit for short-stay non-EU/EEA travellers; UK FCDO says the digital record is valid for 3 years and registration is free. Onward ticket and funds: UK FCDO says that at the border you may need to show a return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation, travel insurance and enough money for your stay, and that the amount varies with your accommodation. No opened page states these as fixed conditions with a figure (a search-result summary of the UDI page mentioned NOK 500 per day, a return or onward journey and no work, but the UDI page itself was not opened, so treat that as an unverified lead and check udi.no before you travel), and no page opened states a blank-page requirement, so those fields are left unset. Cash: Norwegian Customs (toll.no, page updated 27/11/2025) says currency worth more than NOK 25,000 must be declared when bringing it to or from Norway, covering Norwegian and foreign notes, coins and other means of payment such as gift cards, with a fine of 20% of the whole amount for failing to declare; UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada word the threshold as NOK 25,000 or more, so declare if you are at or near that amount. Internal Schengen border checks may be reintroduced temporarily (Global Affairs Canada). Visa-free visitors cannot work in Norway (Global Affairs Canada says work visas are required).

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (especially for rural areas or street food)
Hepatitis B (CDC: unvaccinated travellers under 60; Global Affairs Canada: recommended for all travellers)
Tick-borne encephalitis (CDC: travellers with extensive tick exposure from outdoor activities; Global Affairs Canada: present in some areas, mainly April to November)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None mentioned on CDC's Norway page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Norway page says the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026), and Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) says there is no yellow fever risk in Norway. CDC lists a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and no malaria section. CDC says rabid dogs are not commonly found in Norway and that rabies is found in some land wildlife on Svalbard, with post-exposure vaccine usually available across most of Norway but possibly limited on Svalbard; Global Affairs Canada says rabies may be found in wildlife including bats. UK FCDO says UK nationals can use a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that this is not an alternative to travel insurance and does not cover private care or repatriation, and gives 113 for an ambulance. Global Affairs Canada says polar bears are a serious risk in Svalbard and visitors should stay within settlements unless they have a guide and proper equipment. No page from Norway's health authorities (FHI, which has no English travel-health pages reachable from its English home page, or Helsenorge) was opened for this guide, so CDC, UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada are used as fallbacks.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Norway says 'debit and credit cards are accepted almost everywhere', that almost all establishments accept electronic payment by card or phone (including Google Pay and Apple Pay in many places), that post offices and some grocery shops or supermarkets do not accept foreign credit cards although they take debit cards, and that Visa and MasterCard are the most commonly accepted credit cards with far fewer accepting Amex or Diners. The page is undated.
money.cash_culture: Visit Norway says cash is no longer the main payment method but it is still a good idea to carry a bit for small purchases, and that foreign currency is rarely accepted, so you need Norwegian kroner. The page is undated.
money.tipping: Visit Norway says tipping is not common for the most part, except in bars and restaurants where locals tip when happy with the service or food; there is no fixed rule but tips tend to stay within 5-15% of the bill, and tipping is entirely up to you. The page is undated.
money.atm_notes: Visit Norway says there are cash machines in towns and cities and that in most rural areas there is at least one place to withdraw money. No withdrawal fees are stated by any opened official page. The VAT-refund scheme was not researched.

power.voltage: 220 V AC (as stated by Visit Norway)
power.adapter_note: Visit Norway's travel tips A-Z page says '220 volts AC (50 Hz) is the Norwegian standard' and that Norway uses the continental European standard socket. It does not name plug types (C/F), so none are listed here. The IEC's World Plugs was not opened to cross-check. The page is undated.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Norway page gives police 112, ambulance 113 and fire 110; Global Affairs Canada gives the same three numbers; Visit Norway's A-Z page lists 110 fire, 112 police, 113 ambulance, 120 emergencies at sea, the Poisons Information Centre on 22 59 13 00 and 1412 as a text phone for the deaf or hearing impaired; the police website (politiet.no/en) shows 'Emergency 112' in its English navigation. 112 is therefore the police number in Norway, not a general all-services line, so `universal` is left unset. No dedicated tourist police line was found. Global Affairs Canada lists the Canadian Embassy in Oslo at +47 22 99 53 00 and its Emergency Watch and Response Centre on 00-800-2326-6831; UK FCDO lists 020 7008 5000 (24 hours) for its London line.

getting_around.summary: Visit Norway describes long-distance travel by train (Vy, including the Oslo to Bergen line, with some overnight sleeper trains), express coaches between major cities, ferries and express boats, domestic flights and the Hurtigruten coastal voyage, and says Entur is the tool for tickets on almost all public transport journeys in Norway. It lists no journey times, fares for a given route or rail passes, so none are given here (its 'from' prices are for listed operators, not a timetable). UK FCDO says you can drive on a UK photocard licence for up to 90 days, you must use winter tyres with a minimum 3 mm tread if there is snow or ice on the road, and headlights must be on (dipped) in the daytime all year; Global Affairs Canada says roads are good but some northern roads are narrow and can be impassable in winter, wildlife collisions are common at night, and an international driving permit should be carried. Visit Norway's safety page says weather can change quickly and braking takes much longer on icy roads. Oslo's city transport (Ruter) and rail passes were not researched.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visit Norway's travel tips A-Z page says a local prepaid SIM may be the cheapest option for calling home and that mobile data coverage is patchy in sparsely populated areas. No operator, price or registration rule was stated by an official page.

timezone_note: One time zone for the whole country. The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism's Oman at a Glance page says the Sultanate 'follows the GMT+4 time zone'. It does not mention daylight saving; the IANA database places Asia/Muscat at UTC+4 all year.
passport_validity_rule: The official visa-free entry list (Ministry of Heritage and Tourism) states: passport valid at least six months from the date of entry. UK FCDO says the passport must have an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive, and Global Affairs Canada says it must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date of entry. The Duqm Airport immigration page also says a passport valid for more than 6 months is needed to obtain a visa.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA-FREE IS 14 DAYS, FOR A LIST OF NATIONALITIES, WITH CONDITIONS. The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism's visa page (experienceoman.om/visa) links an official 'List of Countries with Visa-Free Entry to Sultanate of Oman'. It has a 1st list of 73 countries (it names Britain, Ireland, Germany and other EU states, Australia, Canada, Singapore, the United States, Brazil and others) and a 2nd, conditional list of 30 countries (it names India, Peru, Mexico, Egypt, Jordan and others) whose nationals qualify only if they are residents of a GCC country in listed professions or hold a valid entry visa for the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, a Schengen country or Japan. The conditions printed on that list: passport valid at least six months from the date of entry; the visitor 'must hold a return ticket, hotel reservation, health insurance, and' funds to cover expenses; the stay is 14 days, 'which cannot be extended or transferred'; no work, and the entry cannot be converted to any residency visa; overstaying is fined at 10 riyals per day. FCDO confirms 14 days visa-free for British citizens, adds that you must show a return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation and travel health insurance at border control, and says overstay fines are up to 10 rials a day capped at 500 rials, with possible detention. Everyone else, and anyone staying longer, needs a visa: the Royal Oman Police e-visa portal (evisa.rop.gov.om) takes online applications (FCDO: choose the unsponsored visit visa as a tourist), and Global Affairs Canada says a visa can also be bought on arrival at Muscat International Airport, while the tourism board says it is 'preferable to obtain the visa prior to travel'. One wording catch: the tourism board's visa page describes the exemption for about 103 countries in terms of transit, but the official list itself and FCDO describe a 14-day visit; the Royal Oman Police e-visa pages that would state fees and visit-visa lengths could not be read (they returned only login prompts), so no fee or longer-stay length is given here. GCC citizens need no visa. LAWS THAT CATCH VISITORS OUT (FCDO and Global Affairs Canada). Dress: the tourism board says the clothing code is modest, men in long trousers below the knee and sleeved shirts, women covering shoulders, chest and knees; headscarves are only necessary when entering mosques; swimwear is for private beaches and hotel pools and must be modest on public beaches. FCDO: clothing should cover the tops of your arms and legs (below the knee). Alcohol: it is illegal to drink alcohol in public (FCDO) and Canada says not to drink outside licensed hotels and that public intoxication is an offence; drink-driving is illegal. Customs allows non-Muslim arrivals up to 2 litres of wine and 48 cans of beer, and Muslims are not allowed to import alcohol. Drugs: no distinction between soft and hard drugs; FCDO and Canada both say the death penalty can apply. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal (FCDO; Canada). Photography: do not photograph people without permission; photographing some government buildings, public buildings and military or police vehicles is prohibited. Drones: FCDO says flying one without a valid licence is illegal; Canada says you must get authorization before importing or operating one. Ramadan: during daylight do not eat, drink, smoke or chew gum in public, including in a car (FCDO); Canada says Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin on or around 7 February. Oman does not recognise dual nationality (FCDO). Mobile phone use while driving is illegal with fines up to 3,000 rials or up to 3 years in prison (FCDO). MEDICATION AND CASH. FCDO: some UK prescription and over-the-counter medicines are illegal in Oman; carry a copy of your prescription and check with Oman's Ministry of Health before you travel (the Ministry of Health site gave no importation rule that could be read, so none is stated here). Oman Customs (customs.gov.om, traveller services): currency, bearer securities, banknotes or convertible precious metals or gemstones that 'exceed (6000 riyals)' must be declared on arrival or departure; the page also says the form is required for 6,000 Omani rials or more or the equivalent, so declare if you are at the figure. SEASONS AND HAZARDS. Khareef is Dhofar's monsoon season: the tourism board says it lasts from mid-June to September (its Dhofar page says June to September) with mist and light showers. FCDO warns tropical cyclones from the Indian Ocean sometimes affect Oman in July and August, and that wadis are prone to flash flooding after heavy rain from October to March. Global Affairs Canada says the rainy season runs May to September and that seasonal flooding can disrupt overland travel; it does not mention Khareef by name. SECURITY. Global Affairs Canada (page updated 6 August 2026) advises avoiding non-essential travel to Oman because of the volatile regional security situation; FCDO's safety page is the other place to check before you book. Check both before travelling.

health.malaria_risk: Very low. Global Affairs Canada: 'Limited malaria transmission may occur in this destination, but risk to travellers is very low' and antimalarial medication is not recommended for most travellers. CDC's Oman page carries no malaria statement.
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccine tied to entry, and only conditionally. FCDO: you need a certificate if you arrive from Rwanda, Tanzania or a country listed as a transmission risk. Global Affairs Canada says there is no risk of yellow fever in Oman itself. CDC (page last reviewed 25 August 2026) counts transits or layovers longer than 12 hours in a risk country. Everything on the recommended list is advice only and is not checked at immigration. CDC also notes rabies in dogs and wildlife, schistosomiasis in fresh unchlorinated water, and insect-borne diseases such as dengue, leishmaniasis and CCHF. FCDO lists dengue and MERS as health risks, says extreme heat has caused deaths from dehydration and heat exhaustion, and warns that uninsured visitors who cannot pay charges may be stopped from leaving the country; British nationals must use private healthcare. Get travel health insurance: it is also a stated condition of visa-free entry. The Ministry of Health's travel-medicine page gives no vaccine list, so entry vaccination rules are cited to FCDO, CDC and Global Affairs Canada.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada states: 'Credit cards and U.S. dollar traveller's cheques are widely accepted.' No Omani government page gives more detail, so smaller shops and rural areas are not covered.

emergency.notes: Global Affairs Canada: 'Dial 9999 for emergency assistance.' FCDO: call the Royal Oman Police on 9999 after a serious traffic accident, and 'Call 9999 and ask for an ambulance.' The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism's Key Contacts page also lists 'Emergency Number: 9999'. No source we could read states a separate fire number, so fire is left null; 9999 is the number to try. We found no official tourist police number. FCDO suggests using the Nidaa/CDAA service for emergency updates. English is widely spoken (tourism board), but no official page guarantees English from the emergency line.

getting_around.summary: Oman's tourism board lists five airports (Muscat International, Salalah, Duqm, Sohar and regional oilfield airports), with Oman Air as the national carrier (over 50 destinations) and SalamAir as the low-cost carrier (over 30). Within Oman it names Oman Taxi, O Taxi, Marhaba Taxi, Tasleem Taxi and the Mwasalat bus operator; Muscat's Sultan Qaboos Port (Muttrah) handles cruise ships and intercity ferries, and Oman National Ships Company runs high-speed catamarans between Shinas and Musandam. By road, the Rub' al Khali crossing is the principal link from Saudi Arabia and there are numerous crossings from the UAE. Distances are long and public transport between regions is limited in what these pages describe, so most visitors hire a car or a driver. FCDO advises watching for camels and goats on roads outside Muscat, notes it is illegal to use a mobile phone while driving, and says that for desert or mountain trips you should travel in convoy, carry water and a phone and tell someone your plans. Intercity bus timetables, car hire rules and the Hafeet Rail service are not covered by the pages read, so they are not described here.

timezone_note: One zone nationwide; Panama does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset from North American and European clocks shifts when those countries change.
passport_validity_rule: Panama's own immigration service (Servicio Nacional de Migración, SNM) lists as a tourist entry requirement an original passport or travel document 'con un mínimo de 3 meses de vigencia' (a minimum of 3 months' validity) on its Preguntas Frecuentes page; the Autoridad de Turismo de Panamá (page updated July 2025) says the same ('at least 3 months of validity'). Neither Panamanian page says which date the three months are counted from. Global Affairs Canada says 'valid for at least 3 months beyond the date you expect to leave Panama', and the structured fields therefore use 3 months counted from the departure date, the stricter of the two readings. The UK FCDO states a stricter rule: expiry at least 6 months after the day you plan to leave Panama (and at least one blank page). That is not on any Panamanian page read here, but airlines frequently apply the stricter rule at check-in, so a passport with under 6 months left is a risk worth avoiding. Sourcing note: the SNM tourist-requirements pages sit behind a login (lara.migracion.gob.pa) and the public Artículo 43 page gives no validity figure; the FAQ page was used instead, with the tourism board, Global Affairs Canada and FCDO as cross-checks.
entry_requirement_notes: PROOF OF FUNDS: the SNM FAQ page requires proof of economic solvency for the stay that 'en ningún caso podrá ser inferior a quinientos balboas (B/.500.00)' (balboas are at parity with US$); under-18s are exempt. The tourism board says a minimum of US$500 in cash, credit card, bank reference or similar, and warns some nationalities may be asked for more. Global Affairs Canada says US$500 or a credit card. The UK FCDO says you may need to prove US$1,000 or a credit card. The structured guidance is US$500 per Panama's own SNM; carry evidence of more if you can, since the border officer decides. ONWARD TICKET: SNM's FAQ lists a 'reserva comprobada de salida del país, dentro del periodo establecido' (a confirmed booking out of the country within the permitted period) as a requirement, and Article 43 of the migration law (SNM Turistas page) requires a return ticket to the country of origin or residence 'cuando la categoría migratoria lo requiera'. The tourism board says to carry a return ticket to your country of origin or your next destination. The FCDO notes officials may ask for a return or onward ticket, especially for those arriving by land from Costa Rica. STAY LENGTH (official sources disagree; check at the border): the tourism board says citizens of most countries can stay a maximum of 90 days; SNM's own material cites Decreto Ejecutivo 320 (2008) Art. 16 for tourist visas of no more than 90 days; the UK FCDO says up to 3 months and normally not extendable; Global Affairs Canada says no tourist visa is needed for stays up to 180 days; and the Embassy of Panama in the USA (embassyofpanama.org/visas) says US and Canadian citizens may stay up to 180 days under Resolución 22706 (September 2021) while also giving 3 months for visa-exempt nationals on its list and 30 days for people entering on the strength of a visa or residence from another country under Decreto Ejecutivo 196 (2024). No single figure is asserted here; the officer sets the days stamped, so do not book non-refundable travel beyond what is stamped. VISA: the SNM template page cites Decreto Ejecutivo 521 (6 August 2018, modified by Decreto 196) which waives the visa for nationals who need one but hold a valid visa or residence from Canada, the USA, Australia, South Korea, Japan, the UK, Singapore or an EU state; that page is marked 'Borrador para revisión institucional' (draft), so treat it as indicative. Check the Panamanian embassy list for your passport. Arrival by sea on a non-cruise vessel needs a visa (FCDO). CASH DECLARATION: the tourism board says to declare cash, objects or documents valued at more than US$10,000 using the online traveller's affidavit (QR code) and that no form is needed otherwise; the customs authority ANA publishes the Declaración Jurada de Viajero at declaraciondeviajero.ana.gob.pa. The exact threshold wording was not confirmed on an ANA page (ANA's news pages describe prosecutions for under-declared cash but do not state the rule in the text read), so rely on the tourism board's figure and ask ANA. OTHER: the FCDO lists a departure charge of US$40, usually included in the ticket price; Global Affairs Canada says biometrics (fingerprints and a facial scan) are registered at the port of entry and that failing to get an entry stamp carries a US$1,000 fine. Free tourist medical insurance applies for the first 10 days for air arrivals under age 86 (tourism board). The SNM, tourism board, embassy, FCDO and GAC pages were read on 2026-10-19; Panamanian rules in this area have changed several times (stay length, solvency), so confirm with the SNM or a Panamanian consulate shortly before travel.

health.malaria_risk: Per CDC: transmission in Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí, Colón, Darién, Panamá, Panamá Oeste and Veraguas provinces and in the Emberá, Guna Yala (Kuna Yala) and Ngäbe-Buglé comarcas, with rare cases elsewhere; no transmission in the Canal Zone and Panama City. Chloroquine resistance is reported east of the Canal. CDC recommends prophylaxis for Darién, Emberá, Guna Yala and Panamá province (chloroquine is not an option there) and for Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí, Colón, Ngäbe-Buglé, Panamá Oeste and Veraguas; other transmission areas need bite precautions only.
health.notes: YELLOW FEVER (sources differ): Panama's Ministerio de Salud (article dated 8 July 2025) states 'en Panamá no se está exigiendo a los viajeros que ingresan al país la tarjeta de vacuna contra la fiebre amarilla', and the tourism board (updated July 2025) says it is no longer mandatory to present a vaccination card on entering, while advising the vaccine and saying that travellers from Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Brazil or Africa should carry proof, and that Panama reserves the right to request it. By contrast CDC's Panama page states the vaccine is required for travellers aged 1 year and older arriving from countries with risk of yellow fever virus transmission (its yellow-fever section was last updated 23 April 2025), and the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada likewise say proof is needed if arriving from a risk country. The structured required_vaccinations is therefore empty because Panama's own health ministry says the card is not being demanded, but if you have been in a yellow-fever-risk country (for example in South America or Africa) carry a valid international certificate, ideally given at least 10 days before arrival (MINSA recommends vaccinating 10 days before travel). CDC also recommends the vaccine for all travellers aged 9 months and older going to mainland areas east of the Canal Zone, and not for travel limited to the Canal Zone or areas west of it. Separately, MINSA says the certificate for foreigners costs B/100.00 if you are vaccinated in Panama. Dengue is a year-round risk (CDC notice updated 2 October 2026). CDC lists risk-of-malaria areas below; a medical consultation is advised.

money.cash_culture: Global Affairs Canada states that the balboa (PAB) is Panama's currency and is used interchangeably with the US dollar, and warns of counterfeit US$50 and US$100 bills, advising travellers to carry only small US dollar bills. No official source read gave figures for cash-only businesses, so none are asserted.

emergency.notes: 911 is the national emergency number: Panama's Ministerio de Salud (article of 4 September 2025) describes it as free, reachable from anywhere in the country, coordinating Bomberos, Sinaproc, Cruz Roja, Minsa and other institutions. Police 104 and fire 103 are taken from the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages, which agree (GAC gives medical assistance 911; the FCDO lists 103 for ambulance as well as fire, so if 911 does not connect for an ambulance, 103 is the other number named). The Panamanian police and fire-service pages that were meant to confirm 104 and 103 could not be fetched (connection reset), so those two numbers rest on the two foreign governments. No tourist-police number was confirmed by an official source, so none is listed. Free tourist medical assistance for the first 10 days for air arrivals: call centre +507 840 4585 (tourism board).

getting_around.summary: Per the official tourism board: in Panama City, buses and the metro (both air-conditioned) need a MiBus card, sold at the airport or at an official sales point, and the MiBus app adds credit and plans routes. Domestic flights from Panama City reach destinations in under an hour, from Tocumen (PTY) to David and from Marcos A. Gelabert (PAC) to David, Changuinola, Isla Colón and Chitré, with Panamá Pacífico (BLB) to David and charters to places such as Guna Yala and the Pearl Islands. Long-distance buses mostly depart from the Gran Terminal Nacional de Transporte in Albrook, and trips to Bocas del Toro may need transfers in Changuinola or David. White Special Tourism Service (SET) taxis have standardised rates and are found at Tocumen and near large hotels. Car hire is available at PTY, BLB, Río Hato and David (valid licence, credit card and mandatory insurance). The Panamá-Colón highway toll is cash only. Fares, journey times and the Panama Canal railway are not given on the page, so none are stated.

passes.worth_it: Required rather than optional: the tourism board states you need the MiBus card to ride either. It is a stored-value card topped up by app or at sales points, not a time-limited tourist pass, and no fares are published on the page, so no saving can be calculated.
