timezone_note: Peru uses a single time zone nationwide and does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset is UTC-5 year round (IANA zone America/Lima).
passport_validity_rule: PROMPERU (the official tourism board) states that entry requires a legitimately issued passport with a minimum validity of six months from the date of entry into the country. The UK FCDO states the same rule for British nationals: the passport expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date of arrival.
entry_requirement_notes: Official sources state the permitted stay differently and none could be reconciled today. PROMPERU (peru.travel) says the maximum stay granted is 90 days and cannot be extended; Global Affairs Canada says no tourist visa is needed for a stay of less than 90 days per 365-day period; the UK FCDO says visitors normally get up to 90 days in any 180-day period, with officials able to grant a maximum of 183 days in 365 as a visitor. Peru's Foreign Ministry visa table and Migraciones (migraciones.gob.pe, gob.pe) could not be opened today (the government portal blocks automated browsers), so whether a 90-day stay can be extended once was not confirmed. Plan around 90 days and check the permitted stay recorded on your own entry record on the Migraciones website. Arrivals at international airports are registered digitally through the Tarjeta Andina de Migracion (TAM) and passports are not stamped (FCDO, Global Affairs Canada); if you enter overland you must get an entry stamp yourself, and an overstay is a penalty payable on exit. Declare anything dutiable or prohibited; Global Affairs Canada states that carrying more than US$10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure. Stays for business, study or work require the relevant visa from a Peruvian consulate before travel. Peru's Ministry of Health (DGE) also asks travellers returning from Ebola (Bundibugyo virus) outbreak zones to notify CDC Peru in advance and self-monitor for 21 days. Whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed: no Peruvian authority page that could be opened states it either way, and Global Affairs Canada says only that customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation and sufficient funds, which is a possibility, not a stated requirement. Carry an onward ticket anyway; airlines also apply this check at departure.

recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid (if visiting areas with poor sanitation or staying over a month)
Yellow fever (for travel below 2,300 m in the listed eastern jungle regions, including parts of Cusco and Puno; not recommended for Lima, Cusco city, the Inca Trail or Machu Picchu)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, varicella, polio, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: No transmission in Lima Province, Cusco city, Machu Picchu, the Sacred Valley, Lake Titicaca or anywhere above 2,500 m. Transmission occurs below 2,500 m east of the Andes (including Iquitos and Puerto Maldonado), where chemoprophylaxis is recommended; rare cases occur in Tumbes and Piura.
health.notes: No yellow fever vaccination is required for entry: the US CDC states Peru does not require proof of yellow fever vaccination for entry, and Global Affairs Canada says the same. Peru's own Ministry of Health (DGE) says authorities recommend prior vaccination and that a vaccination certificate may be requested at some forest-area entry points considered endemic; no official page found limits a requirement to travellers arriving from risk countries, so that wording is not asserted. If you are going to the Amazon, carry a certificate to be safe. The real health risk for a typical Peru itinerary is altitude, not disease. The CDC Yellow Book records Cusco city at 3,339 m (about 11,000 ft) and Lake Titicaca at 3,812 m (about 12,500 ft), and states that travellers going above 2,500 m (8,200 ft) are at risk of altitude illness - acute mountain sickness, high-altitude pulmonary edema and high-altitude cerebral edema. It specifically flags the Lima-to-Cusco flight, which gains roughly 3,350 m in about an hour, as an ascent rate that raises the risk, and notes that acute mountain sickness affects close to half of travellers during their first 48 hours in Cusco, though it is usually mild. CDC guidance is gradual ascent and, for travellers at risk, acetazolamide prophylaxis prescribed in advance - so this is a conversation to have with a doctor before booking, not after landing. Practical consequence for planning: do not schedule the Inca Trail or a high pass in the first day or two after flying into Cusco.

emergency.notes: Police 105, fire 116 and SAMU ambulance 106 are the numbers published by the Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros on the Peruvian state platform (gob.pe/547-telefonos-de-emergencia, read earlier and not reopenable today); the same page lists highway police 110 and Defensa Civil 115. Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/peru, updated 15 October 2026) agrees on police 105 and fire 116, but lists 116 for medical assistance as well and gives a tourist police WhatsApp line, +51 980 122 335, which is the tourist-police number shown (it is a WhatsApp number, not a voice short code). Where the two disagree on the ambulance, the state platform's 106 is kept; if 106 does not connect, try 105 or 116. SAMU on 106 is listed for Lima and a named set of regions (Amazonas, Ancash, Ayacucho, Huancavelica, Huanuco, Junin, La Libertad, Loreto, Madre de Dios, Piura, Lima Region, Tacna, Tumbes, Ucayali, Lambayeque and Pasco); Cusco is not on that list, so in Cusco or Puno expect to reach an ambulance through the police on 105 or directly through a clinic. No single general emergency number is published, so none is shown; whether 911 or 112 connects is not confirmed by any official source found.

getting_around.summary: Distances are long and the Andes make roads slow, so most visitors fly between Lima, Cusco and Arequipa and then travel by road or rail locally; the Lima-Cusco hop is the one most itineraries are built around, and it is also the altitude jump that needs a rest day at the other end. In Cusco and the Sacred Valley, movement is by road (colectivo, bus or hired transport) plus the rail line to Aguas Calientes/Machupicchu Pueblo, which is the only way in other than walking. The part of a Peru trip that genuinely cannot be improvised is Machu Picchu itself: entry is capacity-capped by ministerial resolution, tickets are sold only by the state, and the popular dates go early.

passes.name: Llaqta de Machupicchu entry ticket (boleto de ingreso)
passes.covers: Timed entry to the Machu Picchu citadel on a specific date and circuit. Sold exclusively by Peru's Ministry of Culture through tuboleto.cultura.pe - the ministry's 2026 capacity resolution states sales are only through that portal, so any other seller is a reseller.
passes.worth_it: Not optional - you cannot enter without one. Entry is capped by ministerial resolution at 5,600 visitors per day on the specific high-season dates listed in the resolution and 4,500 per day for the rest of the year. The Ministry of Culture opened the whole 2026 season for advance reservation on 17 November 2025 (Machu Picchu reservations from midday), moving the opening forward from December to November specifically to avoid saturation on the busiest dates - so the realistic advice is to book as soon as the following year's window opens, and certainly several months out for June-August, rather than weeks out. Reserve on the portal and then pay on the same platform within the published payment schedule or the reservation lapses.

passes.name: Red de Caminos Inka permit (Inca Trail)
passes.covers: Trekking permit for the Inca Trail network into Machu Picchu, sold through the same official platform, tuboleto.cultura.pe, and only through a licensed operator.
passes.worth_it: Permit numbers are limited and the whole year opens for reservation on one day - for 2026 that was 17 November 2025, with Inca Trail reservations opening at 08:00, four hours before the Machu Picchu citadel tickets. Treat the trail as something you book the moment the window opens, up to roughly a year ahead, not something you add to a trip that is already dated. Hard constraint to plan around: the Ministry of Culture closes the entire Inca Trail network for the whole of February every year for maintenance and conservation, reopening 1 March, so a February trip cannot include it. Closures for heavy rain outside February have also happened.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month of the year in Cusco, 145 mm. Afternoon downpours are the norm and trail and road conditions suffer.
climate.crowd_note: Low season apart from a short New Year bump; the citadel is at its 4,500-a-day cap rather than 5,600.

climate.precipitation_note: Still deep in the wet season, 134 mm, with the heaviest sustained rain of the year around Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: Quietest month, but the entire Inca Trail network is closed 1-28 February for maintenance, so a trek-based itinerary is impossible.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain easing but still substantial at 107 mm; the landscape is at its greenest.
climate.crowd_note: Inca Trail reopens 1 March and is far less contested than mid-year.

climate.precipitation_note: Sharp drop to 43 mm as the wet season ends; clear spells return.
climate.crowd_note: Green scenery with dry-season skies arriving and far fewer people than June-August - arguably the best value month.

climate.precipitation_note: Effectively dry at 9 mm. Nights are getting cold at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Dry-season conditions before the July-August crush.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest stretch of the year, under 2 mm, with warm days and near-freezing nights in Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: High season. Inti Raymi on 24 June fills Cusco; permits and hotels for that week go furthest ahead of anything else.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry, 4 mm, with the coldest nights of the year at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month alongside August; expect the 5,600-a-day high-season cap and sold-out dates.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry at 9 mm; windy and dusty in the highlands.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the peak. Book entry and permits many months ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: First light rains return, 22 mm, with mostly settled weather.
climate.crowd_note: Crowds thin noticeably after the northern-hemisphere holidays while conditions stay good.

climate.precipitation_note: Warmest days of the year in Cusco with rain building to 39 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Comfortable shoulder month; afternoon showers become likely.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet season arriving in earnest, 72 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet, and the month the following year's Machu Picchu and Inca Trail reservations open.

climate.precipitation_note: Back into heavy rain at 123 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Wet, but Christmas and New Year bring a short local and holiday-travel surge.

timezone_note: A single time zone applies to the whole country, including Palawan and Mindanao, and there is no daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: The Philippine government's official e-visa portal states that visa-free temporary visitors' passports must be "valid for at least six (6) months beyond the applicant's date of departure" from the Philippines. The UK FCDO's Philippines page words it as an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive. The stricter of the two readings, six months beyond your planned departure date, is the one recorded here.
entry_requirement_notes: Four things beyond the passport rule. (1) Onward travel: visa-free visitors "must also possess return tickets to their country of origin or outward-bound tickets to their next country of destination", per the official e-visa portal; the UK FCDO's Philippines page says most visitors are expected to have proof of return or onward travel and that officials and airlines may ask to see it. (2) eTravel: registration at etravel.gov.ph is required for all arriving foreign and Filipino passengers and you show the QR code to the airline before boarding. It is free and, per the official eTravel FAQ, may be done within 72 hours (3 days) before arrival; the UK FCDO says the same ("within the 72 hours before your arrival"). A green QR code goes straight to immigration, a red one means a Bureau of Quarantine check first. Diplomats, foreign dignitaries and their delegations, 9(e) visa holders and diplomatic/official/service passport holders are exempt. A Bureau of Immigration advisory page on mandatory eTravel registration is published only as an image that could not be read, so no earlier-than-72-hours rule is recorded. (3) Visitors must have no derogatory record with the Bureau of Immigration. (4) Cash: per the UK FCDO, you cannot take in more than 50,000 Philippine pesos, and foreign currency over US$10,000 must be declared. Stay lengths, per the official e-visa portal: most visa-free nationals get an initial 30 days; Brazil and Israel get 59 days; Hong Kong SAR passport holders get 14 days. Indian passport holders: since 8 June 2025, 14 days (non-extendible, non-convertible, tourism and business) with a confirmed hotel booking and proof of financial capacity; Indians holding a valid American, Japanese, Australian, Canadian, Schengen, Singapore or United Kingdom visa get 30 days for tourism on a valid passport plus a return or onward ticket. Older Philippine consulate pages still describe a 14-day (extendible to 21) rule for Indians holding such visas; the e-visa portal is the more current source and is followed here, so check your own nationality on the e-visa policy page. Apart from the Indian 14-day route above, no proof-of-funds or mandatory travel-insurance requirement was found on any official Philippine source. The Philippine Embassy in Tokyo's visa-free page could not be opened (blocked to automated access), so its wording was not checked directly.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid
Japanese encephalitis (stays of a month or more, or extended rural/outdoor exposure)
Rabies (for travellers with likely animal contact)
COVID-19
health.malaria_risk: Present in the province of Palawan and the Mindanao island group. Metro Manila and other urban centres are malaria-free. CDC advises prescription antimalarials for travel to risk areas.
health.notes: Only the yellow fever certificate is an entry condition, and only for arrivals from a yellow-fever risk country (CDC: required from age 9 months, including layovers over 12 hours in such countries; not required for direct travel from the US). The UK FCDO adds that proof of polio vaccination may be needed if arriving from certain countries with a transmission risk. Everything else on the recommended list is advisory and is not checked at the border. Dengue is a year-round mosquito-borne risk and the UK FCDO notes heightened dengue risk during the June-to-October rainy season, so insect-bite avoidance matters more than any vaccine for a typical short visit.

emergency.notes: 911 is the Philippines' national emergency hotline, covering police, fire and medical response. The UK FCDO's Philippines health advice tells travellers to "Call 911 and ask for an ambulance". The Department of the Interior and Local Government has been consolidating more than thirty separate local emergency numbers into this single nationwide 911 line. The Philippines' own emergency-hotline pages (e911.gov.ph, gov.ph/the-government/hotlines, officialgazette.gov.ph/emergency-hotlines) all return HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the number here is cited to the UK FCDO's page about the Philippines rather than to a first-hand Philippine source. Whether 112 also connects, and whether English is reliably answered outside Metro Manila, could not be verified from an official source.

climate.precipitation_note: Deep in the dry season: 19mm normal for Manila. PAGASA classes December to February as the cool dry season, and January as the coolest month nationally (mean 25.5C).
climate.crowd_note: Busiest stretch of the year for foreign visitors; book Palawan and Boracay well ahead. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month in Manila's normals at 7.9mm. Still within PAGASA's cool dry season.
climate.crowd_note: Reliable weather and high demand; prices stay at dry-season levels. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 11.1mm in Manila. PAGASA's hot dry season runs March to May, so heat starts building.
climate.crowd_note: Good sea conditions with the heat still manageable. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Manila's hottest average high (33.5C in the normals) with only 21.4mm of rain.
climate.crowd_note: Holy Week is the busiest domestic travel week of the year; beaches and inter-island ferries fill up. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Rainfall jumps to 165.2mm as the dry season ends. PAGASA records May as the warmest month nationally (mean 28.3C).
climate.crowd_note: Hot and increasingly wet; the transition month, with rates starting to soften. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: PAGASA's rainy season begins: 265.0mm in Manila as the southwest monsoon sets in.
climate.crowd_note: Quieter and cheaper, but afternoon downpours and the first tropical cyclones disrupt island-hopping. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 419.6mm in Manila. PAGASA puts the peak of the typhoon season at July through October, when nearly 70% of typhoons develop.
climate.crowd_note: Low season; ferry cancellations and flight disruption are common. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Manila's normals at 486.1mm, inside PAGASA's July-to-October typhoon peak. The Philippines averages about 20 tropical cyclones a year in its area of responsibility, 8 or 9 of which cross the country.
climate.crowd_note: The month most likely to have a trip rearranged by weather; Metro Manila flooding closes roads. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 330.3mm in Manila, still inside the typhoon peak.
climate.crowd_note: Cheapest fares of the year, but the least dependable for a fixed island itinerary. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 270.9mm in Manila. The last month of PAGASA's typhoon peak; rainfall starts easing late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Improving toward month end, but still worth building slack into flight connections. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 129.3mm in Manila. PAGASA's rainy season formally runs to the end of November, but conditions improve markedly; late-season cyclones still occur.
climate.crowd_note: A good-value window before December rates rise. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 75.4mm in Manila as PAGASA's dry season begins; the cool dry season runs December to February.
climate.crowd_note: Dry, comfortable weather but a heavy domestic travel period around Christmas and New Year. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

timezone_note: Poland has one time zone (IANA Europe/Warsaw). On 19 October 2026 it is on central European summer time (CEST, UTC+2); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The Polish Tourist Organisation's practical-information page gives CET (UTC+1) with CEST (UTC+2) in summer; the exact changeover date comes from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Polish government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Poland is in the Schengen area. The Polish Ministry of the Interior and Administration (MSWiA) states that a travel document must be valid for at least three months after the intended date of departure from Schengen territory and must have been issued within the previous 10 years (an emergency may justify waiving the validity requirement). The EU's Your Europe portal and UK FCDO's Poland entry page give the same two conditions (FCDO adds that passports renewed before 1 October 2018 may be invalid for entry because of their issue date). Visa-free short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. The MSWiA page is undated, so confirm with a Polish consulate or the Border Guard if your passport is close to either limit.
entry_requirement_notes: CURRENCY: Poland is in the EU and Schengen area but its currency is the zloty (PLN, 1 zloty = 100 groszy), not the euro; the Polish Tourist Organisation (poland.travel) states that Poland's legal tender is the zloty. No euro adoption date was found on an official page opened for this guide. ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and gives a fee of EUR 20; a later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026', that the exact date will be communicated later, and that the authorisation will be valid for 3 years or until the passport expires. No page opened gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is already live: the Commission says it 'became fully operational on 10 April 2026'; UK FCDO says it involves biometric registration (fingerprints and a photo) at no cost, with a digital record valid for 3 years. TEMPORARY BORDER CHECKS: per MSWiA (gov.pl, 1 October 2026), Poland extended its internal-border controls with Germany and Lithuania for the period 2 October 2026 to 30 March 2027 (they began on 7 July 2025). The Border Guard says that at these borders travellers must cross at designated points, carry documents to show and allow vehicle checks. The MSWiA page does not list crossing points or documents, and no check on the Czech or Slovak borders was stated. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). BORDER CHECKS: per the Border Guard and MSWiA, a third-country national entering must hold a valid travel document and a visa if required, state the purpose and conditions of the stay, have enough funds for the stay and the return, and not be listed in the Schengen Information System. MSWiA's page gives minimum funds of PLN 300 for stays up to 4 days and PLN 75 per day for longer stays, higher if you have no return ticket and lower for some categories of traveller; that page is undated, so treat the figures as unconfirmed for today. UK FCDO says Polish border control may ask you to show a return or onward ticket and prove you have enough money; no page opened states that an onward ticket is a fixed condition, and none states a blank-page requirement, so those fields are not stated. CASH: the Polish government portal powroty.gov.pl (page current as of 22 May 2026) says cash worth EUR 10,000 or more carried into or out of the EU must be declared in writing, in Poland to the customs-fiscal service (Sluzba Celno-Skarbowa), and that failing to declare, giving false information or not presenting the cash on request is a fiscal misdemeanour punishable by a fine. It adds that member states may set their own rules at internal borders. GOODS: poland.travel (undated, copyright 2023) lists allowances for non-EU arrivals aged 17 and over (for example 1 litre of spirits over 22% ABV, 2 litres of wine, 40 cigarettes by land or 200 by air or sea) and says animal products from outside the EU are banned except certain infant products, with meat and milk needing a special permit; FCDO likewise says meat, milk and products containing them cannot be taken into the EU, with exceptions such as baby food. poland.travel also says the public drinking of alcohol outside licensed venues is prohibited. ID: neither poland.travel nor FCDO states a general legal duty to carry ID for visitors.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 and older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure from planned outdoor activities; may be considered for others)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider; present in some wildlife)
Mpox (only for adults with specific higher-risk activities)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Poland page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Poland page states the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page carries a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis among non-vaccine-preventable risks, and advises repellent and tick checks after outdoor activity. Poland's chief sanitary inspectorate (GIS, via a regional sanitary station page that carries no date) says several hundred tick-borne encephalitis cases are recorded each year, highest in the north-east (podlaskie and warminsko-mazurskie), that the basic vaccine schedule is three doses with boosters every 3-5 years, and that the vaccine does not protect against Lyme borreliosis. Emergency care: dial 112 (see emergency numbers). No page from the Polish health ministry was opened for this guide; CDC, GIS (regional page) and FCDO are used instead.

money.card_acceptance: The Polish Tourist Organisation (poland.travel) says cards are widely accepted, especially in major towns and tourist attractions, and are standard in supermarkets and most shops (Visa, Mastercard and American Express named). The page carries no date beyond a 2023 copyright footer, so treat it as general guidance.
money.cash_culture: Prices are in zloty (PLN). poland.travel says currency can be exchanged at banks, exchange offices called 'kantor', hotel receptions and ATMs; kantors usually open 9 am to 7 pm on weekdays and until 2 pm on Saturday, and transactions in a kantor cannot be reversed. 24-hour exchange is usually available at major tourist hubs such as train stations, border crossings and airports. Those hours are the page's undated figures.
money.atm_notes: poland.travel says Poland has a dense ATM network (about 10,000 machines, over 1,000 in Warsaw), connected to international networks, operating 24 hours and found near banks, rail stations, airports, supermarkets and town centres, and advises checking foreign-use charges with your own bank or card issuer. The ATM count is an undated figure.

emergency.notes: The Polish government's 112 page (gov.pl/web/numer-alarmowy-112) calls 112 the national emergency number and says calls go to one of 17 emergency notification centres (CPR), one in each voivodeship capital and in Radom; calls to 997 (police) and 998 (fire) also reach CPR operators, and 999 (ambulance) is not yet fully integrated but is to be handled by CPR centres eventually. UK FCDO's Poland page lists ambulance 999, fire 998 and police 997 and does not mention 112, so dialling 112 is the safe single number if unsure. The 112 page says nothing about English-language service. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page. The same gov.pl page also lists 116 111 (child and youth helpline) and +48 222 309 900 (helpline for crime victims), and the Alarm112 app for people who cannot make a voice call; these are not emergency numbers.

getting_around.summary: Warsaw's city transport authority (ZTM) is covered by the City of Warsaw's 19115 portal, which lists 24-hour, 72-hour and weekend tickets by zone (below); the Polish Tourist Organisation says city tickets are sold at 'Ruch' kiosks, grocery shops or from the driver, must be validated, and that travelling without a validated ticket can mean a fine (amount not stated there). The national long-distance operator PKP Intercity (intercity.pl) says Warsaw-Krakow takes 2 h 21 min on Express InterCity Premium (EIP, Pendolino) and 2 h 54 min on InterCity (its Warsaw-Krakow page is undated). EIP requires a ticket bought before boarding and conductors cannot sell tickets on board except to passengers with disabilities. Seat reservations (Poland prices, per PKP Intercity's reservation guide updated 11 September 2026): EIP always mandatory at PLN 43; EIC recommended at PLN 3; IC mandatory only on trains marked 'R' (PLN 3); TLK recommended (PLN 3). Regional rail, buses, airport transfers and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.name: Warsaw 24-hour, 72-hour and weekend tickets
passes.covers: Per the City of Warsaw's 19115 portal (page updated 20 November 2025; the tariff's effective date is not stated): a 24-hour ticket is PLN 15 for zone 1 (PLN 7.50 reduced) or PLN 26 for zones 1+2 (PLN 13 reduced); a 72-hour ticket is PLN 36 for zone 1 (PLN 18 reduced) or PLN 57 for zones 1+2 (PLN 28.50 reduced); a weekend ticket for zones 1+2 is PLN 24 (PLN 12 reduced) valid from 19:00 Friday to 08:00 Monday, and a weekend group ticket for up to 5 people is PLN 40. All are valid at P+R car parks and run from validation.
passes.worth_it: Single-journey prices and the airport fare were not confirmed here, so a break-even against single tickets cannot be stated; check ztm.waw.pl or warszawa19115.pl for the journeys you plan.

passes.name: PKP Intercity point-to-point tickets
passes.covers: Tickets for Intercity trains (EIP, EIC, IC, TLK) sold at ticket offices, ticket machines, ebilet.intercity.pl and the PKP Intercity app; EIP and some IC trains need a seat reservation (prices above). Interrail pass holders can use the trains but must still buy the reservation.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey. Fares were not read for this guide (PKP Intercity's EIP page says tickets start at PLN 29, on a page last updated 29 November 2019, so confirm current fares).

climate.precipitation_note: 31.0 mm mean monthly precipitation total; mean daily max 1.0 C and min -4.0 C. Calculated for this guide as the 1991-2020 mean (30 of 30 years present for every month) of the monthly values IMGW (Instytut Meteorologii i Gospodarki Wodnej, Poland's national met service) publishes as open data for the Warszawa-Okecie synoptic station (code 352200375; listed as WARSZAWA-OKECIE in some years and WARSZAWA in others, same code). It is not a table copied from an IMGW normals publication, so it can differ slightly from IMGW's own published normals.
climate.crowd_note: Freezing nights and short days; quiet apart from the New Year period and ski areas (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: 29.8 mm mean monthly precipitation total; mean daily max 2.6 C and min -3.3 C. Calculated for this guide as the 1991-2020 mean (30 of 30 years present for every month) of the monthly values IMGW (Instytut Meteorologii i Gospodarki Wodnej, Poland's national met service) publishes as open data for the Warszawa-Okecie synoptic station (code 352200375; listed as WARSZAWA-OKECIE in some years and WARSZAWA in others, same code). It is not a table copied from an IMGW normals publication, so it can differ slightly from IMGW's own published normals.

timezone_note: Primary zone is Europe/Lisbon, which covers mainland Portugal; Madeira (Atlantic/Madeira) keeps the same clock as the mainland, while the Azores (Atlantic/Azores) run one hour behind it (UTC-1 in winter, UTC+0 in summer). The Azores and Madeira are not separate entries in this guide; the zone differences are from the IANA database, not from a page opened for this guide. Summer time follows the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, so on 17 October 2026 mainland Portugal is on WEST (UTC+1) and clocks go back to WET (UTC+0) on Sunday 25 October 2026 (the last Sunday of October that year). A web search listed the Observatorio Astronomico de Lisboa (oal.ul.pt) as giving 25 October 2026 for the change, but its pages could not be opened (expired TLS certificate), so the date rests on the last-Sunday rule rather than on a page cited here.
passport_validity_rule: Portugal is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (counted from the day you enter). UK FCDO's Portugal entry page gives the same two conditions. Portugal's own visa portal (vistos.mne.gov.pt), for visa applicants, asks for a travel document valid over 3 months after the date of exit. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. This applies to the mainland, Madeira and the Azores.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (17 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. A later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be communicated later, and the French foreign ministry (April 2026) says it is 'not yet operational'. No page opened for this guide announces an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation (not a visa) for visa-exempt nationals: the Commission gives a fee of EUR 20 (people under 18 or over 70 exempt from the fee) and validity of 3 years or until the passport expires. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; per UK FCDO it replaces manual passport stamping, you may be asked to register fingerprints and a photo at the border, and the digital record is valid for 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and vistos.mne.gov.pt). Official pages say border officers may ask for proof of enough money and an onward or return ticket (FCDO), and Portugal's visa portal requires a return reservation and bank statements from visa applicants, but no page opened for this guide states that visa-exempt visitors must hold an onward ticket as a fixed condition or gives a proof-of-funds figure, and the consulates quote differing figures, so an onward ticket, blank pages and a funds figure are not stated here. FCDO's entry page gives no separate entry rules for Madeira or the Azores. Cash: Portugal's customs authority (info-aduaneiro.portaldasfinancas.gov.pt, page titled 'Viaja com 10.000 euros ou mais em dinheiro? Nao se esqueca de o declarar!') and Global Affairs Canada say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash (or equivalent) into or out of the EU must be declared to customs; this does not apply to travel within the EU. Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) also says ETIAS applications are 'not yet open' and that customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds, which fits that: a request, not a fixed condition. The ETIAS site (travel-europe.europa.eu/en/etias, opened 18 October 2026) still says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation'; the Commission's EES page says EES 'became fully operational on 10 April 2026'.

health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Portugal page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Portugal page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (page section last updated 23 April 2025; the page was last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. The page has no malaria section, carries only a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and has no notices specific to Madeira or the Azores. It also names leptospirosis, leishmaniasis (sand fly bites), hantavirus and tuberculosis under non-vaccine-preventable risks and says road crashes are a major risk. Emergency care is via 112. For non-urgent medical advice, UK FCDO's health page lists SNS 24 on +351 808 24 24 24 on the mainland (press 9 for English), +351 800 24 24 20 for Madeira and Porto Santo, and +351 808 24 60 24 for the Azores, and says a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance. CDC and FCDO are used as fallbacks because no page from Portugal's health ministry (sns.gov.pt / dgs.pt) was opened for this guide.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Portugal pages (a fallback; no Portuguese government emergency page could be opened) list one number, 112, for ambulance, fire and police, and say the police are the PSP (Policia de Seguranca Publica) in cities and the GNR (Guarda Nacional Republicana) in smaller towns and rural areas. Police, ambulance and fire are therefore all shown as 112. For non-emergency medical advice FCDO lists SNS 24 on 808 24 24 24 (mainland; press 9 for English), 800 24 24 20 (Madeira and Porto Santo) and 808 24 60 24 (Azores). No dedicated tourist police line and no separate direct ambulance or fire number was found on an official page, so none is listed here. Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/portugal) independently says 'Dial 112 for emergency assistance' and the European Commission (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/112) says 112 reaches ambulance, fire brigade or police and is available everywhere in the EU free of charge.

getting_around.summary: Long-distance travel on the mainland is led by CP (Comboios de Portugal). Per CP's own pages, the Alfa Pendular is its fastest service (maximum speed 220 km/h, introduced 1999; 301 seats, free Wi-Fi, a cafeteria and bar carriage) with Braga to Faro and Lisbon to Porto given as typical journeys, and Intercidades is a separate intercity service connecting the main cities (Minho to the Algarve, Lisbon to Porto, the Alentejo and the Centre). CP advertises up to 65% off when you buy Alfa Pendular or Intercidades tickets in advance. No official journey time or fare for any route was opened for this record, so none is given: check the CP timetable and fares on cp.pt. Lisbon and Porto each run their own operator fares (see the passes below). Carris Metropolitana (the regional bus network around Lisbon), the Madeira and Azores bus and ferry networks, and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.name: Lisbon Carris/Metro single ticket and 24-hour tickets
passes.covers: Metro de Lisboa's 2026 fare sheet (effective 1 January 2026) lists a Carris/Metro single ticket at 1.90 EUR (one journey on the whole Carris/Metro network within 1 hour of first validation, not valid for consecutive Metro rides) and a 24-hour ticket for unlimited travel on Carris and Metro at 7.25 EUR, with variants adding Transtejo (Cacilhas) at 10.35 EUR and CP at 11.40 EUR. The sheet does not say which CP lines the 11.40 EUR ticket covers.
passes.worth_it: A 24-hour ticket at 7.25 EUR equals roughly four single tickets, so it pays off on a day of four or more separate journeys. The sheet also lists a navegante occasional card at 0.50 EUR to hold the ticket; confirm the current figures with Metro de Lisboa or Carris before buying.

passes.name: Porto Andante Tour and Andante 24 (Z2)
passes.covers: Metro do Porto's tariff in force from 1 January 2026 lists Andante Tour 1 at 7.75 EUR (24 consecutive hours from first validation) and Andante Tour 3 at 16.55 EUR (72 consecutive hours), and an Andante 24 ticket for zone Z2 at 5.35 EUR (24 hours in the zones bought). The Andante site says the Tour card works across the Andante intermodal network but not on the Funicular dos Guindais or the STCP tram, and cannot be topped up.
passes.worth_it: The Tour passes are for visitors using metro, bus and train widely, while the Andante 24 (Z2) is cheaper if you stay inside the zones you bought. Which zone your trips need was not checked, and the Metro do Porto page gave an Andante Azul (occasional) card at 0.60 EUR and a Z2 single at 1.40 EUR; check andante.pt for the zone map.

passes.name: CP long-distance tickets (Alfa Pendular, Intercidades)
passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets for CP's Alfa Pendular and Intercidades trains, sold on cp.pt; no national rail pass was found on an official page.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey. CP advertises up to 65% off for advance purchase, so for fixed travel dates buy early; the discount terms were not read in full.

timezone_note: One time zone for the whole country. Visit Qatar's travel tips give the time zone as GMT+3, and the WMO World Weather Information Service entry for Doha lists +0300 with daylight saving 'N'. Qatar does not use daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Sources differ, so check before booking. Visit Qatar (visa page) says the passport must be valid for at least three months from the date of arrival. UK FCDO says visitors' passports should be valid for at least 6 months from the date you arrive, and Global Affairs Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Qatar (and that transportation companies may apply stricter rules). The structured figure is the stricter 6 months from entry; Qatar's own tourism board states 3 months. Entry is refused with a passport reported lost or stolen.
entry_requirement_notes: PASSPORT VALIDITY IS WHERE THE OFFICIAL SOURCES DISAGREE. Visit Qatar (the Qatar Tourism visa page) says "The visitor's passport must be valid for at least three months from the date of arrival in Qatar". UK FCDO says visitors' passports should be valid for at least 6 months from arrival, and Global Affairs Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Qatar. The structured field uses the stricter 6 months because airlines can apply it at check-in and a refused boarding costs far more than renewing early. VISA: Visit Qatar says 102 nationalities enter visa-free ("Visa-free entry is now the new term defining previously 'visa on arrival'. Nothing changed except the name."), GCC citizens need no visa, and everyone else applies for an e-visa on the Hayya platform (hayya.qa). The fee is QAR 100, paid at the airport for visa-free/on-arrival entrants who are charged, or online after approval for Hayya visas (categories A1 tourist, A2, A3 depending on nationality). The Visit Qatar page is an interactive checker, so the result for your own passport is not published as a static list - run it before booking. Hayya is presented as optional for visa-free nationalities ("Enter visa-free OR apply now for a Hayya A1 Entry Visa") and compulsory for the nationalities listed as visa-required; for the A1 application a hotel reservation is needed. For some groups, visa-free entry needs a confirmed hotel booking on arrival or a registration booked through the Discover Qatar website before travel, as the Ministry of Interior requires. One group is listed as needing a confirmed round-trip ticket, and the page does not label which nationalities. STAY LENGTH: Visit Qatar gives no single visa-free length. It states that US citizens receive a visa valid two years or until the passport expires, multiple entry, with each stay up to 90 days. It also describes a Qatar-Oman Joint Tourist Visa issued on arrival, valid 30 days for both countries and extendable for another 30 days for a fee, for listed nationalities that include Australia, Canada, Germany, Singapore, the UK and the US. UK FCDO says full British citizens can get a tourist visa on arrival, that holders of other British passport types need a visa in advance, and that stays over 30 days need the visa waiver extended before it expires (a fine, payable before departure, applies otherwise). Global Affairs Canada says tourist visas are not required for Canadians. PRE-ARRIVAL REGISTRATION: no page we could read states a separate mandatory 'Digital Travel' or arrival-registration form for visitors. The only digital pre-arrival system named by Visit Qatar and hayya.qa is Hayya (e-visa, host family and friends, and vehicle pre-registration for the Abu Samra land border). The Ministry of Interior portal (portal.moi.gov.qa) returned 'Request Rejected' to automated fetches, so this could not be checked there; confirm on hayya.qa and portal.moi.gov.qa before you fly. HEALTH INSURANCE: sources differ. Visit Qatar says it recommends insurance and that you can buy a policy on arrival; UK FCDO says stays over 30 days need health insurance from a Ministry of Public Health registered provider bought before travel (standard premium QAR 50 per person per month); Global Affairs Canada says you need health insurance recognised by the Ministry of Public Health. Take cover for the whole trip regardless. MEDICATION: FCDO says some prescribed and over-the-counter medicines are controlled in Qatar; you need a prescription and a medical report in English or Arabic issued within the last 6 months, and the Ministry of Public Health runs an electronic permit service for controlled medicines for personal use (fli.moph.gov.qa, as linked by FCDO; that page was not opened here). FCDO states no quantity limit. Drugs carry zero tolerance, including in transit. CUSTOMS: Visit Qatar says cash or equivalents (including jewellery, precious metals or stones) of QAR 50,000 or more must be declared on arrival; FCDO says more than QAR 50,000, and Global Affairs Canada says more than QAR 50,000 on entry and exit, so declare at or near the figure. Vapes, e-cigarettes, their liquids and electronic shisha pipes are illegal to import, sell or buy whatever the quantity (FCDO). OTHER: Global Affairs Canada warns entry can be denied if your passport carries an Israeli visa or stamp, or you have a prior arrest, conviction or deportation in Qatar. FCDO says transit passengers cannot stay in the transit area more than 24 hours. Visit Qatar lists a Qatar Airways transit visa for passengers with a layover of at least 6 hours who are not visa-free (and a transit visa up to 4 days for longer stays). SECURITY: FCDO's current page (checked 19 October 2026) reports strikes and retaliatory attacks by Iran in the region since 8 July, including in Qatar, with a risk of airspace closures and flight cancellations - check flights and FCDO or your own government's advice immediately before travelling. Blank pages and proof of funds are not stated by the sources read.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (certificate required for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for travel direct from the USA)
Polio (UK FCDO says a certificate may be required in some circumstances; it does not say which)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
COVID-19
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60, per CDC)
Typhoid
Measles
Rabies (consider, depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.notes: Yellow fever is the entry-linked vaccine, and only conditionally: CDC says travellers arriving from countries with yellow fever transmission risk must be vaccinated (aged 9 months and older) and does not recommend the vaccine for Qatar itself; Global Affairs Canada says there is no yellow fever risk in Qatar and proof of vaccination is required only if arriving from a country where it occurs. FCDO also says a polio certificate may be required in some circumstances. Everything in the recommended list is medical advice, not checked at immigration. Malaria: CDC's Qatar page does not mention malaria, and neither does the Global Affairs Canada page, so malaria_risk is left null rather than asserting none. Other risks named by CDC and Global Affairs Canada: MERS (avoid camels and camel products, and sick people), rabies (dogs infected with rabies are sometimes found in Qatar, so avoid stray animals), a measles travel health notice, and low typhoid risk. Medication: bring a prescription and a medical report (English or Arabic, within 6 months), and check whether your medicine is controlled; FCDO links the Ministry of Public Health permit service. FCDO says healthcare facilities in Qatar are similar to those in the UK and that visitors pay for treatment, so make sure travel health insurance covers local treatment and evacuation. CDC's Qatar page was last reviewed 25 August 2026.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada says credit cards are widely accepted in Qatar. Visit Qatar's travel tips page does not state card acceptance. (Fallback: a foreign government's page about the country, not a Qatari source.)
money.cash_culture: Visit Qatar advises carrying cash for tips, and says the Qatari riyal is the only currency used in the country. It is pegged to the US dollar; Visit Qatar gives the rate as 3.64 QAR to the dollar.
money.tipping: Visit Qatar: most restaurants and hotels already add a service charge, but "a tip of 10-15% as a gesture of satisfaction is appreciated"; the page suggests carrying cash for tips. Check the bill for an included service charge first.
money.atm_notes: Visit Qatar says ATMs are common in malls, hotels and across Doha. It does not publish card networks or fees. Cash or equivalents of QAR 50,000 or more must be declared on arrival.

power.adapter_note: Visit Qatar's travel tips page says "The standard voltage is 240 V and the frequency is 50 Hz", that plugs match UK-style sockets (Type G is inferred from that wording), and that devices rated 100-127 V need a voltage converter. Anything rated 220-240V works unmodified; US 110V-only equipment needs a converter, not just a plug adapter.

emergency.notes: Visit Qatar's travel tips list 999 for police, fire and ambulance, and its safety page names 999 as the emergency response number; Global Affairs Canada lists 999 for police and ambulance, and UK FCDO says to dial 999 and ask for an ambulance. Other numbers on Visit Qatar: Traffic and Patrol Police 4890666; deaf visitors can reach 992 by video call, SMS, or email at 992@moi.gov.qa; Qatar Tourism hotline 106 (inside Qatar) or +974 44069921 (from abroad), for general information rather than emergencies. We could NOT confirm from any official source that 112 reaches Qatari emergency services, and no official page read states a tourist police number or a guaranteed language of response (FCDO says some medical staff speak English). Canadian Embassy in Doha: +974 4419-9000; British Embassy in Doha: +974 4496 2000 (per Global Affairs Canada and FCDO).

getting_around.summary: Doha has a three-line metro (Red, Green, Gold) meeting at Msheireb Station and serving Hamad International Airport (Terminal 1, on the Red Line), West Bay, Education City and Al Wakrah. The Lusail Tram (four lines, 25 stations) connects to the metro at Lusail and Legtaifiya stations and is ridden with your metro travel card; the Msheireb Tram (about 2 km loop) and Education City Tram are free. Karwa Bus is run by the government-owned Mowasalat, with Metrolink feeder buses to metro stations. Karwa taxis are turquoise and can be hailed or booked through the Karwa Taxi app (airport taxi line +974 800 8294 per Visit Qatar); Uber is also used, and Avis, Budget, Europcar and Hertz rent cars. Friday morning metro service is shut for Friday prayers. Taxi and bus fares are not published on the pages read.

timezone_note: Romania has a single time zone (IANA Europe/Bucharest). On 19 October 2026 it is on Eastern European Summer Time (EEST, UTC+3); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to EET (UTC+2) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Romanian government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Romania is a full Schengen member, so the Schengen short-stay rules apply. UK FCDO's Romania entry page says the passport must have an expiry date at least 3 months after the date you plan to leave the Schengen area and must have been issued less than 10 years before arrival. Global Affairs Canada gives the same 3-months rule. Romania's General Inspectorate for Immigration (igi.mai.gov.ro) states the same two conditions for short-stay visa applicants (valid at least 3 months beyond the visa's validity, issued within the last 10 years). Visa-free stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. This is a 3-months-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule. No blank-page minimum is stated on any page opened.
entry_requirement_notes: Romania joined the Schengen area in two steps: the European Commission's home-affairs page (opened 2026-10-19) says checks at internal air and sea borders were lifted from 31 March 2024, and that Romania and Bulgaria became full members on 1 January 2025 when checks at internal land borders ended. Visa position depends on passport; this guide does not list nationalities. For visa-exempt nationals such as UK and Canadian citizens, UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say up to 90 days in any 180-day period in the Schengen area, counted from first entry, with earlier Schengen visits counting towards the 90. Romania's IGI (igi.mai.gov.ro, opened 2026-10-19) states that a short-stay (type C) visa allows up to 90 days in any 180 and cannot be extended, and that some nationals who normally need a visa may enter visa-free if they hold a valid Schengen visa, a Schengen or long-stay visa or residence permit, or a long-term EU residence permit, with the 90/180 limit still applying; check igi.mai.gov.ro and evisa.mae.ro or the nearest Romanian mission for your passport. Romania's e-visa portal (evisa.mae.ro) is an application and appointment system, not an instant authorisation: it says to apply at least two weeks and no more than three months before travel, that processing counts from the in-person appointment at the mission or consulate, and that a visa is only one entry condition. Entry/Exit System: FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say the EES records facial image and fingerprints of non-EU travellers at the Schengen external border; FCDO says it is free. ETIAS: both FCDO and Global Affairs Canada (pages opened 2026-10-19) say applications are not yet open, so no ETIAS authorisation can be obtained or is required today; check the official EU website before travel. UK FCDO says you may need to prove you have enough money for your stay and may need to show a return or onward ticket, but gives no figure; neither Romania's MFA nor IGI page opened stated a proof-of-funds amount or an onward-ticket condition, so onward_ticket_required is left null (carry one anyway). Declare cash or cheques of EUR 10,000 or more when entering or leaving the EU (FCDO and Global Affairs Canada). Global Affairs Canada says you must carry photo identification at all times and that a photocopy of the passport is acceptable. Registration of foreigners: IGI's page says hosts must notify the competent police unit within 3 days of accommodating a foreigner, and that, per the Romanian-language text of its registration portal, hotels and similar accommodation report guests within 24 hours; hotels normally handle this for guests. FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both warn that Romania may briefly reinstate checks at internal Schengen borders, so carry your passport when crossing. The Romanian foreign ministry (mae.ro), romania.travel, ANAF and the customs site returned errors (503, 403 or TLS failures) to automated fetches, so the UK, Canadian and EU pages above stand in for them where stated.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)

health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Romanian border for vaccination: CDC says Romania does not require yellow fever vaccination for entry and does not recommend it, and Global Affairs Canada says proof of vaccination is not required. The CDC Romania page opened (updated 23 April 2025) does not mention malaria, and no malaria statement was found in the Global Affairs Canada health summary either, so malaria_risk is left null rather than stated as none. CDC also flags leptospirosis, leishmaniasis, hantavirus and tuberculosis as non-vaccine-preventable risks and says rabies is present in some wildlife. Global Affairs Canada says medical facilities may not match Canadian standards, private hospitals in cities are often better equipped, and most facilities expect cash payment at the time of service. The Ministry of Health site (ms.ro/en) was opened but its travel-advice card was truncated, so nothing from it is relied on here.

money.card_acceptance: Global Affairs Canada says the Romanian economy is mainly cash-based but credit cards are widely accepted in major cities. This is a general official statement, not a rule for any particular shop; carry some lei for smaller places.
money.cash_culture: Global Affairs Canada says the currency is the leu (RON), that changing money on the street is illegal (exchange only at recognised places such as exchange shops, banks and hotels), that merchants may refuse worn banknotes, and that traveller's cheques are not widely accepted. UK FCDO says criminals have copied cards in some bars and restaurants and that theft is a risk near money exchanges.
money.atm_notes: Global Affairs Canada advises using ATMs in well-lit public areas or inside a bank or business and covering the keypad when entering your PIN. No official page opened gave ATM fees or limits.

emergency.notes: Romania's telecom regulator ANCOM (ancom.ro, opened 2026-10-19) states that 112 is the single number for alerting the police, fire brigade, ambulance, SMURD (mobile emergency, resuscitation and extrication service) and gendarmerie, reachable free of charge from fixed and mobile phones; that the 112 service receives calls in the main international languages; that foreign citizens in Romania may call it; and that the Apel 112 app (Android and iOS, needs data and GPS) can send the caller's location. UK FCDO's getting-help page lists 112 for police, ambulance and fire, and Global Affairs Canada lists only 112. No separate police, ambulance or fire numbers were found on an official page, so all three structured fields carry 112. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page.

getting_around.summary: CFR Calatori, the national passenger rail operator, runs a daily train between Bucuresti Nord station and Henri Coanda airport that its page says takes about 20 to 25 minutes. CFR says tickets can be bought online (bilete.cfrcalatori.ro), in the CFR Calatori app, at station offices up to 30 days ahead for domestic travel, at vending machines in major stations, or by contactless terminal on the train. UK FCDO says most Bucharest taxis should list prices on the side and display a company name, that drivers sometimes overcharge foreign visitors, and that apps such as Uber and Bolt are generally reliable; it also says a rovinieta road toll is required on national roads and can be bought at border points and most petrol stations. timezone_note: Rwanda uses a single time zone, Africa/Kigali (UTC+2), all year. Visit Rwanda's practical-information page gives 'Central Africa Time (GMT/UTC + 2 hours)' and the Rwandan High Commission in Pretoria's practical-info page says 'The time in Rwanda is GMT +2'. No daylight saving is stated by either page; the IANA database also has Kigali at fixed UTC+2.
passport_validity_rule: Passport (or other accepted travel document) valid for at least 6 months. Rwanda's Directorate General of Immigration and Emigration (migration.gov.rw, 'Visitors visa' page) lists the requirement as 'Any genuine acceptable travel document valid not less than 6 months', without saying from which date it is counted. The UK FCDO says the passport must have an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive and at least one blank page for entry stamps. Global Affairs Canada words it differently: valid 'at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Rwanda'. Because the two foreign advisories count from different dates and the DGIE page names none, the record stores the shorter reading (6 months from entry); a traveller whose passport has under 6 months left at departure should not rely on it, and airlines often enforce the stricter reading at check-in. The one blank page is from the FCDO only; DGIE's page does not mention blank pages.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA: Rwanda's DGIE (migration.gov.rw) says the tourist visa (V1) is 30 days single-entry or 90 days multiple-entry, issued on arrival at the border post or applied for online (Irembo) or at a Rwandan mission; fees on that page are USD 50 single / USD 70 multiple, free for nationals of countries with a visa-waiver arrangement. Visit Rwanda's 'Immigration & Visas' page says citizens of all countries can get a visa on arrival without applying in advance, that citizens of African Union, Commonwealth and La Francophonie countries get a free 30-day visa on arrival, that EAC citizens get a free entry visa for six months, and that citizens of Angola, Benin, Central African Republic, Chad, Cote d'Ivoire, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Ghana, Guinea, Indonesia, Haiti, Mauritius, Philippines, Senegal, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Sao Tome and Principe, Singapore and Qatar get 90-day free visas on arrival. It also caps fees at USD 50 single / USD 70 multiple entry. The DGIE page lists an East African Tourist Visa (V11) at USD 100 covering the signatory countries (Global Affairs Canada names Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda and says the first entry must be the issuing country if obtained before departure). The UK FCDO says Commonwealth citizens can get a free 30-day visa on arrival. Neither page lists the full visa-exempt country list, so check the passport against Irembo or a Rwandan mission. ONWARD TICKET / FUNDS / INSURANCE: none of the DGIE, Visit Rwanda, FCDO or Global Affairs Canada pages opened state an onward-ticket, proof-of-funds or health-insurance requirement, so onward_ticket_required is null (not confirmed either way). EBOLA ENTRY RESTRICTIONS (check before booking): Rwanda Biomedical Centre's notice of 16 June 2026 (also in its traveller info note dated 22 May 2026) says all foreign nationals who have travelled to or transited through the DRC within the last 30 days are denied entry; Rwandan nationals and foreign residents with proof of residency may enter but face mandatory quarantine if they were in the DRC in that window; health screening is reinforced at DRC land borders and enhanced entry controls apply at Kigali International Airport; the notice says tourism and travel within Rwanda continue as usual and gives no end date. The UK FCDO (page updated 4 September 2026, still current on 19 October 2026) mentions updated border measures in response to the DRC Ebola outbreak, says the DRC border crossings could close at short notice and advises against all but essential travel to parts of Rusizi District within 10 km of the DRC border (including the Lake Kivu islands and Kamembe Airport). These are the positions on those dates, not a forecast. PLASTIC BAGS: Visit Rwanda says plastic bags are 'Banned by law since 2008' and that 'any plastic bags in your luggage will be confiscated at the airport or other point of entry'; the FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say the same (Canada says non-biodegradable bags are prohibited and bags brought through Kigali airport will be confiscated). The RRA prohibited-goods page opened does not itself list plastic bags. E-CIGARETTES / VAPES: the FCDO says vapes and e-cigarettes are banned, with confiscation and a fine possible; Global Affairs Canada says they are illegal to import or use. DRONES: the FCDO says drones must be declared on arrival and may be confiscated or held until you leave, and that flying one to photograph a prohibited area without a permit can bring imprisonment or a severe fine; photographing some government buildings is prohibited. CASH DECLARATION: the Financial Intelligence Centre's Cash and Bearer Negotiable Instruments declaration form says anyone entering, transiting or leaving Rwanda with cash or bearer instruments worth more than USD 10,000 (or the equivalent) must declare it, with an immediate administrative fine of 5% of the amount for a false or missing declaration, without prejudice to criminal sanctions (form file dated 2022; not an RRA page). CUSTOMS: RRA's prohibited-and-restricted-goods page covers items such as narcotics, counterfeit goods, pornographic material, ivory and CITES products, arms and ammunition and historical artefacts; no duty-free allowance table was opened, so none is stated. The FCDO says travellers must declare anything prohibited or subject to tax or duty.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate for travellers arriving from or having recently been in a yellow-fever risk country (Rwanda Biomedical Centre notice; Rwanda says the list of countries is dynamic and the WHO list applies). CDC: not required for direct travel from the United States.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR; early dose for infants 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers aged 1 year or older)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Typhoid (recommended for most travellers)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be discussed with a provider; rabid dogs are common)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Cholera (consider for areas of active transmission, which CDC places in Western Province)
Mpox (only for adults with certain anticipated activities)
health.malaria_risk: CDC says malaria transmission occurs in all areas of Rwanda, mainly Plasmodium falciparum, with chloroquine resistance, and recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine (section updated 23 April 2025). Global Affairs Canada also says malaria is a risk and antimalarial medication is recommended for most travellers. Visit Rwanda's health page says much of Rwanda lies at too high an elevation for malaria to be a major concern but that the disease is still present, so anti-malarial drugs are recommended and travellers should protect against bites between dawn and dusk. The sources differ in emphasis; the conservative reading (take prophylaxis advice from a travel clinic) is the one stored. No Rwanda Biomedical Centre malaria page could be opened (the URL tried returned 404).
health.notes: ENTRY: the Rwanda Biomedical Centre's traveller info note (dated 22 May 2026) says a yellow fever vaccination certificate is mandatory from endemic countries and countries with active transmission, that travellers should be vaccinated at least 10 days before departure, that a certificate issued less than 10 days earlier is invalid and the traveller is quarantined until it becomes valid, that travellers without a certificate are vaccinated on arrival, and that travellers pay for quarantine or vaccination. The note gives both a 24-day and a 30-day window in different places and skips a list number, so confirm details with Rwandan authorities. The same note says testing and the Passenger Locator Form for COVID-19 are no longer required. EBOLA: see the entry notes for the DRC-related entry ban; RBC states there were no cases in Rwanda as of 16 June 2026. Its toll-free health line is 114 (24/7). The FCDO also records that Rwanda announced the end of the Marburg outbreak on 20 December 2024 (last confirmed case 30 October 2024). CDC notes Rift Valley Fever suspected cases in Rwanda, spread mainly through contact with infected animals or mosquito bites; CDC page last reviewed 25 August 2026. Visit Rwanda advises not drinking tap water and says King Faisal Hospital in Kigali is the most advanced in the country. All of this is medical information, not advice.

money.card_acceptance: The Rwandan High Commission in Pretoria's practical-info page (undated) says 'A growing number of places accept credit and debit cards, with Visa being more widely accepted than Mastercard' and advises checking when booking.
money.cash_culture: The same page says the Rwandan franc is the principal currency, that US dollars are widely accepted, that cash is preferred for local services, and that larger costs such as gorilla tracking and upmarket hotels often take US dollars or other hard currency. Global Affairs Canada says Rwanda is largely cash-based. Visitors carrying more than USD 10,000 must declare it (see entry notes).
money.tipping: The Rwandan High Commission in Pretoria's practical-info page (undated) says tipping is optional but appreciated, cash is usually preferred, and suggests US$10 per day for guides and drivers and US$2 for trekking porters. It is a diplomatic-mission page, so treat the amounts as guidance rather than a rule.

power.adapter_note: Visit Rwanda's practical-information page states 'Electricity 230v 50Hz'. It does not name the plug or socket types and no official source opened did, so plug_types is left empty; check the socket type with your accommodation or the IEC World Plugs list before travelling.

emergency.notes: Rwanda National Police's homepage lists the toll-free numbers 112 (Emergency), 113 (Traffic Accidents), 111 (Fire and Rescue), 110 (Maritime Problems), 997 (Anti Corruption), 3511 (Abuse by Police Officer) and 118 (Driving License Queries). Global Affairs Canada also lists police 112. AMBULANCE (official sources disagree): the UK FCDO says 'Call 112 and ask for an ambulance'; Global Affairs Canada lists medical assistance on 912 and gender-based violence on 3512; an RNP article of 25 November 2016 lists 912 among the national toll-free lines without saying what it is for and calls 114 'the ambulance helpline', while the Rwanda Biomedical Centre's homepage now lists 114 as its 24/7 toll-free line for health information and symptom reports. The stored ambulance number is 112, the general emergency line named by both RNP and the FCDO; if 112 does not connect, 912 and 114 are the other numbers named by official sources. No tourist-police number was found, so none is listed.

getting_around.summary: Visit Rwanda's 'Getting Around' page says Rwanda has no rail services; the most convenient way to travel the country is by car, either self-drive or with a driver arranged by a tour operator; main towns are linked by paved roads but smaller roads are frequently unsurfaced and can be worse in the rainy season. Taxis operate in larger towns, motorbike taxis are common (travel insurance may not cover them), shared minibuses are the most popular public transport, and Kigali buses use a smart card system called Tap&Go. The page does not give fares, timetables, ride-hailing apps or domestic-flight information, so none is stated.

climate.precipitation_note: Kigali: 76.9 mm normal rainfall; mean daily max 26.9 C and min 15.6 C (1961-1990 base period, as published by the WMO World Weather Information Service for Kigali; this is an old base period, and the Rwanda Meteorology Agency's own climate-normal page held no data table when opened). Visit Rwanda gives two rainy seasons, mid-February to May and mid-September to mid-December, and a dry season from June to mid-September.
climate.crowd_note: Short drier spell between the two rainy seasons; moderate demand (editorial judgement).

climate.precipitation_note: Kigali: 91.0 mm normal rainfall; mean daily max 27.4 C and min 15.8 C (1961-1990 base period, as published by the WMO World Weather Information Service for Kigali; this is an old base period, and the Rwanda Meteorology Agency's own climate-normal page held no data table when opened). timezone_note: Serbia has a single time zone and observes EU-style daylight saving. Per the IANA tz database for Europe/Belgrade, summer time (CEST, UTC+2) began 29 March 2026 and ends 25 October 2026, when clocks return to CET (UTC+1). Checked against the IANA database on 2026-09-28; the label above reflects the state on that date.
passport_validity_rule: Serbia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states the passport must be valid at least 90 days after the intended date of departure from the Republic of Serbia, contain at least two consecutive blank pages, and have been issued within the past 10 years. This is a 90-days-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa position depends on passport. Serbia's MFA (visa-regime pages, opened 2026-10-17) lists ordinary passports of, for example, the USA, UK, Singapore and Brazil as visa-free for up to 90 days in a six-month period counted from the date of first entry. India is different: the MFA page for India says diplomatic and official passports need no visa for up to 90 days, but ordinary passports require a visa. Under a 2014 Government decision, however, holders of national passports with a valid Schengen, UK or EU member state visa, or a visa of the United States, and holders of foreign passports with a residence permit in the Schengen area, the EU or the US, may enter and stay up to 90 days in a six-month period within the validity of that visa or permit without a Serbian visa (a residence permit issued as a separate card must be shown with the passport). The MFA page does not name a UK residence permit. Since 23 April 2025 Serbia also issues electronic visas, the Digital Travel Authorization, but only to nationals of countries enabled on welcometoserbia.gov.rs and only if low-risk and reciprocity conditions are met; otherwise a sticker visa applies. The pages opened did not list which nationalities are enabled, so Indian eligibility is not confirmed here: check welcometoserbia.gov.rs or the nearest Serbian mission before booking. Foreigner registration (the 'white card') is still in force: the stay must be registered with the police within 24 hours of arrival or of accommodation being provided. Hotels and other paid accommodation providers register guests; for visitors staying in a private home the host is legally responsible for registering them within 24 hours (MFA registration page and the police page). Permanent residents have eight days. Whether registration can also be done online was not confirmed from the official pages opened today, so do not assume it. Serbia's MFA also states entry may be refused without sufficient funds, defined as 50 EUR per day of stay shown by cash or a bank statement; health insurance covering at least 20,000 EUR of medical costs is recommended, not mandatory; and border officers may ask to see a return flight ticket and proof of a paid hotel booking, though Serbia does not state an onward ticket as a condition of entry. UK FCDO advice (2026-10-17) agrees: visa-free up to 90 days in any 6 months, passport valid at least 90 days after departure, register with local police within 24 hours.

getting_around.summary: Serbia is compact and mostly covered by road: the government's own visitor portal describes roughly 1,000 km of motorway, putting Belgrade about an hour from Novi Sad and under two hours from most of the north and south. The headline rail service is the modernised 'Soko' high-speed train, which the same portal states runs Belgrade to Novi Sad in about 35 minutes with free Wi-Fi; tickets and timetables come from Srbijavoz, the national passenger rail operator. Within Belgrade, GSP runs more than 150 bus, tram and trolleybus lines plus over 20 night lines.
