timezone_note: Singapore uses a single time zone, Asia/Singapore in the IANA database, fixed at UTC+8 with no daylight saving. This comes from the IANA database; no Singapore government page opened for this guide states the offset, so it is not independently sourced here.
passport_validity_rule: Singapore requires at least 6 months of passport validity for everyone except Singapore passport holders. ICA states "All travellers, except Singapore passport holders, must ensure their passport has a minimum validity of 6 months." UK FCDO says the passport must expire at least 6 months after the date you arrive, and the Government of Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you enter, including for passengers in transit; ICA itself does not say whether the count starts at entry or departure, so NextStamp counts from entry. Catch: your airline may refuse boarding on the same rule, so a passport inside the 6-month window should be renewed before booking.
entry_requirement_notes: CHECKED 18 October 2026. (1) SG Arrival Card (SGAC) with Electronic Health Declaration: IN FORCE and required. ICA states "All travellers are required to submit the SG Arrival Card with Electronic Health Declaration before arriving in Singapore"; this includes Singapore citizens, Permanent Residents and Long-Term Pass holders (except residents entering through the Woodlands and Tuas land checkpoints). Not required of passengers transiting or transferring without seeking immigration clearance. Submit within 3 days before arrival, counting the day of arrival (UK FCDO and Government of Canada say the same: up to three days before). It is free: ICA says it does not endorse or support commercial services that charge a fee to submit it for you. Submit only through ICA's SGAC e-Service on ica.gov.sg or the free MyICA app (choose the Foreign Visitors option); an acknowledgement email goes to the address you declare. If your health status changes after you submit, use the 'Update SGAC' feature; a false health declaration can be prosecuted under the Infectious Diseases Act. The SG Arrival Card is not a visa. (2) Passport validity: ICA states "All travellers, except Singapore passport holders, must ensure their passport has a minimum validity of 6 months." UK FCDO words it as an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive; the Government of Canada says at least 6 months beyond the date you enter, including in transit. ICA does not say whether the 6 months is counted from entry or from departure; the UK and Canadian pages count from arrival, so that basis is used here. (3) Visa: depends on your travel document; ICA publishes the list of documents that need a Singapore entry visa and notes that a visa is not an immigration pass and does not guarantee entry. The length of stay is set by the Visit Pass the officer grants at the checkpoint, not by a visa; UK FCDO says it is normally between 30 and 90 days for British citizens. Overstaying is an offence; a Visit Pass extension can be applied for. NextStamp's visa rules hold the per-passport answer. (4) Onward ticket and funds: ICA says "Short-Term travellers should have sufficient cash and proof of onward travel (tickets, visas)". The wording is 'should' rather than 'must', so treat it as an expectation the officer may check; the Government of Canada says officials may ask for a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds. No amount of funds is stated on the pages opened. (5) No blank-page requirement was found on any official page opened, so none is listed. (6) Yellow fever: not required from most countries, but ICA requires a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate from any traveller, residents included, who has been in a country with risk of yellow fever transmission in the six days before arrival, or who spent more than 12 hours in airport transit in such a country; the certificate becomes valid 10 days after vaccination. ICA's country list is marked correct as of 18 November 2022, so check it. (7) Customs and declarations: ICA says you must declare if you carry cash and bearer negotiable instruments (CBNI) totalling more than S$20,000 or the foreign-currency equivalent. Electronic cigarettes and vaporisers are on ICA's list of prohibited goods; UK FCDO and the Government of Canada both say bringing them in is illegal even for personal use and can bring a fine or jail. Medicines are controlled goods: carry a doctor's prescription for prescription-only medication, and take the Red Channel if an import licence or authorisation is needed. Drug penalties are severe (the Government of Canada and UK FCDO mention caning and the death penalty for trafficking, and FCDO says this includes drugs found while transiting the airport; Canada says customs can drug-test on arrival). Biometrics (iris, face, fingerprints) are recorded on entry and exit per the Government of Canada. Duty-free allowances were not confirmed from an opened page, so none are stated.

health.notes: Dengue is the main mosquito-borne risk: UK FCDO lists dengue, and the Government of Canada says there is no vaccine or medication to prevent it, so avoid bites at all times; CDC advises covering skin and using repellent with 20% or more DEET. CDC carries a Level 1 (usual precautions) travel health notice for measles. UK FCDO describes Singapore healthcare as of a high quality and expensive and advises travel insurance covering treatment and repatriation. The recommended list is CDC medical advice, not something checked at immigration. The yellow fever entry rule is ICA's (see entry_requirement_notes); CDC and the Government of Canada do not consider Singapore itself a yellow fever risk. Malaria risk was not addressed on the pages opened, so it is left null.

power.adapter_note: Singapore's Consumer Product Safety Office says the 13A three-pin fused plug (Type G) is suitable for most electrical appliances in Singapore. It also names Type M (15A, three round pins, generally air-conditioners) and Type C (2.5A, two round pins, low-power appliances, used with a fused conversion plug) and says Schuko plugs (10A/16A) are not suitable for use in Singapore. That page does not state the mains voltage or frequency, and no opened official page did, so those are left null; check your device's rating before plugging in.

emergency.notes: SCDF runs 995 for fire and ambulance and says to call it only for life-threatening emergencies; calls assessed as non-life-threatening can be referred to the NurseFirst helpline (6262 6262) for advice. SMS 70995 is for people who are deaf, hard of hearing or speech-impaired (SCDF encourages everyone else to call). Singapore Police Force lists 999 for immediate police assistance and SMS 70999 if it is not safe to talk; its non-emergency Police Hotline is 1800 255 0000 (crime-related information). SCDF's non-emergency ambulance line 1777 is being discontinued from 1 January 2027 (use go.gov.sg/pao for private ambulance operators). The Government of Canada and UK FCDO give the same 999 and 995 numbers. No official source opened gives a separate tourist-police number or a general international emergency number, so those are left null.

getting_around.summary: Singapore's Land Transport Authority describes the public transport payment options for visitors: you can tap a foreign-issued contactless Visa, Mastercard, American Express or NETS card (or a phone or smartwatch wallet such as Apple Pay or Google Pay) at MRT gates and bus readers at the adult fare, with no SimplyGo registration needed, though LTA says an admin fee applies to cards issued outside Singapore (the amount is not stated on that page). Fares are based on total distance travelled and transfers between buses and trains carry no extra boarding charge within set time limits. Tap in and out with the same card or device. Paying cash on buses costs more per ride and no change is given, so pay the exact fare. SimplyGo EZ-Link cards are sold at SimplyGo Ticket Offices. LTA's Fare Calculator estimates trip costs. No journey times between places are stated here because none were taken from an operator page.

passes.name: Singapore Tourist Pass
passes.covers: SimplyGo lists the Singapore Tourist Pass as an all-day pass for unlimited travel on trains and basic bus services, sold as 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- or 5-day passes at a fixed cost per pass: S$17 (1 day), S$24 (2 days), S$29 (3 days), S$37 (4 days), S$45 (5 days). It does not cover premium services such as the Sentosa Express, RWS8, express buses and other premium or niche bus services. Sold at selected SimplyGo Ticket Offices, selected SimplyGo Ticketing Service Centres and the 24-hour Automated Kiosks.
passes.worth_it: Whether it pays off depends on how many rides you take; fares are distance-based and no per-ride fare table was opened, so no break-even is claimed. The SimplyGo page does not mention a deposit or refund, so confirm that when buying. The price list was read on 18 October 2026 and fares change.

passes.name: Foreign-issued contactless bank card or mobile wallet
passes.covers: LTA says Visa, Mastercard, American Express and NETS contactless cards, and phones or smartwatches with wallets such as Apple Pay or Google Pay, can be tapped for adult fares on MRT and buses without SimplyGo registration. An admin fee applies to cards issued outside Singapore (amount not stated on the page). Mastercard charges post after 5 days or once transit spending reaches S$15, whichever is first; Amex, Visa and NETS charges accumulate daily and post after 3 days.
passes.worth_it: The no-purchase default for most visitors: no card to buy or top up, but check your card issuer for foreign-transaction fees on top of the LTA admin fee.

timezone_note: Slovenia uses a single time zone, Europe/Ljubljana in the IANA database (Central European Time, UTC+1 in winter). The European Commission's summertime page states that under Directive 2000/84/EC Member States switch to summer time on the last Sunday of March and back to standard time on the last Sunday of October; the last Sunday of October 2026 is 25 October, so Slovenia returns from CEST (UTC+2) to CET (UTC+1) on 25 October 2026. The label above reflects the state on 19 October 2026. That Commission page does not list members by name, so Slovenia's membership of Central European Time rests on the IANA zone, not on a page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Slovenia applies the Schengen rules (the Slovenian police's Entry/Exit System page refers to 'Slovenia and all other Schengen Area member states'; the UK FCDO and Government of Canada entry pages for Slovenia give Schengen rules). The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (page last checked 19 August 2026). The UK FCDO says the same: issued less than 10 years before arrival and expiring at least 3 months after you plan to leave the Schengen area. The Government of Canada also states the 3-month margin beyond the date you expect to leave the Schengen area. The Slovenian police page on entry conditions says only that foreigners must hold a valid travel document and, for visa applicants, that its validity must exceed the visa's by at least three months. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area (the police page words it as a maximum of 90 days within a period of six months, counted from the day of first entry), and time in Slovenia counts toward that total.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS: no confirmed start date was found. The European Commission's ETIAS page on home-affairs.ec.europa.eu (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS is 'currently not in operation' and that no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point, and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; the Government of Canada's Slovenia advice (updated 11 August 2026) says applications are not yet open and to apply only through the official EU website once it launches. The UK FCDO entry page does not mention ETIAS. Re-check the Commission page before travelling; when it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation for visa-exempt nationals, not a visa. Entry/Exit System (EES): the Slovenian police EES page says Slovenia began EES on 12 October 2025, that the Slovenian external border crossings (air: Ljubljana Brnik, Maribor Slivnica and Portoroz; sea: Koper and Piran) have been fully operational since 10 March 2026, and that from 10 April 2026 entering data in EES is mandatory for third-country nationals; it says non-EU travellers must give a facial image and four fingerprints each time they cross the external Schengen border. The FCDO says fingerprints and a photo may be taken at no cost, that the digital record is valid for 3 years, and that children aged 11 or younger are not fingerprinted. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality: see the visa rules for your passport and the Slovenian police entry-conditions page. Onward ticket and funds: the FCDO says that at Slovenian border control you may need to show a return or onward ticket and may need to prove you have enough money for your stay; the Slovenian police entry-conditions page does not state an onward-ticket rule, a proof-of-funds figure or a minimum number of blank passport pages, so none is stated here. Police registration: the FCDO says you must register with the police within 3 days of arrival, that registered hotels and guesthouses usually do it for you, and that failing to register can bring a fine; the Government of Canada says that if you stay 3 or more days in private accommodation and are not an EU citizen you must register with local police within 72 hours of arrival. The police entry-conditions page gives no registration timeframe, and a 2009 'for foreign tourists' entry on policija.si (which may be outdated) says guesthouse and tourist-accommodation hosts must register guests regardless of length of stay. Border checks: the FCDO notes there are checks at Slovenia's land borders with Italy and Austria. Cash: FURS (the Slovenian tax and customs administration, page refreshed 13 August 2024) states that cash of EUR 10,000 or more must be declared in writing to customs at the control point when entering or leaving the EU, that no declaration is needed travelling between Slovenia and other EU states unless customs or the police ask for it, and that authorities may detain undeclared cash and impose penalties; the FCDO adds that without a certified declaration money could be seized on departure. ID and conduct: the FCDO advises carrying a copy of your passport (a fine of 50 to 200 euros if you cannot show ID when asked) and says wild camping is illegal, with fines of 40 to 500 euros. The Slovenian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (gov.si) and its police registration rules were not opened for this guide, so the UK FCDO, Government of Canada, EU and policija.si pages are relied on.

health.malaria_risk: CDC's Slovenia page contains no malaria information, so no malaria risk is stated here.
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Slovenia page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry and not recommended, and the Government of Canada also says proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required; the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) and carries a Level 1 notice about rising global measles cases dated 28 May 2025. The UK FCDO says UK travellers need a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that it is not an alternative to travel insurance, and advises insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation; to get an ambulance it says to dial 112. The Government of Canada advises avoiding getting freshwater in the eyes, mouth or nose, especially after heavy rain or flooding. Slovenia's tourist board (slovenia.info) states 'you can drink tap water, since it is pristine', but also that drinking-water quality varies around the country and that after heavy rainfall it is advisable to avoid tap water as it can be turbid. The Slovenian National Institute of Public Health (NIJZ) and the Ministry of Health had no traveller page opened for this guide, so CDC, the FCDO, Canada and the tourist board are used as fallbacks.

money.atm_notes: The European Central Bank states that the euro became legal tender in Slovenia on 1 January 2007, and slovenia.info gives the currency as the euro (EUR). slovenia.info says you can withdraw money at Slovenian ATMs using MasterCard, Visa, Maestro, Cirrus and Visa Electron Plus cards, including outside working hours, and that you can exchange money at exchange offices, hotel receptions, travel agencies, service stations and major shopping centres. The Government of Canada says ATMs are rare in mountain regions and small villages, so carry sufficient cash there. No official source opened states how widely cards are accepted in shops and restaurants, tipping norms, withdrawal fees or limits, so those are not stated.

power.adapter_note: slovenia.info (Slovenian Tourist Board, practical information page) lists mains voltage as 230 V at 50 Hz and says Slovenia uses sockets type C and F, which have two round pins (it also labels the socket CEE 7/16); if your device is not compatible with 230 V you may need a voltage converter.

emergency.notes: slovenia.info lists '112 Notification centre - emergency medical assistance, fire brigades, veterinary assistance, rescue units', '113 Police - emergencies' and 1987 for the Automobile Association of Slovenia (roadside assistance and towing). The Slovenian police site (policija.si) lists 113 as the police emergency number and does not mention 112. The UK FCDO says to dial 112 and ask for an ambulance and to call 112 for mountain rescue; for a breakdown on a motorway or expressway it gives 1970 (or +386 1 518 8 518). The Government of Canada says to dial 112 for emergency services. There is no separate ambulance or fire number in the sources opened, so those fields repeat 112. A Slovenian tourist police number was not found on any official page opened, so tourist_police is null. Sirens are tested at 12:00 on the first Saturday of each month (FCDO); a siren at any other time means follow the authorities' instructions.

getting_around.summary: Ljubljana: city buses are run by LPP; Visit Ljubljana (the city tourist board) states a single journey fare of EUR 1.50 within one zone (EUR 2.50 across two zones, EUR 3.50 across three, with a note that prices may change), that the Urbana card costs EUR 2.00 and can hold up to EUR 50.00 of credit, and that a fare covers an up to 90-minute journey however many buses you change; you can pay with a Visa or Mastercard card instead, but changing buses within 90 minutes is then not free. The same tourist board says the Kavalir electric vehicles offer free rides within the pedestrianised city centre and that BicikeLJ bicycles can be picked up at one station and returned at another (it gives no price or hours). Driving: slovenia.info says you need a vignette to drive on motorways and expressways in your own vehicle or camper van, and the UK FCDO says you must buy an e-vignette (weekly, monthly or yearly) at petrol stations, post offices, DARS offices or the official DARS website; the FCDO also says winter equipment is required from 15 November to 15 March and in winter conditions (fines of 125 euros, or 417 euros if you also cause delays), and that the drink-drive limit is 0.05% (none for drivers under 21 or licensed under 2 years). E-vignette prices could not be confirmed because the DARS site refused connection when opened, so none are given. Trains and buses: slovenia.info says international buses run regularly to Slovenia and that Ljubljana Bus Station has moved to a temporary site about 200 metres from its previous location with timetables unchanged; the Slovenian Railways (Slovenske zeleznice) site returned an access-denied error when opened, so no train times, fares or passes are stated and no intercity journey time could be confirmed from an official page. Safety on the move: the FCDO says to call 112 for mountain rescue and to check whether mountain cabins are open.

timezone_note: South Africa uses a single time zone, Africa/Johannesburg (UTC+2), all year. The South African Tourism UK-market page 'Know before you go' gives the time as GMT+1 when the UK and Ireland are on summer time and GMT+2 when they are on winter time, which is consistent with a fixed UTC+2 and no clock change in South Africa.
passport_validity_rule: Passport must be valid for at least 30 days after the date you intend to leave South Africa, and must have at least two blank (unused) pages. The South African mission in Ottawa (DIRCO) states: 'The passport must be valid for a period of at least 30 days after the planned departure from South Africa' and 'Two unused blank visa pages are required when a person reports to a port of entry. Non-compliance will result in refusal of admission to South Africa.' The UK FCDO's South Africa entry page gives the same rule (at least 30 days after you leave, two or more blank pages). Home Affairs' travel-documents page states 'Passports must be valid for at least 30 days after the intended departure date' and 'at least two blank pages for entry stamps. These pages must be facing', but that wording sits in its section on South African passports and does not itself say it applies to foreign visitors, so the mission and FCDO pages are the support for visitors. Stored as 1 month beyond exit; the rule is precisely 30 days, so a passport with 30 days left on departure day is acceptable.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA: Home Affairs' 'Exempt Countries' schedule (issued 9 December 2025, marked 'subject to change without notice') lists 90 days visa-free for ordinary-passport holders of the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil; for India the page text as read showed 90 days only for what appeared to be diplomatic, official and service passports and no ordinary-passport entry could be confirmed, so Indian ordinary-passport holders should check the visa rules and the DIRCO or VFS pages. The UK FCDO page adds that you can visit without a visa for up to 90 days for business or tourism. CHILDREN (two official sources disagree on wording): Home Affairs' 'Travel requirements for children' page (marked revised November 2019, following the first amendment to the Immigration Regulations that took effect 1 December 2018) asks for a 'birth certificate / equivalent document', defined as an extract from the Birth Register containing the child's and parent(s)' particulars, and says consent from the parent(s) cited on the birth certificate is needed when a parent is not travelling with the child, with the consent letter not older than 6 months. It does not use the word 'unabridged'. The South African Consulate-General in Toronto's page for children under 18 (no date given) still says parents 'must produce an unabridged-birth certificate' and, for one parent travelling, an affidavit from the other parent, a court order or a death certificate. Home Affairs' page lists exemptions, including children in direct transit at an international airport and children whose passport names the parent(s); it does not state whether the rules are currently enforced as written, so carry the full birth certificate showing both parents plus consent documents. A 2015 Home Affairs tourist advisory PDF also says 'unabridged' but pre-dates the 2018 amendment and is not relied on. Official pages opened for this guide did not state an onward-ticket requirement or proof-of-funds figure, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. ELECTRICITY SUPPLY: Eskom's media statement of 8 July 2026 reported more than 413 consecutive days without loadshedding, and separately a 'load reduction' measure still affecting some areas, mainly in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, with five provinces (Western Cape, Northern Cape, Free State, North West, Mpumalanga) free of it; Eskom itself calls the two 'fundamentally different challenges'. That is the position on 8 July 2026, not a forecast; no newer Eskom page was opened. TRAVELLER DECLARATION (in force): SARS's notice 'Required Online Traveller Declarations from 1 July 2026' says all travellers entering or leaving South Africa through air, land, sea and rail ports must submit a declaration before travelling, through the SARS Customs Online Traveller Declaration portal, the SATMS app or Scan-to-Declare QR codes; its FAQ says to submit no more than 24 hours before departure (for journeys with stops, the last leg to South Africa), that it includes foreign travellers, that each traveller including children and infants needs one (a parent or guardian can complete it), and that air or sea transit passengers who stay in the transit area are excluded. SARS says travellers will not be denied entry solely for not having completed it in advance, and can be helped at the port, but a false or missing declaration can mean delays, detention, forfeiture or penalties. The UK FCDO page also tells visitors to submit an online traveller declaration. CURRENCY (sources disagree): SARS's Travellers page (updated 19 August 2026) and FAQ give R100 000 as the threshold above which written South African Reserve Bank permission is needed, and say declaring currency below that is voluntary; the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages still say to declare more than R25 000 or USD 10 000. SARS is the issuing authority, so R100 000 is treated as the better-supported figure; the older figures appear on foreign advisories. ETA: the Electronic Travel Authorisation was launched on 12 August 2026 (SAnews, Minister Schreiber's launch speech on gov.za), initially for China, India, Indonesia and Mexico, at OR Tambo, Cape Town, King Shaka and Lanseria airports, with land and sea ports to follow. The Minister said it 'will progressively become compulsory' for short-stay visits from countries that require visas and voluntary for visa-exempt travellers; the pages opened do not say it is yet compulsory for any nationality or give a fee. Indian citizens need a visa to visit (Department of Tourism, September 2025), so for India the ETA is the online route, not a visa-free entry; check eta.dha.gov.za or the nearest mission before booking. USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil passport holders do not need an ETA for up to 90 days.

health.malaria_risk: Malaria is a notifiable condition in South Africa with three endemic provinces: KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo (Department of Health). The NICD says transmission generally occurs in low-altitude areas of northern KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Mpumalanga, with the high-transmission season generally September to May. CDC lists Kruger National Park and uMkhanyakude (KwaZulu-Natal), Mopani and Vhembe (Limpopo) and Ehlanzeni (Mpumalanga) districts as areas where prophylaxis is recommended. Cape Town, Johannesburg and the Garden Route are not among the areas named.
health.notes: ENTRY: The National Department of Health's 'Health Protocols for Travellers Arriving in South Africa' (on health.gov.za) says all travellers over 1 year old arriving from a yellow fever risk country must produce a valid International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, that those without may be refused entry or quarantined for up to 6 days or until the certificate becomes valid, and that a signed waiver letter from a travel health practitioner is needed for medical exemption (those travellers are placed under quarantine surveillance). The protocol points to the WHO list of countries with risk of yellow fever transmission rather than naming them, so check that list. CDC's page says the vaccine is not required for travellers coming direct from the US, and that yellow fever vaccination is not recommended for South Africa itself. Travellers carrying medicine for personal use are required to have authorisation from SAHPRA (same protocol, section 5). All arrivals can be subject to entry screening including temperature checks. MALARIA: the Department of Health advises consulting a travel clinic or doctor before travel to decide whether prophylaxis is needed, and taking steps to avoid mosquito bites outdoors in the evening in endemic areas; CDC recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine for the districts above and lists mosquito avoidance only for other transmission areas (King Cetshwayo, Zululand, Capricorn, Greater Sekhukhune, Waterberg). CDC's malaria and yellow fever sections were updated 23 April 2025 and the page was last reviewed 25 August 2026; the NICD article is dated 3 November 2025. CDC also carries a rabies alert about Cape fur seals (South Africa and Namibia): do not approach or touch seals. All of this is medical information, not advice.

money.tipping: South African Tourism's UK-market page says 'South Africa is similar to the UK, with 10-15% customary in restaurants and for tour guides.' That is a UK-edition tourism-board page with no date, so treat the range as guidance rather than a rule.

emergency.notes: The Western Cape Government lists Police Flying Squad 10111, Ambulance 10177 and 'Cell Phone Emergency' 112 (MTN, Vodacom, Cell C, Telkom), and also states 'Currently, there's no single emergency number in South Africa'; it says for fire and rescue to 'see your district municipality for emergency contact numbers' (page undated). The national Department of Tourism's safety page lists police 10111, 112 'from a cellphone' and 10177 for ambulance/fire. Because the two official pages differ on fire, no fire number is shown rather than assuming 10177 covers it; ambulance 10177 is supported by both. No dedicated tourist police number was found, so none is listed here. The Department of Tourism page gives tourism complaints on 012 444 6000 or 0860 686 747, which is not an emergency line. RE-CHECK 18 October 2026: the Department of Tourism safety page lists 'Police (SAPS) 10111', 'Police from cellphone: 112' and 'Ambulance/ Fire: 10177'; the Western Cape page again lists no fire number ('Please see your district municipality') and says there is no single emergency number; Global Affairs Canada lists 'firefighters: 10111 or 10112 from a cellular telephone' and 'medical assistance: 10177'; the UK FCDO lists police 10111 and 'emergency services on 112 (mobile only)'. Three official pages give three different answers for fire, so no fire number is shown. Police 10111, ambulance 10177 and 112 from a mobile are each supported by at least two of these pages.

phrases_language: Mixed sample: isiZulu, isiXhosa and Afrikaans, each labelled in brackets. South Africa has many languages and this is a small sample for greetings and basic needs, not a complete phrasebook; these phrases were written from general knowledge, not taken from an official page. The government's gov.za 'South Africa at a glance' page lists 11 official languages, and Parliament's release of 3 May 2023 says South African Sign Language would make 12 once the President signs the Bill; the signing was not confirmed from a page opened for this guide. English is one of the official languages.

timezone_note: South Korea uses a single time zone nationwide, Korea Standard Time (Asia/Seoul in the IANA database), and does not currently observe daylight saving time. The Korean government pages used for this guide give times in KST (for example the K-ETA exemption runs to 31 December 2026 KST and the e-Arrival card window is counted in KST).
passport_validity_rule: Korea sets no minimum remaining validity beyond the trip itself: the passport only has to stay valid throughout the stay. The Embassy of Korea in Singapore (mofa.go.kr) answers the question directly: you may enter with a passport that has less than 6 months of remaining validity "as long as your passport remains valid throughout your stay." Government of Canada advice says the passport "must be valid beyond the date of expected departure from South Korea" and UK FCDO says it must have an expiry date after the date you leave (for stays up to 90 days; FCDO adds 6 months from arrival for long-term visas). Two catches: a K-ETA lasts 3 years or until the passport expires, whichever is sooner, so a passport that expires soon shortens the K-ETA; and your airline or a transit country may still apply its own six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: CHECKED 17 and 18 October 2026. (1) K-ETA (Korea Electronic Travel Authorization): IN FORCE as the general rule for visa-free visitors, but TEMPORARILY WAIVED for 22 nationalities/regions until 31 December 2026 (KST). Korea's Ministry of Justice extended the waiver for one year, 1 January to 31 December 2026, per Korean MOFA notices dated 29 December 2025 and 5 January 2026. A Korean MOFA notice dated 18 March 2026 (Embassy in Estonia) also names Estonia among the countries covered, and Global Affairs Canada ("exempt ... until December 31, 2026") and UK FCDO ("temporarily exempt ... until December 31, 2026") confirm the end date for Canadians and Britons. The KTO (VisitKorea) page lists the exempt nationalities (Estonia is not on it): Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Macau; United States (including Guam), Canada; United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, Poland, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Belgium, Denmark, Austria; Australia, New Zealand. Of the eight passports NextStamp covers, UK, USA, Canada, Australia, Germany and Singapore are on that list; India and Brazil are not and need an approved K-ETA before boarding (if they are visa-exempt at all; check visa.go.kr). Nothing opened for this guide says the waiver continues past 31 December 2026, so a trip that starts on or after 1 January 2027 should assume a K-ETA is needed and check k-eta.go.kr (its notice list shows an item dated 2026-03-20 titled as a temporary-exemption extension notice whose text could not be opened here). Facts for those who do need or want one: fee KRW 10,000, non-refundable even if refused; usually assessed within 72 hours but can take longer and there is no express service; valid 3 years or until passport expiry, whichever is sooner; must be approved before boarding; approval does not guarantee entry (the immigration officer decides). An exempt traveller can still apply voluntarily, which also spares them the arrival card. Beware look-alike sites; apply only at k-eta.go.kr or the official app. Transit passengers who do not clear immigration at Incheon do not need one. (2) e-Arrival card: IN FORCE. Government of Canada states all travellers must submit an entry declaration, online up to 3 days before arrival (e-arrivalcard.go.kr, free, counted in KST) or on paper on arrival; UK FCDO says paper forms are still available. A 2025 KTO article said the paper card was planned to end after December 2025, which the 2026 FCDO and GAC pages contradict, so expect the online form to be the faster route. K-ETA holders do not have to submit it. Beware fake e-Arrival sites (Korea Immigration Service notice of 9 March 2026). (3) Q-CODE: NOT a blanket registration. It is required of travellers who have visited or transited an area on KDCA's Quarantine Inspection Required lists. The KDCA list for Q4 2026 (as of 1 October 2026) has two tiers: for 'strict' areas (including India, Brazil, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, and the US states of New Mexico, Michigan and Washington) everyone arriving from or via them must submit a Q-CODE or health declaration form; for the wider 'quarantine inspection required' list (which includes, for example, the rest of the US, Canada, Australia, Japan, Singapore, Germany and England) it is mandatory only if you have symptoms. Registration opens up to 7 days before arrival (GAC, KTO), the fine for non-compliance is up to KRW 10 million, and the list is revised quarterly, so re-check kdca.go.kr before travel. (4) Stay length is set by nationality: UK FCDO says up to 90 days for tourism or short business; Government of Canada says Canadians need no visa for up to 180 days; KTO and Korean MOFA direct travellers to visa.go.kr for their nationality. UK FCDO states you must hold an onward or return ticket; the Korean and Canadian pages opened for this guide did not mention it, so the onward-ticket rule rests on FCDO alone. No blank-page requirement was found on any official page, so none is listed here. UK FCDO says you must declare anything prohibited or subject to tax or duty; Korea Customs Service says bringing in up to USD 10,000 (foreign currency, KRW notes or cheques) needs no declaration, and anything above that must be reported on the Traveler Declaration Form (tick the currency item and hand it to a customs officer); a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration cannot be issued once you have passed immigration, and failing to report can mean up to one year in prison or a fine of up to KRW 100 million. Korea Immigration contact centre: 1345 (+82-2-1345 from abroad).

health.malaria_risk: Limited. CDC lists a limited risk of Plasmodium vivax malaria in rural northern parts of Incheon, Gangwon and Gyeonggi provinces, including the DMZ, March through December, and recommends antimalarials for travellers to those areas. No risk is described elsewhere in the country.
health.notes: No vaccination is required for entry: CDC states the yellow fever vaccine is not required and not recommended, and the Government of Canada says proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required. CDC carries a Level 1 (usual precautions) travel health notice for measles. The recommended list is medical advice from CDC, not something checked at immigration. Separate from vaccination, the Q-CODE health registration rules in entry_requirement_notes can apply depending on where you have travelled recently.

power.adapter_note: The Korea Tourism Organization states the standard is 220 volts at 60 Hz and that outlets take two round holes. It does not name a plug-type letter, so none is recorded here. Without a multi-voltage adapter you can borrow or buy one at a hotel front desk, and KTO lists airports, retail stores, duty-free shops and convenience stores as sources.

emergency.notes: The Korea Tourism Organization lists 112 for police and 119 for fire and medical emergencies; the Government of Canada's South Korea page gives the same (112 police, 119 medical and fire). KTO says if you do not speak Korean, say "English please" or "Interpreter please" when the call connects. KTO also lists +82-1339 for infectious-disease emergencies; for a life-threatening emergency use 119. The 1330 Korea Travel Hotline (+82-2-1330 from abroad) is run by the Korea Tourism Organization for non-life-threatening help such as transport questions and interpretation, 24 hours a day, with phone support in Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, Thai and Malay (some languages have shorter hours). No tourist-police number appears on the KTO page, so none is listed here, and no source opened confirms that 112 works as a general international emergency number in Korea, so no general emergency number is shown. UK FCDO (getting-help page) lists Ambulance 119, Fire 119, Police 112 and the Danuri Call Centre 1577 1366 (24/7 interpretation); Global Affairs Canada gives police 112, medical 119, fire 119.

getting_around.summary: The Korea Tourism Organization describes the KTX as a high-speed train running at up to 330 km/h from Seoul, Yongsan and Cheongnyangni stations to Busan, Pohang, Mokpo, Yeosu, Gangneung, Andong and other cities; the Seoul to Busan Gyeongbu Line is 447.1 km and the busiest route. SRT is a separate high-speed service (up to 300 km/h) from Suseo Station towards Busan or Mokpo. Tickets can be bought at ticket offices, on the KORAIL website or KORAIL+ app, at kiosks, and through NAVER Train Booking or KakaoT; sales open one month before departure at 07:00 and close 20 minutes before departure. KORAIL's English customer centre is +82-1599-7777 (08:00-20:00). KTO gives no Seoul to Busan journey time, so none is stated here. In cities, a rechargeable transport card (T-money, among others) pays for subways and buses. KTO pages were last updated in August 2026.

passes.name: Korail Pass (KORAIL Pass)
passes.covers: KTO: a train pass exclusively for international travellers, sold as 2-, 3-, 4- or 5-day flexible passes usable within ten days. It gives unlimited use of standard cabins during the pass period, up to two seat reservations a day, unlimited standing tickets, and first-class booking at 50% of the original first-class fare. It does not cover SRT, subways or temporary tourist trains. KTO says it is booked through korail.com (English, Japanese, Chinese).
passes.worth_it: No current prices were found on a page that could be opened, and older price tables conflict with the pass structure now described (KORAIL changed pass types and age categories from 11 December 2025, per a search result not opened in full), so no figure is given and no verdict on value is offered. Check the price against your planned KTX journeys on korail.com before buying.

passes.name: T-money card
passes.covers: KTO: a rechargeable prepaid card costing 3,000 to 5,000 won, sold at convenience stores nationwide (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven and others) and at information centres in Seoul subway stations on Lines 1 to 8. It works on public transport and at affiliated shops showing the Tmoney logo, and also at expressway toll gates. Reloading is at subway ticket machines, up to 500,000 won. KTO notes a transit-fare transfer discount when using a transportation card.
passes.worth_it: Not a discount pass but the practical default for city buses and subways. Refunds of more than 50,000 won are only possible at Tmoney Town at Seoul Station; smaller balances can be refunded at convenience stores, so top up modestly. KTO also lists a foreigner-only Mpass (fixed-period unlimited-ride card, bought with Korean won cash only) and says its separate Climate Card became limited to use within Seoul from 1 October 2026.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: KTO states visitors can rent a Wi-Fi egg or smartphone and buy SIM cards at the roaming centres at Incheon, Gimpo, Gimhae and Jeju airports (fees are on each provider's site). Physical USIMs are also sold at convenience stores such as CU, GS25, 7-Eleven and Emart24, though stock varies by branch. An eSIM can be bought online and activated by scanning a QR code; check your phone is eSIM-compatible. Free public Wi-Fi is available at most public locations including airports and subway and train stations (wififree.kr).

timezone_note: Mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands use Europe/Madrid: CET (UTC+1) in winter and CEST (UTC+2) in summer. The Canary Islands are on Atlantic/Canary, one hour behind the mainland (WET, UTC+0 in winter; WEST, UTC+1 in summer), which spain.info confirms in its practical-tips page ('UTC +1, except in the Canary Islands, where UTC +0 (one hour behind) is used'; clocks change twice a year). Offsets and the 2026 clock-change dates were checked against the IANA tz database (via Python zoneinfo) on 2026-10-17: summer time began 29 March 2026 and ends 25 October 2026, when mainland clocks return to CET (UTC+1). The label above reflects the state on 2026-10-17.
passport_validity_rule: Spain applies the Schengen rule. The EU's Your Europe portal states the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the previous 10 years on the day you enter. Spain's consulate in Washington gives the same condition: valid until at least three months after the planned date of departure from the Schengen territory. This is a 3-months-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Spain follows the Schengen short-stay rules: up to 90 days in any 180-day period for visa-exempt nationals (Your Europe), and tourists of some nationalities need a visit visa. Spain's consulate in Washington lists a round-trip or return ticket as required 'in all cases', and spain.info says a tourist must prove the availability of economic resources for the planned stay and for the return or transfer to another country. Funds: the Spanish consulate in Washington gives 122 EUR per person per day in 2026 with at least 1,099 EUR for stays of 9 days or more; the Spanish embassy in Canberra gives 122.10 EUR per day with a 1,098.90 EUR minimum. The two differ by rounding; the Canberra figure is the more precise one and the amounts are re-set each year, so carry proof of funds (cash, card, bank statement) and check the figure for your travel year. ETIAS: the European Commission's ETIAS page says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' (page last updated 6 October 2025), and a Commission news item of 28 April 2026 says it is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026 with the exact date to be announced later in the year. Spain's Washington consulate likewise says it is expected to become operational in the last quarter of 2026 and that no action is required from travellers yet. No start date had been confirmed in any source opened on 2026-10-17, so ETIAS is NOT in force today; re-check before travel. EES: the Commission's 28 April 2026 news item states the Entry/Exit System has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; non-EU travellers are registered (including biometrics) on entry and exit instead of having passports stamped. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens may enter with a national identity card or passport. These rules apply to mainland Spain, the Balearic and Canary Islands; no source opened here gave separate rules for Ceuta or Melilla, so none are stated. Border checks: Global Affairs Canada and the UK FCDO both say officers may ask for a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds (the Spanish consulate in Washington lists a return ticket as required in all cases). Both also say the passport needs 3 months' validity beyond departure from Schengen (FCDO adds: issued less than 10 years before arrival). Global Affairs Canada (checked 2026-10-18) says ETIAS applications are not yet open; the Ottawa embassy page gives CAD 197.40 per day and CAD 1,776.60 minimum for 2026, consistent with the Canberra EUR figures.

health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Spanish border: the CDC states yellow fever vaccination is not required for entry and does not recommend it for Spain. The CDC Spain page does not list a malaria risk, so no risk is stated rather than asserting 'none'. The CDC notes dengue and leishmaniasis (spread by mosquitoes and sand flies) and advises avoiding bites. On care for visitors, spain.info states emergency treatment is guaranteed for everyone in hospitals and some health centres, care at private centres is always paid for, free care for illness or accident under the European Health Card applies to citizens of the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, and it recommends always travelling with international medical insurance. Medicines are bought at pharmacies, identified by green crosses.

money.card_acceptance: spain.info states that bank cards, especially Visa and MasterCard, are accepted in most shops, restaurants, hotels and museums, that cash is also accepted, and that withdrawal or currency-exchange fees are often charged. For local buses, spain.info's airport FAQ adds that fares are usually paid on boarding and cash is usually the only payment allowed, with change often limited to 20 EUR.
money.atm_notes: spain.info says withdrawal or currency-exchange fees are often charged; it names no specific ATM network and no official source consulted gave fee levels.

emergency.notes: Opened 2026-10-18. 112 is the single emergency number for police, ambulance and fire (UK FCDO 'Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance'; Global Affairs Canada 'Dial 112'; DGT table 'Centro de emergencias 112'; spain.info). 091 is the Policia Nacional emergency line (policia.es tourist safety leaflet: 'the National Police emergency telephone number'; DGT table). 062 is the Guardia Civil (guardiacivil.es: 'En el número 062, la Guardia Civil te atendera directamente, las 24 horas'; DGT table); 092 is local police (DGT table). Ambulance and fire are given as 112 because that is what official foreign-ministry pages state; 061 is a regional health-emergency line (for example Galicia, per Xunta de Galicia) and 080/085 fire lines are local, so none is stated as a national number. The Policia Nacional's tourist telephone complaints line (not an emergency line) is 902 102 112. No dedicated tourist-police emergency line was confirmed.

getting_around.summary: Spain's tourism board describes high-speed AVE trains connecting major destinations such as Barcelona, Seville or Valencia with Madrid in three hours or less; its table gives Madrid to Barcelona 2 h 30 min, Madrid to Seville 2 h 30 min, Madrid to Valencia 1 h 40 min and Madrid to Zaragoza 1 h 35 min. Long-distance and AVE trains are run by Renfe, which also operates Cercanias commuter networks around major cities. In Madrid, Renfe's Cercanias page says one-way fares can be paid at the turnstiles with a contactless bank card or phone and that tickets must be validated at the departure and arrival stations. For city buses and the metro, spain.info's airport FAQ says metro and train journeys are paid for at the station (usually from ticket machines), while bus fares are usually paid on boarding, often in cash only.

passes.name: Renfe Spain Rail Pass
passes.covers: Renfe's pass for people with residence outside Spain: you choose 4, 6, 8 or 10 trips and Standard or Comfort seats (Premium is not available). It covers Long Distance trains including AVE, and regional Media Distancia and Avant trains with seat reservation. The pass is personal and non-transferable.
passes.worth_it: Renfe's page states no price, so whether it beats point-to-point tickets cannot be judged from the official source. Each journey must still be validated by booking a ticket for that specific route (online under 'My passes', at ticket offices, travel agencies or by phone), you have up to 6 months from purchase to make the first trip, and the pass is valid for one month after the first trip.

passes.name: Madrid unlimited-travel transport pass (30-day and annual)
passes.covers: Renfe's Cercanias Madrid page says the pass allows any number of trips by bus, metro and Cercanias during its validity; options include 30-day and annual passes, loaded onto a Public Transport Card that can be topped up at station self-service machines.
passes.worth_it: Renfe's page gives no price and does not say whether visitors can obtain one, so it is listed for awareness only; single one-way tickets and contactless turnstile payment are the stated alternatives for a short stay.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: spain.info states that visitors using non-EU phone numbers may pay extra for calls and mobile data, depending on their provider, and suggests buying a prepaid SIM card with a data package suited to your needs. It adds that travellers from the EU use their phones at the same roaming rates as at home. No official source opened here covers eSIM availability or any ID or registration requirement for a prepaid SIM.

timezone_label: Sri Lanka Standard Time (UTC+5:30, no DST)
timezone_note: One zone for the whole island, offset by 30 minutes from whole hours and with no daylight saving. Half an hour ahead of Nepal-style offsets is a common mix-up; it is the same clock as India.
passport_validity_rule: The Department of Immigration and Emigration states as a general condition of entry that you must hold "a passport valid for a minimum period of six months from the date you arrive in Sri Lanka". The UK FCDO states the same rule for British travellers: the passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the day you arrive.
entry_requirement_notes: The Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is a MANDATORY ADVANCE authorisation, not a visa on arrival. The Department of Immigration and Emigration states that "all foreign nationals, including nationals of the above-mentioned 40 countries ... are required to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) prior to arrival in Sri Lanka" (immigration.gov.lk/pages_e.php?id=60, and the same wording on eta.gov.lk). With effect from 25.05.2026 the tourist ETA is issued FREE OF CHARGE to nationals of 40 countries (including the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, India, China, Japan, Germany and France), plus Maldives, Seychelles and Singapore; the fee waiver does not remove the requirement to apply before travelling, and ETA fees paid before 25.05.2026 are non-refundable. The free tourist ETA is valid for 30 days from first arrival with double entry permitted (90 days for Maldivian nationals); longer stays require a paid extension through the immigration portal. Two further conditions are stated by immigration.gov.lk: a visit-visa holder must hold "a written assurance (ticket) to return to the country of domicile or a visa to the next country of destination", and Immigration must be "satisfied that you have adequate funds for your maintenance whilst in Sri Lanka and for the payment of your return passage" — no figure is published for what counts as adequate, so none is stated here. No blank-passport-page minimum is published by Sri Lankan immigration. The free-ETA list (as published on immigration.gov.lk and eta.gov.lk, checked 2026-10-17) does not include Brazil: Brazilian passport holders are among "all other foreign nationals" who must still obtain an ETA before arrival under the general ETA rules. Neither official page states a fee amount for those nationalities, so none is stated here; check the fee on eta.gov.lk before paying, and pay only through that site. Singapore is not among the 40 but gets a free ETA under a reciprocal arrangement, as do Maldives and Seychelles.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required for travellers aged 9 months and over arriving from, or having transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Typhoid
Japanese encephalitis (for longer stays or rural/outdoor itineraries)
Rabies (risk-based)
Routine vaccines including MMR and COVID-19
health.malaria_risk: None — WHO certified Sri Lanka malaria-free on 5 September 2016 and the WHO Sri Lanka country office reaffirmed ten years of sustained elimination in April 2026.
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country; everything in the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. Sourcing conflict worth naming: WHO's certification and its 2026 follow-up are unambiguous that there is no local malaria transmission, while the CDC destination page still carries generic 'malaria is a risk in some parts of Sri Lanka, fill your prescription before you leave' boilerplate. The WHO certification is the better-supported position and is what the malaria entry above reflects; a traveller who sees the CDC wording should know it is not a Sri Lanka-specific finding. Vigilance against re-introduction (imported cases) is a WHO theme, but that is a public-health programme concern, not a traveller prophylaxis recommendation.

money.card_acceptance: Sri Lanka Tourism states that most hotels, restaurants and shopping centres accept credit cards, and warns that some establishments illegally try to add a surcharge for paying by card. Outside those settings — small eateries, tuk-tuks, markets, rural areas — assume cards are not accepted.
money.atm_notes: Sri Lanka Tourism says it is easy to withdraw money island-wide at ATMs using international credit or debit cards. The UK FCDO is more cautious and is worth heeding: ATMs exist in major towns but not all of them accept international cards, most major banks allow Visa and Mastercard cash withdrawals, and bank card fraud is common — use ATMs inside a bank or hotel where possible and check the machine for signs of tampering. Bank hours are 0900–1300 Monday to Friday, with some city branches open until 1500 or on Saturday mornings.

power.adapter_note: Sri Lanka Tourism publishes the supply as "230–240 volts, 50 cycles AC" and advises bringing a stabiliser for laptops, but does not publish which socket types are in use, and no other Sri Lankan government source states them — so plug_types is left null rather than guessed. A traveller from a 230V country needs no voltage converter; the socket shape is the only open question and is worth checking with the accommodation.

emergency.notes: No Sri Lankan government source publishes a single consolidated emergency-number list that could be found, so the police and fire numbers here come from the UK FCDO's Sri Lanka travel advice — a foreign government's page used as a fallback, not a first-hand Sri Lankan citation. FCDO lists police as "118/119" (119 is given here as the primary; 118 is worth trying if it does not connect), fire and rescue as 111, ambulance as "011 2691111 or 1990", and tourist police as 011 2421052. Sri Lanka Tourism's own travel-tips page independently confirms 1990 for the ambulance service (the state-funded 1990 Suwa Seriya service) but gives a DIFFERENT tourist police number, +94 11 2382209, and adds a 1912 tourism hotline — both sets are reproduced here rather than one being picked silently. Whether 112 reaches an emergency operator in Sri Lanka was not confirmed by any official source, so no general emergency number is shown. No official source was found confirming whether English is answered.

getting_around.summary: Sri Lanka Railways runs the intercity network and is the way most visitors cover long distances; seats can be reserved in advance through its seat-reservation system and the Pravesha smart-ticketing platform rather than only bought at the counter, and it markets scenic services such as the Ella Odyssey and Dunhinda Odyssey to tourists. Road transport (buses, hired cars with driver, tuk-tuks) covers everything the railway does not, but no official Sri Lankan source setting out fares, coverage or booking for those was found, so nothing is asserted about them here.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon. The west and south coasts are in their dry half — Colombo averages only 58mm over about 5 rain days, one of its two driest months. The opposite is true on the other side of the island: the northeast monsoon is soaking the east and north, so Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Arugam Bay are wet and the eastern sea is rough.
climate.crowd_note: High season on the southwest and south coasts; the first week is still busy with the New Year tail. Editorial judgement, not a sourced measurement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month on the southwest coast — Colombo averages 73mm over about 5 rain days — as the northeast monsoon weakens. The east coast is still on the wrong side of that monsoon, though it is easing there too.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the southwest-coast season; beach towns and whale-watching out of Mirissa are at their busiest. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon begins: rain arrives island-wide as afternoon and evening thunderstorms rather than as monsoon rain, and Colombo's total climbs to 128mm. This is the brief window when neither coast is monsoon-hit — the east is drying out while the southwest is still mostly fine.
climate.crowd_note: Still high season in the south and west but thinning after February. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon at full strength: 246mm in Colombo over about 14 days, almost all of it convective afternoon storms that clear. Hottest month of the year by daytime maximum. Both coasts are workable, which is unusual.
climate.crowd_note: Sinhala and Tamil New Year falls in April and domestic travel surges around it; transport and coastal accommodation get tight. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The switch. Southwest monsoon onset makes this Colombo's second-wettest month (392mm, about 16 rain days) and hits the southwest coast and the hill country hardest — Sri Lanka Tourism describes it as heavy rainfall on the southwest coast and hills. Simultaneously the east and north dry out, and Trincomalee, Arugam Bay and Jaffna enter their good season.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest beach season ends; east-coast season begins. Low prices on the west, rising on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Southwest monsoon established. Colombo's total drops sharply from May (185mm) but rain falls on about 16 days, so it is persistent rather than heavy, and the hills stay wet. The east coast is dry and settled — this is when Arugam Bay's surf season is running.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet on the southwest coast, building on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month of the southwest monsoon in Colombo (122mm) — the monsoon's rain is concentrated on the hills and the far southwest rather than the city. The east and north are at their driest and sunniest of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season on the east coast and through the cultural triangle; European summer holidays add to it. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: As July: 120mm in Colombo, the southwest monsoon still running but at its least intrusive on the west-coast lowlands, and the east coast dry. The best single month to be on the eastern side of the island.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month on the east coast and the second high season nationally. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The southwest monsoon's tail, and Colombo's rainfall jumps back to 245mm over about 15 days. The east coast is still fair but its season is closing as the second inter-monsoon approaches.
climate.crowd_note: Thinning on both coasts; a genuine gap between the two high seasons. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Second inter-monsoon — the one time of year both coasts are wet at once. 365mm in Colombo over about 17 rain days, the highest rain-day count of the year, with heavy thunderstorms and squalls island-wide. Neither coast offers a reliable escape from the other.
climate.crowd_note: Lowest visitor numbers of the year and the widest choice of closed restaurants and hotels. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Colombo (414mm) as the second inter-monsoon runs into the onset of the northeast monsoon. Rain is widespread; the east and north are moving into their wet season just as the southwest starts to clear late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Still low, though the southwest coast starts reopening towards the end of the month. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon takes hold and the pattern flips back: Colombo drops to 175mm and the southwest and south coasts move into clear skies and calm seas, which Sri Lanka Tourism calls peak season there. The east coast is now the wet side.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest-coast high season restarts; Christmas and New Year are the most heavily booked fortnight of the year. Editorial judgement.

timezone_note: Sweden has one time zone (IANA Europe/Stockholm). On 19 October 2026 it is on central European summer time (CEST, UTC+2); under the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, clocks go back to CET (UTC+1) on Sunday 25 October 2026. The zone and the changeover date come from the IANA database and that EU rule, not from a Swedish government page opened for this guide.
passport_validity_rule: Sweden is in the Schengen area. The Swedish Police page for third-country nationals says the passport must be valid on entry, "can not be older than 10 years" and "should be valid at least 3 months after planned departure date"; Migrationsverket says a passport "valid for at least three months after you plan to leave the Schengen area", Visit Sweden says "at least three months beyond your planned departure date from the Schengen area", and the EU's Your Europe portal and UK FCDO add that it must have been issued within the 10 years before the day you enter. Visa-free short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. EU/EEA citizens can travel to Sweden with a valid national ID card or passport (Visit Sweden).
entry_requirement_notes: CURRENCY: Sweden is in the EU and the Schengen area but its currency is the Swedish krona (SEK), not the euro. Visit Sweden states: "While Sweden is a member of the European Union, it has not adopted the euro", and that euros are generally not accepted for cash purchases, so pay in kronor. ETIAS is NOT in force today (19 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) says ETIAS "is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point", that the start date will be announced several months ahead, and gives a fee of EUR 20. Visit Sweden's passport page says "ETIAS will start operations in the last quarter of 2026" with no action required of travellers yet, and the Swedish Police page says it is not possible to apply yet and there is no exact implementation date. No page opened gives an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it "became fully operational on 10 April 2026" (the Swedish Police page, which has not been updated to match, says 9 April 2026, so the date is taken from the Commission); it registers name, travel document data, fingerprints and a facial image for non-EU short-stay visitors and logs entry, exit and refusals, and UK FCDO says there is no cost, the digital record is valid for 3 years and long-term Schengen residents are exempt. Entry conditions for visa-exempt visitors: the Swedish Police page says third-country nationals must hold a valid passport on entry that is not older than 10 years and valid at least 3 months after the planned departure date, must show sufficient funds for the entire stay, and "need a return ticket or sufficient funds to purchase this"; stay is limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries; entry can be refused if documents or purpose of travel cannot be shown. Migrationsverket's page for people who do not need a visa lists a passport valid for 3 months after you plan to leave the Schengen area, a round-trip ticket with the return journey within 90 days, an invitation from the person you stay with or a hotel booking confirmation, and states "Sweden requires that you have SEK 700 for each day of your visit" (it says the amount may be lower in some cases, such as for younger children or when meals and accommodation are prepaid or you stay with relatives or friends). The Police page gives no figure for funds; FCDO says border officers may ask for a return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation, proof of travel insurance and proof of enough money. Migrationsverket's "at least two blank pages" is stated in its visa-application section, not as a rule for visa-exempt entry, so no blank-page requirement is recorded here. Cash: Tullverket (Swedish Customs) says you must notify customs when travelling to or from Sweden with the equivalent of EUR 10,000 or more in cash or equivalent assets (notes and coins, travellers' cheques, cheques, promissory notes, investment gold of at least 99.5 % and gold coins of at least 90 % gold content); the page says that from 1 April 2026 the requirement also covers travel to or from another EU country. Notification is free and can be made online or on a paper form given to a customs officer at the border. The page does not state penalties. Other: Migrationsverket notes in a news item (21 September 2026) that Russian non-biometric passports are no longer recognised from 1 October 2026. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport). Temporary internal Schengen border checks and the national rules on carrying ID were not covered by any page opened for this guide.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
COVID-19 (eligible travellers up to date)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (consider for most travellers; especially smaller cities, villages and rural areas)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60)
Tick-borne encephalitis (travellers with extensive tick exposure; may be considered for outdoor activities in tick areas)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Sweden page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: the Public Health Agency of Sweden (Folkhalsomyndigheten) states "There are no vaccination requirements in order to visit Sweden or before leaving the country", and CDC's Sweden page says the yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025; page last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is CDC's medical advice only. TBE: Folkhalsomyndigheten's risk-area page (updated 5 May 2026) classes most of central and southern Sweden as risk area 1 (moderate to high occurrence), Stockholm city, Gotland and parts of the south and west as area 2 (low), and most of the north plus Malmo, Lund and Helsingborg as area 3 (very low to none); about 20 municipalities in Stockholm county are in area 1. CDC advises checking for ticks after outdoor activity and using repellent. CDC's page carries a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and names leptospirosis, hantavirus and tuberculosis among non-vaccine-preventable risks. Emergency care: dial 112 and ask for an ambulance (UK FCDO). FCDO says a UK GHIC or EHIC is needed for medically necessary state healthcare, is not an alternative to travel insurance and does not cover private care or repatriation. The Swedish health-advice number 1177 and visitor charges for care were not covered by any page opened for this guide.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Sweden states that major credit cards such as Visa and Mastercard are widely accepted, that some places might not accept American Express so an alternative card is prudent, and that you should bring a chip-and-PIN card because magnetic-stripe cards are often unsupported.
money.cash_culture: The currency is the Swedish krona (SEK); euros are generally not accepted for cash purchases (Visit Sweden). Visit Sweden says carrying large amounts of cash is not necessary and that small amounts can be withdrawn from ATMs, which are readily available in cities and towns. It also says Swish, the common mobile payment app, requires a Swedish bank account and a personal identity number, so it is inaccessible for most tourists. Whether individual shops, public transport or taxis take cash was not stated on any official page opened for this guide.
money.tipping: Visit Sweden says tipping in Sweden "isn't as established as in many other countries. It's always welcome but not expected"; when eating out it is common to round the bill up (its example is a 280 SEK bill rounded to 300 SEK), a service charge is sometimes included but will be clearly stated on the bill, and a suggested nice tip is about 10% of the final bill. It gives no guidance for taxis, hotels or bars.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are called "Bankomat" or "Uttagsautomat" (Visit Sweden). Fees were not stated on any official page opened for this guide; check your own bank's foreign-withdrawal terms.

emergency.notes: 112 is Sweden's single emergency number: the Swedish Police say it is for emergency assistance when there is danger to life, property or the environment, that calls route to the nearest emergency centre where you can reach police, fire, ambulance and other services, and that operators speak Swedish and English; UK FCDO lists "112 (ambulance, fire, police)". The police non-emergency line is 114 14, staffed around the clock in Swedish and English for all matters except urgent police help (reports, tip-offs, information); from abroad or from a foreign mobile in Sweden call +46 77 114 14 00. The Police page also notes that 112 cannot be dialled in Sweden from another country. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page. UK FCDO says pickpockets target tourists in major cities and reports gang-related violence in Malmo, Stockholm and Gothenburg.

getting_around.summary: Rail: SJ is the national rail company and other operators include Snalltaget, Vy, Inlandsbanan and VR (Visit Sweden). Visit Sweden warns that tickets cannot be bought on board trains: buy on the operator's website or at the station beforehand, and book early for the best prices; there are discounts for under-26s and over-65s, and children under 15 often travel free depending on operator and trip. Visit Sweden gives no journey time for Stockholm-Gothenburg or Stockholm-Malmo (and one of its city pages gives figures that conflict with its train page), so no times are stated here; check sj.se for the journey you want. City transport: Stockholm's public transport is run by SL and Gothenburg's by Vasttrafik (Visit Sweden); tickets are sold at kiosks, information centres and through mobile apps. SL's own pages could not be read for fares for this guide (its visitor-ticket pages did not return content to the fetch tool), so no SL prices are given. Airports (Visit Sweden): Arlanda Express runs every 10-15 minutes and takes 18 minutes to Stockholm Central (price not stated on the page; buying on board costs extra); the commuter train takes about 38 minutes; Flygbussarna coaches take about 45-55 minutes; a taxi or car takes about 40-45 minutes depending on traffic. At Gothenburg Landvetter, Flygbussarna takes about 40 minutes to Gothenburg Central with 2-3 departures an hour. At Bromma, a Tvarbanan tram takes about 30 minutes to Stockholm Central with a change. Taxi prices are not regulated, so they vary by company.

passes.name: Eurail / Interrail pass
passes.covers: Visit Sweden describes Eurail and Interrail as passes exclusively for international travellers, letting you hop on and off trains; on Stockholm-Gothenburg or Stockholm-Malmo routes you need a valid pass or separate tickets. Which Swedish operators and trains accept them, and reservation fees, were not read for this guide.
passes.worth_it: Not assessed: no pass prices or Swedish coverage details were found on an official page opened for this guide. Compare against point-to-point SJ fares booked early.

passes.name: Inlandsbanan 14-day pass
passes.covers: Visit Sweden lists an Inlandsbanan 14-day pass for travellers without a Eurail or Interrail pass; Inlandsbanan is the rural inland line (including the Wilderness Train).
passes.worth_it: Only relevant if you plan to travel the inland line; price and validity were not read for this guide.

passes.name: SL visitor tickets (Stockholm)
passes.covers: SL (Stockholm's public transport operator) has a Visitor tickets section on sl.se including single journey tickets; fares, validity and payment methods could not be read because the pages did not return content to the fetch tool.
passes.worth_it: Not assessed: check sl.se for the current visitor-ticket prices and the SL app.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: PTS (the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority) says operators in the EU and EEA may not charge anything beyond your home rate (Roam Like At Home), though operators may apply a fair-use policy that caps data used while travelling, so you cannot expect to use as much data abroad as at home even on an unlimited plan. Outside the EU and EEA, PTS says operators set their own roaming prices and no cap applies; you also pay for incoming calls and for checking voicemail, and you can switch roaming off in your phone settings. The PTS page does not cover prepaid SIMs, eSIM, SIM prices or registration, and no official page opened for this guide does.
